stories.Headline: Michael Burry claims he warned investors about AI companies following a market rout
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry claimed he warned investors about Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Shares for these three companies fell that day during a recent rout of artificial intelligence stocks. Burry wrote on X that he provided the information needed to sell these specific assets. He clarified that he never told anyone to short the stocks. The former Scion Asset Management fund manager issued these comments as markets declined.

Burry holds Nvidia puts struck at 140 dollars that expire in February 2027. He doubled his put options on the Nasdaq-100 index in a November 12 Substack post. He also rebuilt a put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which includes Nvidia. Nebius holders lost 9.4 percent Thursday, CoreWeave holders lost 6.1 percent, and Nvidia holders lost 3.3 percent. Nvidia shares fell 19 percent since November 8, 2026.

Burry argued that CoreWeave, Nebius, ASML, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company leaned on the market power of Nvidia. He stated that he tried to warn investors about semiconductors and the mentioned companies. He claimed that his provided information was sufficient for those who wanted to sell. Burry has previously made a name betting against the 2008 housing bubble. He also issued a market warning in October.

Interim CEO Colette Kress rejected concerns about neoclouds, stating that the biggest cloud operators are not pulling back. CoreWeave and Nebius are affected as neoclouds that sell access to Nvidia-powered servers to developers. Nvidia shares closed at 145.98 dollars on Thursday, which is 39 percent below their October high. CoreWeave shares had fallen close to 26 percent in the week before November 23. Investors debated how AI infrastructure would be financed.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO four days after admitting extramarital affairs to staff on November 8. Revenue in the first post-Huang report jumped 103 percent to 115.8 billion dollars. CoreWeave reported third quarter revenue of 3.66 billion dollars and a net loss of 709 million dollars. CoreWeave debt stood at 47.5 billion dollars with a backlog of 132.5 billion dollars. The company expects 2026 revenue between 13.0 billion and 13.3 billion dollars.

Nvidia's board restored Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, November 23, 2026. This move caused Nvidia shares to rise near 30 percent and CoreWeave shares to rise 23.55 percent. Burry's Nasdaq-100 puts run into early 2027 to test his views on market power. The articles leave open whether credit worries will return to unwind the sector recovery. stories.Headline: University of Indianapolis uses $8.5 million Lilly grant to launch AI center for human performance
stories.Summary:
The University of Indianapolis received an $8.5 million grant from Lilly Endowment Inc. to establish a new Center for Artificial Intelligence for Human Performance. The award was announced on November 23, 2026, and the three-year initiative is expected to begin in January. The funding will significantly expand the use of artificial intelligence across the university's campus. University President Tanuja Singh said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how people live and work at breathtaking speeds. The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which supports Indiana colleges and universities.

The initiative calls for creating or revising up to 330 courses to incorporate artificial intelligence into the curriculum. The university will also develop nine AI-focused micro-credentials and provide students with opportunities to work on industry-sponsored projects. Faculty members will receive additional training and resources to incorporate AI into their teaching, with an emphasis on critical thinking and ethical decision-making. The university plans to introduce AI-powered tools to improve academic advising, student support services, transfer credit evaluations and data security. The new center will be located in a renovated section of Krannert Memorial Library on the university's campus.

University of Indianapolis President Tanuja Singh said higher education has a responsibility to prepare students not just to use new tools but to think critically about how and why they are used. She said the investment helps the university build on its strengths in experiential learning and student-centered education. Singh also said the university must ensure that technology serves people, not the other way around. UIndy Provost Chris Plouff said the center pairs faculty expertise with student creativity and problem-solving abilities to address real-world challenges facing Hoosier businesses and organizations. Plouff said students will benefit greatly from hands-on experience gained by applying classroom lessons to real-world problems.

Ted Maple, the Endowment's vice president for education, said the rapid rise and growing ubiquity of AI may be one of the most significant challenges higher education institutions have ever faced. Maple said faculty and staff are concerned about the potential for AI to impede original and independent thinking and threaten social connections. He also said colleges and universities have recognized that AI may present unprecedented opportunities to enhance teaching, learning, student services and research capabilities. Small businesses and nonprofits that lack the resources or expertise to implement AI independently will be able to access customized consulting services through the center. The center will serve two primary purposes: encouraging discussions about the relationship between artificial intelligence and human performance, and providing practical assistance to businesses and nonprofit organizations.

The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which is providing funding to 35 Indiana colleges and universities. The initiative is designed to help higher education institutions respond to the growing influence of artificial intelligence and prepare students, faculty and staff for technological changes. The University of Indianapolis has already begun exploring the technology's impact through events such as its inaugural AI Summit in April. That summit brought together business leaders, educators, technology experts and policymakers to explore the opportunities and challenges of AI. The university plans to hold another AI Summit in fall 2027.

The initiative is expected to begin in January and builds on the University of Indianapolis's ongoing work in artificial intelligence. One strategic pillar of the center will be thought leadership, serving as a hub for both campus and community conversations about how AI intersects with human performance. The other strategic pillar will focus on applied learning and consulting by providing customized services to nonprofits and small businesses. The articles do not specify which businesses or nonprofits will receive consulting services first. They also do not state how many students will participate in industry-sponsored projects or when the renovated library space will open.

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs five-year ban on AI chatbot toys
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill on November 24, 2026, establishing a five-year pause on AI chatbot toys in New York. The legislation, S.9408A/A.11144B, prohibits the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots. Such toys include talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with kids. The signing took place in Albany as consumers began their holiday shopping season.

The new law takes effect 90 days after signing, meaning it will not be in effect this holiday season. Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation, enforced by the Attorney General. The moratorium covers the manufacture, exchange, distribution and sale of AI-powered chatbot companion toys for children in New York. Governor Hochul urged parents and caregivers to consider the potential risks of AI chatbot toys before purchasing gifts for young children this holiday season.

Governor Hochul said parents shopping for gifts should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk. She said that as New York’s first mom governor, protecting kids is deeply personal to her, and when unregulated artificial intelligence poses a threat, it is her job to put New York families first. New York Attorney General Letitia James said AI chatbots in children’s toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk. James said her office will not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm.

State Senator Andrew Gounardes said the rush to sell AI-powered toys to young children is the latest chapter in a repetitive story where Big Tech puts profits before kids’ safety and families pay the price. Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay said consumer protections, especially those that protect youth, must keep up with rapidly evolving technologies. Mothers Against Media Addiction Policy Director LaVita Tuff said parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, meaning toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design. Common Sense Media Founder and CEO James P. Steyer said this moratorium on AI toys in New York could not come soon enough, and their research shows they are not safe for kids.

According to a national consumer watchdog that tested a sample of chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3-12, some talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave. These toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued. Some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face. In October, the Governor signed legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit conversations. The signing builds upon Governor Hochul’s efforts to protect children from emerging technology risks and address the youth mental health crisis statewide.

Governor Hochul encouraged parents and caregivers to look beyond a toy’s packaging and consider whether it includes an AI companion, what information it collects, and whether it allows open ended conversation with a child. Although the moratorium will not be in effect this holiday season, the signing of this legislation highlights these concerns now, before families make purchasing decisions. The articles do not state whether any specific companies or products will be immediately affected by the ban. The articles also do not say how the Attorney General will identify or test toys that violate the moratorium once it takes effect. The articles leave open whether other states will follow New York’s example with similar bans on AI chatbot toys.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three AI providers after security tests reveal customer data leaks
stories.Summary:
OpenRouter removed three AI providers from its platform in November 2026 after security tests revealed data policy violations. The company took this action after discovering that these providers had exposed sensitive customer data. Together AI, Phala, and Novita were the three inference providers dropped by the AI model broker. This decision followed an investigation into leaked prompts and secrets that had escaped the providers. OpenRouter also notified all potentially affected customers about the security incidents.

The company revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution. Together AI admitted a coding agent exposed a repository credential on GitHub during June and July. Phala reported a server compromise between October 21 and November 8 affecting DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests. Novita stated a misconfiguration sent MiniMax requests to the official MiniMax API from May 28 to November 11. Atlas Cloud voluntarily withdrew its models pending security testing after a third-party security incident.

OpenRouter stated that there was no breach on its own internal systems. The company said it will keep raising the bar for providers wanting to be on the platform. A spokesperson for Stripe, which owns OpenRouter, confirmed that the customer warning emails were legitimate. The providers involved said they are tightening security controls and strengthening their data deletion policies. They advised potentially impacted users to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed.

Dragos, an operational technology security company, alerted OpenRouter after sending two million test prompts with tracking links. These researchers found that an unidentified Chinese AI lab accessed links in over half of some prompts. Customers who shared sensitive company information, private conversations, or passwords are the primary parties affected. Some seeded credentials were used in the wild to access canary AWS accounts and test systems. Researchers also detected attempts to download private code repositories referenced in the test prompts.

OpenRouter acts as a broker letting developers access various AI models using a single API key. The platform forwards requests to providers who run the models and pass the answers back. This incident follows other cyber incidents at platforms like Fireworks AI, Railway, and OpenCode since October. Other infrastructure companies including Prime Intellect and GMI Cloud also disclosed security incidents or investigations recently. The events highlight limited visibility into which companies ultimately handle sensitive developer conversations.

OpenRouter is adapting the Dragos tests for ongoing use to check for further data leaks. The company will require validation before restoring Zero Data Retention eligibility to any removed endpoint. Providers must now meet higher standards to remain on the platform and ensure privacy commitments. The articles leave open whether other providers are currently routing private data to third parties. It remains unclear how many customers actually had their secrets stolen by unauthorized parties.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for 43.9 billion dollars to secure AI agents
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler on a Monday in November 2026 to improve security for AI agents. This massive deal combines endpoint protection with zero-trust network security to help enterprises control their systems. The acquisition aims to provide chief information security officers with a single supplier for various security controls. It unites the visibility of endpoints and cloud workloads with the inspection of network traffic. The transaction is intended to stop unauthorized AI agents from sending sensitive data to unapproved models.

The stock deal is valued at 43.9 billion dollars and surpasses a 32 billion dollar Google acquisition. CrowdStrike is based in Austin, Texas, while Zscaler is located in Santa Clara, California. The companies expect to close the transaction in the second half of fiscal 2028. Zscaler reported record revenue of 3.35 billion dollars in fiscal 2026 and serves 11,000 global customers. The deal will eventually bring Zscaler offerings into Falcon Flex under a single subscription model.

CEO George Kurtz said the proliferation of AI agents has changed the role of network security. He stated that the network now connects agents to data rather than just connecting people to places. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said the combination allows for coordinated policy enforcement across cloud environments and networks. CFO Burt Podbere noted that the two companies will operate independently until the deal officially closes. Kurtz also claimed that the brand promise of a single software agent will not change.

Analyst Frank Dickson said the combination fundamentally changes the competitiveness of the cybersecurity industry by 100 percent. He believes the deal increases the importance of partnerships and niche differentiation for other security vendors. Customers are affected by the shift toward a smaller number of companies protecting more global networks. Some chief information security officers may worry if a broader platform limits their choice of security products. Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick questioned how the deal affects customers using other secure access service providers.

Zscaler provides cloud-based products that replace traditional virtual private networks which are often targeted by state-sponsored hackers. CrowdStrike uses the Falcon Guardian to discover AI agents and protect them during their runtime operations. Zscaler operates in over 185 countries and serves more than half of the Fortune 500 companies. The two companies already share 16 integrations and send data into a next-generation security information event management. Zscaler has not turned an annual profit since it went public in the year 2018.

CrowdStrike expects to generate 1 billion dollars in annualized revenue savings within 30 months after closing. The company plans to introduce an agent identity provider around January to provide just-in-time access controls. The companies must still turn their existing integrations into unified enforcement while supporting other competing products. It remains open whether the combined portfolio can fully provide necessary registry and authentication for AI agents. The articles leave open the specific delivery date for the combined single-agent software architecture.

stories.Headline: DGEN Technologies completes acquisition of exclusive license to HumanOS artificial intelligence assets
stories.Summary:
DGEN Technologies Corp. completed its previously announced acquisition of an exclusive and irrevocable license to the artificial intelligence software, automation technology and related assets of HumanOS Technologies Inc. on November 23, 2026, in Vancouver, British Columbia. The transaction was completed pursuant to a license agreement dated November 12, 2026, between the two companies. DGEN announced the completion in a news release issued on November 23, 2026, at 5:36 p.m. Atlantic Standard Time. The licensed assets include software, source code, systems, platforms and tools developed and operated by HumanOS under the HumanOS name. These assets include the HumAIn, Matspace, Media Studio and Automation Lab products and the HumanOS scan tool.

The license also includes the HumanOS trade name, the 1humanos.com domain and associated websites and social media accounts. It further includes client and customer lists containing names and contact details only, along with related information and documentation. The license permits DGEN and its affiliates to use, commercialize, further develop and sublicense the licensed assets. HumanOS retains ownership of the licensed assets, while any improvements developed by or for DGEN will be owned by DGEN. In consideration, DGEN issued 4,000,000 common shares at a deemed price of $0.25 per share, for aggregate deemed consideration of $1,000,000.

DGEN also issued 4,000,000 common share purchase warrants, each entitling the holder to acquire one common share at an exercise price of $0.32 per warrant share until November 23, 2029. The consideration shares, consideration warrants and any warrant shares are subject to restrictions on resale until March 24, 2027. These restrictions are in accordance with applicable Canadian securities laws and the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange. DGEN stated that it is arm’s length from HumanOS, and no finder’s fees or commissions are payable in connection with completion of the transaction. The company described itself as a Vancouver-based technology company developing a cloud-based payment platform intended to integrate point-of-sale, kiosk and mobile payment systems.

DGEN’s platform is currently in beta stage and not yet in use by any business, and it has not yet been commercialized or generated revenue. The company said the license permits it and its affiliates to use, commercialize, further develop and sublicense the licensed assets. DGEN cautioned that forward-looking information in the news release is based on management’s current expectations, estimates, projections, beliefs and assumptions as of the date of the release. These assumptions include that the licensed assets will perform as expected and can be integrated into the company’s business. The company also assumed it will have access to sufficient financing and personnel, and that there will be no material adverse changes in applicable regulatory requirements.

DGEN identified risks including the ownership, validity and enforceability of intellectual property rights in the licensed assets, including third-party claims. Other risks include the possibility that the licensed assets do not perform as expected or cannot be successfully integrated, developed or commercialized. The company also noted dilution resulting from the exercise of the consideration warrants, and the fact that its platform remains in beta stage and has not generated revenue. DGEN said readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on forward-looking information, which speaks only as of the date of the news release. The Canadian Securities Exchange has not reviewed, approved or disapproved the contents of the news release, and does not accept responsibility for its adequacy or accuracy.

DGEN stated that except as required by applicable securities laws, it undertakes no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking information. The company did not disclose any specific timeline for integrating the HumanOS licensed assets into its existing payment platform business. The news release did not state whether any employees of HumanOS would join DGEN as part of the transaction. It also did not disclose the current revenue or customer base of HumanOS Technologies Inc. The release left open how DGEN intends to prioritize development of the licensed artificial intelligence products relative to its beta-stage payment platform.

stories.Headline: Fakeeh Health and Boston Health AI sign agreements to bring AI clinical documentation to UAE clinicians
stories.Summary:
Fakeeh Health and Boston Health AI signed two strategic agreements on the sidelines of the 5th Annual Fakeeh Health International Conference in Dubai on 24th November 2026. The signing took place in the presence of Sheikh Ahmed bin Hasher bin Ahmed Al Maktoum, according to a press release from Awareness Marketing Management DWC LLC. Together, the two organisations will introduce AI-supported clinical documentation across Fakeeh Health and jointly develop new AI solutions for healthcare providers in the UAE and the region. The first agreement focuses on giving clinicians more time for their patients by taking on routine documentation in the background. The second agreement involves Takamul Innovative Health Solutions partnering with Boston Health AI to build new healthcare solutions.

The first agreement requires that AI handle routine documentation while the physician remains in control of the clinical record. Patient data must stay in the UAE and be protected in line with national regulations. The second agreement requires Takamul and Boston Health AI to develop new solutions that help healthcare providers work more efficiently. It also requires building local expertise in clinical AI through education and research. The agreements support the UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 and the Dubai Universal Blueprint for Artificial Intelligence.

Dr. Mohaymen Abdelghany, Group CEO and Board Member of Fakeeh Health and CEO of Fakeeh University Hospital, said the philosophy of Care & Beyond puts the patient at the centre of every decision. He said that starts with the doctor's full attention, and with Boston Health AI they are giving physicians more time with patients. He added that through Takamul they will build new AI solutions together for healthcare providers across the UAE and the region. He said this is in line with Dubai's vision for a digitally enabled healthcare system. Dr. Adil Haider, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Boston Health AI, said physicians did not go into medicine to type.

Dr. Haider said Fakeeh Health shares the belief that technology should give clinicians their time back. He said that makes Fakeeh Health the right partner not only to deploy the platform but to build the next generation of clinical AI. He added that they are proud to build in the UAE with a local team and with patient data that stays in the country. The agreements affect clinicians across Fakeeh Health, who will receive AI-supported clinical documentation. They also affect healthcare providers in the UAE and the region through Takamul Innovative Health Solutions.

Fakeeh Health is a UAE healthcare group brought to the UAE by the founders of Fakeeh Care Group, building on more than four decades of clinical excellence, research and innovation. Its flagship, Fakeeh University Hospital in Dubai Silicon Oasis, is a smart academic hospital that brings together clinical care, medical education and research. Takamul Innovative Health Solutions is Fakeeh Health's healthcare services company, providing consulting, operations and business services to healthcare providers in the UAE. Boston Health AI is a clinical AI company founded by surgeon-scientist Dr. Adil Haider. Its platform, developed by physicians and engineers, supports care teams across the patient journey, with clinical authority always resting with the physician.

The agreements will now be implemented, with AI-supported clinical documentation introduced across Fakeeh Health and new solutions developed through Takamul. The articles do not specify a timeline for when the AI documentation will be fully deployed or when the first jointly developed solutions will be released. They also do not state the financial value of the agreements or the number of clinicians who will use the platform. The articles leave open which specific healthcare providers in the region will adopt the new solutions. They also do not detail the exact nature of the education and research programmes that will build local expertise in clinical AI.

stories.Headline: PostSig wins best AI for infrastructure and operations at 2026 buy-side awards for its CPM product
stories.Summary:
PostSig announced on November 24, 2026, that it has been named Best Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure & Operations at the 2026 WatersTechnology Buy-Side Technology Awards. The company made the announcement from San Francisco, California, through a press release distributed by ACCESS Newswire. PostSig received the award for its PostSig CPM product, which is powered by PostSig LineageAI. The award was presented by WatersTechnology as part of its annual Buy-Side Technology Awards program. PostSig did not state the exact date or location of the awards ceremony in its announcement.

PostSig CPM connects the agreements that govern a firm's vendor relationships with its spend, invoices, products, and entitlements. The product helps teams identify billing discrepancies, track changing commitments, and prepare for renewals with evidence from the underlying records. An amended fee schedule can change the correct invoice amount, and a service order removing a product can expose continued billing for that product. Usage data can reveal that a renewal includes licenses the firm no longer needs. Recent product expansion brings spend, inventory, product and fee schedules, vendor oversight, and Financial Terminal management into a shared commercial context.

Phil Kim, Chief Product Officer and Co-Founder of PostSig, said teams should be able to trace an invoice, product, or renewal back to the terms that govern it. He explained that LineageAI connects those records as they change, giving teams a consistent basis for checking charges, managing entitlements, and making renewal decisions. Hendrik Bartel, CEO and Co-Founder of PostSig, said buy-side firms need AI-native solutions that can explain what they are paying for, what they are entitled to, and where action is needed. He added that this requires understanding which commitments apply today, how they have changed, and the evidence behind every answer. Bartel said the award recognizes how PostSig brings that intelligence into daily operations.

PostSig also provides evidence-backed conversational access through LineageAI Assistant and governed access through PostSig MCP, extending that context to approved enterprise applications and AI agents. Procurement, finance, and operations teams can validate invoices against agreed pricing, trace price changes, manage products and entitlements, allocate costs, and prepare for renewals using the same underlying commercial context. PostSig extends the value of contract lifecycle management beyond signature by connecting governing commitments to financial and operational activity. The platform works alongside existing CLM, ERP, CRM, procurement, and finance systems without requiring firms to replace their systems of record. PostSig describes itself as the AI platform for the people that run the business, with applications including PostSig CPM and Investor Rights Intelligence.

PostSig LineageAI maintains context to determine what governs now, what changed and why, with the supporting evidence behind the answer. A superseded fee schedule can change what should be paid, and a later service order can reveal continued billing for a product that was removed. Inventory and utilization can change a renewal's economics. PostSig did not provide details about the judging criteria or the number of competing entries in its announcement. The company did not disclose the names of other finalists or winners in other categories at the 2026 WatersTechnology Buy-Side Technology Awards.

PostSig directed readers to visit postsig.com/bestai to see why it won and how the product works. The company did not announce any specific product changes, pricing updates, or customer additions in connection with the award. PostSig did not state whether it plans to attend future WatersTechnology events or how the award will affect its business strategy. The announcement leaves open whether PostSig will pursue additional awards or expand its product offerings further. Media contact Tiffaney Fox Quintana of PostSig, Inc. was listed for further inquiries.

stories.Headline: UC faculty criticize $1.2 million OpenAI deal giving students free ChatGPT access
stories.Summary:
The University of California is procuring full access to ChatGPT Edu for all students and faculty as part of a $1.2 million agreement with OpenAI. The one-year partnership takes effect in December and is an extension of a 2024 agreement with OpenAI. UC students, staff and faculty will also have access to OpenAI's coding agent Codex. The agreement surprised members of UC's Academic Senate, who raised concerns late last month that administrators had not sufficiently consulted faculty. Administrators met with UC faculty after the Academic Senate raised concerns in an October letter.

The partnership costs $1.2 million and runs for one year, beginning in December. It extends a 2024 agreement with OpenAI and gives all UC students and faculty full access to ChatGPT Edu. UC students, staff and faculty also gain access to OpenAI's coding agent Codex. The Academic Senate raised concerns in an October letter dated October 30 about data privacy, intellectual property protections and the impact on student learning. UC announced additional training opportunities as part of the expanded partnership with OpenAI.

Academic Senate Chair Susannah Scott said the case is far more serious than a routine software purchase. She said the Academic Senate believes it is unwise to provide students with universal access to a tool capable of performing academic work required to earn a degree. Scott said faculty wants administrators to engage in genuine consultation with faculty experts so UC can provide appropriate tools and guidance. A UC spokesperson said administrators have discussed the OpenAI partnership with Academic Senate leadership and other faculty members since this spring. The spokesperson said the University will continue working with the Academic Senate and other faculty groups on best AI practices.

Camille Crittenden, executive director of CITRIS at UC Berkeley, said the agreement helps UC maintain a forward-looking position on AI adoption. Crittenden acknowledged faculty's concerns but said large universities need to ensure students, staff and faculty have appropriate tools for the 21st century. UC San Diego Chancellor Pradeep Khosla said he has seen AI tools used in novel ways by faculty and staff on his campus. Khosla applauded the OpenAI partnership for expanding ChatGPT access to students, faculty and staff. He acknowledged AI could create wealth and enhance abilities but also lead to further inequities.

During the September board of regents meeting, UC administrators proposed adopting systemwide access to AI tools produced by OpenAI or Anthropic. The Academic Senate would be consulted before an agreement was signed, according to the update from UC's Office of the President. Academic Senate leadership said they were not made aware of the purchase agreement with OpenAI until a month later. Scott told UC President James Milliken in her October letter that providing students with ChatGPT would be perceived as endorsing students' AI use in all courses. Scott requested that the Academic Senate be allowed to provide feedback before UC finalized an agreement with OpenAI.

Scott said the core concerns raised in the October 30 letter remain unresolved. She said the Academic Senate must establish ethical and pedagogical guidelines before UC widely distributes AI tools into the curriculum. UC Chief Information Officer Van Williams acknowledged faculty's desire to give input but said the university needed to move quickly on the deal. Williams said the current negotiating window gives a timely opportunity to lower costs, strengthen enterprise protections and broaden access. Milliken said in a Thursday letter that the decision has the full support of all UC Chancellors.

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Cisco launch Shirudo, an open-source runtime that shields Linux systems from exploits while patches roll out
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Cisco introduced Shirudo on November 23, 2026, an open-source runtime that helps protect running Linux systems while teams roll out patches. The project combines OpenAI’s frontier AI, security, and infrastructure research with Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise. In a controlled test, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. The two companies are inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. Shirudo is Japanese for “shield.”

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, and security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading, and Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules. Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. The project is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI, said defenders are getting better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today does not mean every system can be patched tomorrow. He said OpenAI is partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. Brockman added that because so many teams rely on the same software, it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer, said there is nothing more important than giving security teams tools to match the speed of AI-driven threats. Patel said Cisco is proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI as an important step toward self-defending infrastructure.

OpenAI said on X that Shirudo lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches. The company called the initiative a first step toward self-defending infrastructure that can adapt to new threats while services continue to run. Cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build they use, or show where it breaks legitimate traffic. The project aims to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches. Operators can use hardware-backed evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks, and protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline, so Shirudo is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities Java4Shell and a PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats.

A technical walkthrough from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host. The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI’s Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java’s Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. Developers can follow the VM quickstart to sign, load, and verify a test protection, explore Shirudo through Isovalent’s self-guided lab, or register for the December 15 webinar.

stories.Headline: AI lets companies predict individual consumer behavior from purchases and personal data, Jeff Gaus says
stories.Summary:
Companies are using artificial intelligence to process vast amounts of customer data and personal information, narrowing advertising down to the individual level. Jeff Gaus, now CEO of the Provenance Chain Group, described the change on November 24, 2026, comparing his earlier work with drugstore cash-register data to today’s AI systems. What once took multiple days and several number-crunching humans can now be worked out in minutes or seconds by artificial intelligence, he said. The article from TIME describes how AI draws on purchases, opinions, preferences, personal stories, geolocations, photos, and videos from search engines and social media platforms. Gaus said that five years ago companies were at a five or six on a ten-point scale of customer knowledge, but today they are at about 9.2 or 9.3.

The new AI systems can create constantly evolving “digital twin” models of specific people or small populations to predict consumer behavior based on a matrix of financial and personal data points. Retailers use purchase patterns, credit-card charges, AI chatbot inquiries, and even voting patterns to understand product preferences down to specific ZIP codes. Gaus recalled a fellow panelist who had formerly worked in government intelligence describing a map that plotted a person’s consumer purchases on all credit cards over 45 days, where his car had driven, and what telephone calls he had been making. The data came from private corporations, according to the panelist’s account. A separate report from the Institute for Corporate Productivity found that just 10% of companies are focused on continuous organizational redesigns alongside AI implementation.

Justin Sherman, founder of Duke University’s Privacy and Democracy Project and now CEO of Global Cyber Strategies, said AI can draw commercially beneficial information out of even anonymized records. He noted that a company or research organization or consumer might share information thinking that it is quote-unquote anonymized, but AI-advertising technology companies and data brokers can mash it all together and link it back to people. Callie Schroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights Program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said AI can go through information so fast and sort and parse out what it wants to pull from it. She argued that it would be better for society if laws and norms caught up to the need for a shared approach to what consumers should be able to expect. Kevin Martin, chief research officer at i4cp, said the companies that come out ahead in 2027 will be the ones that are better at the art and science of changing.

Sherman said he has bought plenty of things through targeted ads he has gotten online, and he particularly appreciated recommendations on music and video streaming services. He said the thing to watch out for is a situation in which consumers are not offered a meaningful way to give or withdraw consent for use of their personal data. Schroeder said she had to manually go through all the settings on a new phone and turn off a whole bunch of machine-learning things, and that it is a lot of work and unfair that consumers have to do it. A 2026 Gallup study found that 50% of CHROs surveyed were not confident that their company’s managers were able to guide employees’ AI use at work. The i4cp research found that 56% of organizations where HR was in charge of AI adoption said they were either mostly or fully AI-ready, compared to only 18% when AI adoption was led by IT teams.

In 2009, Ars Technica wrote about how data scientists had shown they could re-identify sets of supposedly anonymized information, from medical records to AOL searches, with remarkable ease. That piece was based on research by Georgetown University law professor Paul Ohm, who was quoted as saying, “Data can either be useful or perfectly anonymous, but never both.” Gaus said that fifteen years ago his firm bought drugstore cash-register data and could tell pharma reps that “Dr. Smith has three people with this condition” and instruct them to go pitch their wares to that doctor. The i4cp study found that as more routine analysis and entry-level tasks are given to AI, companies risk losing the kinds of developmental routines that help teach judgment and critical thinking. The report said this could result in “a talent shortage created from within.”

Gaus said the depth and breadth of data available sometimes surprises even him, and the specificity of what companies are able to know about their customers is only going to get more astounding. The i4cp report said CEOs will be examining how investments in AI have changed their companies and their workforces, making the role of CHROs in managing and implementing AI adoption increasingly important. CHROs said their main internal obstacles included competing priorities at 43%, change fatigue at 33%, and resistance to change at 30%. The articles do not say whether new laws or regulations will be introduced to address data ownership or consumer consent. They also leave open whether companies will adopt the culture and organizational design changes that i4cp says are needed to sustain superior market performance.

stories.Headline: California Republican expects Congress to pass AI bill before January
stories.Summary:
Rep. Jay Obernolte, a California Republican, said on Sunday that he is optimistic Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence bill before the end of the year. He made the statement during an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” even though Democrats are preparing to take control of the House in January. Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said lawmakers have made significant progress on the Great American AI Act, known as GAIA. He noted that major pieces of the legislation have already passed through the relevant policy committees and are now queued for action on the House floor.

The Great American AI Act is a package of proposals that would establish federal safeguards for the rapidly developing technology. Obernolte said the legislation has six bipartisan co-sponsors, and portions of it have already attracted support from lawmakers in both parties. He acknowledged that any bill would require cooperation across party lines, regardless of which party controls Congress. He explained that anything passed would need 60 votes in the Senate to avoid the filibuster and would also require the signature of the president of the United States.

Obernolte has been among the leading voices in Congress pushing for federal AI legislation as states move ahead with their own regulations. He said all 50 states are going in 50 different directions on AI regulation, which has caused concerns in the industry over a patchwork of conflicting rules for tech companies operating nationwide. He added that lawmakers must strike a balance between protecting Americans from the misuse of AI and allowing the technology’s benefits to reach the economy. The push comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of the House following this month’s midterm elections, potentially complicating efforts to reach an agreement on AI oversight.

Obernolte said he is optimistic that lawmakers can get the job done before the current Congress ends. He told host Chris Stirewalt that the relevant policy committees have passed major pieces of GAIA and that the legislation is queued up for action on the House floor. He said, “We actually could get this done this year.” The California Republican did not provide a specific timeline for a floor vote or for Senate consideration of the bill.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship to review and approve GitHub pull requests for teams
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a new feature called Claude Ship on Monday, November 23, 2026, to help developers ship code faster. This tool allows the AI to review, fix, and approve GitHub pull requests based on the specific policies of a team. The company released the feature in beta for users who have Claude Team and Enterprise tier subscriptions. It is designed for individual developers or companies that want to move faster by delegating coding tasks to agents. The system aims to ship code as fast as teams can write it by automating the review process.

The tool uses two new agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, alongside the Code Review feature released in March. PR Steward handles failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback, but it cannot approve or merge any pull requests. Claude Approvals uses a repo file provided by the team and other signals to approve changes autonomously if allowed. Individuals with Pro, Max, or Ultra subscriptions can access the feature using the /ship command within Claude Code. Certain Enterprise organizations can claim at least 10,000 dollars in credits by January 15, 2027, to use within 30 days.

Anthropic stated that teams remain in control of where the tool runs and which changes require a human. The company said the goal is to ship code as fast as teams write it through these agents. They recommended that most customers first enable additional checks in observe-only mode to build confidence before requiring a green light. Anthropic noted that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs. The company explained that users of the /ship command will not notice any significant increase in token usage.

David Gewirtz, a senior contributing editor, said the idea of shipping code at writing speed raises the hair on his neck. He mentioned that the tool could save money and send fixes to customers faster for certain deployment processes. Gewirtz expressed concern that the tool might shut junior members out of roles where they add value and grow skills. The feature affects developers who use GitHub, though those with zero-data-retention policies or other privacy configurations lack access. He added that the effectiveness of the tool depends on the team workflow and the kind of development.

The articles state that coding agents are becoming popular and are changing the nature of professional development work. Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI tools like OpenAI's Codex in very large numbers. Some developers still prefer to check code themselves before pushing it rather than handing the last step to AI. Developer platforms are adapting, such as Entire, a GitHub competitor built for developers working side-by-side with AI agents. Admins can select which repositories the feature runs in and set spending limits for the PR Steward agent.

Next, users can enable the feature for an entire repo so that developers do not need the /ship command. Team and Enterprise users will be billed on tokens, which means their overall bills may change based on usage. The articles leave open whether more developers will be comfortable handing the final approval step over to an AI. It remains unclear how many Enterprise organizations will claim the available credits before the January 2027 deadline. The text does not specify when the beta period for Claude Ship will officially end for all users.

stories.Headline: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urges nations to create an AI risk management framework within a year
stories.Summary:
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for global artificial intelligence oversight during a conference in Barbados. He made this request on Monday, November 23, 2026, at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety. Guterres urged member states to coordinate efforts to manage the risks posed by advanced technology. He wants the world to develop a multilateral framework for risk management within the next year. This proposed system would be principles-based, globally inclusive, and backed by independent and credible oversight.

The framework requires shared safety measures, a testing regime, and basic requirements for independent oversight. Guterres mentioned that the UN, the world trade system, and the international financial architecture need reform. He noted that current global governance institutions correspond to the reality of the world in 1945. The UN-supported Global Network for Exchange and Cooperation on AI Capacity-Building already has 27 centres of excellence. Guterres also proposed a global fund to help various countries build their own AI capacity.

Guterres stated that controlling AI is necessary for humanity to maintain control of our world. He argued that the UN is the right place to lead because it represents the whole world. The Secretary-General said that safeguards have fallen behind the growing capabilities of artificial intelligence. He believes that countries exposed to the technology should have a voice in decisions about it. Guterres claimed that an independent international scientific panel found that AI safeguards were trailing technology capabilities.

Some tech leaders, including Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Dario Amodei, called for an AI development slowdown. Other executives, such as Mark Zuckerberg and Jensen Huang, want to move full steam ahead. US regulators appear unlikely to intervene immediately despite the fast pace of development in the United States. President Donald Trump hosted tech executives in September who agreed to a voluntary AI safety code. The US, China, and the EU remain far apart on the issue of binding AI rules.

Guterres has become vocal about safety measures to avoid a future where killer robots are a reality. He previously backed an IAEA-style AI watchdog in June 2023, but no such body exists today. In 2023, he and the ICRC urged states to conclude an autonomous weapons treaty by 2026. The United States and Russia have resisted new binding limits on those specific autonomous weapons. Guterres noted that recent cyberattacks and technology outages show the risks of digital technology without controls.

Guterres will advise his successor, who takes office in the new year, about the need for AI control. The Secretary-General leaves his office in December, before the proposed one-year deadline for the framework arrives. The articles leave open whether any single government has agreed to the twelve-month timetable for oversight. No enforcement mechanism was set, and no specific body was named to run the proposed oversight. It remains unclear if the superpowers will agree on a shared document for AI risk management.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s IPO spotlights how ordinary investors already hold AI stocks through index funds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, completed its initial public offering on the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on November 19, 2026. The event generated considerable wealth for the company's leadership and early investors, and it prompted widespread public attention. Many ordinary people watched the closing bell ceremony and wondered whether they had missed out on similar financial gains. The IPO served as a visible reminder of how concentrated the rewards from the artificial intelligence boom have become.

The articles explain that everyday investors are not necessarily excluded from these gains, because large technology companies are already common holdings in broad investment funds. Many retirement accounts and index funds include shares of major firms that are deeply involved in artificial intelligence development. This means that a person who owns a standard diversified portfolio likely already has indirect exposure to the sector's growth. The wealth created by a single IPO may look distant, but the underlying technology companies are often embedded in ordinary portfolios.

NPR produced the episode and identified its production team, including producers Sophia Paliza-Carre and Karen Zamora, with audio engineering by Maggie Luthar. The episode was edited by Mallory Yu and Tinbete Ermyas, and the executive producer is Courtney Dorning. NPR stated that it does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews, and it warned that anyone making such an offer does not represent the organization. The program framed the discussion around the contrast between visible IPO wealth and the quieter participation of everyday investors.

The episode is part of NPR's Consider This podcast, which is supported by public media funding and offers perks through NPR+ for over 25 podcasts. Listeners are encouraged to support the show to unlock bonus episodes and sponsor-free listening. The articles do not describe any specific future events or policy changes beyond the ongoing availability of the podcast. The central message is that while the artificial intelligence stock boom has made some individuals very rich, ordinary investors may already hold a stake in that boom through their existing funds.

stories.Headline: New York attorney general Letitia James forms ASSET unit to enforce AI safety laws
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the creation of the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit on November 17, 2026. The unit, known as the ASSET Unit, is positioned inside the Office of the Attorney General’s Economic Justice Division. It will serve as the attorney general’s primary enforcement and investigative arm for AI matters. The announcement came six weeks before the Responsible AI Safety and Education Act takes effect on January 1, 2027. James said the unit will investigate potential violations, develop policy proposals, and provide technical assistance across her office.

The RAISE Act requires large frontier AI developers operating in New York to register with the state, publish safety frameworks, and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. All frontier developers, regardless of size, must also publish model-transparency reports and report qualifying critical incidents. Administration of the RAISE registration and reporting portal falls to the Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust, known as DIGIT. New York’s chatbot law takes effect on June 1, 2027, and prohibits covered companies from offering specified unsafe or deceptive conversational features to minors. Companies must provide more than one age-verification method, and the law is reported to include a method that does not rely on government-issued identification.

Attorney General Letitia James said promising new technologies like artificial intelligence should never come at the expense of New Yorkers’ safety and privacy. She also said her office has always stepped up to enforce the law to protect New Yorkers when big tech companies try to take advantage of them. The ASSET Unit will focus on how emerging technology affects data privacy, digital scams, cybersecurity, and online safety. It will work alongside state agencies that administer the underlying reporting systems. The unit is positioned as the attorney general’s enforcement and investigative arm once violations are suspected.

Reported civil penalties reach up to $25,000 per violation, though that figure requires confirmation against the enacted law. Additional remedies reportedly include restitution and disgorgement of profits. A public website maintained by the attorney general will allow consumers to submit complaints about potential violations. Reported prohibited features include presenting a chatbot as human or emotionally alive, using flattery or sycophancy, and drawing on certain personal or health data from prior sessions. The attorney general may also designate additional features that simulate companionship or interpersonal relationships, though that delegated authority requires a primary statutory source to confirm.

The RAISE Act allows the state to transmit critical-incident reports or summaries to other government entities. Whether the underlying reports submitted by developers or members of the public will be publicly accessible is not established in available official material. Several broad statutory terms will require interpretation through implementation, enforcement, or litigation. What separates ordinary conversational responsiveness from prohibited sycophancy is not settled. Regulations, enforcement actions, or litigation could clarify the terms before the law’s June 2027 effective date.

Several questions remain open before both laws take effect. These include the precise scope of covered chatbots, what constitutes an acceptable anonymous verification method, how the state will define unsafe features, and whether enforcement standards will be published before the laws become operative. The articles do not state whether the underlying incident reports will be publicly accessible. The articles also leave open whether the $25,000 civil penalty figure and the age-verification provisions will be confirmed against the enacted statutory text. The delegated authority for the attorney general to designate additional prohibited features also remains subject to primary statutory confirmation.

stories.Headline: Chinese resellers sell illicit access to American AI models to bypass bans
stories.Summary:
Chinese resellers in Beijing's Haidian district sell illicit access to American AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to bypass bans. These resellers operate from an office building and advertise their services openly on Telegram, Taobao, and GitHub. They take payments in yuan using Alipay or WeChat to facilitate these illegal transactions for Chinese customers. The resellers forward requests to models through accounts registered abroad to hide the users' actual locations. This activity has created a growing token black market to meet high Chinese demand for advanced AI.

Resellers create tens of thousands of accounts using virtual credit cards, stolen cards, and fake email addresses. They use other people's home internet connections to disguise the origin of the accounts they run. By using free trials, they sell Claude at 70 to 90 percent below the American price. Team Cymru counted over 80,000 servers enabling this illicit access in September. The market serves customers including Baidu, Tencent, Alibaba, Peking University, and Tsinghua University.

The White House denounced these deliberate, industrial-scale campaigns that give advanced AI to China in mass. Anthropic identified seven Chinese labs, including Xiaomi and SenseTime, that distill models through these fraudulent intermediaries. Alibaba, DeepSeek, and Moonshot ran over 185 million exchanges with Claude between May and July. Moonshot forwarded 300,000 requests in 10 days through 5,380 fraudulent accounts to its Kimi model. China's Ministry of Commerce called these American distillation charges groundless and legally unsound.

The U.S. government says this market allows Chinese companies to copy American models through industrial-scale distillation. This process lets adversaries narrow the U.S. lead in AI by imitating teacher models' capabilities. National security risks include the use of AI for cyberattacks, military planning, and dangerous biological research. Russian weapons developers, Iranian paramilitary units, and Chinese state-security bureaus have used Claude through these networks. Virologists at a military research institute also used the market to access Claude for bioweapons research.

The Commerce Department found in May that China's most capable model lagged the American frontier by eight months. American models are used by Chinese chip designers, military researchers, and the country's most important companies. A state-backed chip-design center bought an overseas cloud account specifically to access the Claude model. Many developers use Claude Code, and Alibaba used Claude to build internal infrastructure for model development. OpenAI and Google have also observed adversaries relying on the black market to access their models.

The Department of Justice could prosecute these services for wire fraud and access-device fraud. The Treasury Department can sanction relay networks and suppliers to freeze assets and cut financial access. The Department of Homeland Security could create a system for companies to warn each other about accounts. Intelligence community advisories warn that relays obfuscate user metadata to avoid detection by AI safety teams. The articles leave open whether the U.S. government will actually implement these specific legal actions.

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs law restricting unsafe AI companion features for minors
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S9051B into law on October 28, 2026, restricting certain artificial intelligence functionalities in interactions with minors. The legislation adds a new Article 48 to the General Business Law and takes effect on January 1, 2027. It prohibits operators from providing “unsafe AI companion features” to minors in the state of New York. The law broadly covers generative AI systems with natural-language interfaces that provide ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs. Digital health companies and healthcare providers offering chatbots or conversational AI tools to patients or consumers must assess whether their tools fall within the law’s scope.

The law defines a “covered AI companion” as a generative AI system with a written or spoken natural-language interface that provides ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs. An “operator” is any person or business entity, or any member, affiliate, subsidiary or beneficial owner of a business entity, that provides a covered AI companion to a user. Prohibited unsafe features include presenting the system as human, alive or capable of human emotions, or claiming a personal or professional relationship with the user. The law also bars features that express opinions, make emotional appeals, flatter the user, or bring up the user’s emotions beyond what is needed to respond directly to the prompt. Features that draw on information the user shared about mental or physical health, well-being or personal life more than 12 hours earlier or in an earlier session are also prohibited.

The law is enforced by the New York Attorney General, who may seek injunctive relief, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation. Disgorgement includes destruction of unlawfully obtained data and algorithms trained on that data. Any contract provision that seeks to waive, preclude or burden enforcement of liability arising from a violation is void as a matter of public policy. Courts must hold affiliated entities jointly and severally liable if they find the entities structured themselves purposely and unreasonably to avoid liability in a way that would frustrate recovery. The law applies to conduct occurring in whole or in part in New York, but not where the user is physically located outside the state.

The law does not create an express private right of action. Until applicable age-assurance regulations take effect, operators must use a reasonable age-assurance method that guards against circumvention and minimizes data retention. Operators may rely on self-declaration only when a user self-declares as a minor, since a user’s self-declared adult status is not sufficient. Operators must offer more than one method, including at least one that either does not rely on government-issued identification or allows the user to remain anonymous to the operator. Information collected for age assurance may be used only for that purpose and must be deleted immediately after the age determination attempt, unless other law requires otherwise.

The law follows S3008C, passed in 2025, which requires providers of AI companions in New York to include functionality for detecting and responding to expressions of suicidal ideation. The prohibition does not apply where a system is made available solely for customer service or information strictly related to a business’s customer service, including its products, services or customer accounts. It also excludes systems used solely for efficiency improvements, research or technical assistance, or for a business’s internal purposes or employee productivity. For the first two exceptions, the system must be unable to respond on topics outside the specified purpose. A separate proposal, S7263A, introduced April 7, 2025 and amended May 26, 2026, would prohibit operators of AI chatbots from knowingly permitting a chatbot to impersonate a licensed professional.

Healthcare and digital health organizations that offer chatbots or other conversational AI tools to New York patients or consumers should prepare before S9051B takes effect on January 1, 2027. Recommended steps include inventorying externally deployed conversational AI tools, determining whether each tool falls within the statutory definition or an exception, and confirming whether minors can access it. Organizations should assess the features of each covered tool against the unsafe AI companion features described in the law. They should also review age-assurance workflows to confirm they are reasonable, resist circumvention and delete age-assurance data as required. The articles leave open whether S7263A will pass and what specific age-assurance regulations the Attorney General will adopt.

stories.Headline: DeepHealth wins FDA clearance for AI that predicts five-year breast cancer risk from 3D mammograms
stories.Summary:
DeepHealth, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of RadNet, Inc., announced FDA 510(k) clearance for Mammo Risk on November 24, 2026. The company, based in Somerville, Massachusetts, described Mammo Risk as the first FDA-cleared image-based breast cancer risk prediction solution for 3D mammography. The clearance covers combined 3D and 2D imaging workflows and applies to supported systems from multiple vendors. DeepHealth stated that 3D technology is now available at more than 90 percent of mammography facilities nationwide. The solution assesses three-, four- and five-year breast cancer risk using existing completed mammogram images with no additional scans required.

Mammo Risk enables providers to personalize patient pathways and optimize screening workflows by identifying patients who show no apparent signs of cancer but may have elevated risk. An estimated 321,910 women in the U.S. will be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in 2026, according to the announcement. When cancer is diagnosed early, five-year relative survival approaches 100 percent compared with 34 percent when it has spread to distant parts of the body. The American Medical Association established a Category III CPT code effective January 1, 2027, to track utilization of image-based breast cancer risk assessment technologies. The code supports collection of evidence that may inform future reimbursement decisions.

Niccolò Stefani, M.D., Business and Product Leader for Clinical AI at DeepHealth, said every woman deserves a clearer, non-invasive, more predictive path for her future. He stated that launching the world’s first and only image-based risk assessment software for 3D mammography moves beyond detecting cancer towards enabling preventive pathways. Stefani added that unlocking predictive insights directly from a routine scan can reduce uncertainty and give providers and patients insights into risk years before cancer would be diagnosed. He said this enables personalization of care in a way that can truly save lives. Victoria Smart, SVP of Mission at Susan G. Komen, said everyone’s biology and breast cancer risk are different, yet too often a one-size-fits-all approach is taken to screening and care.

Smart said better approaches have been long overdue and that personalized approaches help people understand their risk, make decisions about their health and get care as early as possible. She described this as the innovation essential to ending deaths from breast cancer. Mammo Risk uses AI trained on 220,000 studies to derive personalized risk insights directly from routine mammograms, unlike traditional risk assessment models that rely on extensive patient questionnaires and clinical information. An independent, multicenter pivotal study involving more than 65,000 screening mammograms across 10 U.S. clinical sites demonstrated strong predictive performance of future breast cancer risk. The study included a diverse patient population, and performance was consistent across important subgroups, including Black women and women with dense breasts.

These groups have historically experienced poorer breast cancer outcomes, and traditional models have been less accurate in assessing their risk. Mammo Risk builds on earlier generations of DeepHealth’s image-based breast cancer risk assessment technology designed to predict breast cancer risk up to two years ahead. That earlier technology is CE-marked and commercially available in Europe, with clinical validation across European and U.S. screening populations using both 2D and 3D mammography. A peer-reviewed study led by researchers at Karolinska Institute and published in Science Translational Medicine drew on a U.S. screening population of more than 154,000 women undergoing 3D mammography. The earlier technology demonstrated an estimated 2.4-fold sensitivity compared with the Tyrer-Cuzick risk model when considering supplemental screening for the 12 percent of women at highest risk.

The newly FDA-cleared Mammo Risk extends the risk prediction horizon to three, four and five years, supporting longer-term personalized breast cancer screening strategies. With this clearance, Mammo Risk is now part of DeepHealth’s Radiology AI Suite, which brings together native clinical AI, workflow tools and performance analytics on one platform. The solution complements the recently launched Mammo Dx technology, representing a new generation of AI-powered image-based breast cancer detection and risk prediction. Mammo Risk is now commercially available to healthcare providers across the U.S. seeking to enhance their breast cancer screening capabilities and differentiate their screening services. In the coming months, Mammo Risk will be part of an integrated offering within RadNet’s mammography screening initiatives, including RadNet’s Enhanced Breast Cancer Detection program.

stories.Headline: China and Singapore agree to expand cooperation in artificial intelligence and green industries
stories.Summary:
China and Singapore agreed to expand their cooperation in artificial intelligence and green industries during meetings held in November 2026. Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang met with Singaporean leaders to discuss these emerging fields. The discussions took place in Singapore on November 22 and November 23. Ding Xuexiang is a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee. These talks aimed to upgrade traditional cooperation and explore new avenues for technological innovation.

The leaders co-chaired the 22nd China-Singapore Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation Meeting in Singapore. They also held the 27th China-Singapore Suzhou Industrial Park Joint Steering Council Meeting. The 18th China-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City Joint Steering Council Meeting was conducted during this visit. They met for the 10th China-Singapore Chongqing Demonstration Initiative on Strategic Connectivity Joint Steering Council Meeting. These meetings yielded 29 outcomes in financial cooperation, health, and other emerging and frontier areas.

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang said that practical cooperation between the two nations has achieved remarkable results. He stated that bilateral relations are all-round, high-quality, and future-oriented in their nature. Ding said China is ready to align its 15th Five-Year Plan with Singapore's national development priorities. He noted that both sides should adapt to changing circumstances to support their respective modernization efforts. He also emphasized the need to utilize bilateral cooperation mechanisms to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore is willing to deepen cooperation in the services sector and connectivity. He stated that Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had productive exchanges with Chinese leaders during a recent visit to China. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong expressed his belief that the mechanism meetings would consolidate and expand all-round cooperation. Wong said Singapore looks forward to strengthening cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence. He also noted that the two sides should enhance people-to-people exchanges to boost mutual understanding.

The articles state that the bilateral cooperation mechanism meetings have continuously enriched their dimensions over time. These meetings have yielded new achievements that lay a solid foundation for the partnership. The two countries have a history of close exchanges in education, science, technology, and culture. This existing public foundation is intended to support the growth of bilateral relations. The partnership is described by the officials as an all-round high-quality future-oriented partnership.

Singapore will assume the rotating chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in 2027. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore is ready to use this opportunity to advance ASEAN-China cooperation. The two nations will continue to explore ways to make better use of intergovernmental projects. The articles leave open the specific details of the 29 outcomes reached in emerging areas. They do not specify the exact nature of the planned green industry projects.
