stories.Headline: DePauw University receives $5 million from Lilly Endowment to fund its Launch AI campus strategy
stories.Summary:
DePauw University received a grant of $5 million from Lilly Endowment Inc. to support the liberal arts college’s holistic approach in artificial intelligence. The award was announced on November 24, 2026, in Greencastle, Indiana. The three-year award will go toward Launch AI, DePauw’s campus-wide strategy. The strategy spans AI literacy, experimentation, teaching practices and institutional policy development. As an implementation grant, the support follows a related award from Lilly Endowment that DePauw put toward AI planning.

Launch AI is being funded through Lilly Endowment’s Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education. The initiative is designed to support colleges and universities in Indiana as they develop and implement approaches for using AI. DePauw is one of 35 colleges and universities in Indiana receiving funding through the initiative. Under Launch AI, DePauw will concentrate grant support from Lilly Endowment in areas including AI literacy, fluency and ethics. Students, faculty and staff will receive tailored AI training, and opportunities to complete an AI Achievement credential, library instruction in a first-year seminar and a pilot sophomore seminar will focus on learning and ethical use of technology.

University President Lori S. White said AI offers historic capacity to amplify learning and achievement while the university reinforces the essential place of critical thinking, individual judgment and relationships. White said strategic AI use creates more time and space to focus on these irreplaceable human functions at the heart of a DePauw education. White said the university is honored and grateful to have support from Lilly Endowment for its AI approach. White said the foundation’s commitment helps position DePauw as a leader among liberal arts institutions in the ethical, deliberate integration of AI. White said DePauw graduates will be ready to lead with AI as they incorporate its advancements responsibly into both work and life.

Dave Berque, vice president for academic affairs at DePauw, said AI is an invaluable complement to abilities and skills inspired for centuries by the liberal arts. The university leverages a “cloister and starship” practice for AI adoption, identifying spaces where the technology would hinder intellectual growth, such as reading, writing and discussion, while supporting ethical AI integration where it has the potential to enhance human-centered learning and work. Sarah Steinkamp, vice president of communications and strategy and chief of staff at DePauw, who will work with Berque on grant oversight, said the liberal arts have never been more essential. Steinkamp said the skills developed at DePauw, critical thinking, ethical reasoning, clear communication and the ability to ask the right questions, are exactly what it takes to use these tools well. In surveys, half the parents of prospective DePauw students ranked AI competence as their top priority for college.

More than 20 faculty AI liaisons will help identify where AI fits each academic department. Faculty will redesign student assessment in the context of AI and lead summer research projects with students. Among other steps, an AI-assisted advising pilot will focus on first-year, first-generation and pre-health students. A set of approved AI tools with privacy protections will be available to the university community, offering a digital “sandbox” for safe experimentation. The university will advance AI policy, data security and governance frameworks.

Campus partners supporting AI work at DePauw include the university’s Prindle Institute for Ethics, Tenzer Technology Center and Roy O. West Library. Under the Lilly Endowment grant, DePauw will share frameworks, curricula and outcomes with peer institutions across the state. White said the support is instrumental as the university maximizes AI for learning engagement, graduates’ long-term growth and the university’s own institutional resilience. White said the next generations of critical, creative and capable DePauw graduates will benefit enormously from the foundation’s generous vote of confidence. DePauw University was founded in 1837 and is a liberal arts college located in Greencastle, Indiana.

stories.Headline: Avanade's Ben Beath says firms must redesign work to gain 200% to 300% from AI
stories.Summary:
Ben Beath discussed how to create value from artificial intelligence during a video interview with ISMG. This conversation took place on November 24, 2026, at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. Beath serves as the chief AI officer for the company known as Avanade. He explained that organizations must redesign business processes to maximize the return on their AI investments. He argued against simply layering new technology onto existing work patterns to achieve better results.

The AI Reality Report from Avanade found that only 18% of global organizations fundamentally reshaped their AI usage. However, 75% of these organizations claim they are doing better with AI than they actually are. Layering AI onto existing processes yields about 30% productivity gains according to the data provided by Beath. Building AI into the business can yield 200% to 300% through new revenue opportunities for the company. This approach requires alignment and a specific perspective on both governance and security for the enterprise.

Ben Beath is responsible for scaling AI adoption and integrating agentic systems into various enterprise operations. He stated that rethinking how a business operates is hard work for any organization to undertake. Beath believes that velocity is the right way to think about AI adoption rather than focusing on speed. He noted that human oversight must evolve as AI agents gain authority to make decisions of consequence. He also explained how Avanade uses Agent 365 to help employees build more intelligent AI agents.

The reports indicate that many global organizations are affected by what Beath calls the AI reality gap. These companies claim higher success rates with AI than their actual process redesigns would suggest. C-suite leaders are the primary group Beath works with to scale these complex AI adoption strategies. The data shows a significant difference in value between simple layering and full business reinvention for firms. Most organizations are currently failing to fundamentally reshape how their teams use these new artificial intelligence tools.

Beath has more than 20 years of experience in digital transformation and innovation for various businesses. His professional expertise includes enterprise AI strategy as well as generative AI and machine learning technologies. He previously co-founded the digital agency Loud & Clear along with PlayHQ Sports and FanHub Media. He was also a co-founder of the company called Sidekicker before his current role at Avanade. These experiences inform his view that business reinvention is necessary for achieving high returns on AI.

The next step for organizations is to move beyond simple productivity gains toward new revenue opportunities. Companies must decide if they will continue layering AI or commit to the hard work of redesigning. The articles leave open how exactly human oversight should evolve as agents gain more decision making authority. It remains unclear how many organizations will close the AI reality gap in the coming years. The text does not specify the exact timeline for achieving these 300% gains in revenue.

stories.Headline: North Carolina treasurer Brad Briner says state's $250 million Anthropic stake is now worth $950 million
stories.Summary:
North Carolina invested $250 million in the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, State Treasurer Brad Briner said, and that figure was worth $950 million after the company went public last week. Briner said the state found Anthropic's Series G round, raised in March of this year, extremely compelling when the company was worth $380 billion. The investment is emblematic of a broader shift of strategy since Briner took office in January 2025, which has seen a more aggressive approach in investing. Briner said North Carolina had long run a roughly 45% equity and 55% cash and debt portfolio. The state's investment grew to $950 million after Anthropic's public debut, the articles reported.

Briner said the average pension fund in the country runs 70% stocks and 30% bonds, so much higher risk than North Carolina's. He said the state has changed that fundamentally and is now roughly 65% stocks and equities and other things like that, 35% debt and cash. Briner said the state delivered a 13% rate of return in its first full fiscal year, which is double of what it is trying to do at 6.5 percent. Other notable investments include Andruil, Revolut, Databricks, and Bending Spoons. Briner said the state cannot sell its entire Anthropic position at once because there are 23 different expiration dates governing when shares can be sold.

Briner said the goal is very clear to get to 100% funding and to reinstate cost-of-living adjustments on a permanent basis for state employees. He said the state will get a little bit in a couple weeks and then unlock slowly thereafter. Briner said the state will begin selling that stock through its investment manager when it can, and it is a lot for the state in a single position. He said the state wants to take some of those profits in reinvestment of other things. Briner said the state's retirees haven't had a cost-of-living adjustment in nine years.

Wendell Powell, President of the State Employees Association of North Carolina, said if the state makes $700 million in gains, that will definitely go a long way toward helping retirees get a COLA and putting money into the benefit package so employees can get raises in the upcoming year. Powell is a Correctional Captain at Harnett Correctional Institution. Powell said stronger pension performance could also help the state attract workers by giving employees confidence that their retirement benefits will be available. He said people want to make sure there is money there so they say they want to come to North Carolina and get into its pension system and work for the state because they know they have a defined benefit waiting. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly, whose new session will begin in January, will utilize the additional funds.

Powell said the association is happy that the Treasurer is finding ways to enhance the pot, making the pot bigger so the legislature can have tools and revenue streams to pull from to take care of state workers. The performance is especially noteworthy to public sector employees and retirees. The articles said Anthropic's IPO made major headlines last week, and in the case of North Carolina, major money. The articles were reported by Michael Perchick and published Monday, November 23, 2026 at 11:11 PM. The articles were datelined Raleigh, N.C.

The state will take a piecemeal approach to selling its Anthropic shares, with a little bit coming in a couple weeks and unlocking slowly thereafter. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly will utilize the additional funds when its new session begins in January. The articles leave open how much the state will ultimately realize from the position and what the General Assembly will do with the funds. The articles leave open whether retirees will receive a cost-of-living adjustment and whether employees will get raises in the upcoming year. Clients have already shown interest in paying premiums for AI-assisted work product, Kim said. stories.Headline: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO and AI credit markets swing on debt fears
stories.Summary:
Credit markets for artificial intelligence experienced significant volatility on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, as investors reacted to the return of Jensen Huang. Huang was reinstated as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on Monday, November 23, after having stepped down on November 12 due to allegations of multiple affairs. This return sparked fears among credit investors regarding the massive amounts of debt used to fund the buildout of artificial intelligence.

The market shift caused the stock of CoreWeave to drop 13 percent and the yield on its 9.75 percent bond due in 2031 to exceed 17 percent. Credit default swaps for CoreWeave jumped 8.5 percent to over 1,200 basis points, while Oracle saw its five-year spread rise 7 percent to 355.68. Spreads for Meta Platforms and Amazon.com increased by more than 2 percent, and Nvidia's own credit default swaps rose 3.4 percent. Nvidia reported having 118 billion dollars in guarantees to support AI projects as of October 25.

President Donald Trump stated on Monday that he convinced the board to bring Huang back to the company. Ben Emons of FedWatch Advisors described the subsequent market dip as a waning of the Jensen effect, suggesting that government involvement creates credit risks. Larry Holzenthaler of Catalyst Funds noted that traditional credit investors typically dislike the drama and uncertainty surrounding this reinstatement. Meanwhile, investor Steve Eisman predicted that Huang will double down on circular financing for AI chips and data centers.

The situation remains unstable as Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. An independent investigation is being conducted by Nvidia, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a separate probe. Although Attorney General Todd Blanche stated the federal government lacks evidence of unlawful conduct, economist David Rosenberg believes more information will emerge. Market participants continue to monitor the neocloud sector while waiting for more clarity on long-term supply and demand.

stories.Headline: International Bar Association ranks AI first among seven legal priorities for 2026
stories.Summary:
The International Bar Association published its Legal Agenda 2026 on Monday, November 23, 2026, to identify the most pressing issues for lawyers. This organization ranked artificial intelligence as the first priority among seven key concerns facing the global legal profession during this period of disruption. The report highlights how technological advances are currently reshaping legal service delivery, talent development, pricing, client relationships, and general access to justice. This new ranking marks a change from the 2025 Agenda, which placed the rule of law as the foremost concern for lawyers. In that previous 2025 list, artificial intelligence was ranked in second place among the seven priorities identified by the international legal organization.

The 2026 Agenda lists AI governance and its impact on service delivery, pricing, talent, client expectations, and access to justice as priority one. Priority two covers the rule of law and the rules-based international order, including the erosion of legal protections and threats to judicial independence. Priority three focuses on the rule of law through recruitment, talent development, retention, and the long-term attractiveness of the legal profession for workers. Priority four involves law firm business models, including ownership, investment, and evolving approaches to the structure, financing, and delivery of legal services. The final priorities are client relationships and ethics, cybersecurity and operational risk, and diversity, inclusion, and workplace evolution including leadership imbalances.

IBA President Claudio Visco stated that the adoption of artificial intelligence is becoming the most impactful technological advancement of our current time. He said that lawyers must embrace innovation without compromising the professional standards, ethical responsibilities, and independence that underpin the practice of law. Visco noted that lawyers have a crucial role in promoting proper governance and regulating AI to help shape the future of society. Immediate Past-President Jaime Carey remarked that AI overtaking the rule of law does not diminish the fundamental importance of that legal principle. Carey stated that the legal profession must remain a steadfast defender of individual rights, professional independence, and justice during geopolitical uncertainty.

The report notes that divergent national and regional approaches to AI regulation create complexity for international law firms and businesses across multiple jurisdictions. Young people entering the profession are affected because technology now performs many tasks that were historically undertaken by junior lawyers in firms. The legal profession faces competition for talent from other high-income careers, specifically those found in the finance sector and Big Tech. Women are affected by retention issues, and the Agenda suggests that greater workplace flexibility is important for balancing professional and family responsibilities. International firms also face challenges from differing moral and regulatory expectations in jurisdictions such as Russia and China regarding certain mandates.

The IBA Legal Agenda was launched in 2023 by former President Almudena Arpón de Mendívil Aldama as part of a five-year strategic focus. This strategic plan for 2023 to 2028 was developed following consultations with leaders of major national and international law firms in London and New York. To support these goals, the organization launched the IBA Artificial Intelligence Institute in June 2026 to serve as a key reference point. In March 2026, the IBA collaborated with the Danish Bar and Law Society to launch the IBA Rule of Law Educational Project. This specific project was designed to raise awareness of the rule of law among secondary school students located within the country of Denmark.

The priorities outlined in the 2026 Agenda will serve as the foundation for the strategic initiatives and partnerships of the IBA next year. The organization will continue to use the Agenda to promote practical solutions to the challenges facing the global legal community and practitioners. The IBA Diversity and Inclusion Council will provide continued institutional commitment to address persistent gender imbalances at senior levels of legal leadership. The Association also intends to play a more active role in strengthening the rule of law globally through advocacy and closer coordination. The articles leave open the specific results of the consultations that will continue in 2027 to inform the next edition of the Agenda.

stories.Headline: Sierra Leone children share AI concerns at Freetown policy dialogue
stories.Summary:
Children in Sierra Leone shared their experiences and concerns about artificial intelligence during a national policy dialogue. This event took place in Freetown on November 23, 2026, to commemorate World Children's Day. Government partners and young participants gathered to discuss child rights in the digital era. The dialogue focused on how the youngest users are already utilizing new technology. These contributions will now feed into a global UNICEF initiative regarding children's rights and AI.

The dialogue was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Freetown on November 23, 2026. It involved children aged 10 to 17 from various backgrounds across the entire country. The event will help strengthen the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill. It also informs the National AI Readiness Assessment to guide the national AI policy and strategy. These efforts aim to protect personal data and ensure the best interests of the child.

Mariko Kagoshima of UNICEF said AI is already part of the present for children in Sierra Leone. She stated that responsibility for AI lies with Parliament, Government, and technology and telecommunications companies. Minister Chernor Bah said children must be involved in shaping policies, not just in conversations. Minister Isata Mahoi reaffirmed the government commitment to stronger online child protection and personal information safeguards. Minister Kenyeh Barlay stressed integrating children's rights into national development planning and digital investments.

Children expressed worries about misinformation, privacy, cyberbullying, harmful content, and an over-dependence on these new tools. They called for safe and fair access to AI instead of blanket bans on the technology. Twelve-year-old Halimatu said children must have a voice because today's decisions shape their future opportunities. Aissatou Diallo of the World Bank Group said children need AI taught in schools and affordable tools. Seraphine Wakana of the United Nations reaffirmed support for an inclusive and rights-based digital future.

The dialogue was organized by UNICEF and the ministries of Information and Civic Education and Gender and Children's Affairs. It also included the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation as a partner in the event. The process built upon a national consultation with children who had varying levels of AI experience. A national pledge on child online protection was presented last week in Manila at a global conference. UNICEF has worked for children globally for 80 years and in Sierra Leone for over four decades.

Children's recommendations will now help build accountability, participation, and inclusion into the National AI Readiness Assessment. AI could potentially be used to simplify laws and translate policies between English and Krio. The dialogue does not establish new binding regulations but provides policymakers with direct accounts from young users. Future goals include reducing inequalities in access for girls, children with disabilities, and those in underserved communities. The articles leave open how the government will specifically implement these recommendations into binding law.

stories.Headline: Indian AI companies raise 1.6 billion dollars in first nine months of 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian AI companies raised 1.6 billion dollars in equity funding during the first nine months of 2026. This total represents a 96 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025. The funding occurred between January and September of 2026. Data intelligence platform Tracxn provided these figures in a recent report. This amount is the highest nine-month total recorded by the report since 2019.

The funding total was 1.6 billion dollars, which is 162 percent above the 616 million dollars raised in 2024. Mumbai became the largest recipient of AI funding, raising 765 million dollars for a 48 percent share. Bengaluru raised 711 million dollars, which was a 44 percent share of the total. Neysa in Mumbai raised 600 million dollars in February, while Sarvam in Bengaluru raised 255 million dollars in June. Sarvam raised another 90.4 million dollars in August, and Yotta raised 150 million dollars in July.

Tracxn reported that a small number of large deals drove the surge in funding. The platform stated that around 90 percent of the total capital was raised in just 10 rounds. Tracxn noted that the number of deals fell from 149 in 2025 to 87 in 2026. The report indicated that the average deal size more than tripled to 18.5 million dollars. This increase was up from an average of 5.5 million dollars a year earlier.

Fortune India noted that a handful of deals drove the surge, showing a concentration of capital. Seed-stage founders are affected as they compete for a thinner slice of investor attention. Early-stage and late-stage funding rose by 191 percent and 4 percent, but seed-stage funding fell by 42 percent. This suggests investors favor companies with more mature technology and business models. India accounted for 0.4 percent of global AI money, trailing countries like the US, China, and the UK.

The 2024 base of 616 million dollars was the lowest of the three periods in the report. Funding in the first nine months of 2025 was 822 million dollars. Mumbai's funding was only 15.7 million dollars, a 2 percent share, in the first nine months of 2025. The report tracks equity funding only, excluding debt, grants, and compute credits. India is ranked ninth among countries in terms of AI funding raised during this period.

The reports leave open how much funding went to applications versus infrastructure. They do not disclose the specific investors or individual deal sizes for all rounds. It remains unclear if the funding is driven by infrastructure, enterprise traction, or scarcity. Future durability depends on whether customers renew contracts or compute demand continues. The data does not specify which firms drove the jump beyond the largest named rounds.

stories.Headline: Nestlé opens Swiss deep tech center to test AI and robotics across its food brands
stories.Summary:
Nestlé opened a deep tech center in Orbe, Switzerland last week, the company said, to develop, test and scale advanced technologies across its portfolio of frozen pizza, chocolate chips and coffee. The world’s largest food company said the center will help it develop and test ideas faster, maintain consistent quality and improve efficiency. Nestlé is leveraging artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics to boost growth across its sprawling portfolio, according to Food Dive. The Lean Cuisine and Hot Pockets manufacturer said it will use AI, sensors and rapid prototyping to develop and test ideas faster. Sensors and robotics will handle routine or physically demanding tasks and help maintain consistent product quality and improve efficiency, Nestlé said.

The center will handle consumer experiences, research and development and manufacturing, Nestlé said, and will help create more personalized experiences. Those experiences range from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition, according to the company. The center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations, according to the company. Nestlé said real internal growth, which measures volume, rose 1.8% in North America in its third quarter compared to a 0.6% decline in the prior three months. In the U.S., Nestlé’s biggest market, food and snacks delivered strong growth, led by an improvement in confectionery and in frozen brands like Stouffer’s and DiGiorno that resulted in market share gains, according to the company.

Philipp Navratil, Nestlé’s CEO, said in a statement that innovation at Nestlé starts with the consumer and that for the company technology is an enabler. Navratil said technology helps Nestlé understand consumers better, deliver superior quality, drive smart innovation and run more efficient operations. He said this ultimately supports the company’s growth. Navratil also said Nestlé is still struggling with Gerber and its nutrition unit, which he said underperformed. The company said the snacking giant’s brand is growing 2.5 times faster than the cookie category and is benefiting from consumer demand for high-end treats.

Food Dive reported that CPG companies have turned to advanced technology to help them improve efficiency and more quickly respond to changing consumer demand for healthier offerings. AI and other technologies have proven especially valuable as consumers cut back on spending due to inflation, putting pressure on food volumes, according to the report. International Supermarket News reported that Nestlé is stepping up its investment in advanced manufacturing technology as artificial intelligence, robotics and data-driven production become increasingly important to the global food industry. The publication reported that the initiative reflects a wider shift among major food producers towards factories that can respond more intelligently to changing ingredients, production requirements and consumer demand. The publication reported that the development comes as food manufacturers face pressure from higher operating costs, supply-chain uncertainty and changing consumer expectations.

International Supermarket News reported that one of the biggest challenges in food manufacturing is managing natural variations in raw materials, because milk, coffee, cocoa and other agricultural ingredients do not always behave in exactly the same way. Temperature, quality and composition can influence production, creating challenges for consistency and efficiency, the publication reported. Nestlé’s research is exploring how artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics could help manufacturing systems respond to these variations, according to the publication. Instead of relying entirely on fixed production settings, intelligent systems could use real-time information to adjust processes and improve operational control, the publication reported. The publication reported that better monitoring and more responsive production could help reduce waste, improve quality management and make factories more adaptable.

International Supermarket News reported that moving from research to large-scale industrial application will require substantial investment, and that manufacturers must demonstrate that advanced systems can deliver reliable results, integrate with existing equipment and generate measurable financial returns. The publication reported that for retailers the implications could eventually reach beyond the factory gates, and that more flexible production may help suppliers respond faster to changing demand, improve product availability and manage manufacturing costs. The publication reported that Nestlé’s initiative highlights an important question for the industry about whether the next generation of food manufacturing will be defined as much by artificial intelligence and robotics as by traditional production expertise. Food Dive reported that the center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations. The company said the center will help create more personalized experiences, from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition.

stories.Headline: First Amendment experts debate whether AI speech deserves constitutional protection
stories.Summary:
Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate, titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? ,  A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate,” on November 23, 2026. Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. The debate was moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall. The debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law.

The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. He noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. He said AI output is a joint effort on the part of the user and the AI company and should be protected precisely because of that. He described rights as a speaker trying to generate things to communicate to the public and rights as a listener and information gatherer.

Tsesis argued that large language models lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, so AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers. Tsesis said legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. He contended that in light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against intrusions from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters. He said any restriction on AI in the US will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis. He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality.

Procaccini offered a middle ground. Procaccini suggested that the problems of AI can be addressed doctrinally without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people. She described a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. She argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech.

Defending his position, Tsesis addressed whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. Tsesis established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. He said that when people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. He said that even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, and sexual orientation. He said human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.

Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini said the value is in the ideas shared and that is still something worth protecting as long as it is protected in a tailored way. She also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example of AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment.

He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. She disputed that characterization of the doctrine and said First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way. She said each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. She said what she is doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection.

She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Procaccini said AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context, like those spaces. Volokh argued that Procaccini’s doctrine would set up new rules that would depart substantially from current ones, creating confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs.

He emphasized again that while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government. Volokh agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. He said First Amendment law already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions and they just have the advantage of familiarity. He said it is not buying a pig in the poke and we know roughly where they are and the problems with them.

Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. He said programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. She said traditional property law, civil rights law, and tort law are bodies of law she has a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate when they run up against the First Amendment.

She asked what is to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit. She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. She said uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. The Respectfully Dissent series presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue.

The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. stories.Headline: Congress introduces four bills to block Chinese access to US computing power
stories.Summary:
Congress introduced four bills to stop Chinese access to American computing power. These legislative efforts occurred in late 2026 during a shift in political power. The bills target chip licensing, diversion after sale, chipmaking equipment, and remote rentals. Three of these measures are part of a Senate defense authorization package. Congress expects to take up this package in December.

The AI OVERWATCH Act would codify bans on advanced chip sales to countries of concern. It gives Congress 30 days to block transactions, which the president could then veto. The Chip Security Act requires location verification for covered chips within 180 days. The MATCH Act targets chipmaking equipment and sets a 150 day deadline for allies. RASA would allow the Department of Commerce to license remote access to controlled items.

The bills represent a rebuke of President Donald Trump's approach to the AI race. Trump claimed the government has no reason to believe Jensen Huang poses a security risk. The Department of Commerce issued a rule regarding Chinese firms renting capacity from third countries. Some critics object to the strict deadlines imposed on the Netherlands and Japan. The House passed RASA 369 to 22 in January.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang was reinstated on Monday after resigning on November 12. He resigned over reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Singapore executive. US officials suspect Alice Huang of diverting chips to China and working for Chinese intelligence. The Nvidia board acted after receiving input from senior US officials. These events provide the backdrop for the current legislative efforts in Congress.

The bills assume that access to computing power decides the outcome of the AI race. This premise is one that the Trump administration has rejected in recent years. The administration prioritizes securing global market share over limiting adversarial access to advanced chips. Some technology leaders believe the race depends on who builds the best applications. Chinese efforts to smuggle chips suggest they believe computing power is the deciding factor.

Congress will decide if RASA is included in the National Defense Authorization Act. The effectiveness of the Commerce rule depends on future enforcement and administration willingness. It remains uncertain if the AI frontier is decided by computing power or applications. The bills may undermine efforts to seize global market share by limiting sales. The articles leave open whether the president will veto congressional resolutions to block sales.

stories.Headline: Experts urge caution before linking bank accounts to AI tools
stories.Summary:
As of November 2026, privacy and security experts are urging caution about giving AI tools access to your bank and financial accounts, according to Utah State University. The guidance comes as new tools such as ChatGPT Finance may lead people to wonder whether to link their accounts and let AI weigh in on their budget, credit, or savings and investment plans. Stanford Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence says AI is advancing faster than the testing meant to keep it responsible, which the article offers as one reason to be careful with your money and information. Financial institutions advise keeping account numbers, passwords, and statements out of AI chats.

The article lists four things to consider before linking an account. First, keep your sign-in information private and never type a password or log in to an AI chat, because linking an account means trusting a third party with your financial data under that company's privacy policy. Second, stay in control of your accounts, since some AI tools can log in and take actions for you rather than just view your information, and if you authorize that you may be held responsible for what happens. Third, the rules are still catching up, so it is not always clear how companies can use your financial data, including whether it can help train AI or target ads, and you should read the privacy policy and check what you can opt out of. Fourth, AI can get things wrong by misreading your numbers or giving advice that does not fit your situation, and if a tool can take actions in your account some mistakes cannot be undone, so double-check anything important against your bank's own records.

The article offers a pro tip: if your bank or credit union has an AI assistant built into its app, try that first, because you are already logged in and nothing new is shared. It notes that budgeting apps like Monarch Money and Rocket Money also offer AI features but require information from you to connect to your accounts, so check their privacy settings first. The article says AI can be a helpful money tool but you do not have to link your accounts to get value from it, and it suggests sharing rounded numbers and broad categories, keeping sign-in details and account numbers private, and checking your privacy settings. AI can help you plan, the article says, but let your bank track what is really happening.

stories.Headline: YYForce deploys a trained humanoid concierge robot at Novotel Singapore on Stevens
stories.Summary:
YYForce Inc., which trades as YFOR on the NASDAQ, announced a new humanoid robot for hotel concierge services on November 24, 2026. The company developed this proprietary trained robot to handle live hospitality operations for guests in a real world hotel setting. This specific robot was designed to move commercial embodied AI from training environments into a guest facing service role. The company is an AI enabled provider of robotics, facility solutions, and frontline workforce services operating across Asia and beyond. This launch represents a significant milestone for the company in the field of commercial embodied AI for the hospitality industry.

The robot, named Six Seven by the hotel team, will be deployed at the Novotel Singapore on Stevens in Singapore. It utilizes NVIDIA Jetson edge AI computing and NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulation workflows to achieve reliable performance in dynamic public spaces. The system is integrated into the Workforce OS architecture to combine natural conversational intelligence with real time property and local knowledge. It provides answers about on site restaurants, venue locations, operating hours, dining menus, and daily hotel events or activities. The robot also assists visitors with neighborhood navigation, nearby attractions, transportation options, and curated tourism recommendations across the city of Singapore.

Mike Fu serves as the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of YYForce and spoke about the new humanoid concierge deployment. He stated that the robot would demonstrate how humanoid robotics can provide operational value, accuracy, and genuine warmth on the front line. Fu mentioned that using NVIDIA Jetson and Isaac Sim within the Workforce OS platform accelerates the commercial rollout of embodied AI. He claimed this technology empowers hospitality partners to improve guest experiences while they address persistent challenges with their frontline staffing. The CEO believes this deployment shows the practical application of AI in a live, guest facing hotel lobby environment.

The robot is designed to engage visitors and families with interactive storytelling to create a memorable arrival experience for every guest. It is trained to respond naturally to open ended inquiries from guests who visit the Novotel Singapore on Stevens hotel lobby. This technology affects hospitality partners who seek to elevate the guest experience through the use of advanced commercial service robots. The robot handles a range of interactions, including full hotel and dining concierge services and wide travel guidance for visitors. These capabilities are intended to provide immediate and accurate information to guests regarding both the hotel and the local area.

This deployment builds upon dedicated robotics training and data collection initiatives that YYForce previously conducted in Singapore and in Malaysia. The company brings together intelligent software, people, and commercial robotics into one connected ecosystem to transform frontline work through AI. Its broader portfolio includes digital estate management through 24iFM and intelligent workforce matching via Yolara AI and the YY Circle. The company serves various frontline driven industries, including retail, logistics, facilities management, and the hospitality sector, to improve overall business productivity. YYForce aims to build a future where intelligent technology and people thrive together to create a more sustainable workforce.

YYForce plans to scale its commercial service robots across integrated facility management environments, the retail sector, and the hospitality industry. The company will continue to use its Workforce OS platform to deploy more embodied AI solutions for its various partners. The articles leave open whether the robot will be deployed to other hotels beyond the Novotel Singapore on Stevens. They do not state the specific timeline for the rollout of these robots into the retail or logistics sectors. There is no information regarding the total number of Six Seven robots that the company intends to produce.

stories.Headline: University of Dubai and AIJRF launch guide to agentic AI governance with Arab universities
stories.Summary:
The University of Dubai and the AIJRF announced a guide to agentic AI governance on November 23, 2026. This announcement happened in collaboration with several Arab universities. They will launch the guide during the sixth Artificial Intelligence Journalism World Forum. The University of Dubai will host this forum on November 25 and 26. The guide is titled Professional and Ethical Rules for Assistive Agentic AI.

The guide creates a framework for systems that plan, carry out tasks, and take action semi-autonomously. It provides guidance for government bodies, academic institutions, businesses, and technology organisations in Dubai. The text covers human oversight, accountability, transparency, data protection, and risk management. The University of Dubai, University of Khorfakkan, and Liwa University in the UAE helped prepare it. Badr University in Cairo, Al-Azhar University in Egypt, and the Arab Index for Artificial Intelligence in Universities also contributed.

Dr. Mohamed Abdulzaher is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of AIJRF and he proposed the guide. He said the initiative is a step toward a common Arab framework for governing intelligent technologies. Abdulzaher stated that AI has evolved from content tools into systems capable of taking action with varying autonomy. He said rapid development requires clear operating rules to define what AI agents are authorised to do. He believes technology should advance within clear rules that protect people, institutions, and society.

The guide affects technology developers, organisations using the systems, individual users, and legislative, regulatory, and supervisory authorities. It provides rules for government, media, education, banking, and healthcare sectors to balance innovation with professional responsibility. The guide aims to preserve the role of people in decisions that have significant consequences. It establishes the right of users to know what system they are interacting with. Users can also request human review of automated decisions that affect their rights or interests.

Academics, researchers, and experts from nine countries contributed to the preparation of this governance guide. These contributors represented the UAE, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Libya, and Sudan. The guide builds on previous AIJRF work regarding professional and ethical standards for advanced technology. It extends governance from digital content to the decisions and actions of AI agents within institutions. The guide consists of three chapters covering global developments, ethical principles, and professional responsibilities.

The 2026 forum will examine the future of agentic AI and its role in content creation. It will also look at the role of these systems within the digital economy. The forum will address the challenges of governing intelligent systems and strengthening public trust. The guide explains which tasks AI agents can perform independently and which require direct human approval. The articles leave open how these rules will be enforced across the different participating countries.

stories.Headline: Germany, Italy, Poland and Sweden join France in setting up international AI defense center
stories.Summary:
Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden joined France to set up an international artificial intelligence center for defense, the French Defense Ministry announced. These four European countries officially announced their intention to join the new organization during a first establishment conference held in Rennes. The conference took place on November 19 and 20, and the announcement was made public by the ministry on a Monday. This international effort seeks to create a center that focuses on the use of artificial intelligence for various defense purposes. The participating nations intend to work together to build a new center dedicated to the field of artificial intelligence in defense.

The new organization is called the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence, which is also referred to by the acronym ICAID. The center requires the cooperation of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden to establish its initial operational framework and goals. It aims to build an international community of interest to share best practices and anticipate technological advances in the field of AI. The center will draw on operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions closely meet practical needs and support military operations. The initiative remains open to other like-minded nations that wish to join the effort to accelerate AI readiness for operations.

The French Defense Ministry is responsible for the announcement and the overall coordination of this new international artificial intelligence defense initiative. The ministry stated that France and its partners aim to accelerate AI readiness in support of military operations through the ICAID. They said the center will establish an international network for sharing best practices and anticipating future technological developments in AI. The ministry explained that the center will use operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions address practical defense needs effectively. Officials reaffirmed that the initiative is open to other nations that share similar goals regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

The articles do not provide specific quotes from other individuals, but they mention that other like-minded nations are welcome to join. The nations affected by this initiative include France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden, who are the current founding members. These countries will be affected by the acceleration of AI readiness and the adoption of new technologies for their military operations. The international community of interest will be affected by the sharing of best practices and the anticipation of technological advances. Military operations in these participating nations will be affected by the practical AI solutions developed by the new center.

The background provided is that France initiated the creation of the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence to support military operations. The center was established to create a network where nations can share best practices and anticipate future advances in AI. It was designed to ensure that artificial intelligence solutions are based on operational feedback to meet practical defense needs. The first establishment conference was held in Rennes to formally bring the participating European nations together for this specific purpose. This initiative is part of a broader effort to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence within the defense sectors of Europe.

The next step will be for the participating nations to work together on drafting the founding texts for the center. The goal of the member nations is to reach full operational capability for the center in the course of 2027. The articles leave open which other like-minded nations might decide to join the initiative in the future. It is not stated which specific founding texts will be drafted or how the operational capability will be measured. The articles do not specify the exact funding or the leadership structure that will govern the center once it is operational.

stories.Headline: US Department of Commerce plans to blacklist Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed over chip export violations
stories.Summary:
The United States government intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence company from doing business in America following a recent Nvidia scandal. The US Department of Commerce announced this plan on Monday to blacklist the firm known as Megaspeed Ltd from American trade. This action follows accusations that a former executive of the company worked as a spy for China during a romantic relationship. The relationship was with Jensen Huang, who is the head of Nvidia, and it led to increased scrutiny by US officials. This situation created heightened concerns that the company was funneling advanced AI computer chips from Nvidia into the country of China.

The Commerce Department plans to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are banned from buying or selling US goods. This Singaporean company is mainly a developer of data centres and has significant business dealings in China with the retailer Alibaba. The US intelligence apparatus believes that Alice Huang, a former executive, was working as an asset for the government in Beijing. This specific relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang became public through media reports that emerged during the previous month. The US has blocked China from buying this specific type of advanced AI technology since the year 2022.

The US Department of Commerce stated that it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years before the affair incident occurred. Officials said they suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping Chinese companies obtain advanced chips from Nvidia. President Donald Trump said he convinced the company and made a deal to reinstate Jensen Huang on Monday after his resignation. The board of Nvidia then reinstated the CEO after the intervention by the president of the United States regarding the matter. The White House, the Commerce Department, and Megaspeed were all asked for comment by the BBC regarding the planned ban.

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use this scandal as a pretext. The Chinese government stated that the US should not use the situation to impose a technological blockade on AI technology. The US intelligence apparatus claims that the activities of Alice Huang created national security concerns within the United States of America. The company Megaspeed was not well known within the US until the media reports about the affair surfaced last month. Another alleged affair involving Jensen Huang also surfaced days after the first one, which led to the CEO's initial resignation.

The US government suspects that Megaspeed was helping to get Nvidia chips into the hands of various companies located within China. This activity would violate US export controls that have been in place to restrict Chinese access to AI technology since 2022. Megaspeed is based in Singapore, but its largest customer is the major Chinese online retailer known as Alibaba. The company primarily focuses on the development of data centres as its main business activity before the recent blacklist announcement. The US intelligence community viewed the romantic link between the two individuals as a risk to national security interests.

The US government has not yet specified when the ban against Megaspeed Ltd will officially go into effect for the company. The Commerce Department continues to monitor the situation after its two year investigation into the suspected violation of export controls. The articles leave open whether the US will impose further restrictions on other companies tied to the recent Nvidia scandal. It remains unclear if the Chinese government will take further diplomatic actions in response to the planned American technological blockade. The BBC is waiting for responses from the White House and Megaspeed regarding the announcement made on Monday.

stories.Headline: AMD and Dell post accelerating revenue growth as AI demand rises in 2026
stories.Summary:
Robert Izquierdo of The Motley Fool published the comparison of Advanced Micro Devices and Dell Technologies revenue trends on Nov. 23, 2026. The article appeared on fool.com at 12:02PM EST and on AOL at 5:22 PM UTC the same day. It compared quarterly revenue for the two companies over the last eight quarters, with data from Financial Modeling Prep as of Nov. 20, 2026. AMD closed the World Labs acquisition on Nov. 16 and announced a partnership with Meta Platforms on Oct. 27. Dell partnered with Rackspace on Nov. 17 and collaborated with Mistral AI on Oct. 21.

AMD's year-over-year quarterly revenue growth rate stepped up from the low-to-mid 30% range throughout 2025 to an average of 44% across the first three quarters of 2026. Management projected further acceleration in Q4. AMD revenue was $7.7 billion in Q4 2024, $7.4 billion in Q1 2025, $7.7 billion in Q2 2025, $9.2 billion in Q3 2025, $10.3 billion in Q4 2025, $10.3 billion in Q1 2026, $11.5 billion in Q2 2026 and $13.4 billion in Q3 2026. Those quarters ended Dec. 28, 2024, March 29, 2025, June 28, 2025, Sept. 27, 2025, Dec. 27, 2025, March 28, 2026, June 27, 2026 and Sept. 26, 2026. Dell revenue was $23.9 billion in Q4 2024, $23.4 billion in Q1 2025, $29.8 billion in Q2 2025, $27.0 billion in Q3 2025, $33.4 billion in Q4 2025, $43.8 billion in Q1 2026 and $47.0 billion in Q2 2026, with Q3 2026 not yet reported.

Dell raised its full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $192 billion, implying approximately 69% annual growth over fiscal 2026, thanks to a record $95 billion server backlog. AMD management guided for roughly $17 billion in Q4 2026. Dell generated more than triple AMD's trailing twelve-month revenue, about $151.2 billion versus $45.4 billion. Dell converted its AI server backlog into high-volume revenue at roughly 21% gross margins, exposing it to component cost inflation. AMD captured upstream silicon pricing power with 54% gross margins, meaning each incremental dollar of data center revenue flowed through to operating income at a much higher rate.

The article said Dell's higher absolute revenue total was due to the company selling complete, high-ticket systems such as servers, data center hardware and PCs, whereas AMD sells individual semiconductor components that go into those systems. It said both companies quickly pivoted away from relying on cyclical PC markets to being anchored by enterprise and hyperscale AI infrastructure expansion. It said AMD demonstrated a steady, compounding staircase, climbing 74.7% from $7.7 billion in Q4 2024 to $13.4 billion in Q3 2026. It said Dell saw an even sharper inflection in top-line growth across calendar 2026 as its massive AI server backlog converted into shipments. It said tracking revenue helps investors measure a company's ability to generate baseline sales before accounting for expenses.

The article said AMD makes computer processors and graphics chips, and Dell makes personal computers, servers and storage solutions. It said Dell had significantly higher revenue than AMD in the last two years. It said both AMD and Dell experienced year-over-year sales increases. It said AMD and Dell are seeing revenue growth accelerate in 2026. It said the revenue trends highlight the difference between a systems integrator such as Dell and AMD's fabless chip design approach.

The article said both companies are enjoying massive revenue boosts as the artificial intelligence boom accelerates in 2026. It said the data was sourced from Financial Modeling Prep as of Nov. 20, 2026. It said Robert Izquierdo has positions in Advanced Micro Devices, Dell Technologies and Meta Platforms. It said The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices and Meta Platforms. It said The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

stories.Headline: Wall Street advocates target Jensen Huang to establish government controlled AI
stories.Summary:
An operation targeted Jensen Huang and Nvidia around November 23, 2026, to control artificial intelligence development. The author claims this was a hit run by Wall Street advocates for government AI control. This effort allegedly aimed to eliminate open source and competitive frontier models in the United States. The operation used narrative engineering to tilt public opinion against the Nvidia founder and his company. This event is described as a clash between the founder mindset and the globalist financial class.

The controversy involves Megaspeed, a Singapore based front company run by Alice Huang to send chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that Nvidia removed Megaspeed from its sales list in August of 2025. Senator Tom Cotton expressed frustration that Commerce Secretary Lutnick ignored letters regarding the activities of this specific company. The author notes that fourteen months passed before the New York Times published an article about the matter. This delay is cited as evidence that the issue was used as a political tool.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the government will see if Megaspeed was a pass through for Chinese entities. Senator Tom Cotton stated that the Trump administration is finally coming around but must catalog the damage. The author claims that Wall Street seeks to retain historic systems of control through inverted fascism. This process involves multinationals telling the government which regulations are needed to maintain their status and power. The author argues that the World Economic Forum now seeks to control the era of super intelligence.

The author claims that Anthropic AI expressed interest in joining the big government and big multinational outlook. This company is allegedly pre selected as the winner because it favors a regulatory mechanism for competitive edge. Elon Musk and Jensen Huang are described as representing the Main Street perspective of innovators and patriots. The author asserts that the New York Times and Wall Street Journal assisted in dropping the narrative. These groups are affected by the shift toward a closed and proprietary mindset for AI development.

The author states that Jensen Huang provided American researchers and frontier labs with as much compute power as possible. This approach positioned Nvidia at the epicenter of United States compute power by distributing microchips widely. The text claims that Huang could have made more money by restricting the sales and distribution of chips. The author describes a post World War II shift where globalists retooled the relationship between government and corporations. This background suggests that the current AI race is being managed by the old guard.

The author claims that a singular model of government controlled AI is now underway for the year 2027. A new Big Government congress will reportedly make this control a priority during that upcoming calendar year. Some comments suggest that the Nvidia board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang after the initial attack occurred. It remains open whether the plan to eliminate open source models has failed or will face countermoves. The articles leave open if Main Street will remain a player against the Wall Street system.

stories.Headline: David-Russell urges Tubman University graduates to use AI for Liberia’s development
stories.Summary:
Dr. Elizabeth David-Russell challenged graduates to use innovation and emerging technologies to address development challenges during a keynote address on November 24, 2026. This event took place in Harper, Maryland County, during the commencement ceremony for the 2026 graduating class of William V.S. Tubman University. The former university president urged the students to move beyond their academic qualifications to improve their local communities and lives. She specifically encouraged the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence and other new technologies as tools for solving critical national problems. These challenges include the fight against diseases, the need for infrastructure development, and the ongoing struggle with national food insecurity.

The speaker requested that graduates use their professional skills to create practical solutions for Liberia rather than being passive consumers of technology. She called for agriculture graduates to help achieve rice self-sufficiency and for engineering graduates to address the country's various infrastructure challenges. Education graduates were urged to strengthen community learning, while business graduates were encouraged to provide support for local entrepreneurship efforts. Health sciences graduates should promote disease prevention, and Arts and Sciences graduates should advance research and preserve the cultural heritage of Liberia. These requirements for the graduates were delivered at the William V.S. Tubman University ceremony held in Harper, Maryland County.

Dr. David-Russell stated that the university's commitment to academic excellence must be reflected in professionalism, creativity, ethical leadership, and meaningful national service. She explained that true academic excellence requires the ability to apply knowledge and think critically rather than simply memorizing various pieces of information. The former president cautioned the graduates against compromising their integrity for the sake of personal gain, convenience, or gaining more popularity. She asked the graduates to consider if they would be proud of the person they see when looking into a mirror. She maintained that genuine success is measured by the positive impact individuals make on society instead of just professional achievements.

The graduates of William V.S. Tubman University are the primary people affected by these challenges to integrate technology into their careers. These students are expected to uphold the core values of their institution and become responsible professionals committed to the development of Liberia. The speaker urged them to make their professional decisions based on ethical principles and facts rather than personal interests or convenience. By applying their specific degrees, these new professionals are tasked with solving the diverse problems facing the people of Liberia. They are encouraged to use their education to produce practical results that will benefit their communities and the entire nation.

The articles note that Dr. David-Russell previously served as the president of William V.S. Tubman University during her professional tenure there. During her time as president, she worked to improve the technological infrastructure of the university through the implementation of internet connectivity. She also recalled her efforts to establish intranet systems and provide online academic services for the students and faculty of the institution. This background in technology informs her current challenge to the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence for the benefit of the country. Her previous leadership focused on enhancing the digital capabilities of the university to better prepare students for their future professional roles.

The graduates are now expected to enter their respective fields and apply the innovation and integrity that Dr. David-Russell described. They must now decide whether to become innovators or remain passive consumers of the emerging technologies available in the modern world. The articles do not state if the university has provided specific training in Artificial Intelligence to the 2026 graduating class. It remains open whether the graduates will successfully achieve rice self-sufficiency or solve the infrastructure challenges mentioned in the keynote address. The text does not mention any specific government policies that will support the graduates in implementing these technological solutions.

stories.Headline: Oyo governor's aide urges developers to use AI for governance and to include SMEs
stories.Summary:
Oladayo Ogunbowale, the Special Assistant on Communication to the Oyo State Governor, called on technology developers, innovators and digital entrepreneurs to use Artificial Intelligence to tackle governance challenges and promote economic inclusion. He made the call in a keynote address at the 2026 edition of DevFest Ibadan, held in Ibadan, the Oyo State capital. He spoke on the theme ‘Building the Future: How AI and Digital Innovation Can Transform Governance and Society.’ He urged developers to move beyond commercial products and build solutions that address challenges facing individuals, communities and public institutions. He said technology is a critical instrument for a more responsive, transparent and inclusive system of governance.

He said the Oyo State government was already laying the foundation for digital transformation, citing internally generated revenue of N103 billion in 2025, which he said exceeded the combined revenue of the two preceding administrations. He attributed that to strategic deployment of science, data and technology in government operations, particularly in plugging financial loopholes, reducing fraud and improving revenue in lands and housing. He said the state’s experience shows technology can improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen financial management. He said the ultimate objective of technological advancement should be more accessible government services, greater accountability in public resources and economic opportunities for a wider section of society. He identified small and medium-sized enterprises as the bedrock of Oyo State’s economy and said digital transformation would remain incomplete if SMEs were excluded.

He said that if AI serves only big business and government while SMEs are left on the far side of the digital divide, then digital transformation is a half-finished product. He said Nigeria must move from being a consumer to a creator of technology and must become creators of intelligence rooted in the country’s reality. He said that if the country relies only on foreign AI models, they will not understand its nuances, culture and people. He said the country needs an AI that understands the meaning of words such as ‘akwa,’ ‘ekaabo’ and ‘sannu’ and not just translates them. He said this year’s DevFest theme, ‘Building Safe, Secure, and Scalable Solutions with AI and Cloud,’ captured the technical pulse of the moment with precision.

The Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Kakanfo Inn and Conference Centre, Adedamola Are, said he was delighted to co-host DevFEST 2026 and that the facility hosted the 2026 edition on 21 November 2026. He said the emphasis was on AI and machine learning, agentic AI, Google Cloud, Flutter, Web3, distributed systems, product design, data privacy and tech community and mental health discussions. He said the primary goal of DevFest is to educate developers, builders and tech enthusiasts on Google’s latest technologies while fostering community-driven learning and local networking. The Lead Organiser of GDG Ibadan, Abidemi Tiamiyu, said the team volunteers with Google Developer Group Ibadan, which organises DevFEST Ibadan, to equip young people with skills. He said speakers came from Accra in Ghana, Lagos, Ado-Ekiti and other parts of the world, and that DevFEST has a presence in Accra, Nairobi, Lagos, Ibadan and Ogbomoso.

Tiamiyu said DevFEST recorded 2,500 participants in 2025 and about 3,000 participants at the 2026 DevFEST, and that the crowd was far larger than in 2025. He said the organisers were targeting over 3,000 attendees for the 2026 festival and that training programmes provided by DevFEST for over a decade have helped many youths gain skills to earn a living. The Co-Lead of GDG Ibadan, Joshua Olajide, said one major objective of DevFest was to transform participants from ordinary consumers of technology into independent product builders. He said advancements in AI were making it possible for individuals to develop websites, create graphics and build digital products without depending on external professionals for every task. The Co-Lead Organiser of GDG Ibadan and software engineer at Resilience17, Joshua Odejide, said the programme had equipped many participants with website development capabilities and other digital skills to become self-reliant. He said tasks such as designing graphic flyers could now be completed within seconds using AI tools.

The Developer Ecosystem Programme Manager at Google, Sodiq Akinjobi, said developers, engineers, programme managers and product managers are currently building for Nigeria’s markets. He said they are building their apps in Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo, not just in English, so that information, instruction and technology can reach everyone whether learned or not. He said user research was making it easier to apply these technologies in day-to-day activities. He commended the government for implementing initiatives from secondary schools aimed at utilising new technologies and taking advantage of AI opportunities. He said many participants in the conference hall were within the 22 to 25 age bracket and that he had spoken to a lady building prototypes in robotics for healthcare.

The event was organised by the Ibadan Google Developer Groups in collaboration with Kakanfo Inn and Conference Centre and took place at the facility in Ibadan at the weekend, attracting about 3,000 young people from across Nigeria and beyond. It was the seventh annual Google Developer Groups event. It featured panellists including the Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Zeeh Africa, David Adeleke, investor and community builder Michael Toyinbo, the Director of Expansion, Strategy and Operations at Chowdeck, the Founder of Prine, Gbolahan Alli, and the Developer Relations Lead at ALATPay, Haastrup Adegoke, among other dignitaries. Tiamiyu said many participants were already showing interest in how to use AI to drive products and services. He said taking that away from the event was 100 per cent valuable for anyone.

The articles do not state what specific AI solutions, if any, were commissioned or adopted at the event, nor do they give a date for any follow-up. They do not say whether the Oyo State government made any commitment or announcement in response to the call. They leave open how the target of over 3,000 attendees was set against the figure of about 3,000 participants reported at the 2026 event. They do not say what the 2025 revenue figure of N103 billion will be measured against in future years. They do not state any outcome from the panel discussions or any plan to repeat the SME focus at later DevFest editions.

stories.Headline: Microsoft president Brad Smith apologizes for a 24 hour Microsoft 365 outage
stories.Summary:
Microsoft President Brad Smith apologized for a global outage that affected Microsoft 365 customers on November 12. The disruption lasted for nearly 24 hours and prevented many users from accessing their Outlook mailboxes or sending emails. It also impacted the ability of users to utilize certain features within Teams and Copilot. This event occurred because of a combination of software updates and shifts in network traffic.

The company identified a Windows defect in servers managing connections to the Exchange Online email service as the root cause. This specific defect had remained undetected since July and interacted with a new update and software updated four months prior. To address the failure, Microsoft has already implemented nine corrective steps and plans to introduce 13 additional measures. These changes aim to prevent future recurrences of the technical issues that caused the widespread service failure.

Brad Smith explained in a November 22 interview on CBS's Face the Nation that the event was a perfect storm. He clarified that the outage was not the result of a cyberattack and was not linked to artificial intelligence. Smith noted that AI has accelerated the discovery of code vulnerabilities, which leads to faster patching cycles. He suggested that rapid patching on older infrastructure can increase the risk of errors because there is less time for testing.

Smith urged organizations to upgrade their legacy infrastructure and enhance their current patching practices to avoid similar errors. He also advised individuals to apply software patches promptly to maintain the security and stability of their systems. Furthermore, he stressed the need for concerted action between the tech sector and the government. He specifically called for improved sharing of threat intelligence to better protect global digital infrastructure.
