stories.Headline: Meta rolls out Muse direct messaging on Instagram in five countries
stories.Summary:
Meta began rolling out the ability to direct message its Muse AI agent on Instagram on November 24, 2026, according to The Verge. In a video, Meta showed how a user can ask Muse to help plan a trip based on things the user has saved on Instagram. The feature started rolling out that day on mobile in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Japan and Singapore, TechCrunch reported. Jay Peters wrote the Verge story, which was posted at 5:20 PM UTC.

The Instagram messaging feature is part of a wider Muse rollout that includes the United Kingdom, where Meta announced availability of the personal AI agent for adults the day before, 9to5Mac reported. Meta describes Muse as a helping hand for jobs that pile up, such as chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To do those jobs, users can connect Muse to apps they already use, from email and calendar to retailer apps they shop on. Meta says Muse only works with apps and services a user chooses to connect, and that before it sends an email or buys something it shows exactly what it is about to do and waits for approval. A separate security agent checks Muse's actions and the information it sends against the permissions granted, and users can choose in Settings how often it checks in.

The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum, a forum representing four UK regulatory bodies, warned last month about potential dangers of AI agents, saying they may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. The forum said questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection, including fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information, must be addressed so innovation earns and maintains public trust. Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse accessed personal data without permission, insisting users are in control and must approve important actions. The company admitted to some isolated incidents but said other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app during testing.

At the time of writing, Muse remained the second most popular free app in Apple's US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads, 9to5Mac reported. The outlet also reported the day before that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

stories.Headline: UConn faculty discuss teaching AI agility and critical thinking at economic forum
stories.Summary:
A panel of UConn faculty discussed teaching artificial intelligence at the third annual Economic Impact forum on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. The forum was held at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford. David Bergman, associate dean for faculty and research in the UConn School of Business, moderated the panel. The panelists were Amit Savkar, professor in residence of mathematics, Arash Zaghi, professor of civil and environmental engineering, Kun Chen, professor of statistics, and Molly Land, associate dean of academic affairs at the UConn School of Law. The event focused on AI and how UConn and the state can adapt and collaborate to maximize Connecticut's potential for growth.

The forum aligned with UConn's "AI for ImpaCT" initiative, launched in June under Provost Pamir Alpay. The initiative focuses on advancing artificial intelligence best practices across education, research, innovation, public engagement, and workforce development. Bergman was appointed the provost's special advisor on artificial intelligence as part of the effort. He now chairs an AI Council comprised of faculty, staff, and student stakeholders. The panel also featured faculty from the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, College of Engineering, and School of Law.

Bergman said views on intelligence continue to evolve, from high IQ to emotional quotient, and now a third "q" must be considered. He called it AQ, standing for "agility" or "adaptability" quotient, and attributed the term to author Liz Tran. He said faculty should instill in students the need to move quickly and be agile with technology, ideas, and learning. Land said AI and quantum technology are developing so quickly that graduates must be ready to use these technologies and keep up as they develop. Savkar said that if faculty who are supposedly subject matter experts are struggling with questions of ethics, fluency, and AI literacy, students face great uncertainty.

Zaghi said AI could be a tool for fixing pressing issues in society and described it as an equalizer. He said students at UConn Waterbury are engaged in several AI-related programs that expand skillsets and align with the AI for ImpaCT initiative. He said the university is a designated Minority-Serving-Institution and those skills are key for overcoming achievement and poverty gaps. He warned that if AI is not framed correctly, it will further expand socioeconomic gaps rather than close them. Chen said students need critical thinking skills, the most important thing in the age of AI, because AI can help master technical material quickly but critical thinking remains most important.

The panelists agreed that skills machines cannot replicate should be reinforced in the classroom. The session offered a glimpse into how professors are building curriculum and establishing guidelines around responsible AI use. Faculty are considering how to prepare students for careers that will require learning new technology at breakneck pace and applying it to all fields of study and work. The forum was the third annual Economic Impact forum and focused on AI. The discussion covered different approaches to teaching artificial intelligence and the responsibilities of students and professors.

stories.Headline: Meta gives 49ers suite and club members free AI glasses in sponsorship deal
stories.Summary:
The San Francisco 49ers and Meta announced a landmark multi-year partnership on November 24, 2026, naming Meta the Official Moment Maker of the NFL franchise. The partnership unites two Bay Area-born organizations for the future of the sports fan experience. Headlining the deal, the 49ers and Meta plan to gift all 49ers suite partners and club season ticket members a free pair of Oakley Meta HSTN AI glasses. The giveaway celebrates the 49ers 80th anniversary, and more than 4,700 members will receive the glasses directly to their homes. The 49ers signed Silicon Valley neighbor Meta to a sponsorship described by the parties as a landmark multiyear partnership emphasizing the company's high-end version of its AI glasses.

The newly created category for Meta is official moment maker of the 49ers, and the signature activation at launch is the giveaway of Oakley Meta HSTN glasses to more than 4,700 suite holders and club season ticket holders. Oakley, an NFL sponsor, typically sells the product for $399 or more. Meta's WhatsApp messenger app will become the official instant messenger provider of the 49ers, intended to support the team's global marketing efforts in the U.K., UAE and Mexico in the NFL's global markets program. Meta will be the presenting sponsor of the 49ers' military Salute to Service campaign, with a dedicated focus on blind and low-vision veterans, and Meta will receive digital signage at Levi's Stadium in the deal. Financial terms were not disclosed, and the team negotiated the deal with Meta directly.

Brent Schoeb, 49ers Chief Operating Officer, said innovation and technology are part of the franchise's DNA, from the West Coast offense to Levi's Stadium to the future of the fan experience. Schoeb said Meta has been at the forefront of technology for a long time, and that paired with being Silicon Valley neighbors made this partnership a perfect fit. He said the team is thrilled to continue providing members with exclusive benefits and looks forward to seeing the content they create with Meta's AI glasses. Andrew Bosworth, Chief Technology Officer at Meta, said game day is about being in the moment from the tailgate to victory and the best way to capture it all is handsfree with Oakley Meta glasses. Bosworth said he is a lifelong member of the 49ers Faithful and is fired up that Meta is now an official partner and will help connect fans to the team they love.

Oakley Meta HSTN AI glasses allow fans to capture their fan experience through photos and videos hands-free, listen to music, and get help from Meta AI, all while staying in the moment. Meta has joined the 49ers global marketing efforts in the UK, UAE, and Mexico as part of the NFL's Global Markets Program. Over the next several years, Meta will support the team's mission to reach new fans, grow the game of American football, and leave a lasting impact on international communities. This season, 49ers fans can look forward to seeing 49ers FB Kyle Juszczyk sport Meta AI glasses as a brand ambassador in a new campaign. Meta has signed Juszczyk as a brand ambassador to support the sponsorship, and Meta's current sports sponsorship portfolio includes the UFC and Arsenal F.C.

Meta and the 49ers plan to explore additional opportunities to integrate technology and AI across the organization. The partnership is built on a shared commitment to innovate and create meaningful memories for life. WhatsApp, owned by Meta, has been named the Official Instant Messenger Provider of the 49ers as a first step, enabling fast and efficient communication globally for the team. The giveaway gives more than 4,700 members a first-of-its-kind VIP experience with Meta's next-gen technology. The 49ers and Meta announced the partnership on November 24, 2026, and the Sports Business Journal reported it on November 23, 2026.

For more information, the articles direct readers to visit 49ers.com. The articles leave open the financial terms of the deal, which were not disclosed. stories.Headline: Cloudera launches a digital sovereignty package with Mistral AI models for governed data and AI
stories.Summary:
Cloudera Inc. announced a digital sovereignty package on November 24, 2026, which it said enables organizations to keep control of their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure wherever workloads run. The announcement was dated 06:00 UTC by SiliconANGLE and carried by GlobeNewswire from San Jose, California, and Madrid. Cloudera said the offering combines its Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral AI SAS. Cloudera recently partnered with Mistral, and the integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments with no connection to external networks. Cloudera described the package as a comprehensive solution and partner ecosystem designed to give organizations jurisdictional, operational and technical control across their data, cloud and AI lifecycle.

The solution provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments, according to Cloudera. Cloudera said these capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union's AI Act, the Digital Operational Resilience Act and the Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations. The Manila Times report said the solution supports compliance readiness for the EU AI Act, DORA, CADA, NIS2, the Seals Sovereignty Framework and others globally. Cloudera said governance policies also extend to enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use, and that Mistral's open-weight models can run alongside governed data so organizations can customize models locally and run agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information. Cloudera said its modular hybrid cloud architecture lets users shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data, and that organizations can apply sovereignty controls selectively to sensitive workloads.

Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said enterprises need to know their data, models and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change. Gago said digital sovereignty has to be an architectural decision rather than a compliance exercise after the fact. He said Cloudera is giving organizations a foundation they can build on for the long term so they can adopt the next generation of AI without rethinking their sovereignty strategy each time the technology evolves. Gago said AI is becoming more autonomous and embedded in critical operations. Cloudera said the solution is built on open standards and an open source foundation and allows organizations to determine where individual workloads run and adapt without forced data migrations or proprietary lock-in.

Moor Insights & Strategy Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. Moorhead said a company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on. He said walling off sensitive workloads is not the answer because it makes data and AI harder to manage, and he called extending Cloudera's hybrid data management to open-weight models across sovereign, on-prem and public cloud a logical step. Moorhead said the next step is how quickly customers get the offering into production. Cloudera said regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements rank among the top three barriers to scaling AI, and the offering is aimed at organizations facing those requirements.

McKinsey & Co. reported last year that 71% of executives it surveyed called sovereign AI an existential concern or a strategic imperative, according to SiliconANGLE. Cloudera said its own research found regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements among the top three barriers to scaling AI. Cloudera said digital sovereignty is becoming more pressing as enterprises move beyond managing data residency to ensuring the AI models and infrastructure they depend on remain under their control. Cloudera said it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. Cloudera said it is initially targeting Europe.

Cloudera plans to expand its sovereign partner ecosystem into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions globally after its initial focus on Europe. Cloudera said customers can combine sovereign deployments with other cloud and on-premises infrastructure and apply strict sovereignty controls where required without forcing the rest of their data estate into the same architecture or creating isolated security boundaries. The articles did not say when the offering becomes generally available or how it is priced. The articles did not name the sovereign cloud providers or implementation partners in the network. The articles did not say which specific Mistral models are integrated.

stories.Headline: Netflix retrofits its development lifecycle to let AI agents and engineers ship code together safely
stories.Summary:
Netflix's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle to integrate AI coding agents alongside human engineers, Mark Khuzam reported at QCon San Francisco 2026. Khuzam, a senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the team enabled agents and engineers to ship code together safely. The initiative focused on documentation, consistency, and review rather than on the agents themselves. The team found that agents promised speed but existing systems were built for human developers. An initial attempt to have an agent migrate tests required four tries due to inadequate instructions and a limited context window.

The effort produced 45 Architecture Decision Records, each written for both human engineers and AI agents. Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern, an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. These records link to related documentation and code, and they now ship inside almost every repository. An AGENTS.md file in each project acts as a robots.txt for coding agents, keeping more than 300 other documents findable. The CI pipeline remains deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues, and canaries.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency, and review. He described the fix as context engineering, getting what engineers know into what agents see. The team wrote the 45 architecture decision records to translate engineers' knowledge into a format accessible to AI agents. Khuzam noted that the team borrowed from how search engines read a site when implementing the AGENTS.md file. He closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters.

A review agent now pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns, and looks at what depends on the change. Its first version left 23 comments on a single pull request, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix, and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same pull request.

Changes are not yet auto-merged, and human engineers retain ownership of the code. Netflix reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service. Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web, and TV.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3 before the changes. The team faced challenges with inconsistent documentation across the codebase, because tests were not written the same way everywhere. Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The team saw a 32 percent increase in pull requests year over year, and developer Net Promoter Score improved from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

For cross-service work, the team adopted GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs. Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot, and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line. Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session.

stories.Headline: Galveston police adopt Veritone Investigate AI to speed active and cold case work
stories.Summary:
The Galveston Police Department announced in a November 19 news release that it will begin using an artificial intelligence platform called Veritone Investigate to help move active and long-running cold case investigations along more efficiently, according to Houston Public Media. The Galveston City Council approved the use of the AI-powered tools in a 5-0 vote at a council meeting on November 12. The service package with Veritone runs for one year and costs approximately $75,000, according to city documents. The California-based company Veritone works with about 450 agencies across the U.S. for public safety, most of which are in California, and CEO and President Ryan Steelberg said the partnership with Galveston is one of the company's first entry points into Texas.

Steelberg said police departments are struggling to manage increasing volumes of digital evidence, which makes it harder to find information that moves cases forward. He said the investigative tool would help agencies process audio, video, images and documents and make the material searchable, and would also use AI-driven tools to get information relevant to an investigation. He said the AI is not trying to solve the case for the department but is trying to organize the data. Galveston Police Chief Doug Balli said that entering just one case into Veritone would save the average investigator hundreds of man-hours in reviewing information and generating leads, and that investigators need technology that helps them move from evidence to insight quickly, especially when they are working both active and cold cases. Balli did not respond to Houston Public Media's request for comment about the new technology.

Steelberg said the information used with Veritone Investigate will be safeguarded like any other investigation and that the process for public records requests will not change. He said nothing will change in terms of the controls, audit logging and jurisdiction, and that the purpose is for data to go into a secure environment where the AI models that are invoked are containerized and secure. The department's decision comes alongside heavy scrutiny from residents around Harris and Galveston counties who have expressed privacy concerns about Flock Safety cameras, which use AI technology to automatically read license plates, especially in light of Houston-area cases of alleged misuse by law enforcement. It also comes around the same time that Harris County officials decided to pull a no-bid contract for a controversial AI facial recognition technology, Clearview AI, from a commissioners court meeting agenda.

stories.Headline: Lumexa Imaging appoints Ayis Pyrros as chief clinical AI officer
stories.Summary:
Lumexa Imaging announced on November 23, 2026, that it had appointed Ayis Pyrros, MD, as its Chief Clinical Artificial Intelligence Officer, according to a company release issued from Raleigh, North Carolina. The company, which trades on Nasdaq under the symbol LMRI, described itself in the release as one of the nation's largest providers of outpatient imaging services. Dr. Pyrros brings extensive expertise in radiology, clinical informatics and artificial intelligence to the role, the release said. In the position he will lead the evaluation and deployment of third-party AI technologies while identifying opportunities to develop targeted solutions internally, the company said.

His work will focus on integrating clinical AI into workflows to help improve radiologist efficiency and support high-quality patient care, according to the announcement. The release said Dr. Pyrros is widely recognized for his pioneering research at the intersection of medical imaging and AI, and that he brings more than 15 years of clinical radiology experience along with an extensive background in artificial intelligence research and development. It said he is board-certified in diagnostic radiology, neuroradiology and clinical informatics. In addition to leading Lumexa's clinical AI strategy, he will practice as a radiologist with Connexia, the company's teleradiology practice, and he is scheduled to deliver a keynote presentation and take part in multiple scientific sessions at the 2026 Radiological Society of North America Annual Meeting.

Caitlin Zulla, Chief Executive Officer of Lumexa Imaging, said artificial intelligence has tremendous potential to transform medical imaging and that the company's capital-light, best-of-breed approach positions it to capture that opportunity. She said Dr. Pyrros brings a rare combination of clinical expertise and hands-on experience developing AI solutions for radiology. According to Zulla, his leadership will help the company accelerate the adoption of clinical AI innovation across its platform and enable greater operational efficiency as it scales. Dr. Pyrros said Lumexa has built a strong foundation for innovation through its commitment to clinical excellence and its differentiated approach to technology, and he said he was excited to work alongside the company's radiologists and technology partners to bring meaningful AI solutions into everyday clinical practice, allowing physicians to focus more of their time on delivering high-quality patient care.

The release said Lumexa Imaging is a nationwide provider of outpatient medical imaging with over 5,000 team members and approximately 190 outpatient imaging centers, and that its team conducted approximately 4 million outpatient procedures system-wide in 2025. It described the company as a partner of choice for health systems and radiologists, delivering what it called best-in-class clinical excellence, operations and state-of-the-art technology across its platform. The announcement listed Melissa Weston as media contact and Sue Dooley as investor relations contact. The articles did not say when Dr. Pyrros would begin the role or what happens next beyond his scheduled appearances at the 2026 RSNA Annual Meeting.

stories.Headline: Lenders pull back as investors fear an AI bubble after massive tech spending leads to market declines
stories.Summary:
Large tech companies led a massive investment boom in artificial intelligence that may be the largest in United States history. This surge in spending occurred over the four years following the release of the generative model called ChatGPT by OpenAI. Firms like Amazon and Alphabet spent hundreds of billions of dollars on hardware, software, and data centers to power models. However, investors became spooked in November 2026, causing stocks to tumble due to rising debt and softening revenues. This market decline followed Democratic gains in the midterms and an alleged Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive.

The five largest hyperscalers, including Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, estimate spending over 800 billion dollars on infrastructure this year. This figure represents a 94 percent increase over 2025, while Brookings Institution projects investments exceeding 10 trillion dollars by 2032. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft borrowed 214 billion dollars in 2026, compared to 83 billion dollars for all of 2025. Sona identified 176 circular financing deals worth 3.6 trillion dollars, while Anthropic raised 81.3 billion dollars in an offering. Nvidia lost 1.7 trillion dollars in market value in early November before the board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on November 23.

Rebecca Patterson stated that frontier AI labs use a whatever it takes approach to spending to win the AI race. She noted that financial markets are growing skeptical as the cost of debt rises for many AI related firms. Roger Ferguson said it is too early to declare the boom will burst, but some companies may go under. Vinh Nguyen claimed that long term growth from the diffusion of these technologies will take five to eight years. He also warned that Chinese AI models have effectively closed the performance gap with their United States counterparts.

Investors are concerned about increased government regulation and restrictions on AI, which led them to sell off various tech stocks. Lower income households have not benefited from the stock market rally and still struggle with high inflation and energy prices. McKinsey suggests that AI could displace between six million and sixteen million American workers over the next ten years. Lenders are now pulling back, with Dutch lender ING putting about 500 million dollars in data center loans for sale. Banks like Barclays and HSBC are transferring loan risks to insurers to avoid holding bad debt from the frenzy.

The AI boom has fueled an economic rally where U.S. stock portfolios roughly doubled in value since the year 2022. Goldman Sachs reported that the ten largest AI stocks in the S&P 500 drove about 50 percent of index gains. Bloomberg estimates that growth in 2025 would have been 3.1 percent without subtracting the value of imported AI equipment. Economist estimates suggest the build out created one million U.S. jobs and spurred construction in a struggling sector. However, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta all posted negative free cash flow in their third quarter earnings reports.

President Donald Trump has moved to roll back federal regulations on land use to accelerate the deployment of AI technology. Future growth depends on accessing key inputs, as 90 percent of chips and servers originated in East Asia in 2025. Constraints include a lack of skilled labor and backlogs of two to ten years for importing advanced power equipment. It remains unclear if the recent market slump is the beginning of a larger downturn or just a blip. Experts leave open whether demand for AI will keep up with the massive amounts of money being invested.

stories.Headline: Nocera invests 22 million dollars for a 44 percent stake in Canadian AI data center developer BitRock
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese AI infrastructure firm Nocera entered a binding letter of intent to invest in Canadian developer BitRock on November 19, 2026. The company will pay 22 million dollars in cash for newly issued shares of the Calgary based developer. This transaction will grant Nocera an approximately 44 percent stake in the AI data center developer. The deal was announced publicly on November 23 and November 24, 2026. Nocera intends to use this investment to enter the North American compute market.

The investment is based on a pre-money valuation of 28 million dollars and a post-money valuation of 50 million dollars. Nocera will gain the right to appoint directors, receive financial reports, and participate in major decisions. Funds will build a 10MW facility on 37 acres near Hanna, Alberta, using four 2.5MW prefabricated computing modules. BitRock targets a power usage effectiveness of 1.225 with N+1 redundancy and an uninterruptible power supply. The long-term plan is to grow the campus to 200MW in 10MW modular segments.

Andrew Teng, the Asia director of Nocera, stated that power is the scarce asset in AI infrastructure. He said BitRock is built around its own power, which makes it an attractive investment for the company. Teng described the investment as a measured entry into North American compute with a meaningful ownership position. Nocera believes that grid connections in North America can take years to secure and approvals are harder to win. The company claims that BitRock's self-powered model allows it to bypass these long waits for grid connections.

BitRock will operate on a colocation model where customers install their own equipment in powered data hall space. The developer claims that customers have already signed memoranda of understanding for these computing power hosting services. BitRock is responsible for the day to day operations and the construction management of the Alberta campus. The facility will use on-site natural gas generation to provide its own electricity for the compute load. Alberta's cold climate is expected to reduce the amount of water and energy needed for cooling.

Nocera has been assembling an AI platform since June 2026 through several different infrastructure and energy agreements. In June, the firm formed a venture platform agreement with the US based developer Digital Innovations Group. Nocera announced an agreement to acquire an equity interest in the UK based company INERGX in July. The company also acquired a 30 percent controlling interest in the Taiwanese memory distributor QMAX Technology in July. These deals cover AI software, power, memory, and now self-powered data center capacity for the firm.

The parties have committed to execute a definitive investment agreement as soon as it is practicable to do so. Funding is subject to the completion of due diligence and the receipt of required corporate and regulatory approvals. The letter of intent has a 60 day term that can be extended by 30 days by mutual consent. The articles leave open whether the definitive agreement will be signed on the described terms or at all. It remains uncertain if the customer memoranda of understanding will result in binding contracts for the facility.

stories.Headline: European tech stocks lead a market rebound as the Stoxx 600 rises 0.73 per cent after an AI-driven sell-off
stories.Summary:
European shares recovered on Monday, November 23, 2026, as technology stocks led a market rebound. This recovery followed a sharp artificial intelligence sell-off that caused the steepest weekly decline since late March 2025. The Stoxx 600 index rose 0.73 per cent to 630.24 points by 0933 GMT after five straight sessions of losses. This movement put the index on track for its largest one-day jump since November 9.

The technology index outperformed other sectors with a 2 per cent rise after its worst weekly fall since March 2020. Chip-linked companies including ASML, ASM International, and BE Semiconductor each saw gains between 3 per cent and 5 per cent. Defence stocks advanced 1.8 per cent, while miners surged 1.4 per cent as gold prices recovered from 14-month lows. Abivax jumped 10 per cent after rejecting a short-seller report, and Drax rallied over 7 per cent on profit forecasts.

Kathleen Brooks, the research director for the UK at brokerage XTB, said the previous sell-off established a new era for artificial intelligence. She noted that investors will now provide more scrutiny, though a pullback was expected because the sell-off went beyond just AI pricing. Brooks warned that the current recovery could be a dead cat bounce if investor sentiment remains sour. She mentioned that demand had not changed despite the weakening appetite for artificial intelligence risk.

The market volatility occurred as investors doubted whether massive technology investments would generate returns quickly enough. Concerns grew that valuations had raced ahead of near-term returns, especially after the debut of Anthropic. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron suggested reviving a 2011 proposal for a constitutional golden rule to limit public finances. This move aims to reassure investors amid rising debt and a deeper downturn in the French economy.

stories.Headline: Micron lowers experience requirements to recruit South Korean semiconductor engineers for overseas roles
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology is holding on-site hiring for new graduates and experienced engineers at COEX in Seoul from November 23 to 29. The company is conducting recruitment briefings and interviews to secure South Korean semiconductor engineers during this specific time period. New graduates and applicants with under two years of experience are interviewing from November 23 through November 25. Those with five or more years of experience in semiconductors and related fields interview from November 27 to 29. This large-scale drive takes place in the home turf of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

The company lowered its experience requirement for experienced candidates from eight years to five years to broaden the applicant pool. Micron moved its South Korean hiring schedule up by one month from its usual December timing to November. Hires will be assigned to production and research bases in Taiwan, Singapore, and Japan rather than in South Korea. Roles include HBM advanced packaging, design, quality, and fab processes, including process integration, equipment, and metrology. Japan bases in Tokyo and Kanagawa specifically target Principal Design Engineer positions in 3D stacked memory and ultra-high-speed memory interfaces.

A Micron official stated that the company has large demand for foreign talent and operates programs for local settlement. This official added that there are many opportunities to grow capabilities while collaborating with colleagues around the world. An industry official said South Korean companies must find ways to secure new talent and prevent core personnel outflows. The industry views these changes as an intent to preemptively secure outstanding domestic talent ahead of rival companies. These moves are seen as a way to secure top engineers by advancing the hiring period.

Samsung Electronics began hiring Level 5 equipment and infrastructure engineers for its Device Solutions division in mid-November. SK Hynix has recruited HBM circuit design, engineering, and NAND design talent since October through its Talented Highway brand. SanDisk has also opened a recruitment page for South Korea-based positions ranging from interns to those with five years experience. Industry observers say a large exodus of personnel overseas could deepen labor shortages at smaller South Korean semiconductor companies. Conversely, some say individual engineers now have more options to build English-language work experience and global supply chain expertise.

Micron started its approach to South Korean talent with campus information sessions at major domestic universities in late 2024. The company then moved its recruitment stage to a large exhibition hall this year to conduct direct interviews. The memory industry is currently mass-producing sixth-generation HBM4 and focusing on the development of seventh-generation HBM4E. Securing skilled technical personnel to boost performance and yield of next-generation products has emerged as a core task. The race for talent among the three major memory makers is intensifying as the industry enters a generational shift.

Competition for top South Korean talent is expected to intensify further because the key roles recruited by the companies overlap. The companies are fighting to secure skilled personnel to improve the performance and yield of next-generation memory products. Micron continues to target STEM bachelor, master, and doctoral degree candidates for its various overseas production and research bases. The articles leave open how South Korean companies will successfully prevent the leak of their core personnel to overseas rivals. It remains to be seen if the labor shortages at mid-sized South Korean firms will actually deepen over time.

stories.Headline: Intel draws AI stock screen attention as its chips power model workloads
stories.Summary:
Intel was named in an article on undervalued AI stocks published by Simply Wall St on Yahoo Finance on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. The article was written by Al Bentley and appeared at 4:19 PM CST. Intel was picked for the article's AI screener because its chips and data center hardware sit behind many large language model workloads. The article said an analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St covers how Intel's rebuild around AI and foundry services is expected to play out. The article said Jensen Huang's rapid return to Nvidia and a sharp rebound in chip shares reminded markets that AI is still the main story driving big money flows.

The article said Intel's client computing and physical AI group generated about US$32.9b in recent revenue. It said Intel's Data Center and AI segment generated about US$23.4b. It said Intel Foundry generated about US$22.4b. It said Intel has a roughly US$272.6b market cap. The article said the full screen surfaced 146 more companies not broken out in the article.

The article quoted a statement that Intel plans to strengthen customer trust in its foundry services by ensuring reliability and customer service. The statement said this could potentially lead to an increase in foundry revenue as the company builds its reputation and customer base. The article said what really moves the needle for Intel from here is how one still unresolved shift in AI related demand shapes future margins and cash generation. It said readers could read the full narrative for Intel to see how AI demand, foundry scale and capital intensity could reshape Intel's long term cash machine. The article listed NasdaqGS:INTC earnings and revenue growth as at Nov 2026.

The article said the three undervalued AI stocks covered were just a sample. It said the article was general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It said the articles are not intended to be financial advice and do not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. It said Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned. It said readers with feedback or concerns about the content could get in touch directly or email editorial-team@simplywallst.com.

The article said Intel is a global chip designer and manufacturer. It said Intel's diversified AI linked profile sits on top of its three reported segments. It said the article highlights three undervalued AI stocks across chips, software, and cloud. It said investors start hunting for quality businesses not yet fully priced for the AI theme when capital swings back toward the picks and shovels of the ChatGPT and AI boom. It said readers could go straight to the source and analyze and identify potential high conviction ideas inside the Undervalued Artificial Intelligence/ AI Stocks screener.

The article said the full narrative for Intel maps how AI demand, foundry scale and capital intensity could reshape Intel's long term cash machine. It left open how the unresolved shift in AI related demand will shape Intel's future margins and cash generation. It did not give the outcome of that margin puzzle. It did not say when Intel's foundry revenue might increase. It did not give a date for the analyst consensus Narrative beyond Nov 2026.

stories.Headline: LegalZoom executives meet investors at UBS AI conference on December 1
stories.Summary:
LegalZoom announced on November 24, 2026, that two of its executives will take part in the UBS Global Technology and AI Conference, according to a press release issued from Mountain View, California. The company said Noel Watson, its Chief Operating Officer and Chief Financial Officer, and Madeleine Crane, its Head of Investor Relations, will attend the event in Scottsdale, Arizona, on Tuesday, December 1, 2026. During the conference the two executives will host meetings with investors throughout the day, the release stated. LegalZoom described itself in the announcement as America's number one online legal services company and trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol LZ.

The announcement sets out how investors can arrange time with the company at the conference, which is the main practical change it describes. Investors who want to schedule one-on-one meetings were told to contact their UBS conference representative or to reach Investor Relations directly by email. The release gives no other dates, figures or terms connected to the event beyond the December 1 date and the Scottsdale location. It also does not say whether any part of LegalZoom's participation will be webcast or recorded for later viewing.

LegalZoom presented the conference appearance as part of its effort to keep investors informed, and the release includes background on the company's approach to legal work. It said LegalZoom combines intuitive technology with access to experienced attorneys, either through its independent attorney network or its own law firm. As AI reshapes how legal work gets done, the company said it is at the forefront of a human-in-the-loop approach, in which the speed and efficiency of AI are always backed by the judgment and accountability of qualified professionals. LegalZoom added that it has over two decades of experience and has served millions of customers.

The release places the conference appearance in the context of LegalZoom's broader business, which covers everything from business formation and compliance to intellectual property protection and ongoing legal management and support. It said the company's platform is meant to help individuals and small businesses navigate the legal system with confidence. The announcement did not say what the executives plan to discuss at the conference or what, if anything, will follow from the meetings. It directed anyone seeking more information to the company's website at www.legalzoom.com.

stories.Headline: Norwalk schools curb early-grade devices and YouTube after parent pressure
stories.Summary:
Norwalk Public Schools changed its technology use after parents pressed the district to curb screen time and limit artificial intelligence, the Stamford Advocate and the Norwalk Hour reported on Nov. 24, 2026. District leaders decided early in the school year to stop issuing one-to-one devices to students in grades K-2, the articles said. The district recently banned the use of YouTube on devices at all grade levels, according to the articles. The Norwalk Board of Education approved screen-free recess last month, the articles said. District officials are working on classroom screen time limits for each grade level, the articles said.

Parents at Marvin Elementary School and Nathan Hale Middle School will be able to join a pilot program giving them a dashboard showing how much time their children spend on school devices, the articles said. The program will eventually be rolled out to all schools, interim Superintendent Sandra Faioes said during a Board of Education meeting on Nov. 17, according to the articles. The district will work on AI regulations and update its policy on the technology with a target completion date of March, school board Chair Howard White said, the articles reported. Norwalk Public Schools shut off the embedded AI-Gemini feature in Google Chrome for grades K-8 last month, said Emily Morgan, communications and public relations lead for the district, the articles reported. The district received a $23,000 grant from EDSAFE AI Alliance before the parent letter, the articles said, and the grant is designed to help implement AI policies while protecting student data privacy.

Faioes and White thanked parents for taking part in a recent community forum on AI and screen time and credited parent input for leading to the changes, the articles reported. “We just want to create this meaningful dialogue,” Faioes said, according to the articles. Parent Brandon Buck, who sent a letter to the board in September signed by over 80 parents calling for a pause in AI use in elementary and middle schools, commended officials for responding to parent concerns, the articles said. “You committed to developing an intentional technology policy and you committed to establishing grade level limits on screen time,” Buck said, according to the articles. “Those commitments reflect real leadership and real partnership,” he said, the articles reported.

Kelly-Beth McNicholas, another parent who called for less AI and screen time, praised the district’s response, saying “Norwalk is headed in the right direction on this,” the articles reported. McNicholas still voiced concern about security and privacy issues, particularly with the use of Google, the articles said. The Norwalk parents are joining a growing wave of skepticism and opposition to AI in schools nationwide, the articles said. New York City announced it was banning “student-facing generative AI” and companion chatbots for students in prekindergarten through eighth grade this school year, the articles reported. The Los Angeles Unified School District enacted a moratorium on AI across all grade levels on district-issued devices for the current school year, the articles said.

Across Connecticut, a growing number of parents are sounding the alarm about what they call excessive screen time for their children at school and on school-issued devices, the articles said. The state Board of Education passed guidelines this August calling on all Connecticut school districts to create screen time and technology use policies, the articles reported. The guidelines also call into question the efficacy of technology-based learning, saying educational technology has not produced the widespread gains in academic achievement once anticipated, the articles said. Research from the American Academy of Pediatrics has linked excessive screen time to mental health issues such as increased anxiety and depression, as well as lower academic performance and poor physical health, the articles said. Other studies, including one published by Yale University this year, concluded that the quality of screen time for students may be more important than the quantity, the articles said.

The dashboard pilot will eventually be rolled out to all schools, the articles said. The district will be working on AI regulations and updating its policy related to the technology with a target completion date of March, White said, the articles reported. District officials are working on classroom screen time limits for each grade level, the articles said. The articles did not say when the dashboard pilot begins or which grades the screen time limits will cover. The articles did not say what the AI regulations will contain or what the updated policy will change.

stories.Headline: Scott Snyder outlines four AI trajectories to help business leaders plan for 2030
stories.Summary:
Scott Snyder, a senior fellow at the Wharton School, outlined four AI trajectories for business leaders. He published these scenarios on November 24, 2026, to help leaders plan for 2030. The work aims to help leaders navigate potential risks and rewards. Snyder used conversations with academic and industry experts to develop these views. He focuses on how important uncertainties may unfold over several years.

The scenarios depend on whether trust in AI is high or low. They also consider if AI progress is incremental or advances toward artificial general intelligence. One path sees AGI emerging from a diverse ecosystem of startups and universities. Another path involves a few companies and countries controlling expensive frontier capabilities. A third path describes a generative AI winter where promise exceeds practical impact.

Snyder says scenario planning helps leaders bound an uncertain future. He believes the goal is to be roughly right rather than precisely wrong. He suggests leaders identify forces across social, technological, economic, market, and political domains. He notes that more AI capability does not automatically translate into more trust. He advises separating value creating capabilities from hedges tied to specific outcomes.

Customers and employees are affected by these different potential futures. Some young workers might lose opportunities to develop expertise if displacement outpaces retraining. Customers may expect better experiences at lower costs in a positive AI future. Some employees might struggle with the transition to hybrid working models. Many Americans are currently more concerned than excited about AI technology.

Snyder notes that hyperscalers spent 227 billion dollars on AI infrastructure in Q3. He mentions that OpenAI and Anthropic agents recently compromised various secure systems. He points to EU transparency obligations with a December deadline for watermarking content. He observes that Chinese models account for nearly 70 percent of token consumption. He cites a McKinsey survey where 80 percent of respondents saw productivity improvements.

Leaders must now decide about investing in AI and reshaping their workforce. They need to transform business and operating models to win in 2030. Snyder suggests making no regret moves to build a foundation for transformation. The articles leave open whether the cost of frontier development will concentrate leadership. They do not state which of the four scenarios will actually occur.

stories.Headline: Stony Brook and OpenAI study how AI collaboration shapes human creativity
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University's AI Innovation Institute partnered with OpenAI to study how working with artificial intelligence affects human creativity, according to a Stony Brook news article dated November 24, 2026. The research was led by postdoctoral researcher Babak Hemmatian and AI Innovation Institute Director Lav Varshney. The work drew the attention of Ronnie Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist, and Rachel Brown, a former economic strategist at OpenAI. Through the partnership, OpenAI researchers gave insights on study design and provisioned frontier AI resource access to Stony Brook students in an equitable manner. OpenAI also offered significant credits for the research team to perform AI-driven data analysis, the article says.

Hemmatian said the team wanted to study how working with AI in a collaborative context changes the quality and originality of ideas people come up with. He asked where AI's place in the creative process is, whether it comes from the conversation, from the ideas the machine contributes, or from something the person does better because the machine is there. The article describes the effort as combining cutting-edge technology and rigorous empirical design. Varshney said that with AI advancing rapidly in industry, it is important for Stony Brook to remain at the frontier through direct engagement with leading companies. He said the university, as part of a global AI ecosystem, is developing a scientific basis for how AI can most effectively uplift human creativity.

He called that question poised to be the most important for teaching and learning in our age and a critical factor in how AI is best deployed in numerous societal contexts. The article says building such scientific evidence is crucial to designing the future of education and workforce development. The article says the two organizations are setting the stage for a new era of educational research that moves beyond anecdote and speculation. It says the aim is to establish scientific foundations for how humans and artificial intelligence can best think, learn and create together, focused especially on the human side of the equation. The article directs readers to the full story by Ankita Nagpal on the AI3 website.

stories.Headline: Dhireesha Kudithipudi joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing
stories.Summary:
Dhireesha Kudithipudi, founding director of the MATRIX AI Consortium at UT San Antonio, has been named a member of the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Next-Generation Computing. She is one of only 19 global experts selected to advise global leaders on emerging computing technologies. The appointment, reported by the university in late October 2026, recognizes her leadership in transdisciplinary research. The university says the role positions MATRIX as a contributor to international discussions on the next era of technology.

The Forum's Global Future Councils form a knowledge network of 37 thematic groups with more than 700 experts. Kudithipudi will serve alongside figures from IBM Research, SandboxAQ, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, UC Berkeley, the University of Toronto, Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation and the European Space Agency. The council's work feeds into its Next-Generation Computing Framework, released in October 2026 with the Forum, which guides governments and organizations on the technologies and strategic priorities shaping computing. Kudithipudi also received a special invitation to attend the Forum's Quantum Economy Day in Geneva, Switzerland, in October.

Kudithipudi's own research focuses on neuromorphic AI, artificial intelligence modeled on the brain, with an emphasis on reducing energy use. The article explains that conventional computing separates memory and processing, which contributes to the high energy demands of many AI models, while neuromorphic systems aim to learn and adapt at much lower energy cost. In January 2025 she was lead author of a review in Nature that brought together international experts to examine how neuromorphic computing might scale. She has said her work aligns with the council's concern that computing grow more powerful while staying sustainable and centered on human needs.

MATRIX has grown under her leadership into a network of nearly 90 scientists across three organizations, with expertise in engineering, neuroscience, ethics, medicine and computing. The consortium works on healthcare, energy, cybersecurity and smart cities, and Kudithipudi leads national research efforts. She serves as institutional lead for two Centers of Excellence and contributes to six in total. The university also launched THOR: The Neuromorphic Commons this year, which the article describes as the nation's first open-access hub for brain-inspired computing, funded by the National Science Foundation. The university says the appointment will expand its role in international discussions and create new collaborations.

stories.Headline: Stanford forum speakers urge early policy planning for AI economic disruption
stories.Summary:
The Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research held its Fall Policy Forum, titled “Economic Policy in the Age of AI,” on Nov. 12, 2026, the institute reported on Nov. 23, 2026. Leaders in business, government and academia gathered at Stanford to discuss AI’s potential economic upheaval and how to design policies now. The forum examined a range of possible scenarios, including a labor market meltdown. Neale Mahoney, the Trione Director at SIEPR and the TG Wijaya Professor of Economics at Stanford, kicked off the event. Mahoney moderated a Q&A with Mary C. Daly, president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and a keynote speaker.

Prompted to estimate AI’s contribution to U.S. economic growth in the next three years, economists’ predictions ranged from 1.5% to 30%, said Anton Korinek of the Anthropic Institute. Korinek delivered that data point from his research at SIEPR. Scott Strand, a Google executive overseeing the ATLAS initiative, said AI adoption is “broad yet shallow,” with automating tasks accounting for just 10% of current usage. Elena Patel, co-director of the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, noted that individual incomes make up 85% of federal tax revenues. Jennifer Duff is a member of the Mesa, Ariz., city council, a city of 530,000.

Mahoney said, “We do too much predicting, and not enough planning, around AI.” He said there are real concerns that AI will drive up costs, disrupt jobs and lead to a concentration of wealth and power. Daly said she is both “extremely bullish” about what AI will ultimately mean for the economy and keenly aware of the need for policymakers to be proactive. “The transition dynamic matters,” she said, adding that if the AI economy hasn’t worked the way we want in 10 years, “it won’t be the technology’s fault. This is ours to decide.”

Korinek said of the range of predictions, “That tells you how large the span of uncertainty is.” David Deming, president of Harvard College, delivered a keynote on three potential outcomes: a white-collar jobs apocalypse, a broken career ladder for young workers, and AI as “a normal technology” akin to the internet or personal computer. Josh Zoffer, a principal at CIV who worked at the White House National Economic Council, said bipartisan consensus is possible, citing the right’s call for reindustrialization and the left’s call for electrification. Duff said Mesa is learning from mistakes made when data-center developers demanded non-disclosure agreements and expected hefty tax subsidies. Erika McEntarfer, former head of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and now a senior policy fellow at SIEPR, said, “Our social safety net here in the U.S. is pretty rickety.”

Ioana Marinescu of the University of Pennsylvania and Ben Hyman of UCLA’s California Policy Lab suggested “wage insurance” to subsidize workers transitioning to lower-paying jobs. The articles state that the widespread layoffs many anticipated would strike fast have not happened. The same goes for the widely expected productivity surge that is key to economic growth and improved living standards, the articles state. AI is not infiltrating white-collar work with zero impact on blue-collar jobs, according to the articles, which note that mechanics are using the technology to inspect worn engine parts and farmers to plant crops.

Mahoney said a falloff in income tax revenues could cripple government programs like Medicare and Social Security. With trillions of dollars expected to pour into data-center development in the next few years, Zoffer said policymakers could achieve both goals. Ezra Kagan, executive director of the policy lab at RAISE US, said now is the time to start experimenting and gathering evidence on what works. “It’s imperative, as we think about getting ready for this disruption,” Kagan said, “to start building the muscle at the state level, within our educational institutions, and within the federal government.”

Patel said there is already talk of imposing an AI usage tax and a “windfall” tax on companies profiting from AI, with the added goal of slowing AI’s advance. Panelists also talked about a federal tax on consumption, which could include instituting a value-added tax. Duff said she would like to see a policy framework that smaller municipalities could use to broker more advantageous deals with developers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Eric Josephs studies how AI can design safer personalized CRISPR gene therapies
stories.Summary:
Eric Josephs, an Empire Innovation Associate Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Stony Brook University, has been studying how artificial intelligence can be used to treat genetic diseases more effectively. His research, backed by a seed grant from Stony Brook’s AI Innovation Institute (AI3), recently appeared in Trends in Biotechnology, a prominent review journal. It focuses on engineering CRISPR-based gene therapies for safer genome editing. The work concerns the design of safer personalized CRISPR gene therapies, according to the university. Medicine has experienced a revolutionary shift in the treatment of genetic diseases since the FDA first approved therapeutics using CRISPR ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).

CRISPR, short for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats, was originally discovered as a natural immune defense system in bacteria and archaea. It uses a guide (RNA) molecule and a cutting enzyme (Cas9) to recognize the right target site in a cell’s DNA sequence, match the region with a given genetic sequence as well as its variants, and remove and replace these sequences to restore normal cell function. The article describes this as a kind of semantic “find-and-replace” operation to fix genetic mistakes. Today, researchers are using CRISPR to cut the section of a cell’s DNA that’s causing the disease by altering it in a highly specific way without killing the cell. Josephs said there has been a strong movement by the U.S. government and industry to broaden the use of this technology to treat many different chronic diseases, starting with recently FDA-approved treatments for sickle cell disease and a rare liver disorder in newborn babies.

He said that moving these tools from a controlled laboratory environment into diverse human populations introduces serious risks. The article does not say what specific safety measures his approach would add or how the AI would be used in designing the therapies. The article states that the full story, by Ankita Nagpal, appears on the AI3 website. It gives no further details on the next steps for the research, on when any resulting therapies might be tested, or on how the seed grant will be used. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Northeastern students win $10,000 AI hackathon prize for Earshot device that transcribes EMT calls
stories.Summary:
A team of five Northeastern University students won a $10,000 prize at an AI hackathon held to celebrate the launch of 300, the university’s new hub of global entrepreneurship, for a small orange-and-blue device called Earshot that its makers described as an EMS partner that never forgets. The team behind Earshot beat 16 other groups at the event, which took place over an intense 62-hour period at the historic Horticulture Hall at 300 Massachusetts Ave. in Boston, where student founders gathered to solve specific problems by creating a new product or expanding an existing one. The finals brought together six teams pitching to a panel of five judges, and the judges were Rich D’Amore, Alan McKim, Chet Kanojia, Martha Reyna-Medina and Ashwini Ghogare. Shourya Yadav, a computer science student and one of Earshot’s co-founders, said the result was surreal and that while the team knew it had a good product, he respected many of the other competitors and did not expect to beat them out.

Earshot is the size of an ice cube and uses AI trained on healthcare terms to transcribe ambulance calls and draft patient care reports without needing an internet connection. The device runs a local large language model trained on more than 100 hours of EMT calls so that it can accurately record details of health vitals as they are being discussed, including blood pressure, heart rate and blood oxygen level. The stated goal of the product is to help EMTs spend more time with patients and to reduce their need to rely on memory when filling out patient care reports. Teams at the event were graded on their pitch, the actual product, the investability of it and its societal impact, and up to two bonus points were awarded to those that incorporated AI.

Jack Blundin, one of the event organizers and a second-year student studying computer engineering, said that although the event was called a hackathon, it was really a four-day startup incubator in which teams worked, collaborated and saw that there were people equally as visionary as them at the school. Alan McKim, the founder of Clean Harbors and vice chair of Northeastern’s Board of Trustees, was among the judges and said after the Earshot pitch that he sits on the board of a hospital and that this was exactly what they were looking for. McKim added that if you talk to a doctor, the last thing they want to do is be sitting down and writing notes. The finalists pitched ventures that included everything from an app that makes volunteering sociable to devices that aim to prevent expensive repairs and outages.

stories.Headline: Stanford University hosts conference on societal choices and risks of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Stanford University hosted a conference on October 28, 2026, regarding the risks and choices of artificial intelligence. The event was organized by Stanford HAI and titled Confronting Our AI Future: Hope, Fear, and the Choices Ahead. It brought together a diverse group of participants including technologists, educators, philosophers, and entrepreneurs. A lawyer, a filmmaker, and a Catholic bishop also joined the day of conversations. The gathering focused on the dichotomy between the potential benefits and the fears surrounding AI.

Audrey Tang proposed a global citizens assembly of 1,000 randomly selected people to direct evaluators. She suggested fingerprinting models and using trusted execution environments for double-masked tests by outside evaluators. Tang cited Taiwan's 2024 deepfake fraud deliberation which involved 200,000 text invitations and 1,700 volunteers. This process led to a regulatory package with over 85 percent support and a new law. A pilot is currently underway involving a Gemini model and Singapore's AI institute.

James Landay, the HAI Denning Director, stated that facing fears is important because AI has immense potential. He said independent research at universities helps people address concerns with evidence instead of speculation. Erik Brynjolfsson, a Stanford HAI associate director, noted a gap between AI capabilities and ground reality. He claimed that the rewards of AI wealth might become concentrated but said this is a choice. Andrew Bosworth of Meta urged continuous education to avoid past failures in retraining displaced workers.

Jessica Riskin said AI creates uncertainty about whether students or colleagues truly authored their work. Shane Denson argued that AI is not a neutral tool and reflexively changes who people are. Meghan Sullivan warned against letting software companies fix democratic institutions or universities by selling them products. Bishop Oscar Cantú cautioned that a chatbot is not a person who can love someone. Ion Stoica and Michael Bernstein discussed how human oversight remains a bottleneck for AI agents.

The articles state that some people worry AI will shrink job markets and concentrate wealth and power. Others expect the technology to cure cancer, expand scientific discovery, and improve productivity. Research by Brynjolfsson found a significant decline in hiring early-career workers in coding and customer service. Fei-Fei Li and Jeff Dean discussed recursive self-improvement and the physical limits of training. Anahita Tafvizi noted that AI has increased demands for data security, governance, and accuracy at Snowflake.

The conference concluded that human connection, conscience, and creativity provide value exceeding the capabilities of AI. Future progress depends on whether society and companies make choices that allow workers to share benefits. The articles leave open how the proposed global citizens assembly would be implemented or funded. They do not specify the exact timeline for the Gemini pilot in Singapore. The text does not state if the proposed regulatory models will be adopted globally.

stories.Headline: Northeastern researchers show AI models identify anonymous interviewees nearly half the time
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Northeastern University, Tianshi Li and Jianing Wen, created fictional interviews from public information about real people found through Reddit's Ask Me Anything community, and then asked AI models to identify the speakers after names and obvious giveaways were removed. The bots identified the speakers almost half the time by piecing together small personal details that may seem insignificant on their own, according to the university's news site on November 24, 2026. The research follows earlier episodes in which the generative AI assistant Grok revealed the protected legal name of adult performer Siri Dahl in public posts on X in February, and months earlier broadcast the home address of Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy. The strongest systems identified the speakers in roughly 400 of the interviews, and of the answers the bots labeled with high or very high confidence, about nine out of ten named the right person. The researchers combed the Ask Me Anything community and picked out 822 people with known identities, then turned their backgrounds into fictional interviews about work and technology with telltale names and labels stripped away.

They ran the simulated interviews through 15 different AI settings, some with free rein of the web and others without, and asked the bots to identify the speaker while tracking their search queries and final responses. Web access helped but was not a deal-breaker, because three models still identified 15 to 28 percent of the speakers from what they had learned during training. Wen said that what once took hours or days of detective work takes less than a minute at minimal cost with AI and web search. A second test on a smaller batch of 143 interviews that AI had previously cracked, after removing more potential giveaways, still left plenty of breadcrumbs, such as descriptions of someone's role on a work project. Li, a Northeastern professor of computer sciences, told Northeastern Global News that AI is trained to be very capable at aggregating information and making inferences based on it, and that this can be abused or misused for malicious purposes like re-identification.

The research can help people take back control of their online identities by turning AI's identification methods into practical guidance on what to share, leave out or keep separate across accounts, so they can speak openly without putting their jobs, relationships or safety on the line. The results can also help developers build tools to flag risky tidbits before interviews or online posts go public. They can help police trace anonymous threats and protect the identities of victims and witnesses by connecting messages to potential suspects and spotting details to scrub from documents before release. Doxxing, which means exposing someone's personal information like a name or address, has long been a way to settle scores in internet feuds, but in the age of AI a nightmare might simply start with a chatbot stepping out of line. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the research and its possible uses.

stories.Headline: Texas A&M researchers develop CLARKE AI to speed disaster damage assessments
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M University researchers developed an artificial intelligence tool called CLARKE, which stands for Computer Vision and Learning for Analysis of Roads and Key Edifices, and the university announced on November 24, 2026, that the tool had been selected by the digital media company Semafor for its inaugural Innovation Atlas 2026, a global editorial initiative highlighting real-world applications of AI and emerging technologies. The platform analyzes drone imagery and generates detailed damage assessments of buildings and roads within minutes, helping officials make critical decisions after hurricanes, tornados, wildfires and other disasters. According to the university, 125 emergency responders from 63 agencies across 14 states and Puerto Rico have been trained on the system, including municipal, county and state agencies, urban search and rescue task forces, private sector and drone industry associations, and federal agencies including NASA. The university said the technology was deployed in Florida and Pennsylvania during the 2024 hurricane season following hurricanes Debby and Helene.

The system was trained on drone imagery from more than 21,000 homes damaged in 10 major disasters, including hurricanes Harvey and Ian, and it classifies damage severity for individual buildings in a color-coded, structure-by-structure view while also analyzing transportation networks so crews can identify routes around damaged roads. Tom Manzini, a Ph.D. candidate in computer science and engineering and a member of the development team, said emergency managers need reliable information as quickly as possible after a disaster, and that CLARKE turns drone imagery into actionable damage assessments in minutes instead of 18 to 24 hours. He said the system does not just identify damaged structures but helps responders understand how damage affects the surrounding transportation network so they can plan safer and more efficient routes. The name CLARKE is a nod to science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke, and the university said the research was funded by the National Science Foundation through a grant to the AI Institute for Societal Decision Making.

CLARKE is now part of standard operating procedures for the State of Florida sUAS Remote Sensing Team, known as FL-UAS1. Manzini said seeing the tool incorporated into Florida's operational procedures was incredibly rewarding and that the goal from the beginning was to build something emergency responders could actually use in the field. David Merrick, program director of the Emergency Management and Homeland Security Program at Florida State University and task force lead for unmanned aerial systems for the state of Florida, called the system a game changer for rural counties, saying they can fly drones and immediately understand the extent of damage rather than wait days for information from other sources. The team has continued refining the technology based on feedback from emergency managers and field deployments, and Manzini said Florida's adoption and recognitions like Semafor's reflect growing interest in practical AI systems that address real-world challenges.

Articles.Title: Texas A&M disaster-response AI gains national recognition, expanded use among emergency responders

stories.Headline: Mathematician Terence Tao campaigns to protect mathematics from AI companies
stories.Summary:
On Sept. 8, the tech company OpenAI announced that its artificial intelligence programs had solved the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a theoretical mathematics problem that the Clay Mathematics Institute had offered a $1 million prize for in 2000. According to OpenAI, the company threw 10,000 AI bots at the problem and solved it in just 88 hours. Barely a month later, OpenAI released AI-generated solutions to more than 350 additional mathematical problems across the discipline. Terence Tao *96, a UCLA professor considered one of the world’s leading theoretical mathematicians, has emerged as a spokesman for the AI skeptics. Tao earned his Ph.D. at 20 and won the Fields Medal at 31, and he has joined a public campaign to save math from being cannibalized by AI.

He had been working with OpenAI to improve its programs but stopped around a year ago when he concluded that the company was using him, and the discipline, to boost its share price rather than to advance human knowledge. He co-founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research in 2025 to promote responsible AI use, and at an October meeting of the group he said mathematicians can afford to be slower than this. He said the AI companies are solving major conjectures left and right but are not actually creating any value, and he has described their approach as strip-mining mathematics. Tao and others complain that AI companies have produced hundreds of scientific papers claiming to have solved various mathematical problems but have made it difficult for humans to check whether they have done so, often because their models are proprietary and hide the steps the AI agents took. Upon closer examination, some AI-generated mathematical papers have proven to be incorrect.

Tao argues that the steps taken to arrive at an answer are often equally valuable, both to show that the answer is correct and to point toward other research, and that churning out answers by machine can erase years of painstaking research, often done by younger mathematicians trying to gain a foothold in the field. He fears AI programs may destroy the collaborative nature of higher mathematics, driving scholars to hide their research rather than share it. In a Sept. 2 blog post, Tao suggested that some types of mathematical problems may have to be declared off-limits to AI, in part to give younger mathematicians something to solve on their own. On an Oct. 15 episode of the podcast Numberphile, he said he guesses we are seeing the end of the romantic era of mathematics, the age of heroes, and that math is moving to an industrial era in which people will work in big teams, more like the other sciences.

Articles.Title: Terence Tao *96 Is Fighting AI Companies For the Future of Mathematics
