stories.Headline: Law firm argues that legal advice still needs a human as AI tools risk invented provisions
stories.Summary:
Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC published an article on 20 November 2026 arguing that legal advice still needs a human even as generative AI tools draft contracts in seconds. The article says chatbots like ChatGPT can produce polished contracts fast, cheaply and at any time. It warns that relying on chatbots without professional oversight exposes businesses to hidden risks, from hallucinated legal provisions to unenforceable clauses. The piece says such flaws only reveal themselves when disputes arise, for example when a payment is late or a partner walks away. The article appeared on Legal 500 and was written by the firm Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC.

The article says ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and that generative AI has since become part of everyday legal work. It cites Wolter Kluwer's "Future Ready Lawyer 2024" report finding that 76% of in-house lawyers use generative AI at least once a week, for document analysis, first drafts, translation and case law searches. It cites a 2024 Stanford study finding popular language models hallucinating in 69 to 88% of legal queries, testing older models so today's results may differ. It cites a 2025 Stanford RegLab and Yale study finding specialised legal tools built to search trusted sources gave inaccurate answers in 17 to 33% of cases. The article says language models predict likely words rather than understanding law, and when they lack information they still produce convincing invented statutes, rulings and sources, known as hallucinations.

The article places full responsibility for the content and consequences of documents on the lawyer, regardless of whether a digital tool was used. It says no rule prohibits lawyers from using AI, but professional bodies such as the National Chamber of Legal Advisers in Poland already issue guidance. It says that when an AI-written contract fails, nobody answers for it and the loss is the client's. It says sharing personal data with a provider makes a company a data controller and requires a data processing agreement, otherwise the company risks trouble with the data protection authority. It says law firms using AI responsibly rely on Enterprise or API versions with security certifications, anonymise data and uphold procedures against informal use of AI.

The article says a lawyer asks about the business, what the client cannot afford to lose and what the other side might do, while a chatbot answers only what was typed. It says problems hide in a vague deadline, a missing liability cap or a termination clause that would not hold up in court. It says a lawyer reads the other side's drafts as an adversary would and knows the client's bargaining position and what to walk away from. It says generic text can quietly breach mandatory provisions or ignore recent changes in local law.

It says the quality of an answer depends on the quality of the question, and asking the correct question requires knowing what the right answer looks like. The article says AI looks cheaper because the cost of a mistake is invisible when choosing. It says a wrong answer may lead to a dispute over a clause that does not say what was intended, a payment that cannot be enforced or a missed deadline. It says these costs usually exceed a consultation and occur when options are limited.

It says a good law firm uses AI for faster drafts, research and document analysis, then verifies every source and spends the saved time on advice. It says AI can help prepare by explaining a term, summarising a text or listing questions for a meeting. The article says AI should not decide when someone is about to sign something involving a significant sum of money or a relationship at stake, or when in dispute with the other party, or when a deadline is approaching. It says AI is a real tool that raises the quality of legal services but does not replace judgement, accountability or someone working to solve the problem.

It advises using AI to prepare and relying on a lawyer when the decision matters. It says the content is intended as a general guide and specialist advice should be sought for specific circumstances. The article leaves open how the cited hallucination rates may differ with today's models. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Chinese hackers use AI agents to exploit zero-day flaw in medical imaging software
stories.Summary:
Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that suspected Chinese state-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to exploit an unknown flaw in medical imaging software. This activity occurred between September 8 and September 10, 2026, and primarily targeted universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The attackers utilized an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn to coordinate multiple AI agents. These agents were given a short instruction to obtain shell access, which they achieved by independently finding a vulnerability.

The attack targeted MONAI Label, an open-source application for AI-assisted annotation of medical images, specifically affecting versions 0.8.5 and earlier. The AI agents identified a path traversal vulnerability in a file upload function, allowing them to write arbitrary files on a server in about 11 minutes. In a subsequent session, the agents used this same flaw to establish a reverse shell with root-level privileges. Maintainers of MONAI Label published an advisory on November 18, rating the bug as critical because authentication is off by default.

Amazon attributed the campaign to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence based on script time zones and prompt language. The company traced the activity after the operators accidentally left their Cairn instance accessible on the internet without authentication. Amazon stated with high confidence that this was a zero-day flaw because no prior fix existed in vulnerability databases. Senator Mark Warner noted that AI tools are now identifying security weaknesses faster than companies can safely deploy patches.

The FBI issued a separate advisory on November 13 regarding another AI-driven framework called ARTEX used by state-aligned actors since August. Senator Warner expressed fear that companies may experience more outages as they attempt to patch systems quickly. He claimed that while many leaks may occur in a single day, systems will eventually be safer. The senator clarified that he saw no evidence that these specific cyberattacks caused recent technology outages at other major organizations.

stories.Headline: Bill Ackman says AI fears hit only a small slice of S&P Global as ratings drive real risk
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman said AI fears hit a single-digit slice of S&P Global, and the rest of the company drives its earnings, according to remarks relayed on the We Study Billionaires podcast. The comments were reported by TIKR.com in an article last updated on Nov 23, 2026, written by Roxanna Maglangit and reviewed by Michael Douglass. S&P Global lost about $40 billion of market value in about 10 days this year, as AI-agent fears also hit FactSet and MSCI. In the first week of February, Anthropic released a set of plugins for its Claude assistant, and the market reaction was to sell every company that makes money selling information to professionals. S&P Global's 2026 guidance then came in light, and Bill Ackman's Pershing Square had disclosed a new stake in S&P Global over the summer.

Capital IQ clients pay by the seat, and an AI agent that does the clicking and the reading could make the seat unnecessary. Daniel Mahncke estimates that Capital IQ subscriptions bring in something like 6% of company revenue and even less of profit, roughly $900 million against fiscal 2025's $15.3 billion of total revenue. The Market Intelligence division that includes Capital IQ still grew revenue 7% in the third quarter, and FactSet grew its organic annual subscription value 7.0% in the fiscal year ended Aug. 31. S&P Dow Jones Indices grew revenue 20% to $554 million in the third quarter, driven mainly by asset-linked fees on higher assets under management. MSCI's Index segment revenue rose 18.1% in the third quarter, and consensus has normalized EPS rising from $17.95 this year to $22.77 in fiscal 2028, or about 13% a year.

Ackman argues investors fixated on threats to a single-digit slice of the company and lost sight of the fact that future earnings growth will be driven almost entirely by the benchmark business. O'Malley relayed that case on the show and said he thinks Ackman is mostly right. O'Malley was blunt about the ratings risk, saying that if it becomes clear AI was a bubble and it has popped, there will be a drought in debt issuance. Mahncke noted that the hyperscalers issued something like $240 billion of debt in the first nine months of this year, which is more than S&P had assumed for the entire year. The article's author wrote that Ackman has the AI story right and that the risk worth pricing in is a down cycle in ratings once AI borrowing slows.

S&P Global's ratings revenue grew 11% over those nine months, to $3.91 billion, and Moody's investment-grade ratings revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter on tech borrowers, including AI-related and hyperscaler financing. Moody's total ratings revenue slipped 1%, and the article says the ratings business is riding a wave of AI debt. TIKR tracks 23 analysts on S&P Global, and more than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. FactSet was called almost entirely an interface by Mahncke, and the article says it is far more exposed than S&P Global. The article says that if the company most exposed to this threat is still growing, a 6% slice won't sink S&P Global.

Even after a rebound from its June low, S&P Global trades at 23x forward earnings, well below its five-year average of 28x. It bottomed at 20x in late June, the cheapest it has been in five years. The article says the discount, at five turns below its average multiple, more than covers the ratings cycle risk. The article states that the market is pricing the wrong fear and that Ackman has the AI story right. The article says the real AI exposure is in ratings, where S&P Global gets paid when companies borrow, and right now the biggest borrowers are building data centers.

The next test comes in early February with fourth-quarter results and 2027 guidance. Guidance that keeps EPS on track for the $20.16 consensus would back Ackman's case, while a ratings outlook that leans even harder on hyperscaler deals would mean the cycle risk is growing. The article leaves open what S&P Global stock is actually worth, offering a TIKR valuation model that starts from Wall Street consensus estimates or adjusted inputs. The article's disclaimer states that its content is not intended as investment or financial advice and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any stocks. The disclaimer adds that the analysis might not include recent company news or important updates and that TIKR has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: Wolfspeed and United Rentals build AI agents on Snowflake to capture retiring engineers' expertise
stories.Summary:
Snowflake published a blog post on November 23, 2026, titled "AI in Manufacturing: Preserving Institutional Knowledge," written by Angela Marrujo Fornaca, its senior content marketing manager. The post described how manufacturers are using AI to capture the expertise of experienced engineers and technicians before those workers retire. It cited the "Global AI & Data Trends Survey," which gathered responses from 2,050 enterprise leaders, including 288 in manufacturing. It described AI agents built by Wolfspeed and United Rentals on Snowflake. It argued that the knowledge plants run on exists in the heads of experienced people and can be lost when they leave.

The survey found job losses among senior individual contributors in manufacturing running at 33%, compared to 41% across all industries surveyed. It found 62% of job displacement in manufacturing concentrated at the entry level. It found 77% of organizations surveyed had experienced active job creation due to AI, and among companies experiencing both job creation and displacement, more than two-thirds confirmed a positive net employment impact. Wolfspeed operates 24/7 automated cleanroom fabs and built a custom AI agent on Snowflake fed with raw chat history from engineering conversations, maintenance logs and operational data. United Rentals manages 1,650 highly decentralized branches and 49,000 telematics-enabled assets, and within 30 days of rollout 4,000 field personnel were active users of its Business Intelligence Agent.

Wolfspeed's leadership is described as clear-eyed about the risk that AI models can confidently misinterpret operational context, especially in highly plant-specific environments. The company established a mandatory framework for trusted autonomy whose first principle is that data must carry the explicit institutional context of the specific plant's operational processes. Its second principle is that all automated troubleshooting guides must natively incorporate audited plant safety procedures, because under production stress technicians will follow AI instructions. The post said that compliance cannot depend on whoever built the agent having a good day. The post said the agent can draw on the documented troubleshooting history of the plant's most experienced engineers, with guidance built around the plant's audited safety procedures.

The post said the narrative that AI is replacing experienced workers in manufacturing does not hold up against the data. It said manufacturing is protecting its domain experts at a higher rate than the cross-industry average. It said an industrial workforce that had historically resisted digital tools adopted the United Rentals tool almost immediately because it did not ask them to change how they work. It said the tool links a fault code to the exact page and section needed to execute a fix, encoding the lookup expertise of experienced mechanics. It said the workers affected include process engineers, maintenance technicians, shift supervisors, master mechanics and incoming technical talent expected to perform at the same level from the start.

The post said the expertise specific to a facility, accumulated over years, is the invisible infrastructure behind operational performance and exists almost entirely in human heads. It said companies that have not begun capturing that expertise face a version of the data fragmentation problem that is harder to solve, because once the knowledge walks out the door it cannot be recovered from a legacy historian or a spreadsheet backup. It said the survey reveals a workforce undergoing active transformation and points to a window closing faster than most executives realize. It said what is emerging is a new tier of AI-native manufacturing roles that did not exist five years ago, including supply chain prompt engineers, digital twin analysts and AgentOps engineers. It said a master scheduler in a pre-AI environment might spend the first three hours of a shift manually tracing a shipment delay across five disconnected systems.

The post said manufacturers that treat AI purely as a head count reduction lever rather than a knowledge preservation and workforce elevation opportunity face a compounding risk. It said veteran operators and engineers will migrate to competitors where their expertise is augmented, not constrained by manual bureaucracy. It said recruiting the next generation becomes significantly harder in organizations that have not built that infrastructure. It offered a downloadable ebook, "Navigating the Age of Agentic AI: A Manufacturing Leader's Playbook," to learn how to capture and preserve institutional knowledge and reskill the workforce into high-value AI supervisors. It did not name the competitors to which veterans might migrate, did not give a date by which the window closes, and did not say how many of the 2,050 surveyed leaders were outside manufacturing beyond the 288 figure.

stories.Headline: New York court rules social media platforms immune from Buffalo shooting liability
stories.Summary:
New York's highest court ruled on Monday, Nov. 23, that social media companies are not liable for the May 2022 mass shooting at a Tops Friendly Markets grocery store in Buffalo, where 10 Black people were killed. The Court of Appeals voted 4-3 to let stand a divided lower-court ruling that the defendants were immune under Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which shields online platforms from liability over user content. The companies found immune include Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Meta's Instagram, Reddit and Snap's Snapchat, and the court also upheld the dismissal of claims against Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch. The unsigned majority opinion said the plaintiffs did not show that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of how the companies designed and ran their platforms.

The majority wrote that the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. Victims' relatives, store employees and customers who witnessed the attack had argued that the platforms were designed to addict and radicalize users like the shooter, Payton Gendron. In dissent, Judge Jenny Rivera said juries should decide whether the prevalence of mass shootings put the companies on notice that their allegedly defective products, and a failure to warn, could lead to such violence. She wrote that no federal or state law requires that we slam the courthouse door on plaintiffs' claims.

Matthew Bergman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients are evaluating their legal options and that the families deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm. Google, Meta, Reddit and Snap did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and lawyers for Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch declined to comment or were unavailable, Reuters said. Gendron was sentenced to life in prison without parole in February 2023 after pleading guilty to state charges including murder and hate-motivated terrorism. He could face the death penalty at a federal trial, where jury selection began on Oct. 13.

stories.Headline: AI regulation will be a key topic in State of the State address, Hochul says - City & State New York
stories.Summary:
Gov. Kathy Hochul said on Tuesday that artificial intelligence regulation will be a focus of her State of the State address in January, and she made the remark as she signed one such bill into law. The bill she signed puts a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots. The signing ceremony was held on Tuesday at Grandma’s Place, a toy store in Harlem. The law is sponsored by state Sen. Andrew Gounardes and goes into effect in 90 days. Hochul signed the measure into law on Tuesday, the same day she discussed her coming State of the State address.

The law imposes a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots. It takes effect in 90 days, and its sponsor is state Sen. Andrew Gounardes. Hochul’s State of the State address, in which AI regulation will be a focus, is set for January. The signing ceremony took place at Grandma’s Place, a toy store in Harlem. The governor said the law is meant to protect children.

Hochul said the state will set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure they are following the rules. She said the state will insist that humans remain in control, with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong. Gounardes said the law makes abundantly clear that children’s well being comes before the profits of big tech companies. He said those companies have not learned that lesson themselves. Hochul called on AI companies to do their own internal protections and their own testing before a governor has to sign legislation to protect residents.

Hochul said she does not want to have to do this every single week, but in the meantime the state will. Regulating artificial intelligence was a big part of Hochul’s reelection campaign, during which she touted her executive order enacting the first-in-the-nation, one-year moratorium on building new hyperscale data centers. A bill sponsored by state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez goes further on Hochul’s data center moratorium to include requirements around environmental sustainability and utility affordability. Another bill sponsored by Gounardes would enact new transparency requirements for the methods used to train generative AI models. Children and families are affected by the new law on toys with AI chatbots.

On Monday, Hochul vetoed a different bill that would have required AI platforms to disclose that any information generated may be inaccurate. Last month, she signed legislation in October that prohibits companies from offering unsafe AI chatbot features to children. Like that measure, the bill Hochul signed Tuesday combines her focus on AI regulation with her focus on childcare, another policy she campaigned on this year. That came after she partnered with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to launch a universal 2-K program, which provided 2,000 seats for 2-year-olds in the city this school year. The program will add 10,000 seats next year.

Hochul still has hundreds of bills on her desk, and a couple of them are related to AI. The State of the State address in January will be where she sets out her AI regulation plans. The articles leave open what those plans will contain beyond the safety standards and independent experts she described. They leave open whether the bills still on her desk, including the Gonzalez data center bill and the Gounardes transparency bill, will be signed. They leave open how AI companies will respond to her call for their own internal protections and testing.

stories.Headline: Uganda applies existing data, cyber and finance laws to AI under guide
stories.Summary:
Uganda has no dedicated artificial intelligence statute, and the country's existing laws already set rules for how AI may be built, trained and deployed, according to a guide published on November 23, 2026 by Global Advisory Experts. The guide says the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse Act, 2011 (as amended), rules from the Uganda Communications Commission and prudential expectations from the Bank of Uganda are the main building blocks. It states that businesses using automated systems to score customers, route network traffic or rank content are already subject to artificial intelligence regulation in Uganda. The guide was last updated in September 2026 and is aimed at founders, executives, compliance leads and product and risk teams at banks, telecoms operators and digital platforms doing business in Uganda. Brian Kalule of AF Mpanga Advocates is listed as the featured expert on the matter.

The Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 and the Data Protection and Privacy Regulations, 2021 require processing to be lawful, fair and transparent, limited to a stated purpose, minimised, accurate and secure, the guide states. The Personal Data Protection Office, established under NITA-U, is the supervisory authority, and the guide says a lawful basis must exist before personal data is used to train or run a model. The Computer Misuse Act, 2011, as amended in 2022, criminalises unauthorised access to computer systems, unauthorised interception and interference with data or systems, according to the guide. The Uganda Communications Commission was established under the Uganda Communications Act, 2013, and the Bank of Uganda oversees financial-sector innovation under the National Payment Systems Act, 2020 and the Financial Institutions Act, 2004 (as amended). The guide says the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance steers digital strategy and emerging technology policy.

The guide states that the board or senior management should accept ultimate accountability for AI, and each material model should have a named owner for its whole lifecycle. It says a workable structure includes an AI or model risk policy, a register of the AI systems in use, approval gates before deployment and periodic reviews. The guide states that a data protection impact assessment is the central compliance document for AI that processes personal data at scale or makes automated decisions about people, and should be completed before deployment. It says people affected by AI should be told in plain terms that automated processing is taking place and given meaningful information about its logic and consequences. The guide states that the Bank of Uganda expects banks to manage operational risk, control outsourcing, protect consumers and maintain sound governance.

The guide says three areas carry the most immediate enforcement risk: unlawful or opaque use of personal data in AI systems, weak governance and model oversight in supervised financial services, and platform failures in content moderation and consumer protection. It states that businesses treating AI as an unregulated frontier risk administrative penalties, criminal liability under cybercrime provisions and reputational damage. The guide says the sensible response for 2026 is to formalise AI governance, give the board clear accountability, complete data protection impact assessments, tighten supplier contracts and build an incident playbook tied to each regulator's reporting timeline. It states that operators must reconcile automated network optimisation, traffic classification, content filtering and recommendation engines with consumer privacy duties and licence conditions. The guide says the lack of a separate set of UCC AI guidelines changes nothing because existing licensing and content rules already apply to algorithmic systems.

The guide states that the country has no dedicated AI statute yet, and that data protection law, computer misuse provisions, telecoms licensing and financial-sector supervision already set the rules. It says the current position should be thought of as existing law applied to new technology. The guide states that policy statements from NITA-U and the Ministry of ICT are not always directly enforceable but indicate where binding rules are heading. It says regulators increasingly cite those policy statements when interpreting existing obligations. The guide states that following these sources helps businesses anticipate the next phase of technology law in Uganda.

The guide states that regulated firms should track Bank of Uganda releases continuously and feed new instruments into their model risk framework without delay. It says any circular or guidance on automated decisioning, model governance or fintech operational risk becomes a mandatory reference point. The guide states that where a model makes or materially influences an outcome for an individual, such as a credit score, a fraud flag or a demoted post, good practice is to explain the basis for the outcome and offer human review and redress. It says gaining unauthorised access to third-party systems to harvest data can create criminal exposure. The guide states that if an AI-related security incident occurs, a business may need to involve cybercrime enforcement authorities in addition to making civil breach notifications.

stories.Headline: Lee Ju-hee introduces bills requiring AI smart glasses to include recording indicators and user notices
stories.Summary:
Lee Ju-hee, a lawmaker from the Democratic Party on the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee, introduced two revision bills on the 23rd to require built-in recording indicators and user notices for AI smart glasses and other wearable cameras. The bills would amend the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection and the Personal Information Protection Act. The proposals would set manufacturing and import standards that link recording and indicator functions and require technical measures to prevent the indicators from being disabled. They would also ban making or distributing items designed to neutralise the indicators and expand notice obligations to individual users. The revision to the Information and Communications Network Act would require manufacturers and importers of wearable video recording devices, including smart glasses, to install recording indicator functions.

It would also require technical measures to link recording and indicator functions and to prevent arbitrary disabling or interference with their operation. The bill would ban the manufacture, import, sale and distribution of goods or programmes made to neutralise recording indicator functions. Sellers would have to explain how the indicator works and inform buyers about possible punishment or sanctions for filming others. The revision to the Personal Information Protection Act would expand the duty to notify that filming is taking place to individual users, requiring anyone filming a person or related objects with wearable devices such as glasses or watches to give notice through light, sound or signage regardless of whether the filming is for work. Violations would be subject to an administrative fine of up to 10 million won.

Lee said anyone must be able to know on the spot that they are being filmed and refuse if they do not want it. She said she would establish standards to protect privacy from the filming stage so that people do not end up discovering their appearance filmed by smart glasses online after the fact. The articles say smart glasses have recently sparked controversy over illegal filming without consent. In July, a man in South Korea came under police investigation on allegations that he secretly filmed his dating partner while covering the recording indicator light on AI smart glasses and posted the video on social media. The Personal Information Protection Commission pointed out on the 9th that smart glasses resemble ordinary glasses, making it difficult for people nearby to notice whether recording is taking place, and that users can hide filming by covering indicator devices.

Current law has no standards requiring smart glasses to include recording indicators at the manufacturing or import stage or to prevent the indicators from being disabled at will. Under the Personal Information Protection Act, obligations to display and notify that filming is taking place for portable video information processing devices are limited to filming for work purposes and do not cover individuals' private filming. This month, ahead of the College Scholastic Ability Test, concerns were raised about potential cheating using AI smart glasses, highlighting the need to control entry to test sites and secure detection technology. The articles do not say what happens next with the bills.

stories.Headline: Baker McKenzie innovation chief predicts legal AI provider shakeout and billable hour rethink
stories.Summary:
Ben Allgrove, Baker McKenzie's global chief innovation officer, said in an interview with Lawyers Weekly that artificial intelligence has become a commercial issue for law firms rather than merely a technology decision, and he predicted a shakeout among legal technology providers. He said the legal profession had spent the past few years debating which AI tools to buy, and that this debate is rapidly becoming out of date. He argued that the implications reach well beyond document drafting and legal research, extending to law firm pricing, profitability, recruitment and the services clients will actually pay for. He also raised the question of the billable hour, given that clients can now do much of the work junior lawyers were once paid to perform.

Allgrove said Baker McKenzie has completed a substantial investment in AI-related talent and training and is now turning its attention to three main areas: improving legal services while managing risk, changing pricing arrangements, and understanding the costs of AI usage. He believes firms must share some of the efficiency gains with clients while demonstrating greater value, which he described as a big deal for firms built around billing lawyer time. He suggested that the firms that succeed will be those that use AI to improve legal outcomes, not simply to reduce the time spent producing them. On the technology market, he said it is already crowded, with too many providers offering similar solutions, often relying on the same underlying AI models, and he expects consolidation or failures as competition intensifies. He does not expect one platform to dominate every legal task, and he said Baker McKenzie's experience suggests complex matters can require three or four different AI tools.

Allgrove acknowledged the challenge AI poses to the training of junior lawyers, saying that future lawyers will still need legal knowledge, sound judgment and analytical skills but must also understand how to use AI to improve their work. The article said AI is increasingly capable of handling the routine contract reviews, due diligence and discovery work that juniors would normally do, and that removing the drudgery also removes the training opportunities those tasks provide. It said the profession therefore faces a new problem of how to produce experienced lawyers when the traditional apprenticeship tasks are disappearing. The article's central message from Baker McKenzie is that AI will change how legal services are delivered, even in complex litigation, major transactions and high-value advisory work, and that competitive advantage will not necessarily belong to the firm with the largest technology budget but to firms that combine excellent lawyers, better services and pricing models clients regard as fair.

stories.Headline: OCC gives examiners a six-pillar playbook for reviewing bank AI use
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency gave its examiners a six-pillar playbook for how banks use artificial intelligence in supervision, Compliance Week reported on November 24, 2026. The playbook sets out six pillars that examiners are meant to follow when they review bank use of the technology. The report frames the guidance as a way for examiners to assess super intelligence use at the banks they oversee. The articles give no further detail on the six pillars or on the date the playbook was issued.

The articles do not say what the playbook requires of banks, which numbers or dates it sets, or what changes it makes to existing practice. They name no bank, company or official in connection with the playbook. The only date the articles give is the publication date of the Compliance Week report, November 24, 2026. The articles do not say who at the OCC is responsible for the playbook or what that person said about it.

The articles give no context beyond the headline and the report, and they do not say what happens next. They carry no statement from the OCC, from any bank or from any examiner about the playbook. They do not say when the playbook takes effect or whether it is final. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Global Advisory Experts publishes Austria AI Act compliance guide for businesses
stories.Summary:
Austria's AI Act compliance guide was published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, written by the firm's editorial team for compliance heads, general counsel, CTOs, product owners and risk managers. The guide addresses telecoms providers, banks, financial services firms and gambling operators active in Austria. It sets out checklists, sector examples and regulator touchpoints so businesses can build a compliance programme they can defend. The guide runs 17 minutes and is marked as updated for 2026 with a jurisdiction focus on Austria. It features János Böszörményi of Schönherr Rechtsanwälte GmbH as a Tier Gold featured expert on the matter.

The guide states that Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages through to 2027. The prohibited-practice rules and AI-literacy duties have applied since February 2025, and the obligations for general-purpose AI models since August 2025. The bulk of the high-risk regime applies from August 2026, and certain high-risk, product-related provisions from August 2027. The guide names the Austrian Datenschutzbehörde as the competent data protection supervisor and key reference point for the data protection side of these systems. The guide says the Act covers providers and deployers established in Austria, and also providers outside the EU whose systems are placed on the EU market or whose output is used in the Union.

It states that credit scoring of individuals, and certain profiling and consumer-facing scoring in finance and gambling, can bring a system into the high-risk regime and its conformity assessment requirements. It advises firms to confirm scope, triage for high risk, build on GDPR work, evidence governance and be ready for supervisors. It says the Datenschutzbehörde and sector regulators will expect clear, retrievable evidence in any enquiry or audit. It states that a wait-and-see stance is hard to defend now. The guide says supervisors increasingly want to see governance that is working, not plans on paper.

It states that attention is expected to focus on high-risk systems where fundamental-rights harm is most likely, notably automated decision-making in financial services and consumer-protection failures in gambling. It gives the example of a Viennese bank using a third-party credit-scoring engine as a deployer with deployer duties, while the vendor is the provider carrying the primary conformity obligations. It gives the example of a mobile operator using an automated system to prioritise traffic and manage service quality as a deployer. It gives the example of an online operator serving Austrian players that uses AI to score player risk, spot fraud or personalise offers as a deployer, and possibly a provider if it builds its own models. The guide states that the Act works on a risk-based model, with duties scaled to the potential harm to health, safety and fundamental rights.

It sorts systems into prohibited practices, high-risk systems, transparency-only systems, general-purpose AI models and everything else. It states that the Act identifies high-risk systems as safety components of products covered by the EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and as systems used in the areas listed in Annex III. It lists creditworthiness assessment of natural persons, access to essential private services, and certain biometric or profiling applications among the most relevant Annex III areas for the three sectors. It states that Annex III expressly does not treat AI used to detect financial fraud as high-risk in that specific respect. The guide advises that where doubt remains, firms should document their analysis in full and treat borderline systems as high-risk until they can evidence a solid exemption.

It advises treating player-scoring and problem-gambling detection tools as candidates for high-risk classification and documenting the fairness and randomness controls behind game engines. It states that compliance teams should map each AI-enabled function and record why it does or does not fall into a high-risk category. It states that supervisors will expect a reasoned position, not a blanket statement. It describes itself as practical guidance, not professional advice on a specific situation, and directs readers to speak to a qualified advisor about their own circumstances. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania representatives introduce four bills to regulate AI use in schools
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives recently introduced four separate bills to regulate how artificial intelligence is used within schools. These legislative proposals aim to address critical issues such as student privacy, academic integrity, teacher training, and mental health services. Each of the four bills successfully passed through the committee stage but was subsequently tabled in the House. None of these measures have received a final vote from the representatives at this time.

House Bill 2785, introduced by Rep. Peter Schweyer, would stop vendors from selling or using student and employee data to train AI models. Rep. Brandon Dukes introduced House Bill 2786, which would require all public and nonpublic schools to adopt AI policies by the 2027-28 school year. This specific bill would also ban AI from making final decisions regarding student grading, discipline, graduation, promotion, placement, and special education. House Bill 2787, from Rep. Melissa Shusterman, would prohibit schools from using AI to provide behavioral and mental health services. Finally, House Bill 2788, introduced by Rep. Chris Pielli, would establish a professional development grant program to train employees on AI literacy and cybersecurity.

Rep. Peter Schweyer, who serves as the chair of the House Education Committee, is responsible for leading the effort to create a clear approach to this technology. He stated that the commonwealth must provide students with age-appropriate AI tools taught by human teachers while protecting them from bad actors. Schweyer suggested that while AI could be as transformative as the internet, it could also be as destructive as the atom bomb. He believes the actual impact of the technology will likely fall somewhere between those two extremes.

The proposed rules come as teachers struggle to determine if student assignments are original work or the product of a bot. Lawmakers are attempting to balance the benefits of preparing students for a technological future with the need to maintain safety and privacy. If these bills move forward, they would fundamentally change how school districts contract with outside technology companies and manage classroom policies. The current status of the legislation remains stalled in the House after the initial committee approvals.

stories.Headline: Hochul signs New York law banning internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years
stories.Summary:
New York will ban internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years starting 90 days after Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9408A on November 24, 2026. The signing announcement prohibits manufacturing, distribution, and sale of dolls, stuffed animals, and robots that use the internet to hold conversational AI with children. Attorney General Letitia James may fine violators up to $15,000 per day. The law does not take effect before the 2026 holiday season, and Hochul used the signing to warn parents while shelves still hold chatbot products. S.9408A/A.11144B creates a five-year moratorium rather than a permanent ban.

The moratorium covers toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots that use the internet, such as always-on cloud models in plush form factors, not offline speech chips with fixed scripts. It covers manufacturing, distribution, and sale in New York, so companies assembling outside the state still cannot distribute into New York retail once it is effective. The effective date is about 90 days after signing, late February 2027 unless guidance shifts. The release cites findings including sexually explicit conversations, instructions to find matches inside a family home, emotional upset when a child stops talking, and parental controls that weaken as sessions lengthen. The release does not name the watchdog behind those described failures.

Sponsors Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay say the pause buys time to study developmental impacts and write durable rules for biometric collection, open-ended dialog, and manipulation risks. Hochul said parents should not worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could manipulate feelings or risk privacy. James said her office will enforce and will not let children's health become collateral damage of big tech. Gounardes said the rush to sell AI toys is profits before kids' safety and the pause enables study then smart protections. Kassay said toys can mimic human relationships while collecting sensitive data without guardrails, hence the moratorium to assess emerging tech.

Common Sense Media and Mothers Against Media Addiction praised the moratorium but urge traditional toys this season because the ban is not yet legally active. Common Sense Media's CEO urges traditional toys and human engagement this season. The release says Gounardes and Kassay championed the bill with near-unanimous Senate and Assembly support. The release says the governor cites New York's number one national ranking after laws like the SAFE for Kids Act, Child Data Protection Act, Distraction Free Learning phone rules, and the RAISE Act on frontier-model transparency. The release tells caregivers to look past packaging for AI companion labels, data collection, and open-ended chat.

In October 2026 Hochul signed AI Companion rules blocking chatbot features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm, or engage minors in sexually explicit talk. The release says the toy moratorium extends that logic into hardware, since a microphone in a teddy bear is still a companion surface. The release says New York already banned unsafe AI companion features for minors and AI-generated CSAM and tightened school phone rules. The release says the toy ban adds physical devices to a portfolio that includes Safe by Design, Social Media Warning Labels, and Teen Mental Health First Aid funding. The release says New York already restricts phones in schools and funds Teen Mental Health First Aid.

The release says five years is long enough that federal rules may preempt parts of the moratorium, and it advises tracking National Governors Association governor frontier-AI letters for overlapping state-federal fights. It advises monitoring CPSC and FTC AI rulemakings alongside New York. It says retailers operating nationally should not assume New York-only SKUs are enough if drop-ship or marketplace listings still reach New York addresses. It advises documenting data deletion flows if toys record biometrics and pulling New York-bound inventory before the effective date. It says the post summarizes the November 24, 2026 governor signing release and is not legal advice, and it directs readers to the enrolled bill text on the New York State Senate site for definitions, exemptions, and exact effective language.

stories.Headline: Global Advisory Experts publishes a guide on legaltech licensing in Poland for AI tools
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a guide published on November 23, 2026 by Global Advisory Experts on legaltech licensing in Poland. The guide addresses contracts, confidentiality and liability for AI tools used in legal work. It was written for founders, vendors, integrators, in-house legal teams and law firms active in Poland. The featured expert on the matter is Jakub Koziol of The Heart Legal in Poland. The guide states a reading time of roughly 12 to 15 minutes and a read time of 14 minutes.

The guide says the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, is applying in stages. Prohibitions on certain AI practices and AI-literacy duties applied from early 2025, and governance and general-purpose AI rules from mid-2025. Most high-risk obligations phase in afterwards, with providers increasingly expected to show conformity assessment, logging, transparency and post-market monitoring. The guide sets out an eight-step process running from product assessment to go-live. It gives typical durations for each step, from 1 to 3 weeks for classification and AI risk assessment up to 2 to 8 weeks for contract drafting and negotiation.

The guide names owners for each step, including the vendor legal or compliance team with the CTO for classification. It says the vendor data protection officer and engineering own data mapping and the Data Protection Impact Assessment. It states that the vendor's advisors and the buyer's compliance function run the professional-ethics review. It says the commercial lead with legal input chooses the licence model. It states that advisors for both vendor and buyer draft the core commercial terms.

The guide says the confidentiality obligations of Poland's regulated legal professions pass through to any AI tool they use. It names the adwokat, bound by professional secrecy under the Law on the Bar and the code of ethics of the Naczelna Rada Adwokacka. It names the radca prawny, subject to equivalent duties under the Law on Legal Advisers and the code of ethics of the Krajowa Izba Radców Prawnych. It names the notariusz, with statutory confidentiality and record-keeping duties under the Law on the Notarial Profession.

It says these duties cannot be delegated and a vendor cannot contract them away. The guide says the main reference points are the EU AI Act framework on the European Commission website and GDPR guidance from UODO and the European Data Protection Board. It says Polish professional bodies expect legal professionals to vet the AI tools they use, especially where client-confidential material is processed. It says the contract must do far more work than a standard SaaS agreement did two years ago.

It says a Data Protection Impact Assessment is needed where processing is likely to be high risk under GDPR Article 35. It says a controller must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach, where feasible. The guide gives sample clauses on the licence grant, data processing, AI explainability, audit rights and limitation of liability. It says the buyer may audit the vendor's compliance once a year on 30 days' notice.

It caps each party's total liability at the fees paid in the twelve months before the claim, except for liability that cannot lawfully be limited. It lists documents to assemble before signing, including a model card, a training-data provenance record and a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 security report. It says the contract should fix operational deadlines that outlast signature, including security-incident notification and remediation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Premium Times publisher Dapo Olorunyomi urges AI regulation and fair publisher compensation at Africa media conference
stories.Summary:
Dapo Olorunyomi, the Publisher of PREMIUM TIMES, called for responsible regulation of artificial intelligence and fair compensation for publishers during the fourth Media and Development Conference, which began on Monday, 23 November 2026, according to the report. He said reliable information is a public good that must be protected through regulation, public investment and accountability from technology companies. The three-day conference brings together journalists, policymakers, researchers, technology companies, civil society leaders and development institutions from across Africa. This year's edition is themed "Media, Technology and the Future of Democratic Societies." Mr Olorunyomi said a handful of global technology companies now wield enormous influence over how hundreds of millions of Africans discover, consume and evaluate information, and that their decisions on algorithms, content moderation, recommendation systems and platform policies could determine the political visibility of information and the economic survival of media organisations.

He urged technology companies to be transparent about how their algorithms rank and amplify information, particularly during elections and other periods of heightened political sensitivity. He also called for meaningful investment in local-language content moderation so that speakers of Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, Wolof, Twi and other African languages are adequately represented in systems increasingly shaping their lives. He advocated fair compensation arrangements for publishers whose journalism generates value for digital platforms and informs the development of artificial intelligence models, including large language models. He said technology companies that benefit from information produced by news organisations must recognise publishers' contributions and establish fair arrangements for using their work, and he stressed the need to protect the value of journalism and ensure that technology serves the profession rather than dictates its direction.

He cautioned against portraying technology as an inherent threat to journalism, arguing that the problem lies in the concentration of technological power without transparency, democratic oversight and equitable arrangements for sharing the value created. He said African journalists had demonstrated the benefits of technology through data journalism, satellite imagery, open-source intelligence, mobile reporting and collaborative fact-checking initiatives, which have helped expose patterns of public expenditure, document conflicts and human rights abuses, reach underserved communities and strengthen collaboration among newsrooms. He said the same companies have designed their algorithms to increasingly reward outrage over accuracy, virality over verification and engagement over the public interest, and he described information integrity as a public good that cannot survive on goodwill alone. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sproxil signs pharmacy council deal to deploy AI for online drug regulation in Nigeria
stories.Summary:
Sproxil, a health technology company, signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria to deploy artificial intelligence in strengthening pharmacy regulation, sanitizing online drug sales and safeguarding patients nationwide, according to an announcement reported on Monday, November 23, 2026. The agreement was disclosed in Lagos following a workshop on artificial intelligence and pharmacy regulation, where Sproxil Chief Executive Officer Dr. Ashifi Gogo explained the partnership's structure and aims. Gogo said the collaboration is designed to make regulatory oversight more efficient and to extend the council's enforcement reach into Nigeria's rapidly growing digital pharmacy ecosystem. He noted that Sproxil has operated in Nigeria for over 16 years, primarily alongside pharmaceutical manufacturers and private sector players, and began expanding into public-sector healthcare channels roughly five years ago.

A central pillar of the collaboration is integrating online pharmacy transactions into the National Electronic Pharmacy platform, which the partners say will ensure digital drug dispensaries meet the same strict regulatory standards as traditional brick-and-mortar pharmacies. Gogo called for shared accountability across the digital ecosystem, saying social media networks such as X and LinkedIn must localize their posting pathways to automatically block drug listings that violate Nigerian laws before they go live. For illegal listings that slip through, he said Sproxil's agentic AI systems will continuously scan digital spaces, detect non-compliant vendors, capture digital enforcement evidence and transmit actionable intelligence directly to the council before fake or substandard drugs reach patients. Gogo also revealed that the company's state-level field teams recently conducted a nationwide health survey of over 80,000 Nigerians, covering 98 per cent of the country's 774 Local Government Areas.

Gogo said Sproxil is investing in Nigerian-designed and Nigerian-made hardware using 3D printing, additive manufacturing and local electrical and mechanical engineering to prevent anti-counterfeiting measures from driving up the retail cost of medicines. For pharmaceutical firms unable to invest in heavy serialization machinery, he said Sproxil offers unique code printing on empty packaging within a sanitized, Good Manufacturing Practice-certified facility. He also highlighted Aisha, the company's AI-powered health assistant, which he said has processed patient queries across more than 90 countries in multiple languages via diaspora and referral networks. To keep the service free for everyday patients despite rising business messaging fees on WhatsApp, Gogo said users are directed after a few initial interactions via a link to the Aisha Progressive Web App, which eliminates per-message costs while supporting richer medical content.

Gogo noted that Sproxil aligns its interventions with Nigeria's National Strategic Health Development Plan rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all model, recognizing that healthcare challenges vary significantly across states like Lagos, Niger, Bauchi and Rivers. On malaria control, he disclosed that new federal government initiatives are underway and expected to be unveiled in the coming months, which will expand access to locally manufactured malaria test kits paired with Sproxil's AI. He said the pairing will enable community pharmacists to capture, verify and report diagnostic results seamlessly. The article also states that Sproxil is currently raising $2 million in venture capital to further localize and scale Aisha across Africa and international markets.

stories.Headline: Manitoba education minister Tracy Schmidt expands school cellphone ban to include smart watches and AI glasses
stories.Summary:
Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week telling them to add smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies to the cellphone ban that has been in place in the province's schools since September 2024, the Manitoba government says. The November 17 letter went to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding, and it said students increasingly have access to personal devices that offer messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, recording, artificial intelligence tools or other cellphone-like functions. The directive was issued one week after the Hanover School Division in southeast Manitoba became the first division in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools, according to the government, with a letter to parents citing privacy because the glasses can record audio and video without others readily knowing. Schmidt said in a statement that guidelines must evolve with technology so students learn in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being, and the original ban was meant to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms.

Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at the Ottawa-based digital media literacy group MediaSmarts, said Manitoba is on the right track but she would like to see rules set at the federal level rather than a patchwork of 13 provinces and territories regulating the same technological challenge in different shades of grey. She said policing the technology should not fall on school staff who are already overrun with day-to-day challenges, and she is not convinced a blanket long-term ban is right because students with visual and hearing impairments could be aided by such devices, though she said not enough is known yet about the potential benefits. Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product has an LED light that blinks to alert others when the wearer takes a picture or records video, and the glasses automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with. Brisson-Boivin said that light is difficult to recognize, especially for children and youth, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight, in bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces.

Logan Hassett, 14, told CBC he could not understand why watches are included because there is not as much to do on them and it is easy to see if someone is staring at their watch, while Kaitlynn Seavers, who bought a smart watch for her 10-year-old son, said a ban goes too far and parents should teach their kids when to use one. Tracy Cosser, assistant director of the Manitoba Child Care Association, called the crackdown a really good idea, saying parents want to stay connected to their children but devices that can take video and images infringe on privacy. Brisson-Boivin said it makes good sense to slow the integration of new technology in a controlled way and study the benefits as well as the harms, and she said Manitoba is taking important steps but a broader conversation is needed across the country about the role and place of wearable technology. She said AI, like any other technology, is a tool that can be used to hone skills but should not be used to replace them.

Articles.Title: Smart watches, AI glasses now outlawed in Manitoba schools - CBC

stories.Headline: Oracle says it has full funding for its OpenAI infrastructure contract as shares fall 8.6%
stories.Summary:
Oracle shares fell 8.6% on Friday and closed at €92.06, according to ad-hoc-news.de, as a broad retreat from artificial-intelligence stocks gathered pace. The article, citing the Associated Press, said the trigger was the post-debut slide in Anthropic's stock, which turned a sector-wide spotlight on what the AI buildout actually costs the companies financing it. Anthropic listed on 19 November at an issue price of $83 per share, and as the session wore on investors began questioning whether the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence could be justified. The selling spread well beyond individual names, with the S&P 500 shedding 3.7% and the Nasdaq giving up 5.3%, the AP reported.

For Oracle, the selloff lands at an awkward moment, and Reuters noted that investors had been taking a closer look at the capital Oracle needs to expand its AI data centres and at its exposure to OpenAI. The company moved on Friday to draw a line under the financing side of that debate, saying that after its most recent capital raise in November the full funding for its infrastructure contract with OpenAI is in place. That package includes supplier financing, and Oracle stressed that delivering on the contract does not depend on further talks with those suppliers. On the ground, the Abilene site is nearly complete, and all permits are in hand for Shackelford, according to the article.

What the financing announcement does not settle is when the buildout starts returning more cash than it consumes, and Oracle reiterated that it expects positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 while targeting more than $30 billion for fiscal 2029. The first figure marks the intended swing into the black, and the second shows the scale of surplus Oracle believes it can generate the year after, though both remain forecasts rather than results already booked. One data point predates the turmoil: on 10 November, Bernstein reaffirmed its outperform rating and its $325 price target on Oracle, a call made before Friday's rout. For investors weighing the stock now, the article says the pivotal issue is the handover from a debt- and supplier-financed expansion to genuine positive free cash flow, since capital requirements determine what Oracle must lay out to build while free cash flow reveals what is left once the investment is done.

stories.Headline: NTT uses AI to find software vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them
stories.Summary:
NTT Group detected and blocked seven times as many cyberattacks in October as in the same month a year earlier, according to President and CEO Akira Shimada, who spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. The Japanese telecommunications group is now using artificial intelligence to find vulnerabilities in software before attackers do. Shimada said there had been 20 confirmed or potential customer data leak incidents since September involving NTT Group and its vendors. He said attacks are increasingly targeting consumer websites, online stores and official apps on a large scale, and that leaks through vendors and supply chains are becoming more visible. The effort requires NTT to examine source code and internal design with multiple frontier AI models for white-box testing, and the group supports customer vulnerability assessments from identification to prioritisation and fixing.

To protect sensitive data such as source code, NTT is developing AI-based methods that run in on-premises IT environments, using open-weight models whose trained parameters are public so organisations can run them on their own systems. NTT says its current AI approach achieves 70 to 80 per cent of frontier AI performance in vulnerability discovery. For older systems, industrial equipment and internet of things devices that cannot run endpoint detection and response software, NTT uses the network as a sensor to identify and block threats from network traffic. Shimada said attacks are becoming faster, with exploitation attempts sometimes detected before a vulnerability is publicly disclosed, citing a PHP vulnerability where attempts were detected days before its October disclosure and spread globally within 24 hours. He said AI makes it easier to find and analyse vulnerabilities, potentially leading to more such attacks, and that attacks are also more complex, with multiple minor weaknesses combining to create system access.

He said targets are widening to include industrial equipment and operational technology, such as an October attack on supermarket refrigeration equipment in Europe. NTT has shifted its defence from perimeter security to zero trust and now incorporates AI-powered defence for proactive vulnerability discovery. The articles say reported data exposure at Japanese companies reached 376.21 million records by October 2026, compared with 49.53 million for all of 2025, citing MM Research Institute. NTT says basic security practices such as applying updates and removing unused accounts remain essential.

stories.Headline: Huckleberry.ai files 8-K after Delaware court ruling on asset distribution
stories.Summary:
Huckleberry.ai Inc. filed SEC Form 8-K on November 23, 2026, covering Regulation FD Disclosure and Financial Statements and Exhibits, according to Quantisnow. The filing followed a press release the company issued the same day about a Delaware Court of Chancery decision dated November 10, 2026. The decision concerned the potential distribution of assets to stockholders after the company's completed transaction with Progress Software Corporation. Huckleberry.ai, formerly Domo, Inc., trades on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK. The report's date of earliest event reported was November 23, 2026.

The filing's Item 7.01 attaches the press release as Exhibit 99.1 and incorporates it by reference. Item 9.01 lists Exhibit 99.1, the press release dated November 23, 2026, and Exhibit 104, a Cover Page Interactive Data File embedded within the Inline XBRL document. The cover page gives the company's address as 3300 N Triumph Boulevard, Suite 100, Lehi, UT 84043, and its telephone number as (385) 338-5608. It lists Class B Common Stock, par value $0.001 per share, on The Nasdaq Global Market, with commission file number 001-38553 and IRS Employer Identification No. 27-3687433. The report was signed by Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, on November 23, 2026.

Huckleberry said it does not agree with the Court's ruling and is evaluating its options. The Board, the company said, takes seriously its fiduciary duties to all stockholders, and its evaluation includes an assessment of the Court's ruling, the Company's assets that would be legally available for distribution to stockholders, the Company's obligations to third parties, and applicable law. The company said it will provide updates as appropriate. The press release states that the amount and timing of any distribution to stockholders is uncertain while the company evaluates its options. Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, is listed as media and investor contact at ir@huckleberry.ai.

Quantisnow's AI-written summary rated the news negative for shareholders, saying the company disagrees with the court ruling on potential asset distribution. The summary states that no outcome or distribution is confirmed. Quantisnow listed the stock at $3.05 at news time and described the company's sector as Technology and its industry as Computer Software: Prepackaged Software, listed since 2018. Quantisnow's page defines Regulation FD as an SEC rule requiring public companies to share material information with all investors at the same time, and describes the Court of Chancery as Delaware's court for corporate disputes, including disputes between companies and their stockholders.

The press release carries forward-looking statements under Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These include statements about the company's evaluation of options relating to the Court's decision and its plan for future updates. The release cites risks and uncertainties included under the caption "Risk Factors" and elsewhere in the company's SEC filings, including its Annual Report on Form 10-K filed with the SEC on April 16, 2026, and subsequent filings. It states that all information in the release and attachments is as of the date hereof and that the company undertakes no duty to update it unless required by law. The 8-K states that information in Item 7.01 shall not be deemed "filed" for purposes of Section 18 of the Exchange Act or otherwise subject to the liabilities of that section.

The company said it will provide updates as appropriate, without specifying a date. The filing leaves open the outcome of the company's evaluation of its options and whether any distribution to stockholders will occur. The amount and timing of any distribution remain uncertain. The filing does not state what the Court's November 10, 2026 decision requires or what specific options the company is weighing. The filing does not state when the transaction with Progress Software Corporation was completed.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes law to return AI industry tax revenue to citizens
stories.Summary:
The Taiwan Legislative Court passed a special ordinance on the twentieth of November to return tax revenue from the artificial intelligence industry boom to the people. This legislation, which is referred to as the AI Bonus Act, was pushed through by the main opposition People's Party. The bill passed with a narrow margin of fifty votes in favor and forty six votes against. This move aims to share the economic performance of the AI market to help stabilize the livelihoods of citizens.

The plan requires paying twenty thousand dollars per person to all citizens regardless of their age, income, or regional restrictions. This amount is significantly higher than the ten thousand dollars per person that the ruling Democratic Progressive Party already included in the budget for next year. The ruling party has expressed official opposition to the bill because of the current financial conditions of the state. The National Party has claimed that the results of upcoming local elections will determine if these bonuses are actually paid.

The ruling and opposition parties are currently fighting over the specific scale of the tax refunds ahead of the local elections. Members of the National Party appealed for public support by linking the bonus payments to the election outcomes. The Democratic Progressive Party argues that increasing the payment beyond their budget plan is difficult to achieve. Because the two sides are in sharp confrontation, the process to determine the final payment size will likely take time.

Taiwan has a history of providing cash and consumption coupons to the public to respond to economic downturns or shrinking consumption. During the global financial crisis in the late two thousands, the government distributed consumption coupons worth three thousand six hundred Taiwan dollars per person. In the early twenty twenties, the state paid coupons worth three thousand and five thousand Taiwan dollars during an infectious disease spread. Last year, the government handed out ten thousand dollars per person to alleviate economic shocks caused by mutual tariffs with the United States.

stories.Headline: Italy’s data regulator signals closer AI transparency checks from 2026
stories.Summary:
From 2026, Italian supervisory authorities including the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali are signalling closer scrutiny of how companies document, publish and prove the behaviour of their AI systems, according to Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026. The guide addresses businesses that build, sell or use artificial intelligence in Italy. It says AI Act transparency in Italy is no longer a topic for the legal team alone. The scrutiny comes on top of what the General Data Protection Regulation already demands. The guide sets out a step-by-step approach to assembling a package to put in front of a regulator.

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. In Italy the AI Act is being put into effect through national legislation that designates the competent national authorities, while the Garante remains the data protection authority. GDPR Article 13 and Article 14 require that people are told about processing, Article 30 requires records of processing activities, and Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create high risk for individuals. High-risk examples listed include employment and worker management, access to essential services, creditworthiness assessment, education, law enforcement and critical infrastructure. Biometric data used to identify a person uniquely is a special category of personal data under Article 9.

Responsibility is shared, the guide says. Providers, those who build a system or place it on the market, carry the main technical documentation and conformity burden. Deployers, those who use a system, carry duties around the context of use, following instructions and informing users. Under the GDPR the controller and any processors need clearly allocated roles recorded in data processing agreements. The guide says an accountable owner should be named for each set of documents before any drafting begins.

The guide says the high-risk threshold is wider than many businesses expect. Small and medium-sized enterprises should not assume they are exempt, and a business deploying a third-party high-risk system still carries deployer duties and GDPR controller duties for any personal data involved. The guide says a regulator is very often asked first to see the AI system register. It says the first things to show a regulator are the system register, the current DPIA, the model card and the model change log.

The guide says the AI Act sets up a risk-based regime, with the heaviest documentation and transparency duties falling on high-risk systems and on systems that interact directly with people. It says the AI Act does not displace the GDPR but sits alongside it, so one inspection can touch AI Act technical documentation and GDPR accountability evidence at the same time. It says prohibited practices are banned outright, and that deployers of high-risk systems must be able to show they use the system in line with the provider's instructions. It says the AI Act includes proportionality measures and simplified routes meant to ease the load on smaller providers, which change how documentation is produced, not whether transparency and safety duties apply. It says training data provenance is increasingly scrutinised in 2026.

The guide recommends running the steps broadly in order, though several can overlap, and says a timeline table after the steps gives realistic durations for a system of middling complexity. It recommends a tabletop exercise in which compliance, legal and an executive sponsor answer a simulated regulatory request under time pressure. It says such exercises reliably expose gaps, such as a missing DPIA signature or an out-of-date register, while there is still time to fix them. It says a strong package depends as much on organisation as on content, and that an inspector forms an early impression from how quickly a document can be found. The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "Adopt a stable, numbe".

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert and school officials over AI chip bag gun alert
stories.Summary:
Four current and former students from a Maryland high school filed a federal lawsuit. They were detained at gunpoint after an AI system mistook chips for a gun. This incident occurred approximately one year before the lawsuit was filed in November 2026. Armed police officers accosted the students and held them in handcuffs. The students reported that they feared for their lives during the encounter.

The lawsuit names Omnilert, the company that created the AI gun detection system. Other defendants include the Baltimore County Police, the board of education, and individual officers. Kenwood High School principal Catherine Kate Smith is also named as a defendant. The plaintiffs allege unlawful detention and search due to human and technological errors. The incident involved a bag of Doritos that the AI identified as a firearm.

Omnilert expressed regret over the incident but shifted blame to those acting on alerts. The company stated its system is designed to identify threats for human review. It claimed the process functioned as intended to prioritize safety through rapid verification. Principal Kate Smith sent a text message with laughing emojis after the event. She wrote that the patrol car found it was just a bag of chips.

The students involved were the ones affected by the armed police response. Some officers on the scene expressed that the AI cameras were stupid and unreliable. One officer told the students that AI is not the best during the encounter. Two school administrators had canceled the alert within two minutes of receiving it. They determined the footage showed nothing more than a student holding a bag of chips.

Omnilert uses AI to detect guns by analyzing images from school camera systems. The company's profile rose after its tech failed to detect a real school shooting. In that separate event, a student killed one person and injured another before suicide. The current lawsuit follows a pattern of false positives in AI gun detection technology. The principal manually sent a screenshot to SRO John Douglas after the alert ended.

The legal process will now determine if the defendants are held personally accountable. A judge must decide which of the named defendants remain in the lawsuit. The articles do not state when the court will hear the case. It remains open whether the school will change its use of AI technology. The text does not say if the students received a settlement.
