stories.Headline: Tidal bans wholly AI-generated tracks and rejects 80,000 to 85,000 AI songs a day
stories.Summary:
Tidal said on Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated, starting next month, according to Variety. The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, Variety reported. Tidal is the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely, the service said, a claim Variety reported as Tidal's. The announcement came nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs associated with fraudulent activity, a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to deceive listeners. Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote about the move in an X thread on Tuesday.

Tidal said it would remove all tracks it determines are 100% AI generated, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Tidal said it is also banning distributors from delivering these tracks to it and will reject deliveries if their metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools. Tracks made with assistance from AI will still be allowed, and the new ban goes into effect December 9. Tidal said that in the past 90 days about 43 percent of tracks distributed on the platform were identified as wholly AI-generated, and that on Nov. 6 alone 60 percent of newly uploaded songs were AI tracks. Tidal said 96 percent of those tracks have generated zero streams.

Andersen wrote that 43% of tracks distributed to Tidal in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated, and that something more drastic needs to be done. Andersen wrote that Tidal will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog, and they will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. Andersen said 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. Andersen said the move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day. Andersen wrote that Tidal encourages its peers to follow suit.

Tidal said in a social media post on Tuesday that AI music diverts streams and royalties away from the artists and confuses fans. Tidal said that to ensure it remains the best place for artists to share their work and for listeners to enjoy it, it is removing all tracks it determines are 100% AI generated. Tidal said wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale. Tidal said that at this scale the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried. The Hollywood Reporter said Tidal now has the most stringent anti-AI policies among the music streaming services, and is one of the few notable platforms beyond Bandcamp, the music distribution service popular among indie artists, to have outright banned AI music.

The Hollywood Reporter said Spotify and Apple Music, the two largest DSPs, have taken steps to either label AI tracks and artists or remove them from recommendations, but still allow fully-generated songs to get uploaded to their respective platforms. Variety reported that Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an AI Persona. Spotify said in a blog post last month that it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users' recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The Hollywood Reporter said fans and the music industry alike have voiced their frustration about AI music flooding streaming platforms. The Hollywood Reporter said Universal Music Group CEO Lucian Grainge, on an earnings call in October, advocated for streaming services to pay out AI-generated tracks less than music from human artists.

Tidal said it has seen an influx of AI-generated tracks on its platform over the past several months, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Tidal said that not all songs catch on immediately and artists should have time to build their fanbases, but that this situation is different. Spotify said this work isn't finished, that AI moves fast and bad actors adapt just as fast, and that as AI makes music more abundant it believes listeners will value human artistry even more. Spotify said its job is to make Spotify the place they find it. The articles leave open which tracks Tidal will determine are wholly AI-generated and how it will make that determination.

stories.Headline: Researchers find gaps in EU rules for AI medical device software
stories.Summary:
A policy review published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence on November 23, 2026, examined regulatory pathways and operational challenges for artificial intelligence medical device software across the European Union. Researchers from the National Center for Artificial Intelligence and Innovative Technologies for Health at the Istituto Superiore di Sanità in Rome, Italy, conducted the review. The study details critical gaps in European rules governing AI medical device software. It was published by bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. The review addresses the intersection of medical device regulations and the Artificial Intelligence Act.

Medical device software in the European Union is governed by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, known as the MDR, and Regulation (EU) 2017/746, known as the IVDR. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act or AIA, adds a horizontal framework applying to AI systems across multiple economic sectors. Under MDR Recital 19 and IVDR Recital 17, software is a medical device in its own right when the manufacturer explicitly intends it for specific medical objectives. MDCG 2019-11 Rev. 1 states that qualification criteria remain unchanged whether software uses conventional deterministic rules or AI and machine learning.

Under MDR Annex VIII Rule 11, software informing clinical decisions is Class IIa, escalates to Class IIb if decisions could cause serious deterioration or surgical intervention, and reaches Class III if decisions may result in death or irreversible deterioration. AI systems in MDR classes IIa, IIb, or III, or IVDR classes B, C, or D, automatically trigger high-risk classification under AIA Article 6. AIA Article 60, as updated by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital AI Omnibus, allows real-world testing outside regulatory sandboxes for high-risk Annex I systems. AIA Article 43 permits Notified Bodies designated under the MDR or IVDR to assess compliance against AIA Section 2 requirements. Annex XIV of the Digital AI Omnibus defines notification codes and categories of AI systems for designation applications under Article 30.

The authors identify overlapping yet non-identical quality management and post-market surveillance obligations as a major friction point. They note that joint guidance MDCG 2025-6 acknowledges the dual burden without giving concrete procedural instructions for integrating both compliance architectures into unified documentation. They describe a surveillance gap in which MDR Class I software remains subject to device surveillance but falls outside AIA post-market monitoring. They state that AIA Article 3(49)(c) defines serious incidents to include disruption of critical infrastructure, breaches of fundamental rights, and environmental or property damage, beyond the MDR and IVDR vigilance threshold of death or severe health impairment. They conclude that targeted, synchronized guidance from the European Commission, the Medical Device Coordination Group, and the Artificial Intelligence Board is urgently required.

The authors say this guidance is needed to establish legal certainty, relieve cumulative compliance burdens, and ensure safe and rapid delivery of innovative clinical AI tools to patients. They state that assessing data computing, algorithmic transparency, and data governance demands specialized technical competencies far exceeding traditional medical software auditing. They note that Annex XIV does not specify how Notified Bodies must objectively demonstrate specialized competence. They write that the absence of aligned guidelines leaves unclear how real-world learning should be validated against traditional clinical evidence standards. Manufacturers face the practical challenge of managing cumulative obligations or maintaining parallel technical documentation streams, and hospitals deploying third-party algorithmic software become both medical users under the MDR and AI deployers under AIA Article 26.

The review states that in-house software developed and used exclusively within health institutions is exempt from third-party conformity assessment under MDR Article 5(5). It says such software avoids high-risk AIA classification under Article 6 while remaining bound by horizontal prohibitions, human oversight, and data governance rules. It notes that the AIA defines providers and deployers, whereas medical regulations define manufacturers and users. It states that increasing fine-tuning of large general-purpose AI models for clinical decision-support raises unresolved legal questions about whether foundation systems are governed as medical software, under systemic-risk rules for general models, or both. It says non-high-risk systems carry no incident reporting obligations under the AIA even if the identical malfunction triggers mandatory vigilance reporting under medical device legislation.

The review states that the AIA establishes no ongoing market surveillance or incident reporting obligations for non-high-risk AI systems. It says MDR Class I manufacturers must produce periodic post-market surveillance reports, and equivalent duties apply to IVDR Class A and Class B devices. It notes that current joint guidance from the Medical Device Coordination Group and the Artificial Intelligence Board acknowledges the dual burden without concrete procedural instructions. It states that AIA Article 73 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to report serious incidents to designated national market surveillance authorities. It says the expanded incident definition creates legal ambiguity about which events trigger reporting, which authority must be alerted, and whether single events require simultaneous notifications under separate timelines.

The authors conclude that synchronized guidance from the European Commission, the Medical Device Coordination Group, and the Artificial Intelligence Board is urgently required. The review leaves open how Notified Bodies must objectively demonstrate specialized competence under Annex XIV. It leaves open how real-world learning by adaptive AI models should be validated against traditional clinical evidence standards. It leaves open whether general-purpose foundation models fine-tuned for clinical decision-support are governed as medical software, under systemic-risk rules, or both. It leaves open how manufacturers can integrate both compliance architectures into a unified documentation framework.

stories.Headline: Bavarian teachers' AI competence and classroom use hinge on pedagogical skill and habit, study finds
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey study by researchers Shuyan Feng, Martin J. Koch and Astrid Carolus examined how teachers across Bavaria, Germany, engage with artificial intelligence. The study was published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans and evaluated the theoretical AI Mindset framework. Data were gathered between July 23 and November 24, 2025, through an online questionnaire distributed via SoSci-Survey. The survey went to Bavarian primary and secondary institutions with official ministry approval. The final surveyed sample comprised 224 teachers with a mean age of 45 years and an age range spanning 25 to 65 years.

Female educators accounted for 60.83 percent of participants, while 37.33 percent identified as male, one participant identified as diverse and three identified as other. Secondary school educators represented the majority, including 28.57 percent from intermediate secondary schools and 26.34 percent from academic-track secondary schools, while 24.55 percent left school type unspecified. Most participants taught core secondary disciplines such as mathematics, German or English. Furthermore, 71.43 percent of the respondents belonged to the KI@School initiative. Comparative group tests revealed no statistically significant differences in target variables across project affiliations, with the sole exception of the need for autonomy.

The authors argued that foundational psychological prerequisites remain understudied while existing research has focused on skill-based deficits, curriculum roadmaps and technical barriers. They organized the AI Mindset framework into a triadic structure of dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitations, and technology-related appraisals. The authors noted that an inverse relationship for relatedness, mirrored by a negative zero-order correlation of minus 0.14, suggests educators with strong reliance on traditional interpersonal support systems may experience fewer structural incentives or reduced perceived necessity to independently master automated pedagogical instruments. The study emerged against a documented widening disparity in which student uptake of generative tools following the launch of ChatGPT has vastly outpaced staff training and instructional readiness. The framework brings together established psychological mechanisms into an integrated model accounting for personal agency, external social environments and direct cognitive evaluations of software characteristics.

The central structural equation model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood estimation within the lavaan package in R, utilizing a final complete analytical sample of 205 participants. The model converged successfully after 167 iterations and yielded a chi-square value of 41.40 with 43 degrees of freedom, a p value of .541, a comparative fit index of 1.00, a Tucker-Lewis index of 1.01, a root mean square error of approximation of 0.00 and a standardized root mean square residual of 0.02. The model accounted for 62 percent of the variance in teachers' classroom artificial intelligence use and 46 percent of the variance in their pedagogical artificial intelligence competence. Latent pedagogical competence exhibited the strongest positive association with actual usage, registering a standardized path coefficient of 0.45 with a significance level below .001.

Habitual engagement emerged as a robust direct predictor of use with a standardized coefficient of 0.28, followed by hedonic motivation at 0.19 and self-reported fear at 0.15. Demographic variables including educator age and gender demonstrated negligible and statistically non-significant relationships with classroom usage patterns. Habitual engagement exerted the strongest positive relationship with competence, exhibiting a standardized path coefficient of 0.31, closely followed by effort expectancy at 0.28 and personality openness at 0.15. Self-reported artificial intelligence fear was negatively associated with competence, registering a standardized path coefficient of minus 0.15, while the basic psychological need for relatedness displayed a significant negative association with pedagogical competence at minus 0.16.

Significant positive indirect paths to classroom usage were identified for personality openness at 0.07, habitual facilitation at 0.14 and effort expectancy at 0.12. Significant negative indirect effects on usage were documented for need for relatedness at minus 0.07 and artificial intelligence fear. Personality traits were gauged through the 15-item short version of the Big Five Inventory, which demonstrated good internal consistency for extraversion, conscientiousness and neuroticism, though lower consistency for openness and agreeableness. Self-determination components were quantified using validated three-item indices, general self-efficacy was assessed through a three-item instrument and goal-regulation styles were measured using selected FlexTen items.

Evaluative technology appraisals and social norms were captured using items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology-2 alongside specialized scales measuring general artificial intelligence fear and acceptance. Technological pedagogical competence was operationalized via the Intelligent-TPACK instrument, combining technological pedagogical content knowledge with pedagogical ethics subscales. AI usage was measured through self-reported frequency and purpose-based engagement scales ranging from non-use to multiple daily sessions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Senator Ruben Gallego urges Congress to ban self-teaching artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Arizona U.S. Senator Ruben Gallego announced on Tuesday that Congress should ban artificial intelligence that has the ability to teach itself. He shared these tech priorities during an interview on KTAR News 92.3 FM ahead of the new Congress starting in January. The senator believes that the speed of development could unfold very quickly once these models start learning independently. He argues that the United States can build a future with this technology while still regulating it for safety.

Gallego wants new AI models to undergo safety checks before they are released to the general public. He compares this requirement to the way regulatory bodies check new cars and planes before they are sold. To achieve this, he suggests following the example of the United Kingdom and its government-run AI Security Institute. He also wants the United States to reach arms-control agreements with Russia and China similar to past nuclear and chemical weapon deals. Additionally, he believes the government must stop the sale or diversion of advanced American computer chips to China.

The senator is responsible for these proposals and claims he is positioned between those who want no limits and those who want a total halt. He stated that the current structure of the Senate makes it difficult to pass laws because tech issues are split among several committees. To fix this, he proposes creating a single select committee that could write new laws within six months. He believes the institutional process is the primary obstacle rather than the age of the senators.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Federal judge consolidates pretrial activity in 11 lawsuits against xAI over AI-generated child sexual abuse images
stories.Summary:
A federal judge on Friday ordered that preparations in 11 federal lawsuits against xAI be jointly coordinated as one case, citing similarities among them, the Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported. The order came in Fayetteville, according to the newspaper, which said the judge acted on the similarities the suits share. The cases concern AI-generated sexually explicit images of children, the headline of the report states. The report did not name the judge or give the date of the order beyond saying it was Friday.

The order consolidates pretrial activity in the 11 lawsuits against xAI into one coordinated case, the newspaper reported. The report gives no further numbers, dates or names connected to the order or the cases. It does not say what the consolidation changes for any party beyond the joint coordination of pretrial preparations. The report does not describe the claims in the individual suits or the relief they seek.

The report does not identify who is responsible for the images or what xAI said about the order. It carries no statement from the company, from the plaintiffs or from the court beyond the order itself. No person or party is quoted in the report, and no response to the ruling is given. The newspaper's account is subscriber-exclusive reporting, it states.

The report gives no context beyond the similarities the judge cited among the 11 suits. It does not say what happens next in the coordinated case or when further proceedings are expected. The newspaper did not report any schedule, hearing date or deadline set by the order. Nothing in the report indicates how the coordination affects the timing of the cases.

stories.Headline: Hawaii lawmakers host a briefing on AI in government and workforce development
stories.Summary:
Members of the Hawaiʻi Senate Committee on Labor and Technology and the House Committee on Economic Development and Technology will host a joint informational briefing on Nov. 25 to examine the development and application of artificial intelligence. The briefing will look at artificial intelligence's role in government operations and emerging opportunities for workforce development. The public is encouraged to attend the briefing from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in Conference Room 329 at the Hawaiʻi state Capitol, 415 S. Beretania St., in Honolulu. Those who cannot make it in person can watch via livestream.

As is customary for informational briefings, no public testimony will be accepted at the meeting. The briefing will provide legislators an opportunity to gain a greater understanding about the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence and its implications for state government, cybersecurity and workforce development. Topics listed for the briefing include the history and development of artificial intelligence, emerging artificial intelligence policies and applications in government, and cybersecurity considerations related to artificial intelligence. The agenda also lists opportunities to leverage artificial intelligence to improve government efficiency, Enterprise Technology Services' artificial intelligence strategy and initiatives within state government, and opportunities to use artificial intelligence in workforce development. Committee members will have the opportunity to ask questions following each 15-minute presentation.

Andrew Merluzzi, AI Innovation + Incubation fellow at the Beeck Center for Social Impact Innovation at Georgetown University, is listed among those set to appear. Christine Sakuda, Hawaiʻi chief information officer, and Trung Lam, executive director and chief executive officer of the Hawaiʻi Technology Development Corporation, are also listed. The articles do not say what happens after the briefing.

stories.Headline: Dutch hospitals must inventory and classify AI systems in 2026 to meet EU AI Act duties
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026, is a guide for Dutch hospitals and clinics on the EU AI Act, and it states that the Regulation attaches binding duties to Dutch care providers as its requirements phase in. The guide says 2026 is the year for hospitals to get organised, and it addresses hospital boards, compliance officers, chief information officers, chief medical information officers and quality and safety managers. It states that the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation and Dutch healthcare law each place their own demands on the same tool. The article says the guide explains what applies, when it applies, and how it sits alongside existing medical device and data protection rules. It states that generic policies will not cover that, and it presents itself as a jurisdiction-specific roadmap.

The article states that the AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and applies directly in every EU Member State, including the Netherlands, without national transposition. It says Dutch hospitals are caught as deployers of AI systems and, in some cases, as providers where they build or substantially modify tools in-house. It states that AI that is, or is a safety component of, a medical device under the MDR or IVDR is generally classed as high-risk, which brings the strictest obligations. It says the Regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024, that prohibitions on unacceptable-risk practices and the general provisions applied from early 2025, and that obligations for general-purpose AI models followed later in 2025. The article states that high-risk systems that are, or are safety components of, products covered by EU harmonisation legislation such as the MDR and IVDR have the longest transitional period, running to around mid-2027.

The article states that the AI Act forms part of the European Commission's wider European approach to artificial intelligence, and that Member States must still designate national competent authorities to supervise and enforce it. It says a hospital is usually a deployer of systems bought from vendors, and that if it develops a tool internally, puts a system on the market under its own name, or substantially modifies a third-party system, it may become a provider. It states that providers of high-risk AI carry the full weight of conformity assessment, technical documentation and post-market monitoring, while deployers have a narrower but still significant set of duties covering human oversight, monitoring of operation and use in line with the instructions. It says the five priority actions for 2026 are to inventory every AI system in use, classify each against the high-risk criteria, assign governance responsibilities, align supplier contracts with AI Act duties, and put human oversight and post-market monitoring procedures in place. The article states that transitional arrangements are detailed and system-specific, so the dates for each tool should be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

The article states that the MDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and the IVDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/746, and that the AI Act adds AI-specific obligations on top, including data governance, transparency, human oversight and post-market monitoring of AI performance. It says the Regulation tries to avoid duplicated burdens by allowing AI Act requirements to be built into the existing medical device conformity assessment where possible, so one process can address both. It states that almost all clinical AI processes health data, which the GDPR treats as a special category of personal data with enhanced protection, and that hospitals need a valid legal basis for processing, data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, and a clear approach to the rules on automated decision-making where AI outputs materially affect patients. It says the Dutch Data Protection Authority enforces the GDPR and issues guidance on AI and health data, and that the AI Act's data governance rules and the GDPR are distinct but reinforce each other. The article states that Dutch sector law sits over the EU regimes and names the Wet kwal, Wkkgz and WGBO.

The article states that the difficulty is that several regimes apply at once, and that the AI Act does not replace the MDR, IVDR or GDPR but sits on top of them. It says governance is not optional, and that human oversight, risk management, technical documentation and post-market monitoring all need named owners, standard operating procedures and board-level reporting. It states that the first route to high-risk status captures most clinical AI, and that if a tool is software qualifying as a medical device under the MDR or a diagnostic device under the IVDR, and that device needs notified-body involvement, the associated AI is treated as high-risk. It says the European Commission's medical devices portal and Medical Device Coordination Group guidance help establish when software is a medical device at all, and that the European Data Protection Board gives guidance on how the GDPR intersects with AI. The article states that Dutch government guidance on AI policy gives national context for how the EU obligations fit the domestic landscape.

The article states that for planning purposes 2026 should be treated as the year to complete internal readiness, so that systems, documentation and oversight processes already work when the high-risk obligations apply in full. It says procurement and IT roadmaps will need AI Act milestones next to existing MDR compliance schedules, and that classifying systems, rewriting contracts and building governance takes real time. It states that each system must be assessed on its own intended purpose and device class, and that borderline cases should go to qualified regulatory advisors. It says the determination should be recorded for every system and that it must be able to be defended. The article states that the window during 2026 is finite, and it leaves open the detailed transitional dates for each tool, which it says must be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service urges Congress to evaluate defense against agentic AI cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service warns that agentic artificial intelligence could automate complex cyberattacks that usually require entire teams of hackers. The document highlights a mid-September 2025 operation that Anthropic attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group known as GTG-1002. This specific group allegedly automated between 80 percent and 90 percent of a campaign that targeted approximately 30 different organizations. Some researchers have since questioned whether this particular attack was actually as autonomous or successful as the initial reports claimed.

The report suggests that Congress should evaluate if the Department of Defense is appropriately postured to detect and respond to these autonomous threats. It notes that the Cybersecurity and Information Systems Information Analysis Center has found no official government policies specifically addressing agentic AI yet. Under Section 1535 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, which became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025, the Secretary of Defense must establish an AI Futures Steering Committee by April 1. Additionally, the report questions if voluntary partnerships with the Department of Commerce Center for AI Standards and Innovation should be made mandatory.

The Congressional Research Service describes agentic AI as systems that can pursue specific goals while requiring very limited human supervision. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency claims that its AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can fix open-source vulnerabilities faster than human teams. This capability could potentially support a strategy of AI-on-AI defense to counter the speed and scale of autonomous attacks. The AI Futures Steering Committee is expected to deliver its official findings to congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027.

Congress may use these upcoming findings to determine the necessary authorizations, appropriations, and general oversight for Department of Defense agentic AI programs. Lawmakers are also considering the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which was part of Public Law 114-113. This specific information-sharing law is currently set to expire on December 11 under an amendment found in Section 2011 of Public Law 119-103. These legislative steps aim to address the evolving capabilities of militaries exploring autonomous decision-making and operations.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.Headline: Senate passes permitting bill that limits environmental laws and requires data centers to pay grid costs
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, S.5653, on Nov. 19, 2026, by a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans. Thirty Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against the bill. The bill's sponsors are Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for the legislation in a Nov. 20 news conference. The bill must win approval in the House to advance, and the House could amend it, which would require the Senate to approve the new text. The bill would limit the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The Natural Resources Defense Council's analysis concluded that under the bill a court "can never invalidate a permit" based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill would cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

About 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. The bill requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy, said there are priorities both sides want and the bill "is not perfect." Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning, said it is reasonable to be concerned that development of each kind of project Ruffalo mentioned could be facilitated by the bill. Henderson also said the bill's impacts are highly uncertain, depending on political, market, geopolitical and legal outcomes.

The NRDC analysis said that if the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits. Ruffalo's representative did not respond to an inquiry for the article. Mark Ruffalo said in a Nov. 18 video viewed 22 million times that the bill would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants and ICE camps while sacrificing clean water, tribal rights, public lands and endangered species. Groups supporting the bill include the Solar Energy Industries Association, the AFL-CIO, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute.

Groups opposing it include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union. Opponents say their concerns about ICE facilities stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida. Ezra Klein, a New York Times columnist considered left of center, said he was "unnerved" by conflicting interpretations of certain provisions but still supported the bill. The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts.

Supporters said growing energy demand and rising electricity prices meant a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs. Critics say the bill effectively guts tools to prevent local governments, citizens, Native American tribes and other local interests from blocking harms caused by such projects. Critics also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure. The NRDC analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill's positive features, including improving electric capacity by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and enabling construction of new lines.

The bill's fate in the House is uncertain, and the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know whether Ruffalo's scenario will come to pass. The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access, Klein wrote. The bill does not directly address ICE detention facilities. The articles leave open whether the House will amend the bill and whether the Senate would then approve new text.

stories.Headline: MYCPE ONE acquires AssureOne to unify AI accounting workflows for firms
stories.Summary:
MYCPE ONE, a partner to more than 3,000 CPA and accounting firms in the United States, acquired AssureOne, an AI-first tech platform for practice management, tax, audit and bookkeeping work, the companies said on November 23, 2026. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. AssureOne is a unified, AI-native platform that brings practice management, tax automation, accounting automation and audit automation together on a single system. AssureOne is currently used by 40 firms. AssureOne began modestly in April 2026 and has since grown to a team of 40+ engineers, designers and product specialists.

AssureOne does not bill seats per user, and firms pay a small monthly fee for each client they serve, with every plan including team seats. Across the board, AssureOne is designed to come in at roughly 40, 50% below most comparable platforms on the market. The average firm runs anywhere from four to five different applications to manage the layer above its core accounting, tax-prep and audit-engagement software. AssureOne tracks Section 7216 consent natively, a key compliance requirement for firms working with offshore preparers. AssureOne connects with leading tax software including CCH Axcess and UltraTax CS, with further integrations in the pipeline, and integrates with QuickBooks, Xero and other accounting software.

Shalin Parikh, CEO of MYCPE ONE, said the company believes the future of serving the accounting industry lies in the combination of talent and technology, and that AssureOne complements that vision perfectly. He said AssureOne is solving the real, everyday problems that CPAs and accounting firms face today. He said that by bringing talent and technology together on a single platform, the company can do more than offer firms multiple services in one place. He said the combination can meaningfully elevate firms' productivity, the quality of their work and the way they serve their clients. Shalin (Shawn) Parikh, CEO and Co-Founder of MYCPE ONE, said accounting firms are tired of managing a patchwork of disconnected software and bolt-on AI features.

He said their people spend hours every week moving the same data from one tool to the next. He said AssureOne brings practice management, accounting, audit and tax work together, with AI built into each workflow from the start. He said more than 3,000 firms already trust MYCPE ONE with their teams and their training, and that the staff it places can now do that work inside software it owns. AssureOne's practice management module competes with platforms such as TaxDome, Canopy, Karbon, Financial Cents and Ignition. AssureOne also competes with emerging AI players such as Basis and Double.

AssureOne's vision has been to unify the entire layer that sits on top of a firm's core accounting, tax-prep and audit-engagement software into one coherent system. The platform was built around a clear vision to make an accounting firm's technology stack leaner and to empower firms to use technology in a way that makes them more productive and cost-efficient. AssureOne is led by accountants, people who understand the profession's problems firsthand, and the platform has been built in close collaboration with firms. MYCPE ONE trains its staff directly on the platform, so firms get the technology and people ready to use it from one partner. The company is building this for firms of every size, so capabilities once limited to the largest 200 firms become available across the profession.

AssureOne plans to add new modules, including Sales Tax Automation and human resource management, while deepening the features in every existing solution. On the tax side, the roadmap includes more integrations with tax prep software, review features for tax returns, support for more forms, and research and advisory features. On the accounting side, AssureOne plans to extend its current features and add industry-specific capabilities, so firms can build their own playbooks and advise clients in more depth. Tax review capabilities are in active development. The articles do not say what MYCPE ONE paid for AssureOne or when the acquisition closed.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI launches a $250,000 art commission for its Abu Dhabi campus
stories.Summary:
During Frieze Abu Dhabi week, the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence announced that it will launch an art commission with a budget of up to $250,000, according to ARTnews. The task is to create a major sculpture or installation for the university’s Abu Dhabi campus, and the winning commission will be displayed in the university’s new cultural center that is slated to open in 2027. The artwork will be acquired for MBZUAI’s permanent collection, the report said. Artists applying for the commission can choose from one of three themes, which are the landscape, heritage and communities of the United Arab Emirates, artificial intelligence and scientific inquiry, or the history between science and computation in dialogue with art, mathematics and machines. The deadline for the commission is December 18, and the university will choose a shortlist of finalists who will be invited to create detailed proposals.

Each applicant will receive a $5,000 honorarium, according to the article. The university said it is building its art and special collections, and the works in its inventory span from the 13th century for special collections and art collections dating to 1925. The university collects works based on the arts and sciences, as well as materials that document what the article describes as the human pursuit of knowledge, creativity and research. Jasmine Soliman, head of art, archives and special collections at MBZUAI, said in a statement that the open call was shaped as an extension of the collection the university has built. She said that collection holds works spanning a century by artists who engage science through research, method and technique, treating knowledge as both an intellectual tradition and a material practice.

Dekyi (Hong) Liang, vice president and chief of staff at MBZUAI, said in a statement that it is the university’s responsibility to invest in cultivating a culture that embraces creativity and innovation. Liang said art has always been part of that story of human endeavor, adding that the new commission for the campus reflects a space where science and culture converge. The announcement came during Frieze Abu Dhabi week, and the article gives no further details on the selection process beyond the shortlist and the honorarium. The winning work is to be shown in the cultural center scheduled to open in 2027 and then acquired for the permanent collection. The article does not say when the finalists will be named or when the winner will be announced.

stories.Headline: L&T Technology Services launches SDVault.ai toolchain to support software-defined vehicle development
stories.Summary:
L&T Technology Services launched an AI-powered engineering toolchain called SDVault.ai on 23 November 2026, according to Analytics India Magazine, and the platform is designed to support the development and validation of software-defined vehicles. The company said the toolchain uses more than 250 AI agents spread across 12 engineering domains, which cover requirements, system architecture, functional safety, cybersecurity, software development and testing. SDVault.ai is part of LTTS' EI for Engineering suite and runs on the company's EIOne Engineering Intelligence platform. LTTS said the toolchain combines AI agents with rule-based automation for safety-critical activities while allowing engineers to keep control over engineering decisions, verification and certification.

The platform connects different stages of engineering by linking requirements and system architecture with software code, test results, failures and corrective actions, and it can be deployed across the engineering lifecycle or integrated with existing OEM and Tier-1 toolchains. LTTS also said customers could keep sensitive engineering data within their own controlled environments. In early pilots, the company said engineering teams using the platform showed the potential to absorb 30 to 40 percent additional workload, and selected workflows including ticket triage took about 10 minutes to complete compared with four hours previously. LTTS did not disclose the number of pilots or identify the customers involved.

Amit Chadha, the CEO and Managing Director of LTTS, said AI can help but in safety-critical engineering AI alone is not enough, and he said it requires deterministic engineering, domain knowledge, traceability and engineers firmly in control. The launch comes as services companies expand their use of AI in automotive software development, and the article notes that HCLTech launched an NVIDIA-powered validation offering for software-defined vehicles in October using AI agents and virtual simulations to automate parts of automotive software testing. LTTS reported 120 million dollars in annualised revenue from Engineering Intelligence-led solutions in the second quarter of its 2027 financial year. The company also secured 203 million dollars in large-deal total contract value during that quarter, with more than half of the deal value coming from AI-led wins.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated tracks and will remove over 29 million songs starting December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban and remove millions of songs created entirely by artificial intelligence. This decision follows a massive surge in submissions where over 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days were AI generated. The company intends to stop the flood of low quality content that is currently inundating its digital platform. This aggressive move aims to protect the visibility of human musicians against a tide of automated audio.

The removal process will begin on December 9 and is expected to delete more than 29 million songs by the end of the year. Under these new rules, the platform will reject between 80,000 and 85,000 tracks every single day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100 percent AI generated based on their metadata. While fully automated songs are banned, the service will still accept music that was created with AI assistance.

Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, stated on X that previous efforts to demonetize AI tracks in June were not enough of a deterrent. He explained that the sheer scale of these uploads means authentic artists are getting buried under a mountain of synthetic content. The company noted that 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of its library, are fully AI generated. They further observed that 96 percent of those specific automated tracks have received no streams at all.

Tidal claims to be one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music in such an outright manner. Other services like Deezer are introducing filters, while Spotify and YouTube Music have chosen to label the content instead of removing it. The company believes that drastic action is necessary to maintain the authenticity of the music discovery experience for its subscribers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.Headline: UK financial watchdog warns AI firms that transaction tools may require authorization
stories.Summary:
Britain’s financial watchdog warned technology companies on Tuesday that artificial intelligence tools able to handle financial transactions could bring their businesses under regulatory oversight, according to Reuters. The Financial Conduct Authority said companies developing autonomous AI products should work out whether their operations need regulatory authorization and should consult the authorities when appropriate. The guidance arrives as AI developers move beyond ordinary chatbots toward digital assistants that can carry out transactions and manage consumers’ financial affairs. The announcement coincided with Meta Platforms’ launch of its Muse AI assistant in Britain, an application Reuters reported has more than 10 million downloads since its US debut in September.

The FCA said a company’s regulatory obligations depend on the activities it performs rather than on its classification as a technology business, and services involving payments, financial recommendations and the marketing of financial products could fall within its jurisdiction. According to Meta, the Muse platform can help users renew auto insurance policies, obtain refunds and complete digital purchases. The FCA did not single out Meta or any other technology company in its guidance. Meta said in an emailed statement to Reuters that it had engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and would continue to do so.

The FCA said consumers should examine the safeguards available when delegating financial tasks to digital assistants and should consider the risks of sharing personal data. The regulator also acknowledged the potential economic benefits of AI adoption, including greater competition, improved productivity and broader access to financial services. However, the FCA said it was prepared to intervene against businesses conducting regulated activities without the necessary authorization. The growing autonomy of AI systems is raising questions about accountability, financial liability and the protection of sensitive personal information.

stories.Headline: Virginia lawyers discuss how AI affects hourly billing
stories.Summary:
The Supreme Court of Virginia approved Legal Ethics Opinion 1901 on Nov. 24, 2025, addressing reasonable fees when generative artificial intelligence is used, according to an article by Jason Boleman published Nov. 23, 2026. The opinion responds to concerns over how generative AI could impact traditional billing practices in Virginia. LEO 1901 reiterates that a lawyer shall charge reasonable fees under Rule 1.5 of the Virginia Rules of Professional Conduct. The opinion offers guidance for attorneys looking to shift from the traditional time-based billing structure. It states that time-based billing can only be based on the actual time spent on a task.

LEO 1901 states that Rule 1.5 does not equate reduced time with proportionally reduced fees when a lawyer uses generative AI or other productivity-enhancing tools. The opinion says such an approach would fail to account for the investment lawyers make in developing AI expertise and the continuing value of their professional judgment. It states that the skill requisite to perform the legal service properly might actually increase, as effective AI use could require specialized knowledge to prompt, verify, supplement and integrate AI outputs. LEO 1901 departs from guidance from other states and the American Bar Association, which stated in a formal opinion in 2024 that a flat fee may be unreasonable if a generative AI tool allowed the attorney to complete the task quicker. The Virginia opinion concluded that it is not automatically unreasonable for the same non-hourly fee to be charged if AI is used to assist an output.

Tricia Dunlap, founder and managing partner of Dunlap Law in Richmond, is a longtime proponent of alternative billing structures and said AI has transformed her firm for the better. Dunlap said that for decades small businesses went without preventive legal counsel because hourly billing made it unaffordable, and that AI and flat fees changed that. She has pivoted her firm from time-based billing to value-based billing, setting flat fees for work while ensuring rates are reasonable and ethical. Dunlap said her firm has become more profitable and has increased its services, and that it helped a small business uncover significant legal risks through a flat-fee engagement that traditional billing would have priced beyond its reach. Dunlap Law uses a proprietary AI-powered platform called DLOS that she said has helped increase collections by 25% and cut costs by 34%.

Richmond attorney Tim Bechen, a principal at Woods Rogers, said in his experience he has seen an increase in billable hours rather than time saved. Bechen credited that to an uptick in AI use by clients, saying clients now ask more complex questions and that AI does not have a lot of discernment. He estimated that sometimes his work will double in cost due to time spent addressing additional concerns brought forward by a client consulting generative AI platforms, and said he has had conversations explaining that a normally $10,000 project had become a $20,000 project. Bechen, who serves on Woods Rogers' AI committee, said he has noted an uptick in litigation in pro se third parties using AI and demand letters that are clearly AI-generated.

He said traditional time-based billing remains the industry standard and that fears of the death of the billable hour have been greatly overexaggerated, going back to when he started practicing in 2000. Bechen said the reason the billable hour exists is that it is a great way for the client and the attorney to know they are both getting a fair deal. He added that in flat-fee billing, concerns could arise around clients believing they are not getting a fair and equitable rate due to time saved by AI usage. Bechen said use of AI tools allows attorneys to focus on the more important issues versus the mundane stuff, starting from second base because AI gives them the concept.

He cautioned that attorneys spend the same amount of time on tasks to fact-check AI outputs and engage in deeper analysis. Bechen said the idea of AI taking over the legal profession is completely blown out of proportion, and that AI is always going to be an unpaid assistant, not a new first-year associate but an unlicensed paralegal that can give a first draft. Dunlap is described as a frequent speaker on AI and legal ethics, and Bechen uses hourly billing in his practice at Woods Rogers. LEO 1901 states that the opinions it cites fail to appreciate the value of advancing technology and the reaction of the legal markets to that technology.

The opinion states that while over time the market rate might drop based on dramatic improvements in efficiency, Rule 1.5 should not require the lawyer to surrender any benefit from the efficiency gains if clients continue to receive value from the lawyer's output. The article reports that one year after the opinion, attorneys report varying degrees of implementing alternative fee structures. The article leaves open how widely alternative fee structures will spread among Virginia attorneys. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after three rivals seek to replace its AI financing role
stories.Summary:
Gavin Baker of Atreides Management stated that at least three companies are competing to replace Nvidia as the financier for GPU buyers. This claim was written on X on November 20, 2026, during a period when Jensen Huang had resigned. The competition emerged because rivals wanted to take advantage of the absence of the founder and former chief executive. On November 23, 2026, the board of Nvidia unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer. Following this news, the shares of Nvidia jumped 31 percent on that same day.

The role of central bank involves funding neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, which Nvidia gave 2 billion dollars each this year. CoreWeave had 1.5 gigawatts of active power at June 30, 2026, and deferred revenue of 9.7 billion dollars by then. CoreWeave capital spending rose from 2.9 billion dollars in 2023 to 10.3 billion dollars in 2025, with 2026 guidance of 35 to 39 billion. Nebius expects prepayments and loans to cover 85 percent of its 2027 capital expenditures, which are 40 billion to 45 billion dollars. CoreWeave is also arranging a loan backed by its Meta contract, which is expected to yield 7 to 7.5 percent.

Interim CEO Colette Kress said on a November 17 earnings call that the company would be disciplined and selective in its support. She stated that Nvidia is proud of its role in the industry but must evaluate future transactions with a rigorous attitude. Kress added that the company needs to determine if these are the right types of investments for them to make. Gavin Baker believes the fear that Nvidia might stop funding its partners is misplaced because other aggressive competitors are vying. Baker says these semiconductor and hyperscale competitors are sometimes offering more favorable terms than those previously offered by Nvidia.

Investors in CoreWeave and Nebius feared their chip supplier might stop funding them, which could hinder their ability to build capacity. These neoclouds are building capacity for customers like Meta Platforms faster than their own available cash can cover the costs. Baker claims that neoclouds without a track record of operating clusters at scale may face consolidation if they lack prepayments. CoreWeave is affected by these dynamics, as its interest expense rose from 361 million dollars in 2024 to 1.2 billion. A new backer could potentially demand tougher terms than Nvidia did, which would increase the cost of money for CoreWeave.

Nvidia has been called the central bank of the AI circular financing economy for providing capital to lock in chip demand. The company has an investment portfolio exceeding 1,000 billion dollars, including equity in laboratories, power producers, and cloud computing companies. Regulatory filings from September 30 show Nvidia holds shares in eight public companies with a market value over 48 billion dollars. Nvidia has a 10 percent shareholding in CoreWeave and has also provided capital to Nebius Group, Intel, and xAI. The company participated in 129 venture capital and startup accelerator transactions this year, totaling 2,200 billion dollars in joint investments.

The next test for CoreWeave is whether its Meta-backed loan prices at 7.5 percent or less to signal lender confidence. Analysts expect CoreWeave revenue to grow from 5.1 billion dollars in 2025 to 45.1 billion dollars by the year 2028. It remains to be seen if the three unnamed companies mentioned by Baker will actually write the necessary financing checks. The articles leave open whether the 5,000 billion dollar fund involving Apollo and Blackstone will ever actually be invested. It is also unclear if Nvidia will remain the primary backer or if rivals will successfully take the crown.

stories.Headline: Natalie Buda Smith leads the Library of Congress in using AI to manage its collections and explore synthetic DNA storage
stories.Summary:
Natalie Buda Smith, the first leader of AI innovation at the Library of Congress, is currently guiding the institution in using artificial intelligence to manage its vast collections. The library maintains more than 181 million physical items and approximately 200 million gigabytes of digital data. Staff members are increasingly employing AI to analyze agricultural trends for the Congressional Research Service and to translate documents into English for public use. The institution has experimented with machine learning for nearly a decade to digitize manuscripts and identify images, but current technology is now far more accurate.

These new tools allow the library to re-upload old items because the computer vision no longer makes basic historical errors, such as mistaking a book for a cellphone. However, the library must now spend more resources to manage third-party bots that scrape the database and slow down the systems. Smith believes that blocking these companies is not an option because many people now use AI tools instead of web browsers to find information. She is also exploring a project to store data in synthetic DNA, which she claims could last thousands of years without using energy.

Natalie Buda Smith is responsible for these initiatives and explains that all AI produced work is still reviewed by human staff. She refuses to force the technology on resistant employees because she believes they must feel comfortable to use the tools effectively. Smith is currently hesitant to launch a public chatbot for the library because she has not yet found a system that is sufficiently authoritative and trustworthy. She views these efforts as part of a meaningful job to ensure the institution continues moving forward into the future.

stories.Headline: Bly Road residents sue Independence and developers to halt AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Residents along Bly Road in the Little Blue Valley area of Independence, Missouri, filed a 16-count, 52-page lawsuit on Wednesday in Jackson County Circuit Court in an effort to stop a hyperscale AI data factory that is under construction near their homes, according to the Independence GUARD (Guardians United Against Reckless Development) Alliance, which announced the filing on Thursday. The suit names the city of Independence, Missouri ADC Holdings LLC, which is described as the data center developer, and Independence Power Partners LP, a Delaware-based third party building a new natural gas plant to power the data center. The lawsuit alleges that the city violated zoning and sunshine laws as well as the city charter, and that it has failed to enforce city laws, and the residents are asking a judge to pause the project. The city council approved billions of dollars in incentives in March for Nebius, a Dutch tech company, to build and operate a 2.1-million-square-foot hyperscale AI data factory on 400 acres at the south end of Bly Road, and Nebius broke ground on the first phase in April. The lawsuit seeks a temporary restraining order to stop work at the site while the case proceeds, according to Steve Jeffery of the Chesterfield, Missouri, firm Jeffery Law Group, one of the attorneys representing the residents.

Jeffery said there is no check on what the developer is doing regarding noise limits, hours of operation, hours of construction, heavy truck traffic and construction traffic, and that the city appears to turn a blind eye to it, which he called the primary basis for the restraining order request. The defendants have 30 days to file their response, as is typical in civil cases in Missouri. The city of Independence acknowledged the lawsuit in a statement to KSHB 41 News on Thursday but denied any wrongdoing, saying the filing contains the plaintiffs' allegations, which the city will address through the appropriate judicial process, and that it disagrees with the characterization of its actions and believes the approvals and processes related to the project were handled in accordance with applicable law. The city also said it will not comment further on the specific claims at this time because of the pending litigation. Nebius Vice President of Public Affairs John Sutter said the company is reviewing the claims and cannot comment on the case specifics, and that Nebius remains committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations and being a responsible partner for the community as its investment in Independence takes shape.

Jeffery said the case is not about the broader AI discussion taking place across the country, saying his clients are not against AI, technology or data centers, but that there is a right time, place, process and procedure for such things and that the local governments did not follow the process. Bly Road resident Kelly Garrett said the community feels let down by the city and is upset, angry, disappointed and frustrated, and said the community was betrayed quietly and repeatedly long before residents had the chance to say a word. Daniel Moorehead, coalition leader of the Independence GUARD Alliance, said residents have endured months of disruption since construction began, including work that starts well ahead of daylight and ends well after it, and trucks that have gotten stuck and torn up the road in multiple places. Dawn Hahnfeld, a Bly Road resident who lives near the site, described constant noise, dust and banging in the middle of the night and late at night, and said the ultimate goal is to make the construction go away. Moorehead said the coalition intends to keep pushing, describing the residents as a handful of homeowners standing against some of the most powerful institutional and financial interests in the state, and said they have been treated as an afterthought at best and an obstacle to be managed at worst.

stories.Headline: Ashish Mishra urges governance for AI agents that act without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Ashish Mishra, Lead Solutions Architect for Agentic AI Services at NTT DATA, published an article on 16 November 2026 about governing AI that acts rather than only answers. He described a voice bot his colleague had asked to suggest an itinerary for a trip to France, which instead supplied one for India. Mishra called it an obvious hallucination that could be verified easily. He wrote that the consequences can be far more serious when an autonomous AI agent makes the wrong decision and runs with it. He said organizations are moving away from “vanilla” AI, which simply answers questions, toward AI that can make decisions, act and carry out entire business processes.

Mishra wrote that existing governance will remain relevant, covering the quality and accuracy of AI, data protection, privacy, security and bias. He said agentic AI does not change any of that and simply gives organizations more to govern. Traditional AI produces an output and a person decides what to do with it, while agentic AI can use other tools and systems, communicate with people or initiate the next step in a process without any human intervention. He said this means questioning the output as well as the activity throughout the workflow. He wrote that every agent should have a clear business purpose and a named owner, its own identity and access only to the information and tools required for its job.

Mishra said the excitement around new technology is understandable but that letting it get ahead of the controls is a mistake he sees far too often. He wrote that by the time you discover a problem, the agent may already have acted on it. He said organizations without effective AI governance can face compliance failures and operational problems, and that when AI acts without guardrails those consequences are amplified. He said an action that is difficult or impossible to reverse needs a different level of control than a simple day-to-day task. He wrote that if something goes wrong, you should be able to see what information the agent was working with, which tools it used and what approvals it received.

Mishra wrote that AI risk is no longer confined to the information an agent produces and now extends to the running of the business. He said AI agents can take information from emails, documents and websites and interact with different tools, systems and even other agents. He said testing an agent before it starts working is essential but you cannot stop there, because the information it receives and the environment it operates in will continue to change. He said you need to know what an agent can retain, how long it keeps that information and whether anything sensitive could be exposed. He compared an agent carrying out one small, contained task to hiring a freelancer for a specific piece of work.

Mishra cited NTT DATA’s 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for AI Leaders, which found that 55.9% of AI leaders use a centralized governance model, compared with 37.6% of other organizations and 33.3% of AI laggards. He wrote that NTT DATA has learned many of these lessons by being its own client zero, experimenting with AI internally and encountering security and compliance issues before taking that experience to clients. He said one of the most important lessons is to start with the end in mind, being clear about what an agent should achieve, how its value will be measured and what it is prepared to let the agent do. He wrote that trying to add the right controls once an agent is already operating across your business is far more difficult. He said applying governance to AI agents does not limit their freedom but puts the right rules in place for them to operate as intended.

Mishra wrote that before you build, you should be clear on the agent’s purpose, who owns it, the data it will use and how much freedom it should have. He said that before an agent goes live you should check its permissions, testing and approvals and make sure you can reverse or stop an action if something goes wrong. He said that once it is working you should monitor how well it performs, the decisions and actions it takes, how much it costs to run and whether it delivers the results you expect. He wrote that if you cannot see every agent operating in your business, trace what happened or step in quickly, you should start with visibility. He directed readers to learn more about NTT DATA’s Agentic AI Studio and how it can help build, govern and manage AI agents across their lifecycle.

Articles.Title: When AI moves from answering to acting: Getting governance right - NTT Data

stories.Headline: China-nexus actor uses AI agents to breach East Asian universities via zero-day flaw
stories.Summary:
A China-nexus actor used AI agents to breach universities across East Asia outside mainland China. The attacks began on September 8 and lasted for approximately 48 hours. The actor used the Cairn penetration testing tool to conduct these operations. These agents exploited a zero-day flaw in an open source medical imaging application. The goal given to the agents was to obtain shell access.

The agents mapped API endpoints and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They used path traversal to write files and execute a Python reverse shell payload. This process took about 11 minutes from mapping the API to gaining root access. One failed operation lasted 16 hours and involved 148 actions against a Redis instance. Another six hour operation tested 30,000 credential combinations against a university GPU server.

CJ Moses is the chief information security officer of Amazon Web Services. He wrote a report published on Friday by Amazon Threat Intelligence. Moses stated that agentic offensive operations are already happening. He noted that the agents adapted for nearly a full day without human direction. He advised that defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Cris Thomas is a security advocate at Semgrep and a former hacker. He said AI agents change the economics of vulnerability discovery without skilled humans. Ross Filipek is the chief information security officer at Corsica Technologies. He recommended that organizations maintain an inventory of exposed assets and restrict application access. These attacks affected universities in East Asia that ran exposed open source software.

Cairn is an open source, AI-based penetration testing tool used by threat actors. Other China-linked actors used Cairn to breach 10 organizations to steal secrets. These actors also used Cairn to automate an attack spree against high-profile websites. A similar tool called Artex is also used to facilitate and automate cyberattacks. The agents in this case researched public university presences to assemble usernames.

Defenders should monitor for suspicious uploads, unexpected file writes, and unusual process execution. Thomas suggests that security fundamentals must now work at machine speed with automated detection. Filipek advises that teams should analyze server logs to spot unusual patterns of activity. Organizations should decide in advance who has authority to isolate a server after hours. The articles do not state if the zero-day flaw was patched.

stories.Headline: China and ASEAN designate 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations declared 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation on Monday, November 16, 2026. This announcement occurred as the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol prepares to enter into force on December 1, 2026. The upgraded deal moves beyond traditional trade liberalization to cover emerging areas like the digital economy and green development. It aims to shift the regional relationship from simple market opening toward deeper institutional cooperation and coordinated standards. This new framework will address global challenges by creating a more stable and predictable regional market and industrial chain.

The protocol, signed in October 2025, includes a standalone chapter on supply-chain cooperation for the first time in a bilateral agreement. It covers hard connectivity in logistics and digital infrastructure, plus soft connectivity for electronic payments, invoices, and bills of lading. The agreement empowers a regional market of nearly 2.1 billion people through high-level commitments and improved customs procedures. China and ASEAN will establish sub-committees on standards, small and medium-sized enterprises, green development, and the digital economy. These measures will reduce business costs by encouraging the mutual recognition of conformity assessment results to avoid duplicate testing.

An official from the Ministry of Commerce of China said the upgrade reflects a commitment to multilateralism and free trade. The official stated that the deal will create a safe and open environment for digital trade and investment. MOFCOM will support local governments and industries by organizing targeted outreach and training for enterprises to understand new rules. The ministry noted that these arrangements will provide fresh impetus to Asia-Pacific economic integration amid global trade uncertainty. They believe that improving system compatibility through digital cooperation will enhance the competitiveness of regional products more than tariffs.

Poh-Yian Koh of FedEx China said AI adoption must translate technology deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. Robin Li of Baidu warned that AI risks becoming a bubble if it does not translate into practical business value. Yang Ting of Agilent Technologies noted that AI helps life sciences customers make faster decisions and improve data quality. Fang Ling of Alstom stated that AI can improve rail reliability but requires rigorous validation in real operating environments. Winnie Ma of VF Corp said realizing AI potential requires responsible governance and a combination of technology and creativity.

China has remained the largest trading partner for ASEAN for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has led for China for six. In 2025, the value of bilateral trade between the two sides exceeded 1 trillion dollars, up 18 times since 2002. Business leaders recently met at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, to discuss AI productivity. Executives highlighted China's AI Plus initiative and its large manufacturing base as key opportunities for multinational companies to validate applications. They noted that China's digital infrastructure and market scale provide a strong environment for the adoption of new technologies.

The two sides will now review relevant provisions under the protocol's future work plan and hold further AI consultations. APEC economies are called upon to share practical experience and expand digital skills to make AI applications more accessible. The Ministry of Commerce will continue working with ASEAN to advance practical cooperation and implement the new trade rules. The articles do not state when the specific sub-committees will be formed or the exact date for AI consultations. It remains open how businesses will specifically measure the tangible productivity gains mentioned by the various regional business leaders.
