stories.Headline: OpenClaw Foundation launches ShellBench to show top AI models fail 40 percent of real world tasks
stories.Summary:
The OpenClaw Foundation launched a new benchmark called ShellBench on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, to test various AI agents. This new system evaluates how frontier models handle a set of 100 real world tasks in messy environments. The foundation worked with partners including Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley to design the benchmark. It tests 13 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, DeepSeek, MoonShot, and Nvidia across five different agent harnesses. These harnesses include Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi to see how they perform on everyday work.

The benchmark uses realistic workspaces like emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, receipts, and PDFs to test models with short requests. Top models including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.2, and Gemini 4 Carbon hit a 60 percent completion rate. Meta Muse Wonder 1.0, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, and Claude Sonnet only passed roughly four out of ten tasks during the tests. GPT-6 Astra cost 1.01 dollars per run for a 62.5 percent accuracy rate, while GPT-6.1 Sol cost 17 cents for 61.4 percent. Open source harnesses like Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, and Codex CLI were slightly more accurate than the proprietary Claude Code harness.

Vincent Koc is the chief architect at the OpenClaw foundation and he spoke about the goals of the new benchmark. He stated that the foundation wanted a good distribution of tasks to get clear signals on how the models performed. Koc explained that the primary focus of the testing was on everyday use for the AI agents in the field. He believes that models aligned with personal use will be more effective for enterprises deploying agents at scale for employees. He noted that some of these tasks will eventually become more realistic to meet specific individual needs of the users.

The results showed that 51 percent of task failures were due to information omission even when relevant data was collected. In 87 percent of those failure cases, the agents had actually found the information but failed to include it. GPT-6 Astra showed inconsistency by dropping from a 75 percent accuracy rate to 49 percent over three repeated tests. The findings suggest that these systems may not be as reliable as common benchmarks make them seem to organizations. This research provides a reality check for enterprises that want to embed AI agents into every part of their workforce.

The articles state that 2026 has been the year of agents with many discussions on making them more secure and useful. Most enterprise work is far messier than the clean environments used in benchmarks for complex coding, mathematics, and science. Many major model providers tout impressive coding performance, but ShellBench tests how agents actually perform in messy enterprise contexts. The benchmark was created because the places where everyday work is done are rarely as organized as other AI test settings. This research highlights that paying more for a model does not always result in a more capable AI system.

The OpenClaw Foundation announced that the full results of the ShellBench testing would be available to the public starting today. The benchmark reveals that leading agents fail to fully complete four out of every ten tasks on average during testing. The data shows that the three highest performing models had very little difference in performance despite having wildly different prices. The articles do not state if the model providers will change their systems based on these specific failure rates. It remains open whether the identified information omission issues can be fixed to improve the overall task completion rates.

stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate. The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems.

It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly. Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business.

She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: LexisNexis finds 20% of law firms rely heavily on a few partners for revenue as AI reshapes how expertise is shared
stories.Summary:
LexisNexis published research on 23 November 2026, based on a survey of more than 500 private practice lawyers across the UK and Ireland, which found that 20% of firms are either completely or heavily reliant on a handful of individuals for revenue. The research was presented in an article by a Legal Futures associate, and it describes the traditional rainmaker model, in which a successful partner builds the client relationship, wins the work and becomes closely associated with the revenue that follows. The article says that model is not going away, because legal services are still built on relationships and clients still want advisers they trust, but it argues the model is beginning to shift. The research also found that 65% of lawyers now use AI for legal research, while more than half use it for document analysis, knowledge management and client drafting. The article says the old model concentrates value around the individual partner, including the relationship, the matter history and the commercial context, which can be powerful but also creates risk, since the impact of a partner leaving can reach well beyond the loss of a senior lawyer.

The emerging model it describes is more distributed, still recognising the importance of the partner but placing more weight on the firm's wider platform, including deeper teams, shared knowledge, consistent delivery and technology-enabled ways of working. The article says AI makes it easier for firms to capture expertise, reuse knowledge and deliver work more consistently across teams, which challenges the assumption that much of the value sits in one person's head. It says personal expertise does not become less important, but that it can be turned into a stronger institutional asset. The article says clients increasingly expect the wider firm to deliver consistently, efficiently and transparently, with depth behind the relationship, continuity if people move on, and outcomes that can be explained to the business. It says that if AI can support faster research, document review and drafting, firms will need to show more clearly what clients are paying for, and that the answer will increasingly sit in judgement, quality, speed, commercial insight and confidence in the right result.

The article says the rainmaker is unlikely to disappear, but the role may become less about individual ownership and more about building trust that can scale. It says the most valuable partners will still win work and build relationships, but will also help develop teams, share knowledge and create client relationships strong enough to outlast any one person. The article frames the question for law firm leaders as a practical one: how much of a firm's value sits with individual rainmakers, and how much has been built into the platform around them. It does not say what firms or regulators will do next, and it gives no further dates or figures beyond those above.

Articles.Title: Is AI set to reshape the traditional law firm rainmaker model?

stories.Headline: China names 34 flagship smart factories to expand AI use into consumer goods sectors
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology named 34 facilities as flagship smart factories on Thursday, November 23, 2026. This latest group of recognized sites includes manufacturers of electronics, alcohol, and clothing, showing a shift away from heavy industry. One of these highlighted facilities is operated by the Jiangsu-based HLA Group, where artificial intelligence helps coordinate production. These systems work alongside human operators to turn consumer preference insights into specific design ideas.

The program was launched in 2024 to upgrade supply chains through the use of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. It requires factories to integrate smart systems that can analyze market trends and streamline the manufacturing process. By recognizing these 34 facilities, the government aims to encourage the adoption of high-tech tools across various consumer goods sectors. This transition allows manufacturers to better understand what customers want before a product ever reaches a retail shop.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology is responsible for identifying these flagship factories and overseeing the broader technological upgrade. Officials stated that the goal of the initiative is to modernize the way goods are produced and distributed throughout the country. They believe that integrating AI into the manufacturing sector will create more efficient supply chains for a wide range of products. The government intends to continue promoting these advanced systems to ensure that Chinese industry remains competitive.

Articles.Title: From steel to style: China’s ‘flagship’ AI factories move beyond heavy industry - South China Morning Post

stories.headline_source: From steel to style: China’s ‘flagship’ AI factories move beyond heavy industry

stories.Headline: Expert Institute issues guidance requiring expert witnesses to verify AI outputs and disclose their use
stories.Summary:
Expert witnesses across the country and in New York have submitted reports and provided testimony made with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Gemini in the courtroom, amNewYork reported on November 23, 2026. The article, by Isabella Gallo, said this has led to claims that could not be corroborated, fake citations and unsourced reasoning that AI inexplicably produced. It said reports have included information deemed inadmissible, not credible or otherwise unreliable. In some cases the problematic testimony was struck from the court's record after it had been introduced. The Southern District of New York courthouse at 500 Pearl Street in Manhattan was pictured with the story.

The article said guidelines and rules specifically for how expert witnesses can use AI have remained largely absent from the conversation, especially from official legal organizations like bar associations and court systems. It said the New York City Bar and the New York State Unified Court System have not offered guidelines beyond short statements within guidance for attorney use on AI. Those statements suggest attorneys should be checking expert statements they are commissioning before bringing them into the courtroom. The article said the existing Frye or Daubert standards and general federal rules of evidence require experts to show their technology or scientific methodology is reliable, generally accepted by peers and produces a consistent outcome. It said Expert Institute connects experts with lawyers on roughly 10,000 cases in New York and about 100,000 across the U.S. a year.

Heidi Brown, a New York Law School professor and scholar considering how AI is impacting the legal system, said lawyers, self-represented litigants and judges have gotten into hot water for not checking citations in expert reports or declarations. She said it is problematic if experts cannot show reports can be authenticated or grounded in genuine facts that relate to the case. She said she really does think there needs to be guidance. She said the problem with AI is it is not like a calculator where you get the same answer every time, and the answers can vary wildly. She said experts can and should be permitted to use the tools if they are helpful, but must be aware of reliability and admissibility standards and handle questions about them in depositions or on the stand.

Michael Talve, Expert Institute's CEO, said there have been a number of instances of expert witnesses using AI in an unregulated manner with zero oversight or consideration for the repercussions. He called his company the authority on expert witnesses and the largest company in the expert witness services space, and said creating its own guidelines was an appropriate measure for stewards of an activity critical to the justice system. He said experts need accountability because their opinions can determine the outcome of litigation and this has largely been overlooked. He said AI should improve productivity but certainly should not replace professional judgments, and experts ought to personally verify any AI-generated info and be accountable for their conclusions. He said that without some guidance, experts are prone to run into issues he thinks are avoidable.

The article said one expert was sued in a federal case out of Houston after allegedly using an AI tool to prepare at least 80% of a report for 3M's legal team. It said the report was intended to show whether the manufacturer, accused of being at fault for a Texas warehouse explosion that killed workers, should be on the hook for damages. It said lawyers opposing 3M found the expert had created the report by prompting ChatGPT to show how 3M is 0% at fault for the explosion. It said others have been unable to back up or explain calculations they had an AI tool make, or unable to show demonstrative exhibits relate to the case, leading judges to rule their methods unreliable. It said money clients spent on those experts went down the drain.

Expert Institute began rolling out its guidance last week and will formalize it as part of its terms and conditions in January, the article said. The guidance will generally require experts to verify everything the AI tool puts out themselves, check every data point and statement obtained from an AI tool, and disclose their AI use. It states experts should never defer to an AI tool for an actual opinion or judgement, and may use it for deeper research, summarizing for internal work and organizing records. It states they may not use it for judging the credibility of other witnesses or evidence or drafting or generating an opinion, and may never enter confidential information into a program. The article said Brown thinks clear, explicit guidelines from bar associations and court systems, with examples of expert AI use gone wrong and gone right and current court opinions, would help.

Articles.Title: A shaky stand: New York court’s lack of AI guidance for expert witnesses may put case integrity in danger - amNewYork

stories.headline_source: A shaky stand: New York court’s lack of AI guidance for expert witnesses may put case integrity in danger - amNewYork

stories.Headline: HCLTech and Cohere partner to deliver sovereign AI in Canada and Germany
stories.Summary:
HCLTech and Cohere announced on 17 November 2026, in a release dated from Noida, a partnership to design and deliver what they call sovereign AI solutions to enterprises and public administrations. Under the agreement, HCLTech becomes one of Cohere's preferred global systems integrators in two countries, Canada and Germany. The release presents Canada and Germany as priority markets for HCLTech and says sovereignty is shaping AI adoption by businesses and governments there. The agreement combines Cohere's platform and models, including North, its agent platform, with the integrator's professional services.

Initial developments will target insurance, financial services and industry, with the release citing claims processing that takes jurisdiction into account, secure analysis of sensitive financial data and faster access to technical documentation as examples. Solutions will be installed in the environment chosen by each client to meet data residency, security and regulatory requirements, and Cohere's presentation lists public or private clouds, on-premises installations and fully air-gapped environments as possibilities. Only one certification is cited, ISO 42001, the international standard for AI management systems, which both companies hold. Nothing in the release indicates exclusivity, and the release does not say which entity contracts or where the teams operating the systems are based. France remains outside the announced scope, and the two companies say only that they want to extend the partnership to the rest of the world, with no timeline.

Phil Blunsom, Cohere's chief technology officer, said organisations should not have to choose between the benefits of AI and control of their data, according to the release. Vijay Guntur, his counterpart at HCLTech, and Dave Chopra, who heads the Indian group's Canadian operations, are also quoted, and the only country manager to speak is Canada's. As of 19 November, Cohere's press room did not mention the agreement. HCLTech reports more than 230,000 employees in over 60 countries and USD 14.8 billion in revenue for the twelve months ended September 2026, and its German headquarters is in Frankfurt/Eschborn.

The release mentions none of Cohere's other German elements: its merger with Aleph Alpha, its latest funding round led by the Schwarz Group and its offering on the STACKIT cloud. The Aleph Alpha merger, announced in April, produced a definitive agreement on 16 September, and the combined entity will operate under the Cohere name with headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, keeping the Heidelberg office as a research centre and employing more than 1,000 people. The merger had not been declared closed as of 19 November, and Cohere and Aleph Alpha were expecting in September to close it before the end of 2026, within six weeks of that date. Each partner has other alliances: Cohere announced a global alliance with PwC on 5 October and a partnership with OpenText on 16 September, while HCLTech concluded a Global Premier partnership with Anthropic on 12 October.

Articles.Title: Cohere leans on HCLTech for sovereign AI in Germany - ActuIA

stories.Headline: TGood and LG enter the power resources market to meet AI computing demands
stories.Summary:
TGood and LG have rushed to enter the power resources market during a scramble driven by artificial intelligence. This race for electricity occurred as computing power demand surged, redrawing cost accounts for energy storage and gas-fired power. The scramble extended to gas fields, where advanced gas power has taken 69 percent of the market share. These events were highlighted during a Grid Revaluation Special Summit held on November 19. The summit gathered North American power traders, researchers, and gas-fired power operators to discuss shifting computing power loads.

The U.S. Department of Energy issued a 5.1 billion dollar loan to Alliant Energy last month for gas storage and power. This funding is earmarked for building 1.6 million kilowatts of new gas-fired power capacity in the United States. TGood signed a centralized procurement contract for power cabins at computing power centers worth 250 million yuan. Vertech, a subsidiary of LG Energy Solution, plans for North American production capacity to reach 70 GWh by next year. LG Energy Solution also reported backlogged energy storage orders reaching 160 GWh by the end of the third quarter.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that gas storage facilities function as warehouses for buying gas when prices are low. Tristan Doherty of Vertech stated that idle grid capacity can meet the pulse load of data centers. TGood claims its computing-power-power island solution reduces the construction cycle by about 70 percent compared with civil engineering. LG Energy Solution was selected for the NVIDIA DSX Ready energy storage partner list, which includes only three companies worldwide. These leaders suggest that batteries are now part of computing power infrastructure rather than just backup power supplies.

Residents in Lowell, Massachusetts, sued the state environmental protection department over the expansion of diesel generators at a data center. These residents have seen electricity tariffs rise by more than 50 percent due to the competition for power. Fifteen U.S. states are considering pausing new data center approvals to manage the growing power gap. The National Data Administration noted that China's computing power scale has reached 3.1 million PFLOPS, ranking second globally. The National Energy Administration estimates China's computing power electricity consumption will reach 800 billion kilowatt-hours by 2030.

BloombergNEF projects that new natural gas consumption from U.S. data centers will reach 15 billion cubic feet per day by 2035. This increment exceeds the total national gas consumption of any country except China, Russia, Iran, and the United States. Massachusetts released a regulatory framework in June requiring data centers to provide their own clean power and cover grid costs. Projects with peak power consumption exceeding 25,000 kilowatts must now obtain community approval before applying for official permits. New York State also released an advanced nuclear power master plan targeting 5 million kilowatts of new capacity.

Small modular reactors remain on the drawing board, with Amazon and Meta investing in X-energy and TerraPower respectively. TGood has expanded overseas with computing power center projects in Thailand and Malaysia during the third quarter. The company's total winning bids for overseas business have exceeded 1.3 billion yuan. Financial statements have yet to reflect performance, as TGood recorded a net operating cash flow of negative 188 million yuan. The articles leave open how the real cost impact will unfold as the real bill is yet to come.

Articles.Title: TGood & LG Enter Market Amid AI-Driven Power Resources Scramble: Advanced Gas Power Holds 69% Market Share, Real Cost Impact Yet Unfolds - 36Kr

stories.headline_source: TGood & LG Enter Market Amid AI-Driven Power Resources Scramble: Advanced Gas Power Holds 69% Market Share, Real Cost Impact Yet Unfolds

stories.Headline: Van Hollen pledges AI safety laws and a joint committee in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, and AI regulation has become a major flashpoint in that race, The Washington Sun reported on November 24, 2026. Senators meet Dec. 1 to vote on new leaders for the 120th Congress. Van Hollen is leveraging attention from technology outages, voter anger at AI companies and the costs of their data centers, and the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Congress has long discussed AI and the need for guardrails but has not acted in any significant way. Many see the technology posing an alarming threat to the nation and world.

Van Hollen's audience includes more than 30 Democrats who have not yet pledged their support to either candidate. In a letter responding to Sen. John Hickenlooper over the weekend, Van Hollen pledged to create a joint committee on AI, reform Senate rules and pass basic safety laws in his first 100 days as leader. The rules overhaul he backs comes from Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Steve Daines of Montana, and would need a two-thirds vote to pass, similar to the House's suspension calendar. Van Hollen pointed to a 2022 bipartisan tech antitrust bill that he said got stuck on the calendar after Schumer did not bring it to a floor vote that year.

Van Hollen said his joint committee would not usurp the lawmaking powers of the committees of jurisdiction and that the Democratic leader should not sit on it. Van Hollen told The Sun that tackling AI safety is an urgent matter and that it is an important part of why new leadership is needed for the future. Allison Biasotti, a spokeswoman for Schumer, said Schumer has been working with incoming Democratic committee chairs to develop an ambitious AI agenda before Democrats take over in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Schumer has emphasized the need to regulate the growing industry with a Democratic majority but has not backed a specific plan.

Schumer declared last week that Democrats will investigate the recent outages themselves if the Trump administration won't. Hickenlooper sent a letter to Schumer and Van Hollen last week asking for their day one AI plans, and told The Sun he wants a clear pledge on what the two would do. Hickenlooper said AI touches everything and that a select committee is essential so it can get the priority it needs. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, slated to lead the Senate Finance Committee, has said he needs to see more specifics on what an AI committee would do. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, set to lead the Senate Budget committee, told The Sun he is still in listening mode, though he has a sense of urgency ahead of the leadership elections.

Kaine said the right level of anxiety is somewhere between people saying the sky is falling and Donald Trump saying to relax. Some incoming Democratic committee chairs are unlikely to want to give up their jurisdiction. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Hickenlooper have said a select committee is essential. Van Hollen said in his letter that as Democratic leader he would support mandatory independent testing of leading AI models and hold companies liable for risks from models they never release.

Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, expected to chair the Commerce Committee, has proposed a six-point framework giving the government a role in setting AI safety standards. Sens. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Mark Warner of Virginia, the prospective Senate Intelligence Committee chair, have proposed an AI safety board and enforceable testing standards. As majority leader in the previous Congress, Schumer convened a series of closed-door insight forums in 2023 with tech executives, including Huang. The forums resulted in a bipartisan framework calling for spending at least $32 billion per year on AI research.

A joint committee as proposed by Van Hollen would include members from the House, where a bipartisan group of over two dozen members launched an AI Safety and Innovation Caucus last week. Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas, one of its co-chairs, backed the idea regardless of who leads the Committee, saying a bicameral, bipartisan joint committee puts the right structures and processes in place. The progressive wing of the caucus has called for restricting AI until a federal agency can be formed to oversee it. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 vote or which candidate will win.

They do not say whether the Merkley and Daines rules proposal will come to a vote. They do not say what the six-point framework or the proposed AI safety board would contain. They do not say when the promised comprehensive legislation or the basic safety laws would be introduced. They do not say what the bipartisan framework's $32 billion figure would fund.

Articles.Title: AI Emerges as an Issue in the Senate Leadership Fight - NOTUS

stories.headline_source: AI Emerges as an Issue in the Senate Leadership Fight - NOTUS

stories.Headline: Tenth Circuit requires attorneys to certify human review of AI-assisted filings
stories.Summary:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit adopted a new certification rule on November 23, 2026. This specific mandate requires attorneys to certify that any documents prepared with generative artificial intelligence were reviewed by a human for accuracy. The court claims to be the first federal appellate court in the United States to implement a rule specifically targeting the use of artificial intelligence to prepare briefs. This action aims to ensure that legal filings remain accurate despite the increasing use of automated tools. The new rule introduces two additional sanctions that the court can impose when attorneys fail to comply with the AI mandate.

The court may now deem the affected legal issue waived if the attorney does not follow the certification requirements. Alternatively, the court has the authority to strike the noncompliant document from the record entirely. These new penalties exist alongside other existing sanctions that the court can already apply to legal filings. Every attorney who signs a brief must now adhere to these strict verification standards. The officials at the Tenth Circuit are responsible for enforcing these new requirements for all legal filings.

They have established these rules to prevent the submission of inaccurate information generated by artificial intelligence tools. By requiring a human review, the court intends to maintain the integrity of the judicial process in Denver. The court believes that human oversight is necessary to catch errors that generative tools might produce. More to follow.

Articles.Title: 10th Circuit Adopts Certification Rule for AI-Assisted Filings, Becomes First US Appeals Court to Do So - Law.com

stories.headline_source: 10th Circuit Adopts Certification Rule for AI-Assisted Filings, Becomes First US Appeals Court to Do So

stories.Headline: City leaders say AI will grow demand for specialist skills at Manchester summit
stories.Summary:
More than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester for Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, to explore how AI can improve public services and deliver better outcomes for residents, according to an article by Sarah Wray published on 23 November 2026. The event discussed how AI is changing both the skills governments need and who needs them. Speakers argued that demand for specialist technical expertise will grow even as generative AI enables more people outside traditional digital roles to use and build with technology. The discussions are captured in the report “Make AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities,” which draws on insights from the event. The article says the extract looks into recruiting AI specialists, continuous skills development, and promoting inclusion through building AI literacy among citizens.

A central government leader at the summit argued that AI will reshape the skills governments need but challenged predictions that it will reduce demand for digital professionals, saying “We will indeed need more.” The speaker said demand for real expert frontier skills is expected to grow, with machine learning engineering increasingly recognised as a distinct capability sitting at the centre of developing AI solutions alongside software engineering and data science. The speaker said changing cyber threats are driving demand for advanced expertise, citing machine speed attacks on infrastructure and systems and the need for machine-speed response that cannot be done without frontier AI skills. The speaker said debates around digital sovereignty are triggering introspection and that to stay ahead of the competition you need to hire the very best talent. The article says generative AI is broadening the pool of people able to build digital solutions, with staff outside traditional technology roles increasingly able to create tools that previously required specialist teams and formal investment processes.

Sam Milsom, senior digital strategy officer at Manchester City Council in the United Kingdom, said local governments should not assume people’s level of knowledge on digital and AI. He said one of the biggest things needed is to just ask staff what training they want and need. He said governments go in with a lot of assumptions and that talking to the workforce to find out whether they want to use it, how they are using it and what they need to know has to be the number one thing. Keeley Crockett, professor in computational intelligence at Manchester Metropolitan University in the United Kingdom, stressed the need to tailor training to a diverse workforce including employees of different ages, abilities and levels of digital confidence. Crockett said “We should be adapting to people’s individual needs.

We cannot afford to leave people behind,” and that tech is evolving fast so training must be fast. The article says attendees broadly agreed that as well as recruiting AI specialists, governments at all levels will need to rethink roles, skills and ways of working across the organisation. Several speakers described efforts to upskill the workforce for AI, and one described a tiered approach in which civil servants receive practical training and access to an approved generative AI tool while political leaders are briefed on how AI models work, their potential applications and associated risks. That city also introduced responsible AI policies and governance structures to assess proposed use cases before implementation.

Speakers noted that as digital training scales up, a one-size-fits-all approach does not work. One city leader shared steps including free training centres offering courses in AI and other digital skills, neighbourhood digital support points where residents can receive help accessing online public services, a dedicated citizen service that identifies malware on devices connected to public Wi-Fi and alerts affected users, and free cybersecurity training. The article says established digital roles are likely to change quite dramatically as AI augments existing tasks, increasing the importance of end-to-end accountability and assurance. It says the takeaways include continuing to build specialist AI expertise, with governments needing new and evolving technical capabilities including machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, assurance and oversight.

It says AI capability should be organisation-wide, because as more employees use and build with AI, skills and accountability cannot remain confined to digital and data teams. It says training should start with what people actually need, assessing existing knowledge and tailoring training to different roles, abilities and levels of digital confidence rather than assuming a common starting point. It says skills development should be treated as continuous, with roles, skills and learning updated alongside the technology as AI evolves. The article says the report can be downloaded and that registration is open for Global AI Cities 2027, to be held on 24-25 May in Manchester.

It says the takeaways also include building capability beyond government by investing in residents’ digital and AI literacy, confidence and cybersecurity awareness so that increasingly digital public services do not leave people behind. The article does not say what specific actions governments committed to at the summit or how the report’s priorities will be implemented. It does not give the names of the central government leader or the city leaders who described their approaches. It does not say how many cities have adopted the tiered training approach or the citizen support measures described.

Articles.Title: Reshape and refine: building future-ready AI capability across cities - Global Government Forum

stories.headline_source: Reshape and refine: building future-ready AI capability across cities

stories.Headline: A Munich court holds AI model creators directly liable for memorized copyrighted works
stories.Summary:
The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence and large language models has created unprecedented structural challenges to the foundational doctrines of copyright law across the European Union, according to a legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance. The analysis examines friction points between the European legal acquis, specifically Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market and Regulation 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act. It traces the allocation of liability across an interdependent lifecycle and finds that a settled European legal framework governing infringement remains years away. That leaves a persistent deficit of legal certainty for actors in data gathering, model deployment and downstream application development. The analysis was reported by Bioengineer.org on 23 November 2026.

The analysis divides the generative artificial intelligence value chain into three sequential yet interdependent phases: data ingestion and training, model storage and dissemination, and downstream output. During training, developers harvest literary works, artistic images, music, films and press publications, and the central question is whether computing model weights is an actionable reproduction under Article 2 of the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC or an extraction under the sui generis database right. Article 3 of the Digital Single Market Directive provides a mandatory, non-waivable text and data mining exception for scientific research by research organizations and cultural heritage institutions on lawfully accessible works. Article 4 permits commercial text and data mining by any entity but is conditional on rightsholders not having opted out through machine-readable reservations or other appropriate mechanisms. Article 53(1)(c) of the Artificial Intelligence Act mandates that general-purpose model providers implement internal copyright compliance policies to respect reservations.

The analysis holds that the prevailing view in European legal scholarship is that training inherently involves acts of reproduction, aligning with Court of Justice of the European Union jurisprudence recognizing broad protections for permanent and temporary reproductions incorporating an author's intellectual creation. It notes that advocates of the non-copying thesis maintain that training merely extracts non-copyrightable statistical regularities into mathematical matrices rather than storing expressive works. The analysis states that the operational feasibility of opt-out reservations remains highly controversial when scraping occurs at web scale. It observes that Recital 105 of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the 2025 Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models suggest training falls under the mining provisions. It adds that several scholars and recent judicial opinions argue text and data mining was intended solely for analytical extraction of semantic information rather than the assembly of generative engines competing directly with expressive originals.

The analysis cites the landmark November 2025 ruling by the Regional Court of Munich in GEMA v. OpenAI, which addressed allegations that language models infringed copyright in song lyrics. The court defined memorization as a condition where a model retains training materials so that identical reproductions can be generated in response to targeted user prompts. It ruled that memorization constitutes a complete implementation of the work within the model, taking reproduction beyond the legitimate analytical scope of the text and data mining exception, and placed direct liability on the model creator rather than the user.

The analysis states that European infringement analysis under the Court of Justice's Mio/Konektra ruling requires protected elements to remain recognizable as the author's own intellectual creation. It notes that primary liability at the output boundary will in many practical scenarios naturally attach to the end user who prompts the system and downloads, commercializes or publicly communicates the generated asset. The analysis states that the operational opacity of deep neural networks establishes a profound epistemic barrier for both rightsholders and developers. It says the internal parameters of complex language models are not directly interpretable in a manner disclosing whether, or to what extent, individual protected works have been copied, memorized or transformed within mathematical weight matrices.

It observes that rightsholders struggle to demonstrate actionable copying while developers face symmetrical difficulties proving the absence of reproduction or the applicability of legal defenses. It adds that evidentiary standards and the allocation of burdens of proof have become fiercely contested terrain where statutory transparency duties under the Artificial Intelligence Act may prove insufficient to detect infringement. It notes that European copyright infringement has historically operated primarily under standards of strict liability, while certain aspects of infringement assessments require findings of volition or direct control poorly suited to autonomous or semiautonomous probabilistic engines. The analysis states that disentangling independent user liability from primary or secondary developer liability demands significant recalibration of doctrines governing inducement, accessory participation and contributory infringement across multiple commercial layers.

It notes that courts scrutinize a provider's degree of architectural control, actual or constructive knowledge of recurring violations, and implementation of technical safeguards such as output filters, prompt moderation classifiers and forensic watermarking. It adds that the absence of effective filtering tools where infringing outputs recur predictably can expose providers to negligence findings. It observes that the applicability of pastiche to synthetic imitations of artistic style remains heavily contested, since copyright safeguards concrete original expressions rather than broad, abstract stylistic conventions. It notes that complex doctrinal questions arise when users generate similar works unintentionally without prior knowledge of the training data, challenging traditional concepts of independent creation.

Articles.Title: European Copyright Law Faces Unprecedented Structural Challenges Across Generative Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle - Bioengineer.org

stories.headline_source: European Copyright Law Faces Unprecedented Structural Challenges Across Generative Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle

stories.Headline: South Korea deploys 8,000 metal detectors and seeks 10-year exam bans to curb AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea’s Education Ministry unveiled a set of measures on Nov 24 to tighten exam security, ahead of high school final exams, as AI-assisted cheating spread from national exams into classrooms. The ministry said it will deploy nearly 8,000 metal detectors for use in high schools and seek penalties ranging from expulsion to decade-long bans on the university entrance exam. The move came after three cases of cheating involving smart glasses were detected in high school exams in 2026. Some schools had already acted, including Baehwa Girls’ High School in Seoul, which issued an emergency notice on Nov 22, a day before its senior students’ final exams, and extended the measures on Nov 23 to first- and second-year students. The crackdown also follows last week’s Suneung, during which five test-takers were caught with smart glasses, miniature cameras or wireless earphones, and all five were referred for criminal investigation.

The government plans to distribute 7,989 metal detectors to the country’s 2,387 high schools, allocating three per school, with students screened before or after exams and checked again after restroom visits. Bags must be stored at least 50m from examination rooms, proctors will inspect glasses and clothing for concealed devices, and schools will disable campus Wi-Fi and monitor wireless signals. Students caught cheating with smart devices could receive zeros for all subjects examined that day, while schools will be encouraged to introduce disciplinary measures ranging from suspension to expulsion. The ministry is pursuing amendments to the Higher Education Act to extend bans on entrance exam participation for serious cheating from one year to up to 10 years, and other proposals include legal grounds for metal detector inspections, whistleblower rewards and prison sentences of up to five years for serious violations. The stakes are high because more than 80% of university places for the 2027 academic year will be allocated through early admissions, in which school records play a major role.

The ministry said it plans to obtain prior consent from students and parents to address potential human rights concerns over searches without an explicit legal basis. It also plans to establish a legal basis for metal detector inspections at high schools and to develop technological countermeasures in cooperation with the Science Ministry. Similar security measures will apply to university-administered entrance exams, including essay tests and interviews. Suspicious activity could trigger metal detector screening of an entire examination room.

Articles.Title: Metal detectors, expulsion, 10-year ban: Tougher measures in South Korea to combat AI exam cheating - The Straits Times

stories.headline_source: Metal detectors, expulsion, 10-year ban: Tougher measures in South Korea to combat AI exam cheating

stories.Headline: Korea plans 10-year exam cheating ban and five-year prison terms for AI-assisted cheating
stories.Summary:
Korea's Ministry of Employment and Labor announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it plans to extend the ban on retaking national technical qualification exams from three years to 10 years for people caught cheating, and to raise the maximum prison sentence to five years, which is more than double the current limit. The measures respond to concerns about AI-assisted cheating using smart glasses, miniature cameras and modified calculators. The first case of cheating with smart glasses in a national qualification exam was detected in May, and miniature cameras and modified calculators have since been used in connection with the tax accountant licensing exam. The ministry will also publish the scores of the top two candidates, along with average scores and score distributions by subject, to restore public trust in exam results.

The government has already begun tightening supervision, with stricter electronic device checks, additional proctors and Bluetooth-detection applications, and these measures were first applied to the security instructor licensing exam on Saturday, where six violations were detected among 11,554 candidates, including possession of tablets and smartwatches and failure to switch off mobile phones. Under the tightened rules, proctors will check that all electronic devices are switched off before collecting them, make random calls to test takers' phones before each session, and wear nonwoven fabric coverings to block hidden cameras. Authorities plan to introduce radio-frequency detectors, devices that can identify electronics even when switched off, mobile surveillance cameras and proctors' body cameras by the first half of 2027, and will conduct a comprehensive review of national qualification exams administered this year. The government also plans rewards for reporting cheating, seeks to standardize penalties across professional licensing exams including new criminal sanctions, and intends to expand practical and interview-based assessments.

Separately, the Ministry of Education announced that high school students caught using smart devices to cheat will receive zero scores in every subject tested that day, rather than only the subject in which they were caught, and schools will be advised that disciplinary penalties may include expulsion. Starting with this year's high school final exams, students will be encouraged to wear buttonless clothing or cover buttons with stickers, proctors will check glasses and clothing before each session, schools will collect electronic devices, store bags away from exam rooms and use metal detectors, and Wi-Fi will be shut down during exams while proctors monitor Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals. The new guidelines apply starting this semester, and middle schools are also encouraged to tighten supervision. The education ministry acknowledged that screening all students with metal detectors would be difficult to implement immediately.

stories.Headline: Li Bubai raises tens of millions of RMB across three PandaAI financing rounds
stories.Summary:
Li Bubai, born in 1999 and from Chongqing, completed three rounds of financing for his AI startup PandaAI, 36Kr reported on 23 November 2026. The seed round, angel round and angel+ round were completed in two consecutive months, with total financing of tens of millions of RMB. The rounds were led by Lighthouse Founders' Fund. Li entered the quantitative private equity industry at the age of 20 and once participated in the management of funds with a scale of over 1 billion yuan. He later ran the self-media account "Quantitative Li Bubai", which accumulated more than 200,000 fans.

The funds will be used for the development of AI trading large models, professional QuantSkills, multi-agent collaboration infrastructure and trading Agent development environment. They will further promote the construction of PandaAI OS, EVO and A2A technology systems. Users can ask an investment research question in natural language in PandaAI, and the model embedded in the platform can call data, codes and backtesting tools to assist in data analysis, indicator research and strategy verification. The team aims to help users complete research instead of directly giving trading suggestions. The final investment judgment and trading decision are still made by the users themselves.

Li said another name for trading should be decision-making, because the market gives quick feedback on judgments. He said quantification is first and foremost a research method with specific logic and technology behind it, and should not become a black box only a few professionals can understand. He said the significance of popular science is not only to eliminate misunderstandings but also to enable the flow of knowledge and technology. He said professional capabilities should not be mastered only by a small number of people who have resources and access thresholds. He expects the next-generation product to move towards A2A, an Agent-to-Agent collaboration mode he imagines as an "A2A office".

Some shareholders and customers thought his self-media work deviated from the original business direction. Team members comment that he has strong executive power, and that once he thinks of a direction he usually does not stay at the discussion stage but starts to do research and try to implement it. Early fans and the open source community became the first batch of users of PandaAI. Quantitative users can use it for factor research and strategy development, while subjective investors can use it to analyze research reports, collect data and sort out information. Li believes that in the next two decades Agents will also participate in the process of creating Alpha.

The team initially tried to use Coding Agent to help users write codes, develop strategies and do backtesting, but soon found that being able to write codes does not mean being good at trading. PandaAI therefore gradually shifted from a single-point tool to a complete AI investment research workflow. Li does not want PandaAI to become a company that follows the traditional expression pattern of the financial industry. He hopes it will represent a different temperament: young, technology-driven, and willing to re-enter this ancient industry with a new technology paradigm. The PandaAI logo, which he designed himself, combines a panda with the Iron Man helmet.

Li believes that in the past two decades excellent traders created Alpha relying on experience and research. He said that competition between people will still exist, and new competition will also unfold between different Agents and different research systems. He said what PandaAI wants to do is connect credible data, financial tools, Skills, Agents and the investment research workflow, so that AI can not only perform tasks but also discover rules, verify results and constantly adjust research methods. The articles do not give the dates of the individual financing rounds, the amounts of each round, or the names of any other investors. The articles do not say when PandaAI was founded or where it is based.

stories.Headline: Architect Labs unveils Frostbite, an AI-designed interaction net CPU
stories.Summary:
Architect Labs has introduced Frostbite, a CPU that executes programs as interaction nets in hardware and that the company says its AI agents designed from interaction net theory down to the final GDS. The company announced it in a launch post on X, and the article reporting it is dated November 23, 2026. Programs for the chip are written in Vine, a Rust-like language, and compiled to an intermediate representation called Ivy. The chip is a mesh of tiles, each with its own small local memory, and the company states that the AI agents co-designed the instruction set and chip architecture given only interaction net theory.

The design targets 7 nm, with timing at 800 MHz in synthesis and 500 MHz in final GDS, and one quad of 2x2 tiles plus 4 L3 nodes takes 0.792 mm². In pre-silicon tests the company reports 4.59x the performance per watt of a modern in-order CPU core across 25 workloads, with 6.02x on a 10-workload search set and 3.83x on a 15-workload held-out set, ranging from 23.12x on conv2d to 1.15x on fib, and 8.77x performance per area. The baseline is one core of a modern dual-issue, in-order superscalar CPU that Architect Labs does not name, citing legal reasons, and which occupies 0.895 mm² on the same process. The chip is pre-silicon only, and an FPGA-hosted playground is planned.

The research team used ASL, an in-house, machine-checkable specification language, as the single source of truth for the ISA, the Arcmodel system model, RTL and verification, and the spec translates to Lean, with the project passing 800k lines of Lean. Arcmodel first diverged from RTL by almost 250% in the worst case, and an automated fitting pipeline cut that to under 6% worst case and about 1.5% median, with Arcmodel simulating the full chip 660x faster than RTL. Agents first synthesized papers and built Python models whose output was a 141-page PDF, which was deleted after the first RTL pass because its estimates were physically unrealistic. Across 4 searches and an ablation round, agents tried 58 ideas and kept 37, and the company says the work stealing in which an idle tile takes work from a neighbor emerged during design and was not hand-specified.

Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont at POPL 1990, and in them a program is a graph of nodes whose computation rewrites pairs of nodes connected through their ports, with each node having one principal port so that active pairs never overlap and can fire in any order. Every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state to guard, and a 5-queens net has 3,183 interactions and a 262-step critical path, with about 12 interactions ready per step. Software runtimes such as HVM2 already run interaction nets on GPUs, and Frostbite moves the model into the ISA itself. The chip follows Redwood, an edge AI accelerator the company announced in August 2026.

stories.Headline: New bill aims to hold NY judges accountable for AI-generated court errors
stories.Summary:
State Senator Michelle Hinchey introduced a bill in the New York State Senate last week that would make improper use of artificial intelligence in court orders a sanctionable offense for the judges who issue them, the Queens Daily Eagle reported on November 23, 2026. The bill does not forbid judges from using AI, but instead creates new procedures for disciplining judges whose AI-generated court orders compromise the integrity of a case. Under the bill, if a judge's orders are found to contain fabricated legal authority, meaning statutes or case law that do not actually exist, that would amount to misconduct and the judge could be sanctioned. The State Commission on Judicial Conduct, which the article describes as the only authority in the state with the power to publicly admonish or remove a judge from the bench, would investigate the fabrications and discipline any offending judges.

The commission would be tasked with determining a judge's culpability, whether the fabrications affected the outcome of the case and whether to issue sanctions against the judge, with the exact punishment decided case by case. A spokesperson for the commission said it was reviewing the legislation and had no immediate comment on the bill. Hinchey said AI regulation for New York judges is needed because state and federal judges across the country have admitted to issuing error-ridden court orders created with AI tools, and she said judges make decisions that directly affect people's freedom and rights, so their work must be based on real case law and facts rather than AI fabrications. Hinchey claimed the legislation would be the first in the country to hold judges accountable when their reliance on AI causes real harm, and she said she believes it is critical that New York act now with meaningful guardrails to protect the judicial system.

The article reports that AI has been widely adopted by attorneys and law firms over the past year and is becoming more common in judges' chambers, citing a Northwestern University survey of federal judges released in March in which more than 60 percent of responding judges reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work and around 22 percent reported using such tools weekly or daily. Some judges have been caught citing case law the AI made up, sometimes called hallucinations, and in 2025 federal judges in Mississippi and New Jersey admitted to the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee that they used court orders with AI-generated content containing numerous errors, while an Oklahoma judge also admitted to issuing fictitious citations generated by AI. U.S. District Judge Julien Xavier Neals of New Jersey claimed the fabricated case law was created by a law school intern using ChatGPT without authorization or disclosure, and an order U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate of Mississippi issued for a civil rights lawsuit had incorrect names for both the plaintiffs and defendants and fabricated allegations not included in the original complaint. The bill follows a policy on proper AI use for judges and attorneys introduced by New York court officials, under which AI tools are available to Unified Court System employees through UCS devices only after they complete an initial training course, and use without that course is prohibited.

The policy also limits employees to a list of pre-approved and vetted AI tools, and in January the UCS released a 154-page report on how AI can expand public access to the courts while warning of security and bias risks if it is used haphazardly. First Deputy Chief Administrative Judge Norman St. George said at the time that the courts have a duty to carefully explore and fully understand AI's strengths and limitations so it may be used responsibly in furthering the delivery of justice across the state. In October the courts released further guidance for attorneys filing AI-generated information, saying attorneys are not prohibited from using AI and are not required to disclose it but remain fully responsible for every word they submit, and that fictitious case law could result in serious repercussions and sanctions. Hinchey said she will push to get the bill passed in the upcoming 2027 legislative session.

stories.Headline: Authors propose a human factors framework for designing AI-assisted endoscopy interfaces
stories.Summary:
The articles report a framework for human factors engineering in AI-assisted endoscopy, published in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology on 24 November 2026. The authors outline a design framework for aligning AI information delivery with the perceptual and cognitive processes of the endoscopist. The work draws on human factors engineering, the articles state. The articles say AI is transforming gastrointestinal endoscopy, enabling real-time detection, diagnosis and workflow optimization. The articles state that the clinical impact of AI depends as much on user-interface design as on algorithmic accuracy.

The articles state that poorly designed systems can erode situational awareness, increase cognitive load and diminish trust. The framework categorizes AI outputs into three functional domains, the articles state. The first is perceptual augmentation, including computer-aided detection tools that highlight visual anomalies. The second is interpretive and procedural decision support, encompassing computer-aided diagnosis and emerging interventional guidance systems. The third is integrative performance feedback, including computer-aided quality and post-procedural analytics.

The articles state that effective interface design across these tiers should emphasize clarity, context-specific information flow, explicit uncertainty communication and continuous human control. The articles say that as multimodal and generative AI systems emerge, their outputs must be presented in ways that preserve situational awareness and clearly signal their origin, purpose and reliability. The articles state that by embedding human factors engineering principles into design and regulation, AI tools for gastrointestinal endoscopy can evolve from passive detectors to cognitive partners. The articles say such partners would enhance vigilance, reasoning and procedural safety without displacing human expertise. The articles do not name individual authors or give direct quotations from them.

The articles state that the framework addresses the perception, cognition, action loop underlying endoscopic performance. The articles present a hierarchy of AI-derived information in gastrointestinal endoscopy. The articles describe a human-centred architecture for AI-assisted endoscopy as an adaptive control loop. The articles discuss operational modes and conversational reasoning in AI-assisted endoscopy. The articles do not name specific groups affected beyond endoscopists and patients implied by the clinical context.

The articles cite prior work on computer-aided detection trials, including studies by Repici and colleagues published in Gastroenterology in 2020 and by Gong and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2020. The articles cite a 2025 study by Budzyń and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology on endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to AI in colonoscopy. The articles cite work by Haslbeck and Hoermann published in Human Factors in 2016 on flight deck automation eroding fine-motor flying skills among airline pilots. The articles cite a 2025 Lancet piece by Berzin and Topol on preserving clinical skills in the age of AI assistance. The articles cite a 2026 study by Huang and colleagues in the American Journal of Gastroenterology on computer-aided colonoscopy alert fatigue and its effect on adenoma detection.

The articles do not state what happens next beyond the framework's proposal to embed human factors engineering principles into design and regulation. The articles leave open how the framework would be implemented or adopted. The articles leave open what regulatory bodies would do with the proposal. The articles leave open how multimodal and generative AI systems would be evaluated under the framework. The articles leave open the framework's effect on clinical practice.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Alan Turing Institute opens free 16-week AI deployment programme for UK business leaders
stories.Summary:
The Alan Turing Institute is running a free 16-week programme called the Practitioner's Hub: AI Deployment Studio for senior leaders who are responsible for, or closely involved in, decisions about adopting artificial intelligence. The programme is aimed at UK business leaders and will help participants choose suitable AI use cases, assess readiness, plan deployment, and evaluate results. It will also give participants the chance to develop a case study of their organisation's real-world AI deployment experience. The programme is part of the Alan Turing Institute's BridgeAI programme and is designed to support responsible, practical AI adoption at scale.

The programme includes 14 practical sessions, peer exchange, optional expert clinics and two in-person events. You can express an interest if you work for a UK-registered company in one of the UK's eight Industrial Strategy sectors, which are advanced manufacturing, clean energy, creative industries, defence, digital and technologies, life sciences, financial services, and professional and business services. Your organisation should be considering AI in a business-critical area, such as decision-making systems, operations or industrial systems, or compliance, safety and quality. You do not need technical AI knowledge to take part, and companies can apply as a team but should submit only one application each. Expressions of interest close at 11:59pm on 30 November 2026.

The programme is run by the Alan Turing Institute, which describes it as free and as part of its BridgeAI programme, and the articles give no further statement from the institute about who is responsible beyond that. The articles do not name any individual who said anything about the programme. The context the articles give is that the programme is designed to support responsible, practical AI adoption at scale, and that it sits within the institute's wider BridgeAI programme. The articles say that people can find out more and express their interest in the AI Deployment Studio, and that expressions of interest close at 11:59pm on 30 November 2026.

stories.Headline: Alexandra Cavazos leads a webinar on patent claims for AI-designed biological molecules
stories.Summary:
A complimentary webinar titled “Best Practices for Claiming AI-Designed Biological Molecules” is scheduled for Tuesday, December 8th, at 12 PM CST, according to IPWatchdog.com. The session is part of the SLW Chemistry and Biology Webinar Series, and Dr. Alexandra Cavazos will lead it. The article describes the event as a 30-minute webinar in one place and as a one-hour webinar in another. It says AI platforms now design biological molecules, and a single patent application often must protect both the platform and the molecules it creates.

The webinar will cover where software and life sciences claiming strategies intersect and how to use both to build broader, more durable patent protection. Using examples of AI-designed nucleotide sequences, proteins, and bacteriophages, it will address how to draft claim sets directed to both the platform and the product. Dr. Cavazos will also discuss how to keep those claims together through restriction practice and how to draft them with future enforcement in mind. The article says software and life sciences inventions rarely overlapped until recently, and that the line is disappearing as AI spreads across every industry.

Dr. Cavazos holds a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology (Biochemistry) from the University of California at Berkeley and a law degree from UCLA School of Law. She is a Senior Attorney at SLW, advising biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies, and the article says she has extensive experience with next-generation cell therapies, including CAR-T and CAR-B cell technologies, as well as RNA-based therapeutics. It says she is well-versed in CRISPR-Cas genome editing, bispecific and anti-CD20 antibodies, gene therapy vectors, and large molecule biologics. Ryan Connell, a registered patent attorney at SLW, is also listed in the article with his background in chemical engineering, materials science, biotechnology, and organic chemistry.

The article invites readers to register for the presentation and to share the invitation with a friend or colleague. It does not say what happens after the webinar or describe any other next steps.

stories.Headline: NY Gov. Hochul vetoes bill that would have required AI accuracy warnings
stories.Summary:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed a bill on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, that would have required artificial intelligence platforms to proactively warn users that the information they receive may be inaccurate, according to Gothamist. The bill had been introduced by Assemblymember Clyde Vanel and state Sen. Kirsten Gonzalez, both Queens Democrats, after Meta’s AI platform hallucinated sexual harassment allegations in 2024 against a number of state lawmakers, including the two of them. The state Legislature passed the measure by a near-unanimous vote earlier this year. Had Hochul signed it into law, the owner, operator or licensee of a generative AI platform would have been required to clearly and conspicuously display a notice on the system’s user interface warning that the system’s output may be inaccurate. Some AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, already display such a warning, but the New York bill would have required all platforms to do so, Gothamist reported.

X’s Grok, for example, includes a warning in its terms and services but not directly on the screen users see when they provide a written prompt. In her statement explaining the decision, Hochul wrote that she supports thoughtful, smart guardrails on AI to protect consumers, but she said the bill was too far-reaching and would have applied to artistic or expressive content that isn’t meant to be factual, possibly running afoul of federal free-speech protections. She wrote that the bill takes an inflexible one-size-fits-all approach to require notifications on all generative AI systems regardless of context and that in doing so it may present constitutional and pragmatic challenges. Hochul’s veto came after trade groups representing some of the world’s most prominent tech firms, including OpenAI and Meta, lobbied against the bill and warned of possible constitutional violations, according to Gothamist. Netflix and the Motion Picture Association also lobbied the governor on the measure, according to state disclosure records.

Vanel said he believed he had worked with the industry to come up with bill language that was flexible enough to accommodate different types of platforms. He said he is hopeful he can work with the governor’s office to come up with some sort of compromise next year, when the state Legislature returns to Albany, and that the main thing is he hopes they both agree that some sort of disclosure is important. Hochul has had an up and down relationship with AI companies, Gothamist reported. Earlier this year she unilaterally implemented a temporary moratorium on large-scale data centers, including those used by AI providers, and made it a key part of her reelection campaign at a time when polls showed voters in New York and beyond were deeply skeptical of the facilities. She has not yet taken any action on a more-stringent moratorium that lawmakers approved earlier in the year, which is stridently opposed by tech firms, and she has until the end of the year to sign or veto that bill.

stories.Headline: Bain says enterprises must define agent permissions and oversight before letting AI act
stories.Summary:
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Bain & Company attended a hands-on lab where participants built a data lakehouse and applied sentiment analysis to customer interactions, with Copilot helping write and troubleshoot the code, and its suggestions and corrections were consistently on target. In another session, an IT agent handled a service ticket by diagnosing a device problem, checking policy and identity context, changing group membership, syncing the device, and verifying the fix. The lab showed how quickly teams can build, while the service-ticket demo raised a tougher question about whether an enterprise would let that agent change someone's access rights inside the business tomorrow, and how it would know the agent made the right call. Bain's takeaway was that better models are not enough, because agents need to understand how a business actually works, which definitions to trust, what actions they may take, and how their work gets checked, and Microsoft is building much of its enterprise AI architecture around those needs.

Microsoft's announcements aim at the problem of conflicting definitions, with Copilot moving toward a common interface for work and Microsoft IQ described as its broader context architecture, with Fabric IQ providing governed business data and meaning. Business plug-ins are intended to make context, skills, and tools reusable across agents and processes, and semantic views and Fabric IQ ontologies, both in public preview, are designed to make business metrics, entities, relationships, rules, and available actions reusable across analytics, agents, and applications, building on OneLake and Power BI semantic models. Bain notes that a shared platform does not settle which version of a metric or rule is authoritative, since the same policy might still live in a semantic model, an ontology, an agent instruction, and a security setting, and someone has to own the definition, approve changes, and make sure those changes reach every place they should be used, which the CIO cannot solve alone. The lab also made the development trade-off clear, because Copilot helped write and repair scripts quickly and other sessions showed assistance extending into models, business measures, reports, and applications, which can open data-product development to more teams and can multiply duplicated metrics, inconsistent models, and insecure code, with applications possibly ending up with no clear owner.

Bain describes a useful progression in AI's role as worker, workflow, and workload, where AI helps a person complete a task at the worker level, coordinates a series of steps with people overseeing at the workflow level, and can monitor conditions and act continuously within defined boundaries at the workload level, with potential value rising at each level and so does the cost of a wrong decision. Before putting the service-ticket capability into production, leaders need to set approval thresholds, define exceptions, monitor what the agent does, and work out how to undo a bad action, and Microsoft described unified monitoring across jobs, applications, agents, alerts, and capacity, though several of those capabilities remain in preview. Microsoft also emphasized isolating workloads, reducing single points of failure, containing problems, and testing recovery paths, and Satya Nadella's reference to the recent Microsoft 365 outage added context to those sessions, with Bain stating that the ability to see a failure, limit its impact, and recover belongs in the plan before agents start taking consequential actions. Bain's questions for enterprises are which workflow they are prepared to let an agent complete, which definitions, systems, identities, and policies that agent can rely on, and how they will spot a bad decision and recover, and it concludes that Ignite made the technical ambition easy to see while the challenges it raised reach well beyond Microsoft, with the management conversation harder: which decisions agents can be trusted to make, and what would need to change before they are let act.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Is Your Enterprise Ready to Let AI Agents Act?
