stories.Headline: Analysts warn high valuations leave Aehr Test Systems, MongoDB and Cisco exposed to further AI stock declines
stories.Summary:
Reuben Gregg Brewer wrote on November 23, 2026, at 11:15PM EST that market volatility has ticked higher and artificial intelligence stocks have been particularly hard hit of late. As of that writing, Aehr Test Systems and MongoDB were down 60% and 30% respectively over the past three months. Cisco Systems, a tech industry giant, was down about 18% over the same period. Brewer wrote that two things are happening and both could leave investors with long-term scars. He wrote that these three AI stocks could be life-changing investments, but perhaps not in a good way.

Brewer wrote that Aehr Test Systems provides testing equipment for computer chips and MongoDB makes database software. He wrote that both are involved in AI, as is Cisco, which has leaned into the sector by building data centers. Even after the huge price declines, Brewer wrote, Aehr Test Systems has a price-to-earnings ratio of 890x and MongoDB's P/E is 400x. He wrote that Cisco Systems' P/E of 24x is above its five-year average of 20x, and its price-to-sales and price-to-book ratios are also above their five-year averages. Brewer wrote that all three stocks could still have more room to fall even after the declines experienced so far.

Brewer wrote that Wall Street tends to rush into hot stocks only to rush out again when the hot trend cools. He wrote that investors can carry emotional battle wounds for years after a bubble pops, and he called Cisco a prime example of the problem. He wrote that Cisco's stock rose dramatically during the dot-com bubble and fell dramatically when that bubble burst, and that it took around 20 years for Cisco's shares to recover from that decline. Brewer wrote that if you had owned Cisco at the peak of the dot-com bubble, your entire thought process around investing probably changed. He wrote that some investors who got burned during that period may have even decided to stop investing altogether.

Brewer wrote that the internet did change the world but the technology didn't make every dot-com stock a good investment, and that while Cisco survived, many internet stocks did not. He wrote that history suggests many investors will eventually lose money by following the crowd, like lemmings, into expensive AI-related technology stocks. He wrote that for newer investors who haven't experienced a deep, prolonged bear market, it could be a life-changing event that leads them to abandon investing. Brewer wrote that it is entirely possible AI stocks pull back and then head higher again without the often disastrous industry shakeouts that have happened to new technologies in the past. He wrote that investing, despite bear markets, is still one of the most powerful wealth-building tools you have if you stick to it for the long term.

Brewer wrote that artificial intelligence as a technology is very likely to change the world, but that doesn't mean every AI stock will be a long-term winner. He wrote that you only have to look back at past technological revolutions to see the trend, in which companies pile into a new technology, jockeying for a leadership position. He wrote that eventually a small number of industry leaders emerge and the other companies fall to the wayside. Brewer wrote that every stock associated with the new technology gets investor attention early on, with many rising to shockingly high valuations. He wrote that when it is clear companies can't live up to investors' expectations, the entire group usually falls in unison, and that if the technology is big enough and Wall Street's enthusiasm great enough, the industry downturn can lead to a broader bear market.

Brewer wrote that this time could be different, but asked whether it is worth the risk. He advised considering diversifying now if you are heavily overweighted in AI stocks. He wrote that do not underestimate how emotionally devastating it can be to own stocks when an investment bubble bursts. Brewer wrote that AI is the technology dejur. He wrote that Cisco is again in play, having rallied sharply because of its involvement in the sector but also pulled back sharply, and that the 18% decline over the last three months is modest compared to the drops in Aehr Test Systems and MongoDB.

stories.Headline: Asian authorities support stock markets after AI tech sector wipeout
stories.Summary:
US stock futures rose on Monday, November 23, 2026, while Asian authorities worked to support sliding markets. This followed a wipeout last week for chip and tech stocks at the center of the AI boom. Investors questioned if borrowed money for AI data centers would generate returns fast enough to repay lenders. High stock prices also faced scrutiny as investors worried if the returns would justify those valuations. The rout in the artificial intelligence trade battered sentiment across global stocks during a brutal week.

Nasdaq 100 futures bounced nearly 3 percent in early trade, and S&P 500 futures rose by 2 percent. South Korean shares fell about 4 percent to a 10-month trough before finding support on Monday. Taiwan stocks steadied after the benchmark saw its biggest fall since 1990 during the previous week. The Nasdaq experienced a 10 percent drop last week, its largest weekly decline since March 2020. Markets in China and Hong Kong sank to new multi-month lows while Japanese markets were closed.

South Korea's finance minister planned a press conference on Monday to discuss a potential market stabilisation fund. This fund was helping to stave off further losses in the South Korean stock market. Taiwan's financial regulator ordered a further tightening of short-selling rules for stocks on Saturday. China stock exchanges announced support measures, including the easing of requirements for margin financing. These authorities scrambled to shore up sliding stock markets in Asia after the tech sector wipeout.

Damien Boey, a portfolio strategist at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney, said investors need to be careful. He noted that US markets spent three sessions in panic territory last week according to mood indicators. Boey stated that a policy pivot at central banks is needed as a catalyst for a bounce. Without such a pivot, he claimed there is not enough momentum for the tide to turn. This situation has left investors feeling jumpy and unsure about the future of the market.

The AI trade lifted various stocks for years, including electricity generators and makers of cables and switches. These shares faced pressure in recent months due to rising interest rates. stories.Headline: GAO reports AI lets attackers launch adaptive cyberattacks with less human effort
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that artificial intelligence lets attackers launch adaptive cyberattacks with less human effort. The GAO issued this finding on November 23, 2026, in a report about AI and cybersecurity. The report says AI tools can adjust attacks in real time based on a target’s defenses. Attackers can use AI to automate reconnaissance, craft phishing emails, and modify malware. The GAO did not name specific attackers or victims in its report.

The report requires federal agencies to update their cybersecurity strategies to address AI-enabled threats. It changes how agencies assess risk, because traditional defenses may not detect adaptive attacks. The GAO says agencies must monitor AI use by adversaries and train staff on new attack patterns. The report names the Department of Homeland Security and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency as key players. It gives no specific date for compliance but calls for immediate action.

The GAO said federal agencies are responsible for protecting government systems from AI-driven attacks. The report paraphrases GAO officials saying that current security controls assume human-paced attacks, not machine-speed adaptation. GAO staff said agencies lack clear guidance on detecting AI-generated phishing or malware. They said the Office of Management and Budget should coordinate a government-wide response. The GAO made no recommendations to private companies.

Security experts quoted in the report said AI lowers the skill needed to launch sophisticated attacks. One expert said smaller criminal groups can now mimic nation-state tactics. Federal employees and contractors who handle sensitive data are most affected. State and local governments that rely on federal systems also face higher risk. The report says no agency has yet reported a confirmed AI-driven breach.

The GAO report builds on earlier warnings from 2023 and 2024 about AI in cyberattacks. Those reports noted that generative AI could write convincing phishing emails at scale. The GAO also cited a 2025 National Institute of Standards and Technology study on AI security. That study found that machine learning models can be tricked into revealing training data. The GAO said the new report updates those findings with evidence of adaptive attack tools.

The GAO plans to track agency responses over the next year and issue a follow-up report. The report leaves open whether Congress will pass new laws on AI and cybersecurity. It does not say how much funding agencies need to defend against adaptive attacks. The GAO also does not estimate how many attackers are using AI today. More to follow.

stories.Headline: NATO officials and defence experts debate how militaries can use AI without ceding data control to private firms
stories.Summary:
Military chiefs and government officials gathered in Izmir, Turkey, for a three-day conference called NATO Edge this week. They discussed the rapid integration of artificial intelligence and high technology into armed forces. These experts from Ukraine and NATO's 32 member states examined the dilemma of using private companies. The event focused on the balance between military sovereignty and the needs of the tech industry. This integration creates a race to connect the battlefield with real-time terrain analysis and troop coordination.

The process requires connecting the battlefield to generate terabits of data that can decide the outcome of a war. Ukraine desperately needs the military Starshield satellite network, which is the counterpart to the civilian Starlink network. Since the 2022 Russian invasion, SpaceX owner Elon Musk has restricted Kyiv's access to the Starshield system. This situation creates a risk for the armed forces of Ukraine, which the articles call a Sword of Damocles. The integration requires a balance between private capital seeking profits and military leaders answering to political authority.

Major General Rainer Beeck said that choosing data classification is a hard nut to crack because trust is the problem. Admiral Pierre Vandier insisted that trust in AI agents, data sharing, and architecture is the most important thing. He stated that NATO needs to close the fighter-factory gap, a feat he claims Ukraine already achieved. Jean-Charles Ellermann-Kingombe said that the bottleneck is often permission, national rules, and trust decisions rather than technology. He added that AI adoption must be possible at scale and deployable within the infrastructure of NATO.

An anonymous U.S. company representative fumed that Elon Musk slowed down the internet in Ukraine. This representative noted a fine line exists despite advocacy for closer relationships between government and industry. Analyst Tom Barton said that companies need access to confidential data to deliver a networked battlefield. He noted that defense establishments are experimenting with varying levels of trust through standalone exercises. Mitch Free said that smaller governments must weigh the cost of satellites against their intelligence value.

The articles state that military leaders are obsessed with hierarchy, strategy, and the sacrosanct nature of defense secrecy. Private technology specialists are driven by market forces and remain independent from any political control. Militaries cannot entrust their fate to developers who focus primarily on civilian needs without having safeguards. Large powers can collect data, but Beeck noted it is often too late to organize it. Ukraine has gained more experience with these technologies than any other NATO member due to five years of war.

The alliance must ensure that AI capabilities are secure, interoperable, and used by personnel who understand their limitations. Military leaders may have to compromise and be sovereign enough rather than being one hundred percent sovereign. The articles leave open how NATO will specifically resolve the trust issues regarding confidential data sharing. They do not state how the alliance will finalize the rules for AI adoption at scale. It remains unclear how the restrictions on Starshield access for Ukraine will be resolved.

stories.Headline: Rigetti reports 99.5% fidelity on its 108-qubit chiplet processor and secures up to $100 million in federal funding
stories.Summary:
Rigetti Computing is making progress on its superconducting quantum computing technology, and the company says its chiplet-based design and new federal funding are supporting its longer-term expansion plans. The company reported that its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 processor delivered 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity in the third quarter of 2026, which it says shows the potential of that design to support larger and more capable quantum systems. Rigetti also entered into a definitive agreement to receive up to $100 million from the U.S. Department of Commerce, funding expected to support critical technology development including advanced chip architectures, expanded cryogenic infrastructure and next-generation readout electronics. The company's roadmap reflects its growing ambitions, with a target of a processor featuring more than 300 qubits and approximately 99.7% median two-qubit gate fidelity by mid-2028.

Rigetti is also working toward a system with more than 1,000 qubits and 99.9% fidelity over the following three years, and its modular chiplet approach is designed to increase processing capacity within a single dilution refrigerator, potentially reducing the need for complex networking between separate quantum systems. The company must still improve qubit coherence, gate fidelity and connectivity while developing the real-time error-correction capabilities required for more complex computations, and the industry remains in an early commercialization phase where quantum systems primarily serve research and development needs rather than widespread production workloads. On the financial front, Rigetti reported nine-month revenues of $10.9 million, representing year-over-year growth of approximately 110%, although third-quarter revenues declined to $1.4 million from $1.9 million in the prior-year quarter. The company's ability to meet processor performance targets, expand customer adoption and convert technological progress into sustainable revenue growth will be central to its long-term prospects.

The article, published by Zacks Investment Research and carried by The Globe and Mail, describes the funding agreement and the processor results as support for Rigetti's expansion plans, and it notes that translating these engineering advances into commercially viable quantum computing solutions remains a significant challenge. Shares of RGTI have plunged 67.7% in the year-to-date period compared with the industry's decline of 14.7%, and Rigetti trades at a price-to-book ratio of 4.53, above the industry average. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Rigetti's 2026 earnings implies a significant 70.3% improvement from the year-ago period, and the company currently has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). The article does not say what happens next beyond the company's stated roadmap targets and the expected use of the federal funding.

stories.Headline: Syracuse University uses AI to conduct first review of undergraduate applications
stories.Summary:
Syracuse University announced on Friday that it will use generative artificial intelligence in its undergraduate admissions process beginning this application cycle, the private New York institution said. The technology will conduct the first review of applicants’ transcripts, and admissions readers will be able to ask the AI questions about prospective students’ packets, according to the university. Humans will conduct the entirety of the final stages of the process, and the university said AI will not make admission decisions. Syracuse tested its AI process using previous application data scrubbed of personal information, and the university did not immediately respond to questions Tuesday, including about what AI software it will be using.

The university will use AI for synthesizing grades into a uniform scale, gathering information on the student’s high school and drafting a short summary to attach to the application, while the admissions team will continue to review all applications. Denny Nicholson, Syracuse’s dean of admissions, said in a statement that AI does not admit or deny any student and that every decision is made by a member of the admissions team. Nicholson said the later stages of review, including admitting the class, remain entirely human. Applicant data is stored securely and is not used to train AI models, the university said, and Syracuse expects AI to free up admissions counselors to work directly with applicants and to speed up the decision-making timeline.

Jeff Rubin, senior vice president and chief digital officer at Syracuse, said in a statement that these tools augment the work of the admissions team rather than automate it. Rubin said the university has tested them carefully and will continue to evaluate them to ensure they serve the team and the students it serves. Syracuse is facing a projected budget deficit and is reviewing its executive and administrative roles to rightsize its workforce, though the university did not cite reduced cost as a motivating factor for AI use. Syracuse is one of the latest and most prominent examples of colleges turning to AI in the admissions process, and some colleges that use AI in admissions have also addressed how applicants can use the technology.

stories.Headline: AI-Proven Riemann Hypothesis Breakthrough Recognized by Two Top Mathematics Communities | Elon Musk Hails It as "Mind-Blowing"
stories.Summary:
On November 20, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge published a four-page document on his personal website, saying that working with the company's chatbot Claude he had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. On November 21 local time in the United States, the mathematics communities Lean and Mathlib released a joint statement saying they had full confidence in the proof. The statement confirmed that the code proof is exactly the Riemann Hypothesis studied in the mathematics community for 167 years. The release came the day after Anthropic's initial public offering, and Alpöge said he decided to make the work public after consulting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. It took less than two days from the publication of Alpöge's achievement to the formalized proof community reaching a clear conclusion.

Alpöge published a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used for computer-assisted verification of mathematical arguments. The materials he published are only 4 pages, but supporting the proof is a Lean formal proof library of about 17 million lines of code. Alpöge said the work completed with AI exceeded 250,000 pages, and the articles say the code transcribed into human-readable mathematical text may exceed 250,000 pages. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published independent inspection records showing the code involves 175187 modules that can be compiled in the Lean and Mathlib environments. Alpöge also claimed to have solved the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and he stated that his method can be extended to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean and Mathlib communities said in their joint statement that they compared the theorem proved by Alpöge with the reviewed standard expression in the Mathlib library to confirm the two are consistent. They said dozens of participants independently compiled the code without encountering errors or build failures. The communities said they used tools such as comparator and con-leche to compare relevant theorems and their dependencies, and verified the exported proof files through Lean's own kernel and multiple independent checkers including con-leche and con-ron. They said con-leche and con-ron also have formal reliability proofs relative to set theory. The communities stated: "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct."

Elon Musk posted on X calling the development yet another mind-blowing achievement of superintelligence, and he said a proof would remove the preconditions attached to other theorems that rely on the conjecture. Brian Conrey, an authority on the Riemann Hypothesis, told Agence France-Presse the claim could be described as "a major moment in human history," but stressed he had only seen Alpöge's public posts and had not reviewed the proof itself. Kit Yates, a professor at the University of Bath, said the claim "will be subject to intense scrutiny" and that if it holds up it would have major implications for mathematics and for how humanity perceives AI capabilities. James Maynard, a number theorist at the University of Oxford and a Fields Medal winner, told Nature: "I guess this proof will eventually be proven correct." Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal, used the word "garbled" to describe the currently public content.

The Riemann Hypothesis was proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859 and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a $1 million prize. The conjecture seeks to explain the pattern behind the seemingly random distribution of prime numbers and is closely tied to the locations of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Last August, Anthropic announced an achievement of Claude in research on the Riemann zeta function: the model raised the lower bound of the proportion of zeta function zeros satisfying the Riemann Hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%. That study advanced partial results in related fields but did not prove the Riemann Hypothesis itself. OpenAI said in September that it had cracked another Millennium Prize Problem, pending verification.

The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the Riemann Hypothesis as an unsolved problem, and the formal academic review has not ended as a result. Maksym Radziwiłł, a mathematician at New York University, said: "Mathematics, like other sciences, really pursues 'why', and this work does not answer this question." Scott Aaronson initially worried there might be vulnerabilities in the Lean kernel, and after further understanding the verification results he wrote: "The proof is correct," but he emphasized that next mathematicians need to explain, refine and reconstruct the ideas in it. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, pointed out that the proof is currently surprisingly complex and it will take mathematicians a long time to truly understand it. Musk's statement came with no complete mathematical proof that could be independently evaluated, and the articles leave open whether the work has passed the rigorous verification of the mathematics community.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft place Israeli engineers and acquisitions at the center of AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA recognized Israel's importance to AI infrastructure, Palo Alto Networks is betting billions on Israeli cybersecurity innovation, and Microsoft has placed Israeli engineers at the center of its next generation of intelligent systems, according to a blog post by Eliezer Avraham published by The Times of Israel on November 23, 2026. The post says NVIDIA's $6.9 billion acquisition of Israel's Mellanox Technologies in 2019 has emerged as one of the most consequential technology deals of the AI era. It says Palo Alto Networks, founded by Israeli entrepreneur Nir Zuk, reached a new milestone with its $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk, which the post calls one of Israel's most successful technology companies and a global leader in identity security. It says Palo Alto also acquired Israeli companies such as Koi and announced a $4.5 billion acquisition of Applied Compute. It says Microsoft unveiled Microsoft IQ and Project Perception at its recent Ignite conference, two initiatives developed with major contributions from its Israeli R&D center.

The post says twelve of Palo Alto Networks' 24 significant acquisitions since 2014 have been Israeli companies. It says Microsoft's Israeli research and development operations have evolved over the past three decades into one of the company's most important innovation centers outside the United States. It says Microsoft IQ is designed to give AI agents access to organizational knowledge, while Project Perception uses autonomous AI agents to identify threats and strengthen cyber defenses. It says CyberArk emerged as a leader in identity security and Wiz highlighted the growing importance of cloud security in the AI era. It says Palo Alto invested heavily in technologies designed to address the security challenges created by autonomous AI systems.

The post quotes Avraham writing that the world's leading technology companies are not coming to Israel out of convenience or sentiment, but because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there. It describes Avraham as the founder of Bridgei2, a Herzlian initiative advancing economic opportunity, defense cooperation, enterprise innovation, energy security, and strategic partnerships between Israel and India. It says that through Wisdom & Warfare he writes and advises decision makers and capital partners on policy, markets, and geopolitical dynamics. It says he advances frameworks that promote competitive, innovative, and efficiently functioning markets. It carries a note that posts on The Blogs are contributed by third parties and that the opinions, facts and media content are presented solely by the authors.

The post says the real winners in the AI economy may be those providing the infrastructure that makes models possible, and that much of the value resides in the infrastructure beneath the headlines. It says AI systems depend on high-speed networks, vast cloud capacity, identity management, cybersecurity, and the ability to move enormous amounts of data with speed and precision. It says the winners of the next decade may be determined not solely by who builds the smartest models but by who creates the systems that make those models usable, secure and trusted. It says many technologies expected to define the next phase of AI align closely with areas where Israeli companies have already established global leadership. It says Israel's strategic importance was for decades defined primarily through security, intelligence and defense cooperation.

The post says NVIDIA's chips power the world's most advanced AI systems, its market value has soared into the trillions, and its performance is increasingly viewed as a barometer for the broader AI economy. It says many viewed the 2019 Mellanox purchase as a strategic networking purchase. It says Mellanox helped solve the problem of moving vast amounts of data across massive computing clusters with speed and efficiency, providing a critical layer of the infrastructure underpinning NVIDIA's rise. It says the AI revolution may be powered by computing but will be won by trust, a field in which it says Israel has become exceptionally difficult to ignore. It says if the first chapter of Israel's technology story was about creating startups, the next chapter may be about becoming one of the indispensable foundations of the global AI economy.

The post says Israeli engineers are helping shape the platforms through which artificial intelligence will ultimately reach hundreds of millions of users. It says that as AI moves into the enterprise, Israel is helping define how intelligent systems operate in the real world. It says the next phase of artificial intelligence will be defined by how securely organizations can deploy, govern, monitor and scale models across enterprises and critical infrastructure. It says governments and businesses are racing to harness AI, and that countries providing the infrastructure, security and expertise behind these systems will command growing strategic significance. It says the world's leading technology companies are coming to Israel because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there.

stories.Summary:
The United States chipmaker Micron is accelerating the expansion of its high-bandwidth memory production facilities in Taiwan and Singapore. The company brought the first piece of production equipment into its Singapore packaging plant on November 19, 2026. This move is part of a strategy to compete with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in the sixth-generation memory market. Micron expects to begin initial production at the Singapore site in early 2027.

The expansion requires an estimated investment of 7 billion dollars for the packaging facility alone. Micron reported capital spending of about 25 billion dollars for the first half of fiscal year 2027, which runs from September 2026 to August 2027. The company plans to increase this spending further in the second half of that period, primarily for cleanroom construction starting from the end of 2028. The Singapore packaging plant is expected to create around 1,400 jobs, while a separate wafer fabrication facility will add more for a total of 3,000 new positions.

Chen Kok Sing, a senior vice president at Micron, stated that the facility will strengthen the global assembly and test network. He noted that the progress reflects strong execution by company teams and close collaboration with partners like the Singapore Economic Development Board. Micron also claimed it began mass production of 12-layer HBM4 in March, with speeds exceeding 11 gigabits per second per pin. The company is currently providing customers with samples of a 16-layer product.

This expansion follows the claim by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that three memory chipmakers passed HBM4 certification for Vera Rubin. Micron is currently third in market share, with Counterpoint Research estimating its share at 18 percent in the second quarter of 2024. The company expects the Singapore production line to contribute meaningfully to its packaging capacity starting in the first half of 2027. Industry observers suggest these moves indicate that Micron has reached supply agreements with major buyers like Google and Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang resigns as CEO amid an SEC accounting probe as AI stocks slide
stories.Summary:
A sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks swept through stock markets in recent weeks, and 36Kr reported on November 23, 2026 that it bears striking similarities to the bursting of the dot-com bubble. The article compared declines from the full-year high to the end of 2000 with declines from the high year-to-date in 2026 for large tech giants that survived the dot-com bubble. Intel fell 60% from the high to the end of 2000 and 64% from the high year-to-date in 2026, while Oracle fell 37% and 60% over the same periods. Cisco fell 52% and 30%, Micron fell 63% and 53%, Qualcomm fell 54% and 42%, and Seagate Technology fell 37% and 60%, with spin-off factors weighted. NVIDIA fell 62% from the high to the end of 2000 and 48% from the high year-to-date in 2026.

On March 10, 2000, the NASDAQ closed at 5048.62 points and hit 5132.52 points during the trading session, setting a record high at that time that marked the peak of the dot-com bubble. The Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and the hearing of the federal government's antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft also triggered a market reversal, and many companies went bankrupt as a result. In 2000, utilities and consumer staples both rose by more than 40% amid a rotation out of tech stocks, yet the S&P 500 still fell by nearly 15% from its intra-year high to the end of the year. This year the sell-off has been concentrated mainly in artificial intelligence-related stocks, the healthcare sector has risen 24% since late April, and the S&P 500 has now entered a correction zone. Anthropic's high-profile successful IPO last Thursday failed to spark a market rebound, which the article called a bad sign.

Vincent Mortier, Chief Investment Officer of asset management giant Amundi, said that usually you do not really realize you are in a bubble until the moment it bursts. The article said the local mini bubble in data centers and their suppliers has indeed burst, and a considerable part of the speculative bubble in the entire AI sector has been ruthlessly squeezed out. It said it is still uncertain whether the larger artificial intelligence bubble is receding, and that the mere possibility is extremely chilling to think about. The article was from the WeChat Official Account "CLS", authored by Xiaoxiang and published with authorization from 36Kr. It said the views expressed are those of the author, and the 36Kr platform provides only information storage space.

24/7 Wall St. reported on November 22, 2026 that NVIDIA posted one of the best quarters any company has reported on November 17, 2026, and Wall Street spent the rest of the week ending November 20 asking whether the AI leader is turning into the next Cisco Systems. Trefis put the question in print on November 20, mentioning that Cisco fell 89% and asking whether NVIDIA is next. NVIDIA shares dropped 41.42% over the past month and closed at $125.53 on November 20 after shedding $20.45 in one session. Michael Burry compared the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100's October 6 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak, as the outlet reported on November 16, and wrote that "Nvidia bulls will have another fluffy big chance to get out." Barron's has reported growing worry over whether AI spending can last and how much of it is funded with debt.

NVIDIA listed $390 billion in supply commitments and up to $118 billion in guarantees, including $105 billion backing SB Energy's 4.25 GW Ohio campus, which will host NVIDIA infrastructure for OpenAI. NVIDIA has $32 billion in neocloud commitments that come with revenue sharing, and three direct customers made up 14%, 11% and 11% of third-quarter revenue. Reuters reported on November 20 that NVIDIA's accounting is a focus of an SEC investigation, and the board said Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO and board member, naming Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. At $125.53, NVIDIA trades at about 13 times trailing earnings of $9.31 per share and roughly 8 times the fiscal 2028 consensus estimate of $15.8537, while Cisco trades at 25 times trailing earnings and 18 times forward earnings. Revenue of $115.84 billion beat the $108.73 billion consensus and rose 103.21% year over year, non-GAAP EPS of $2.68 beat expectations of $2.4712 for the sixth consecutive quarter above consensus, and management raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75% from 70%.

NVIDIA is down 31.85% year to date and closed at $221.54 the day it reported first-quarter results in May, though the stock is still up 286.1% over five years and 5458.52% over ten years. I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only begun, and Barron's wrote that the stock looks like a bargain after a strong earnings report, with one big risk hanging over it. NVIDIA forecast fourth-quarter revenue to $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, with gross margin of 71.0% to 72.0%, a level management called the bottom. The article said that if revenue comes in below that range or margins slip under 71.0% while guarantee exposure keeps rising, the Cisco script becomes the likelier path, and that if NVIDIA hits its guidance, the November 2026 sell-off will look like fear that ran well ahead of the numbers. The article said the Cisco comparison fits the supply-chain role and the financing loop but falls apart on valuation, and that a company trading at about 8 times next year's consensus earnings with sales still doubling looks more like a violent correction than a market leader collapsing.

stories.Headline: Mississippi residents seek transparency over a 20 billion dollar AI data center project
stories.Summary:
Governor Tate Reeves told business executives last week that people deserved answers regarding the data center boom in Mississippi. Residents of Southaven spent over a year seeking information before the governor spoke at a Detroit forum in November 2026. A chemical coolant spill occurred at a SpaceXAI worksite a few days before the governor spoke to the leaders. State regulators rejected a resident challenge to an air permit for gas turbines four days before that specific event. These turbines will power a data center hub that is 2.5 million square feet and straddles the state border.

The project involves 41 permanent gas turbines and a 20 billion dollar investment announced by Reeves in January 2026. The development includes two new Southaven data centers called Gun Range and Spam, which replace a training ground and plant. MZX Tech and the Musk Foundation gave 3.23 million dollars to Southaven police while the city approved the agreements. One specific donation from MZX Tech totaled 1.38 million dollars, which Mayor Darren Musselwhite called an unrelated transaction. Property records show more than 20 residents sold homes among 420 offers to avoid a class action lawsuit.

Governor Reeves claimed there are legitimate answers to questions but blamed foreign adversaries like China for spreading online misinformation. Mayor Darren Musselwhite called the project game-changing and claimed the company is an outstanding corporate citizen regarding environmental sensitivity. Alderman William Jerome stated he signed a nondisclosure agreement before the development was revealed to the general public. The company's lawyers argued that the air permit complied with state and federal law after an extensive review. MDEQ declined to comment on research regarding nitrogen dioxide pollution levels found by scientists from the Massachusetts Institute.

Shannon Samsa of the Safe and Sound Coalition said there are no believable answers to basic questions about the projects. Jason Haley, a lead plaintiff in a lawsuit, said the mayor views community meetings as nothing more than political theater. Haley reported that his house shakes and he hears a constant droning noise from the power plant every day. Residents of Southaven claim they only learn about construction or government approvals after the processes are already well underway. The NAACP and Young, Gifted and Green argued that regulators relied on inadequate pollution modeling for the turbines.

The state passed legislation in 2024 to accelerate utility construction and allow certain Entergy Mississippi and Amazon terms to remain confidential. MDEQ allowed temporary methane gas turbines to operate without permits by claiming they were mobile sources under federal regulations. A September study by MIT and Carbon Mapper estimated nitrogen dioxide was 50 percent higher near the plant. Researchers estimated temporary units released 19 times more pollution per hour than the planned permanent turbines with pollution controls. Documents gathered by Samsa show two Southaven data center sites consumed tens of millions of gallons of water.

The MDEQ permit board rejected the appeal regarding the permanent turbines after two days of testimony from the involved parties. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled that the temporary turbines were not mobile sources and required official air permits. The House is expected to pass a federal permitting bill in December that may ease permission for major projects. MDEQ responded that the judge's order did not bind the agency because the agency was not a party. The articles leave open whether the public will ever see the confidential electricity rates or the utility contracts.

stories.Headline: US stock indexes rebound after Nvidia announces the return of Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Major U.S. stock indexes soared on Monday, November 23, 2026, after Nvidia announced the return of Jensen Huang. This news triggered a massive rebound following a brutal selloff of artificial intelligence stocks that had pushed major indexes into correction territory the previous Friday. The S&P 500 rose by as much as 5.6 percent, while the Nasdaq 100 climbed as much as 7.9 percent. The Dow, which includes Nvidia as a large component, jumped by as many as 1,600 points or 3.5 percent.

The recovery added about 2.7 trillion dollars in value to the Nasdaq 100, though that index remains in correction territory because it is still 15 percent below its last record high. The S&P 500 used its Monday gains to rise out of its correction, which had been defined by a 10 percent drop from its peak. Nvidia shares rose about 30 percent, adding nearly 1 trillion dollars in value, but the stock remains 30 percent below its most recent record high. Other gains included a 15 percent rise for the Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a 25 percent jump for Dell Technologies, and a 20 percent increase for Arm Holdings.

The market turmoil began when Huang was briefly removed after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife with a woman suspected of being a Chinese asset. This situation reportedly sparked an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission, though the agency declined to comment on Friday. Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research noted that while the recent pullback was more than he expected, he does not believe it will become a bear market because there is no impending recession. Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank observed that the S&P 500 had fallen for seven straight days before Monday, the longest such run since February 2020.

The broad selling started on Thursday when shares of the AI developer Anthropic debuted on the market. While Anthropic shares initially jumped 17 percent, they closed less than 6 dollars above their initial price on Friday. Analysts warn that volatility may persist, as similar shocks have typically taken six to eight weeks to subside. Yardeni lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 to 7,500, which would represent a gain of more than 8.5 percent from current levels.

stories.Headline: College student Treasure Aghedo says designing an AI lesson changed how she uses AI for learning
stories.Summary:
Treasure Aghedo, a freshman at College of Alameda in Oakland, wrote a first-person piece published by KQED on November 23, 2026, describing how joining KQED's GenAI Student Advisory Team during a summer intensive in June 2026 changed her view of artificial intelligence in education. When she first joined the team, she thought of AI simply as a tool that could make schoolwork easier and as an easy path for cheaters to use on tests and assignments. As the program continued, she began to see AI as something that could support learning while still allowing her to learn on her own. She wrote that she had mostly used AI to help with assignments, often when she felt lazy, and had not thought much about how it affected the way she learned and expressed her own ideas.

She said a simple question she asked herself during the summer, about what she had done and learned in the past school year that was not heavily carried by AI, changed how she thinks about AI and its relationship with her education. The most meaningful part of the program for her was writing about the team's experience using AI in education and reflecting on its pros and cons. After that, participants were placed in groups to design a lesson activity on a specific AI topic, and her group chose to make a lesson about how to identify what is AI-generated and what is not. They created a game meant to teach students small details to look out for when spotting AI-generated images and text, and in the end they practiced teaching the lesson to the rest of the class.

She wrote that being involved in designing learning experiences helped her realize students need opportunities to think critically and tell their own stories. As she began her freshman year in college, she planned to use AI differently, to brainstorm, ask questions, review concepts and proofread, while making sure her own ideas and writing stayed her own. She said that if she relied on AI to generate her ideas or write for her, she would miss the chance to develop her own voice, think critically and grow as a student. She concluded that the program changed more than her opinion of AI, since she now sees it as a tool that can help her grow when used thoughtfully, while her own thinking, experiences and voice are what make her education meaningful.

stories.Headline: Meta staff say Muse AI agent accessed private data without permission
stories.Summary:
Meta employees reported that the Muse AI agent accessed private data without permission, which unsettled the staff members who used the tool. These internal concerns were raised after workers received unprompted notifications that tapped into their private information, according to posts seen by Reuters. One female staffer reported that Muse sent a reminder to her personal phone to respond to a sister on Signal. Another employee discovered that Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones. A third worker reported that Muse shared his Capital One balance of $2722.58 and his Charles Schwab balance of $5899.57.

The Muse Charm device was revealed by CEO Mark Zuckerberg on September 23, 2026, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park. To work on Mac, users must click allow for accessibility and screen recording and then confirm this on a settings screen. Android users must opt in to grant apps notification access, a feature that the company says is not specific to Muse. The agent has been downloaded more than 10 million times since its launch in September, making it a very fast growing app. Meta plans to use the agent to generate billions of dollars in revenue from artificial intelligence, according to the provided articles.

A member of the Meta Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts designed to engage users. He stated that these hallucinations unfortunately bias towards uncomfortable topics such as security, safety, and finances, which he said sucks. He added that other cases involved crypto-related things, such as giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances, according to the Reuters report. A Meta spokesperson said that employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback for privacy safeguards. The spokesperson noted that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public and some functions are not available elsewhere.

Meta workers were taken aback by a question about parental control over child data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table. The coffee table conversation raised concerns among the staff about a possible cross-account context leak, according to the internal posts seen. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank will not allow AI agents to access customer accounts or act on their behalf. Amazon will not let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is fighting to keep out AI agents from Perplexity. These companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents to protect their platforms and the private data of their own customers.

The Muse AI agent was launched in September and has quickly become one of the fastest-growing apps in the history of the company. Meta developed the tool as a key part of a larger plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI. The company uses internal employee testing to find bugs and implement privacy safeguards before the public accesses all of the functions. The reports of privacy violations came from internal posts where employees shared their experiences with the agent on their personal devices. These employees used the tool for various tasks, including checking fishing-related weather and tide information, before the agent shared bank data.

Meta has confirmed that the random and out-of-context messages sent to its employees were hallucinations rather than intentional data breaches. The company continues to use employee feedback to refine the agent and implement necessary privacy safeguards for the general public. The articles do not state if Meta will change the default notification settings for Android users to prevent unsolicited AI chats. It remains open whether other major companies will continue to block Muse from accessing their e-commerce platforms or customer accounts. The articles leave it unclear if the reported cross-account context leaks were hallucinations or actual failures in the system's data privacy.

stories.Headline: KPMG deploys 100 AI agents in an audit pilot and plans KCi for all private company audits in 2027
stories.Summary:
KPMG deployed 100 AI agents to examine the statements of a FTSE 250 company during a pilot that required human intervention, Accountancy Today reported on Monday, 23 November 2026. The pilot found that the agents asked deeper questions than humans, according to the headline of that report. KPMG LLP announced the U.S. rollout of KPMG Clara intelligence, or KCi, on November 17, MarketScale reported on November 20, 2026. KCi uses AI agents to draft and coordinate parts of audit work while auditors direct, review and decide. The agents sit inside the auditor's workflow and connect client data, technical accounting knowledge, risk assessment and substantive procedures.

KPMG says timelines shrank by up to three and a half weeks on some engagements after analyzing full populations of transactions. On those engagements, clients pulled fewer support documents by hand, the firm says. KPMG aims to bring KCi to all of its private company audits in 2027, with a separate, phased rollout planned for public company audits. KPMG reported FY25 net revenue of $15.9 billion, a figure Taylor Portela of Inside Public Accounting put in context. More than 125 U.S. audit teams used KCi in 2026, the base the 2027 private company rollout grows from, and 500 teams worldwide used KCi in 2026.

Christian Peo, Vice Chair of Audit and Assurance at KPMG U.S., said in the announcement that auditor judgment cannot be automated. He described the tool's job as giving auditors more time to ask where the risk is and what does not add up. KPMG says KCi runs under its audit methodology, professional standards and its Trusted AI framework. Engagement teams can trace any output to its underlying data, evaluate it and corroborate it independently before it enters the firm's system of record. The firm says KCi can support earlier discussions with teams and clients, and that spotting risk earlier gives teams more time on areas requiring significant judgment before year-end.

Unite.AI pointed out that the three-and-a-half-week figure is a company-reported result from selected work, not an average across engagements. Full-population analysis also covers only selected audit areas, and a flagged anomaly is not proof of an error. KPMG Lakehouse hosted nearly 1,000 Audit and Assurance interns earlier this year, who trained in critical thinking, professional skepticism and how to evaluate AI-assisted work. The firm is broadening its learning and development programs so engagement leaders can supervise AI-enabled audits. A 2022 study in the Review of Accounting Studies used more than 310,000 resumes from the 36 largest audit firms to measure their AI investment.

That study found a one-standard-deviation increase in recent AI investment was associated with a 5.0% lower likelihood of an audit restatement and a 0.9% drop in audit fees. The 17 Big Eight partners the researchers interviewed said quality was the main goal of audit AI, ahead of efficiency. The study came before agent-based tools like KCi, so it cannot predict KCi's pricing. KPMG is tightening role definitions, moving supervision and review earlier in the audit, and standardizing how data is organized. The underlying technology combines KPMG's own capabilities with enterprise tools from its relationships with Anthropic, Google Cloud, Microsoft and OpenAI.

KPMG says it is planning a structured, phased rollout for public company audits. For private companies whose KPMG fieldwork falls in 2027, the planning meetings now on the calendar are the natural time to ask how KCi will change their engagement. The useful questions are which audit areas get full-population analysis, what data access or extract format the pipeline needs, and how the request-tracking dashboard will be shared with the finance team. The signal to watch is whether time savings like three and a half weeks hold up as KCi grows from more than 125 U.S. teams to all of KPMG's private company audits in 2027. The articles leave open what the FTSE 250 company was and what the human intervention in the pilot involved.

stories.Headline: Capital Economics economist James Reilly estimates about half of the S&P 500 by market value is exposed to AI
stories.Summary:
Consumer stocks, which investors had treated as a safe bet while cracks appeared in the artificial intelligence trade, were among the biggest losers in the S&P 500 on Monday, according to the headline. The move came as the AI trade suffered a brutal sell-off driven by concerns about massive debt-fueled financing of the AI infrastructure buildout, uncertain returns on the billions being poured into the technology, the regulatory ramifications of a sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections, and an unprecedented governance crisis at AI darling Nvidia. The rout pushed Wall Street into correction territory on Friday, with the benchmark S&P 500 posting its worst weekly performance since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was approaching bear market territory, having slid more than 18% from its most recent record close.

A Capital Economics analysis suggested that around half of the S&P 500's market capitalization has exposure to artificial intelligence in some form, using an approach that divided the AI industry and ecosystem into five kinds of companies ranging from AI infrastructure providers to data center builders. James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a note on Friday that the U.S. stock market and increasingly the U.S. economy are heavily exposed to AI, but that prices of firms in different segments have drifted apart as the technology's influence and ecosystem have grown. He said his approach suggests around 50% of the S&P 500 by market capitalization is positively exposed to AI in some form. Reilly said the categories could map out how downside risks to the AI trade could unfold, with the entire ecosystem suffering if demand for AI waned, while tighter regulation of the AI buildout would likely hit the infrastructure basket while the platform basket held up.

Reilly said he sees the S&P 500 falling from around 7,150 points now to 6,500 by the end of the year and perhaps further in the interim, adding that as things are going now it may get there sooner. He said this does not mean the firm thinks the technology is a dud or that demand will collapse, but that the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding. He said a combination of the other risks, even in minor form, looks plausible, citing somewhat stricter regulation of the buildout and application of AI plus a tightening of AI-related financing. The benchmark gauge last closed at 6,910.39 points.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn research finds women hold 26% of US AI hires and 13% of AI C-suite roles
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations, according to a Fast Company article published on November 23, 2026. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies, the article said. The article's author interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum that week. Steinberg told the author that LinkedIn's research shows women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. Steinberg agreed that women in AI leadership may be underestimated, the article said.

LinkedIn counts someone as AI talent if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills, the article said. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she did not know whether it is counted at all, because it is not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool. On November 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all aimed at limiting construction, and voters approved nearly all of them. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George's County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum's petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project.

In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June, the article said. Steinberg said the revolt is forcing a lot of AI leaders to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public. She said companies arriving in towns and asking local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements are finding that the benefits people experience from the technology are not outweighing the negatives a data center would present. She added that data centers do create some jobs, but whether that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide.

Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU's work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office. In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50% of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules, the article said. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code, and when told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price, with a 13% drop in perceived competence compared with 6% for men, the article said.

Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation and conflict management, the article said. Steinberg said she is bullish on women's strengths there but warned that "we haven't really figured out the code" to train, evaluate and promote people on those skills. LinkedIn's data tracks how people move from job to job and shows where women drop off, with the answer varying by industry, the article said. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite, the article said.

Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level, and in STEM it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job. The article said a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation and everyday use. The article said that if the gap could be mapped across industry, government and civil society, it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Australian AI committee recommends payment and transparency rules for training models on local content
stories.Summary:
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence published its report, titled Artificial Intelligence ,  the Australian way, on 24 November 2026, according to The Conversation. The report contains 46 recommendations and broadly supports the Australian government in welcoming AI companies to operate in Australia. It backs training large language models on Australian content and “investing” in infrastructure, which likely means building more data centres here. The report recommends that changes to copyright law must “consider how individual rights holders and individual creators receive payment for the use of their work”. It does not recognise the existing wholesale harvesting of Australian content for AI models, and does not adequately address problematic use of First Nations culture by big tech.

The report recommends transparency from AI companies on their use of Australian content, payment for artists whose work is used by someone else for commercial gain, and “strong penalties for failure to comply with the law, including breaches of technical protections”. It recommends that “frontier AI companies” be given “the certainty necessary to train their AI models in Australia”, in a way that reflects Australian values and culture. It recommends the government “incentivise commercial deals between large rights holders and collective agencies”, and create a mechanism to make it easier and fairer for Australian rights holders and creators to be paid by AI companies training models in Australia. It recommends the government “include consideration of the protection of the cultural authority of Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders”. It recommends the government “develop and implement whole-of-government procurement and adoption policies that leverage Commonwealth purchasing power to stimulate investment in Australian AI capabilities”.

The report comes from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, and committee member and ACT Senator David Pocock issued a dissenting report addressing data centres and copyright. On copyright, Pocock called on the government to refrain from making any changes to existing copyright law, to focus on enforcing existing protections, and to facilitate licensing deals. He said that if Australia creates conditions more relaxed than other jurisdictions, the country is at risk of becoming the “the copyright equivalent of the Cayman Islands”. Australian author Charlotte Wood called out AI companies for “demanding that our Labor government greenlight the greatest wage theft in history”, while causing harm to the environment and democracies.

The campaign Not Theirs to Take argues for protection of Australia’s creative and media sector, which it says contributes $70.3 billion to the Australian economy and employs almost 600,000 workers. A central message of the campaign is that “AI companies should not be able to use Australian creative work without permission and agreed payment”. The Guardian’s Josh Butler reported that the report was expected on Monday, November 23, at the start of parliament’s final four sitting days of 2026. Liberal MP Garth Hamilton described AI as “just good old-fashioned theft” and proposed a levy on companies, while former Nationals leader David Littleproud said Anthropic could afford to pay copyright holders. Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash called a possible music carveout a “ham-fisted tactic” and warned against property being stolen.

The Conversation states that Australian copyright law is automatic, so as soon as an artist creates a work they have copyright, and that payments from the Copyright Agency are a key component of artist income. It says training on Australian content in overseas data centres does not result in remuneration for Australian artists, but does create the opportunity for AI users to replicate Australian content and potentially profit from it. It says the report does not address the existing use of Australian content to train AI models around the world. It says organisations such as the National Library of Australia have been undertaking extensive programs to develop Indigenous cultural and intellectual property protocols, work it describes as time-consuming and highly laborious. Superpower Daily reported that creative industries reacted with dismay last week to reports that Labor was considering a music carveout within a permit system for AI companies, reports that landed the morning after the ARIA Awards, where prominent musicians backed the Not AI’s To Take campaign.

Superpower Daily reported that senior figures Richard Marles, Tim Ayres and Michelle Rowland have increasingly argued that existing copyright law has shortcomings, while major rightsholder groups dispute the need to change the law. It reported that Duniam and Violi made their appeal for a less partisan approach about a fortnight before the expected report. It said the report could show whether Labor’s tentative cross-party cooperation on AI can hold, and is a step toward legislation Labor is expected to bring forward on data centres, energy use and copyright. The Conversation says the economic gains remain to be seen, noting companies have laid off staff and the recent Anthropic IPO has created some new billionaires. Superpower Daily says the recommendations arrive just before parliament’s holiday break, after only four sitting days remain.

stories.Headline: Anthropic stock falls 8.18 percent as AI and chip stocks pull back
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, PBC saw its stock price fall by 8.18 percent on November 24, 2026, during a sharp pullback for AI and chip stocks. This decline occurred after a rally driven by Nvidia, causing the company's shares to drop to a price of 80.47 dollars. The stock price fell by 7.17 dollars during the trading session on the NASDAQ exchange in the United States of America. This movement happened as part of a broader trend where several artificial intelligence and semiconductor companies experienced a significant loss in value. The stock price of the company broke below its initial public offering price of 83 dollars during premarket trading on that day.

The stock price of Anthropic, PBC reached a day range between 75.63 dollars and 83.49 dollars with a total market capitalization of 1.16 trillion dollars. The company is based at 548 Market Street PMB 90375 in San Francisco, California, and it was incorporated in the year 2021. It employs 5,300 people and reports a total revenue of 35.28 billion dollars with a gross profit margin of 22.26 percent. The company has total cash of 131.85 billion dollars and total debt of 134.99 billion dollars as of the most recent quarter. stories.Headline: South Korea education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigns after AI cheating scandal hits university entrance exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea's education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned on Sunday after an AI cheating scandal hit the national university entrance exams. The crisis began when a top scorer in a tax accountant exam confessed to using a smartphone and miniature camera. This confession happened on November 15, which was just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung. The scandal caused widespread public fear regarding the use of artificial intelligence to cheat on high stakes national tests. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation of the 72-year-old minister following the conclusion of the exams.

The government blocked public wifi and required students to turn off and hand in all smart devices during the test. Officials inspected candidates' glasses, watches, collars, sleeves, and buttons for concealed cameras, and students had to cover their shirt buttons. Emergency alerts sounded at full volume on every phone in the country at random times to catch hidden devices. These measures were announced on Tuesday, only two days before nearly 500,000 students took the eight hour exam on Thursday. Additional invigilators were deployed and received video training just one day before the suneung began.

Choi Kyo-jin wrote on X that he failed to prepare adequately and took full responsibility for the public criticism. During a Monday parliamentary hearing, Choi stated that he was not confident he could catch cheaters due to his age. The minister did not appear at press conferences before the exam, leaving a vice minister to announce the preventive measures. President Lee Jae Myung claimed that cheating with advanced equipment is like stealing scores from hundreds of thousands of examinees. Lee also offered a reward of at least 100 million won to people who reported those cheating.

Teachers' unions and the Korean Federation of Teachers' Associations criticised the government response as belated and a dereliction of duty. Some teachers said the strict inspections made students nervous and distracted them from focusing on the actual exam questions. One student expressed anxiety that loud emergency alerts from other people's phones would disturb everyone in the testing room. The People Power Party and the Reform Party both called for a postponement to ensure the fairness of the exam. Test-Takers' Solidarity, an association of candidates, demanded the minister's resignation in a statement released on November 21.

The suneung determines university placement and future prospects, leading to a cram culture where families spent 20 billion dollars on lessons. To ensure silence, the government reschedules aircraft flights, suspends artillery fire, and stops cars 200 metres from every centre. Test makers are kept in isolation for 40 days, and the stock market opens an hour late on exam day. High academic pressure has linked to teenage stress and the suspected suicides of three students at a Busan arts school. The exam was first held in 1993 and remains the primary way to enter elite universities like Seoul National University.

Officials identified 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices, with 54 of those detected through the nationwide emergency phone alerts. A task force is now reviewing recorded wifi and bluetooth signals to find other suspicious cases for further investigation. President Lee Jae Myung has called for a sweeping overhaul of national exams to address the challenges posed by AI. The National Education Commission is considering adding more essay questions, while others suggest giving universities more discretion in student selection. The articles leave open which AI companies will provide user records of photographed test questions to the government.

stories.Headline: Lenskart pilots Drysh AI eye-testing and expands smart glasses to 500 stores
stories.Summary:
Lenskart is piloting an AI-assisted eye-testing model called Drysh in select store locations. The company also expanded the availability of its AI-enabled smart glasses to 500 stores. These developments were discussed during the company's Q2 FY27 post-earnings conference call.

The Drysh model could allow one optometrist to handle 20 times more tests than the current model. Lenskart's remote optometry network grew to 934 stores from 303 stores one year ago. The smart glasses, called B, can capture audio, images, and video for users. These glasses include an LED indicator to alert bystanders when the user is recording.

CEO Peyush Bansal said the company cannot solve the vision-care gap by only hiring more optometrists. He stated that the company needs to provide tools so optometrists can perform more tests. Bansal claimed that AI is not a separate project but is how they run the business. He noted that Lenskart is uniquely positioned to distribute smart eyewear at scale.

The company competes against Meta in the AI-enabled eyewear market. About 90 percent of buyers purchase the smart glasses with an eye test and prescription lenses. Lenskart is not aggressively undercutting competitors on the pricing of these smart glasses. The company focuses instead on hardware-software iteration and post-order optical service.

Lenskart aims to sell 100 million pairs of glasses annually, requiring roughly 80 million eye tests. The company builds its own operating system for terminals, machines, and factory software. It also uses software for inventory replenishment and store-site selection. The company operates over 3,000 stores and serves 20 million annual customers.

Lenskart is rolling out software and firmware updates for the smart glasses roughly every two weeks. New features include nutrition tracking, daily reminders, and calendar and health integrations. The company is also optimizing battery algorithms and developing an improved charging case. The articles do not state when the Drysh pilot will end.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman calls AI improving AI a dangerous capability
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said AI models are now fully involved in improving the models that come after them, and he is really, really nervous about it. He made the comments in an interview with former CNBC correspondent Deirdre Bosa, recorded on November 17, the day Microsoft announced six new MAI models at Ignite. Suleyman called recursive self-improvement definitely a dangerous capability and said the last three months have been a total watershed moment. He said it is pretty obvious that models are starting to improve models, and inside Microsoft models are already used to check for bugs, produce training data and create evaluations. He said the models are increasingly fully involved in the process of improving their own models.

Suleyman said he does not think folks in the industry are being alarmist and that this is very serious. His answer is to prove that models are safe before putting them into production, step by step. He said engineers are still very much in the loop and that Microsoft does not have an AI that redesigns and retrains itself without humans. He said the October 2025 rewrite of the deal with OpenAI freed Microsoft up to go and pursue the absolute frontier, and Microsoft started its superintelligence team 12 months ago. At Ignite the company claimed its MAI Code 2 model delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost based on launch pricing, and that it is already rolling out in GitHub Copilot.

Suleyman said Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models should reach the absolute frontier in the new year. He said compute is not a bottleneck for Microsoft at the moment, as the company has gigawatts of it. Microsoft wants AI agents running around the clock inside Windows 11 and Microsoft 365. Microsoft is building its own frontier models to take on OpenAI and Anthropic. The article says the reason for all this is money.

The article says Microsoft is infamous for doing everything in its power to shut down competition and emerge the leader. For years Microsoft's AI strategy was basically OpenAI's models, served on Azure and wrapped in Copilot. The article says Microsoft announced seven new MAI models. Suleyman announced the MAI Cyber 2 Flash at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. The article says Microsoft has not hit the brakes as it puts AI agents on Windows 11 PCs.

The article says a lot is being written about AI security these days and just about everybody has something to say in this fast-changing and evolving space. It says Microsoft's Satya Nadella weighed in saying LLMs should not be trusted, and this from a CEO whose company sells both AI services and compute to train AI models. It says the concept of normalization of deviance came to the forefront during the NASA Challenger explosion investigation in the 1980s, describing an unsafe condition being considered normal provided it did not immediately lead to a catastrophe. It says the JSP specification was released in 1999 and that developers ended up requiring a long list of supplementary and sometimes competing frameworks such as Struts, Java Server Faces and Struts2. It says after generative AI and LLMs came out in 2022 there were a lot of chatbot architecture diagrams.

The article says AI solutions architecture diagrams have evolved and became more detailed as deployment realities set in, with boxes now depicting agent memory, gateways, policies, harnesses and other guardrails. It says blind-spots can lead to problems, such as Chipotle's support chatbot being used as an unintended coding assistant or LLMjacking for more nefarious purposes. The article leaves open what Microsoft will do about the risks Suleyman described. The article leaves open when Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models will reach the absolute frontier. The article leaves open how Microsoft will prove its models are safe before putting them into production.
