stories.Headline: Study finds AI chatbots refuse hate speech prompts less often in Kazakh than in English
stories.Summary:
Oliver Lopez and Lily Ottinger published a ChinaTalk essay on Sunday, November 22, 2026, about AI chatbot refusal rates. Six chatbots refused crude ethnic hate prompts 76.9 percent of the time when asked in English for Kazakh replies. However, these same chatbots only refused 32 percent of the time when the prompts were written in Kazakh. The study involved 100 questions run through six models in seven languages, totaling 8,400 requests and 8,022 usable answers. This small, independent study was not a formal audit and lacked review by native speakers for the translations.

The study tested Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek V3, and Zhipu's GLM-4.5 alongside OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Meta's Llama 3.3 70B Instruct. Refusal rates for crude prompts were 75.2 percent in English and 25.6 percent in Mongolian, and 79.7 percent in English and 68.1 percent in Mandarin. China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, adopted March 12, 2026, and effective July 1, requires operators to delete ethnic hatred content. Article 31 bars producing content that incites ethnic hatred, while Article 61 provides punishment for operators who refuse to correct failures. Article 63 extends this liability to organizations and individuals located outside of mainland China.

Oliver Lopez, a fourth-year International Relations undergraduate at the University of Edinburgh, argued that obligations have arrived ahead of the ability to meet them. He claimed that most of the content rules in Article 31 were already in force through previous laws and interim measures. Zhou Jianshe of the State Council Information Office Press Bureau called Article 63 a legitimate, lawful, necessary, and workable provision. He stated that Western media had tried to smear this specific provision as long-arm jurisdiction. The author of the study noted that the reported refusal numbers are likely a floor.

Sarah Brooks of Amnesty International said that peaceful advocacy for minority rights could be characterized as undermining ethnic unity. She argued that unity in practice means conformity with the political line of Beijing. Human Rights Watch stated that the September 2025 draft would erase language rights and tighten ideological control. The Jamestown Foundation argued that the final law turns assimilation into a legal duty. Former ACLU president Nadine Strossen argued that such laws can backfire and leave ethnic minorities among those charged.

The articles state that China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law and 2023 Generative AI Interim Measures already obliged providers to stop promoting ethnic hatred. Bilibili users appeared unable to comment in Tibetan or Uyghur script in late October and early November 2021. Talkmate pulled its Tibetan and Uyghur courses and attributed this move to government policies. A September 2026 Anthropic report described a China-based operation using Claude to monitor public opinion and flag dissidents. This operation processed 15 to 30 foreign news articles daily from platforms like Weibo, X, YouTube, Telegram, and Facebook.

The essay's conclusion says Tibetan replies came back as gibberish about a third of the time. Uyghur returned incoherent output on about a fifth of its answers to crude prompts asked in its own language. Only 29 percent of crude Tibetan replies were in Tibetan script, compared to 95 percent of policy replies. The articles leave open why these language-dependent gaps exist across different models and languages. They also leave open whether better minority-language moderation would shield minorities from hate speech or extend state policing.

stories.Headline: Yann LeCun accuses Dario Amodei of trying to restrict access to advanced AI models
stories.Summary:
Turing Award winner Yann LeCun criticised Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei regarding open-weight AI models on November 24, 2026. LeCun used a post on X to publicly question the approach to AI governance used by the chief executive. This exchange reopened an industry debate about whether advanced AI should be openly shared or tightly controlled. LeCun accused Amodei of wanting to restrict access to advanced AI to a small group of organisations. He also claimed a similar desire for control led to Amodei leaving OpenAI in 2020.

Open-weight models allow users to run systems on personal computers or in-house servers without needing cloud subscriptions. These systems have publicly available trained parameters, which allows for local execution and adaptation for specific tasks. Closed models are offered through a company API, where the provider controls access, features, and all barred uses. Kimi K-3 is cited as an example of a model that can be executed locally as open-weight. This approach gives users greater control over their data compared to the dependency created by closed systems.

Dario Amodei testified before the US Congress that widely releasing open-weight models could be risky for the public. He stated that developers lose oversight of how a model is used once it is downloaded and run locally. Yann LeCun argued that limiting AI development goes against the historical progress of technology and a medieval mindset. LeCun claimed that Amodei seeks to keep advanced AI within a limited group of people and organisations. Amodei has not yet responded to the remarks made by LeCun regarding his governance approach and history.

Critics express concerns that open-weight models could be misused to facilitate cyberattacks or spread misinformation without proper safeguards. These users are affected because closed systems simplify the enforcement of safety policies by the provider of the AI. The debate affects developers who must choose between the control of open weights and the simplicity of hosted APIs. Some critics on Hacker News argue that certain available weights are not truly open in an open source sense. The 9to6ai write-up agreed that the Open Source Initiative definition would side with these specific critics of Mistral.

Open-weight models are different from open source AI, which requires exposing the training data and the code used for building. Truly open source systems must allow users to use, study, modify, and share the technology without any field-of-use carve-outs. Most frontier models today do not clear this bar because they do not provide the necessary training data or code. The label open weight is looser and only means the lab publishes the trained parameters for the user to download. Licenses for these weights can be standard texts like MIT or custom terms written by the AI lab.

The industry continues to debate the gap between what a lab calls open and what a lawyer calls open. Future developments remain open regarding whether more flagship models will release weights or remain as hosted API services only. It is not confirmed if Alibaba will release open weights for its newer flagship model known as Qwen4-Max. The articles leave open whether Amodei will respond to the claims about his 2020 departure from the company OpenAI. Legal teams must still determine if specific product features count as services under various modified AI license agreements.

stories.Headline: BTP director Judianne Hoeve fully integrates AI across Sint Maarten telecom operations
stories.Summary:
Bureau Telecommunications and Post Sint Maarten, known as BTP, announced on 24 November 2026 that it has fully integrated Artificial Intelligence across its operations, under the leadership of Director Judianne Hoeve. The organization said a series of strategic AI investments places it and Sint Maarten at the forefront of responsible, innovation-driven regulation in the Caribbean region, a claim BTP makes for itself. At the heart of the strategy is Acuda, a tailored and secure AI platform configured to support BTP's operational and regulatory needs. It is pre-programmed with telecommunications, postal and utilities laws, regulations, policies, industry standards and regional frameworks, and lets staff retrieve, cross-reference and analyze critical information in seconds. A standout feature is its library of expert user profiles, called avatars, each trained on a specific professional role within BTP, from licensing and compliance to spectrum management and consumer affairs.

Alongside Acuda, BTP has launched a formal Internal AI Use Policy governing responsible AI use across all staff, which prohibits uploading any BTP information, including licensing records, enforcement files and stakeholder communications, to external AI systems or Large Language Models. Hoeve said Acuda is not a replacement for BTP's people but a power tool in their hands, and that AI still requires human verification, particularly for regulatory rulings and enforcement decisions. She said the platform eliminates the administrative burden so professionals can focus on sound judgment, fair regulation and serving the people of Sint Maarten. She also said the amount of confidential data being uploaded to the internet through free AI tools is alarming, and that an approved, closed AI model is one of the most effective ways to embrace AI's benefits while protecting entrusted data. The policy is grounded in BTP's core values of integrity, transparency, fairness and accountability, and BTP hopes it will set a governance standard for other public institutions across the region.

BTP's AI strategy extends beyond its internal operations, with an AI-powered virtual assistant now live on its official website at www.btp.sx, available 24/7 to help residents, businesses and visitors with general questions about BTP and about telecommunications, postal services and utilities in Sint Maarten. The initiative is meant to improve public access to regulatory information, reduce routine inquiries to BTP's Consumer Desk and strengthen transparency as a cornerstone of BTP's strategic roadmap. Looking ahead, BTP said it is actively building the institutional knowledge needed to advise the Government of Sint Maarten on AI governance, digital policy and the regulatory frameworks that will be essential as AI becomes further embedded in society. Hoeve has also pledged to engage Sint Maarten's schools to promote responsible AI use and digital literacy from the ground up.

Hoeve said that at BTP embracing modern technology is not optional but a responsibility, and that with Acuda, the Internal AI Use Policy and the public-facing AI widget, concrete steps have been taken to ensure AI works for Sint Maarten rather than the other way around. She said responsible AI use must be championed at every level of society, especially among young people, and that she and her team are committed to engaging students and helping the next generation understand that AI must be guided by ethics, critical thinking and human judgment. She added that BTP stands ready to advise the government on the frameworks Sint Maarten will need to navigate this new era safely and confidently, and that the future is here and BTP is proud to lead the way.

stories.Headline: Draganfly and DOD Solution sign memorandum to integrate AURA AI autonomy into Draganfly drones
stories.Summary:
Draganfly Inc. and DOD Solution jointly announced on November 23, 2026, the signing of a memorandum of understanding to advance integration of DOD Solution's autonomy technology into selected Draganfly unmanned systems. The announcement was made in Kyiv, Ukraine, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 23, 2026. Draganfly is a Canadian-headquartered developer of advanced drone solutions, unmanned systems and software. DOD Solution is an Estonian-Ukrainian developer of onboard autonomy technology. The two companies said the collaboration is designed to combine DOD Solution's autonomy expertise and insights from Ukraine with Draganfly's Canadian engineering and systems-integration capabilities.

The collaboration will explore how lessons from Ukraine can inform autonomy integration and testing against Canadian and allied requirements. DOD Solution's AURA AI platform pairs the AURA SBC onboard computer with AURA OS software, designed to support autonomous functions when GPS or communications are degraded or unavailable. AURA AI brings target detection, recognition, tracking and terminal guidance directly onboard, allowing drones to operate when GPS is unavailable, jamming is active and communications are limited. Draganfly has more than 27 years of experience in unmanned systems. Draganfly's stock is listed on NASDAQ under DPRO, on the CSE under DPRO and on the FSE under 3U8.

Cameron Chell, Chief Executive Officer of Draganfly, said Canada has an opportunity to apply lessons from Ukraine to the way unmanned systems are developed, tested and supported. Chell said working with DOD Solution is intended to connect their onboard autonomy technology and operational understanding with Draganfly's engineering capabilities in Canada. He said the focus is on evaluating how autonomy can help systems perform in demanding conditions. He said the aim is building the expertise to integrate and support those capabilities for customers. Roman Hapachylo, Chief Executive Officer of DOD Solution, said working with Draganfly creates an opportunity to connect their autonomy technology and experience in Ukraine with Canadian engineering and integration expertise.

Hapachylo said DOD Solution wants this level of autonomy to become a core capability of next-generation unmanned systems, and called the partnership another step in that direction. For Canada, the potential benefit includes deeper technical expertise in autonomy integration, testing and ongoing support, alongside opportunities to strengthen Canadian unmanned systems capabilities. For DOD Solution, the collaboration offers a potential pathway to integrate its technology across additional platforms and explore Canadian and allied customer requirements with Draganfly. The initiative is consistent with the broader Canada-Ukraine objective of combining Ukrainian innovation with Canadian industrial and technological strengths through research, testing, technology collaboration and licensing. Lessons emerging from Ukraine highlight the importance of testing unmanned systems under realistic operating conditions, adapting as countermeasures evolve and incorporating user feedback into continued development.

DOD Solution works with unmanned platform manufacturers to integrate AI-powered autonomy across a wide range of defence applications. Its flagship product, the AURA AI platform, combines proprietary software and the AURA SBC onboard computer to enable autonomous navigation, perception, target recognition, tracking and terminal guidance in GPS-denied, contested and communication-constrained environments. Draganfly develops and delivers technologies spanning aerial platforms, autonomy, sensing, payload integration and mission-specific solutions for defence, public safety and commercial applications. Draganfly combines engineering, manufacturing, software and systems-integration capabilities to support customers operating in complex and mission-critical environments. Draganfly says it is driven by a mission to provide innovative, reliable solutions that save time, money and lives.

Draganfly's forward-looking statements address the collaboration contemplated by the memorandum of understanding with DOD Solution and the integration of DOD Solution's autonomy technology, including the AURA AI platform, into selected Draganfly unmanned systems. They also address the anticipated capabilities and performance of such technology, including in environments where GPS or communications are degraded or unavailable. The statements cover the testing and evaluation of autonomy capabilities against Canadian and allied requirements and the expected benefits of the collaboration. Draganfly lists risks including the possibility that the memorandum of understanding may not result in definitive agreements on acceptable terms, on a timely basis or at all. Other listed risks include that the contemplated collaboration and integration activities may not proceed, may not be technically feasible or may not achieve their anticipated performance or benefits.

stories.Headline: Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticizes the US economy for its heavy reliance on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the American economy on Monday, November 23, 2026, for its heavy reliance on artificial intelligence. He spoke after Nvidia stock experienced a massive selloff and a subsequent rally following a corporate leadership scandal. The turmoil began when CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of multiple extramarital affairs emerged. Huang was reinstated as the chief executive on Monday morning by the company board of directors. This sequence of events caused significant volatility for major market indices including the Nasdaq and the S&P 500.

The scandal involved Alice Huang, head of Singapore-based Megaspeed, a former Chinese state-run firm that may have bypassed US chip prohibitions. Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, moved 59 million shares worth $10.5 billion into an irrevocable family trust in March. This transfer used grantor-retained annuity trusts, which the couple first established in March 2016 with $51 million in stock. The company stock hit a low on Friday that was 48 percent below a 52-week high reached one month prior. Even after the rally, the stock remained 32 percent below that peak as of the writing of the report.

Mayor Mamdani stated that working people did not sign up for their pensions to depend on the fidelity of Jensen Huang. He argued that the strength of the United States economy should not be so closely tied to one individual's fate. The mayor noted that a rumored $81 billion divorce settlement could fund universal childcare for 3- and 4-year-olds for one year. He expressed concern that the stock market is disproportionately dependent on stocks related to artificial intelligence technology. Mamdani believes this dominance is evident in both daily public discourse and the overall stability of the national economy.

Public pension funds are heavily affected, with $700 billion invested in AI-related assets as of June 30, 2026. This amount represents 11 percent of the $6.42 trillion held by these systems, making exposure difficult to avoid. AI stocks now account for more than one third of reported public equity holdings across these various pension funds. Market observers noted that while the trust transfers were legal, they could draw ethical scrutiny due to their timing. Wealth management specialists cited by Barron's called the transfer of assets one of the most remarkable they had seen.

The New York Times reported last month that Jensen Huang may have been having an affair with a Chinese spy. Reports also emerged that Nvidia used circular financing, where the company invested in startups that then bought Nvidia chips. Jensen Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and remains the largest shareholder with a stake of about 3.5 percent. His total stake is valued between $130 billion and $150 billion, while his total net worth is $155.2 billion. The company market capitalization fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July of the previous year.

The board previously named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive during the period of Huang's resignation. Lori Huang could receive nearly half of the couple's net worth if they divorce because California is a community property state. The articles leave open whether the allegations regarding the circumvention of US prohibitions on selling chips to China are true. It remains unclear if the circular financing practices will lead to further regulatory actions or a deeper sector-wide economic alarm. The reports do not state if the divorce settlement of $81 billion has been finalized or officially agreed upon.

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger says AI needs a 10,000-fold gain in computing efficiency
stories.Summary:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger said artificial intelligence needs a 10,000-fold increase in computing efficiency, not routine generational upgrades, at the COSM Technology Summit in Scottsdale, Arizona. He spoke in a fireside chat titled "Reality Check: Beyond Chips" alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. The Wccftech report of the summit was published on November 21, 2026, and the TechGig report followed on November 24, 2026. Gelsinger rejected the idea that chip scaling has reached a physical limit, despite industry skepticism. He also posted on X, asking whether Moore's Law is dead and saying it is time to wake it up.

Gelsinger said reviving Moore's Law depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five core engineering fronts, which he named as light, power, cooling, composition and packaging. He said turning one gigawatt of electrical power into ten gigawatts worth of AI token output requires far more than traditional transistor shrinks. He cited U.S. energy capacity growth in the low single digits over the past decade, which he said creates severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. He said new gas turbines face an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear power projects take a decade to construct. He cited NVIDIA's Kyber racks with Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power requirements to 600kW, a figure he said is enough to supply electricity to 500 homes.

Gelsinger is responsible for the argument, made as former Intel CEO and now as a general partner at venture firm Playground Global since March 2025. He said incremental chip improvements cannot satisfy AI and compute demands, and that severe power infrastructure limits are becoming a major bottleneck for innovation. He said, "We need breakthroughs across light, power, cooling, composition and packaging." He said that after 40+ years in semiconductors he believes our greatest innovations are still ahead. He has backed startups targeting these hardware bottlenecks, including U.S. government-supported lithography venture xLight and nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy.

A Harvard study revealed that U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as the country of Chile, despite not having access to all the key metrics, according to the Wccftech report. Major AI foundation models are now shipping roughly every four weeks, the report said. Gelsinger's roadmap points toward optical interconnects and silicon photonics to move data with light rather than copper. xLight aims to push past ASML's 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, the report said. Those affected include hyperscale data centers, which face hurdles from sluggish grid growth, and the hardware and energy startups Gelsinger backs.

Gelsinger's remarks come as U.S. energy capacity has grown only in the low single digits over the past decade, creating severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. Long equipment wait times contribute to the issue, with new gas turbines facing an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear projects taking a decade to construct. On a previous occasion discussing AI hardware, Gelsinger said he strongly believes HBM has a myriad of flaws, calling it a "hideous memory," but said the technology is the best the industry has right now. He proposed Z2RAM, which can potentially offer better density, performance and power draw. The articles give no further background on the summit beyond the panel and the venue.

The articles do not say what specific breakthroughs Gelsinger expects next or when any of them might arrive. They do not say whether xLight or Alva Energy has set targets or timelines for their technologies. They do not give Gelsinger's response to industry watchers who argue traditional Moore's Law scaling is over, beyond his stated view that semiconductor engineering is entering a new era of multi-disciplinary innovation. They do not say what Playground Global's investments in the two startups amount to. They leave open how the 10,000-fold efficiency gain would be measured or achieved.

stories.Headline: Defiance launches 2X long and short Anthropic ETFs for daily trading
stories.Summary:
Defiance ETFs announced on November 23, 2026, the launch of the Defiance 2X ANT Long Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTC) and the Defiance 2X ANT Short Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTQ). The announcement came from Miami, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 23, 2026. Both funds began trading that day on The Nasdaq Stock Market. Defiance described the launch as expanding its lineup of single-stock leveraged ETFs. A prior release dated November 22, 2026, said trading would begin Monday, November 23, 2026, at the 9:30 a.m.

ET open. ANTC seeks daily investment results, before fees and expenses, of 200% of the daily percentage change in the share price of Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT). ANTQ seeks daily inverse results, before fees and expenses, of -200% of the daily percentage change in ANT's share price. Neither fund seeks its stated objective for a period other than a single trading day. Both funds carry total annual operating expenses of 0.71%, a figure that excludes the indirect cost of swaps.

Both funds are series of Tidal Trust II, and shares could not be purchased until trading began. Sylvia Jablonski, Chief Investment Officer of Defiance ETFs, said Anthropic had just completed the largest IPO in history, with more than 800 million shares changing hands on its first day. She said a debut that large draws strong views in both directions. She said ANTC and ANTQ give traders a way to act on a short-term view of Anthropic, long or short, with a defined daily objective and a single ticker, rather than a margin account or an options chain. She described the products as daily tools that reset every session and are built for active traders who monitor positions closely.

Defiance said the funds are designed only for knowledgeable investors who understand daily leveraged results and monitor their portfolios frequently. Defiance said the funds are not suitable for all investors and are not intended for those who will not actively monitor and manage their portfolios. Defiance said an investor could lose the full principal value of an investment within a single day. Defiance said the funds are not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by Anthropic, and an investment in the funds is not a direct investment in Anthropic. The funds obtain exposure through swap agreements with financial institutions and may also use listed options, and they do not own Anthropic stock.

Defiance said the funds rebalance at or near each close so the next session starts at about 200% or -200% exposure. Defiance said a fund's return over any period longer than a single trading day is the result of each day's returns compounded, and will very likely differ from 200% or -200% of ANT's return for the same period. Defiance said the difference tends to widen as volatility rises. Defiance said each fund will lose money over periods longer than a single day if ANT's performance is flat, and either fund may lose money even when ANT moves in its favor over the period.

Defiance said ANTC investors could lose all their money if ANT's share price decreases by more than 50% on a given trading day. Defiance said ANTQ could lose an amount greater than its net assets if ANT's share price increases by more than 50% on a given trading day, and its investors would lose all their money. The launch followed Anthropic's initial public offering, which raised about $93.5 billion and, according to reports, is the largest on record. Anthropic priced the offering at $83.00 per share on November 18, above the $70 to $78 range it had set, and increased the base offering to 980 million shares from 825 million.

The offering closed on November 20 after underwriters exercised in full their option for an additional 147 million shares, and 1.127 billion shares were sold for gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion, alongside a concurrent private placement of $26.0 billion of Class N common stock. Anthropic's Class A common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. ANT opened at $111.50, traded between $92.72 and $115.10, and closed its first session at $97.17, with about 840 million shares changing hands. Defiance said the funds' swap and options capacity may be limited because ANT only recently completed its IPO, and a fund that cannot obtain sufficient exposure may not achieve its objective.

Defiance said fund shares may trade at wider bid-ask spreads or at premiums or discounts to net assets. Defiance said an investor who buys shares at any time other than the close will likely have more or less than 200% or -200% exposure to ANT for the rest of that day. Defiance said each fund's performance depends on one company and each fund is concentrated in the software industry. Defiance directed investors to defianceetfs.com/anthropic-etfs or 833.333.9383 for full fund details and the prospectus.

stories.Headline: GraniteShares launches leveraged long and short Anthropic ETFs on Nasdaq
stories.Summary:
GraniteShares announced on November 20, 2026, that two new exchange-traded funds linked to Anthropic PBC would begin trading on Monday, November 23, 2026. The firm said the GraniteShares 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF, ticker AIL, and the GraniteShares 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF, ticker ANS, would launch on Nasdaq. Both funds offer leveraged and inverse daily investment objectives linked to Anthropic, the developer of the Claude family of artificial intelligence models. The announcement came one trading day before the scheduled launch, according to the company's press release. GraniteShares is headquartered in New York City and was founded in 2016 by Will Rhind.

AIL seeks 200% of the daily percentage change in Anthropic common stock, before fees and expenses, according to the fund table. ANS seeks -200% of the daily percentage change in Anthropic common stock, before fees and expenses, the same table states. Both funds were scheduled to commence trading on Nasdaq on November 23, 2026. Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut on November 19, 2026, under the ticker ANT, following an IPO priced at $83 per share. The offering raised approximately $81.3 billion, and shares opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 on their first trading day, a gain of approximately 17.1% from the IPO price.

GraniteShares described the funds as providing market participants with leveraged and inverse daily investment objectives linked to Anthropic. The company said the launch came just two trading days after Anthropic's debut, expanding its leveraged single-stock ETF range to another closely watched name in artificial intelligence. GraniteShares stated that the funds are designed to be utilized only by knowledgeable investors who understand the potential consequences of seeking daily leveraged and inverse results. The firm said such investors must understand the risks associated with the use of leverage and inverse exposure and be willing to monitor their portfolios frequently. GraniteShares reported that it managed $12.27 billion in assets as of September 30, 2026.

The disclosure states that for periods longer than a single day, the funds will lose money if the underlying stock's performance is flat. It adds that the funds could lose money even if the underlying stock's performance increases over a period longer than a single day. The disclosure warns that an investor could lose the full principal value of his or her investment within a single day. It states that the funds seek daily leveraged investment results and are intended to be used as short-term trading vehicles. The disclosure says the funds are not suitable for all investors and that their investment program is speculative and entails substantial risks.

The disclosure explains that because of daily rebalancing and the compounding of each day's return over time, returns for periods longer than a single day will very likely differ from 200% and -200% of the underlying stock's return over the same period. It states that the volatility of the underlying security may affect a fund's return as much as, or more than, the return of the underlying security. The disclosure notes that shares are bought and sold at market price, not NAV, and are not individually redeemed from the ETF. It says there can be no guarantee that an active trading market for ETF shares will develop or be maintained, or that their listing will continue or remain unchanged. The disclosure states that the funds are non-diversified and include risks associated with concentrating investments in a particular industry, sector, or geographic region.

The disclosure lists risks including effects of compounding and market volatility risk, leverage risk, market risk, counterparty risk, rebalancing risk, intra-day investment risk, and other investment companies risk. It states that the funds are distributed by ALPS Distributors, Inc, which is not affiliated with GraniteShares or any of its affiliates. The disclosure says the information is not an offer to sell or a solicitation of an offer to buy shares of any funds in any jurisdiction where such an offer would be unlawful. It advises investors to consult a tax advisor about the tax consequences of an investment in fund shares. The disclosure states that there can be no assurance that the investment objective of the funds will be achieved.

stories.Headline: Woman says AI-driven system led to her eviction over unpaid rent
stories.Summary:
A woman says an AI-driven nightmare led to her eviction from her apartment when she thought she had until the end of the month to pay her overdue rent, according to reports published on Nov. 24, 2026 at 3:40 AM EST. The articles do not name the woman, the apartment, the city or the company behind the AI system, and they give no further details about what the system did or when the eviction took place. The only account the articles give is her statement that she believed she had until the end of the month to pay the overdue rent. The story was carried by several local news sites, each running the same short account with the same publication time. The articles do not say what the eviction requires of her, what it changes, or which law or process applies, and they give no numbers, dates or names beyond the Nov. 24, 2026 publication time.

No figure for the overdue rent, no deadline and no court date appears in any of the four versions. The articles also do not say whether the AI system set the deadline, sent a notice or took some other step. Because the reports stop at her statement, there is nothing further to describe about what the eviction involves. The articles do not identify who is responsible for the eviction or for the AI system, and they include no statement from a landlord, a property manager, a court or a technology company. The woman is the only person the articles attribute any statement to, and the only words they give her are that she thought she had until the end of the month to pay.

No official commented on the case in the articles, and no one else was named in connection with it. The articles give no context about how the AI system was used in the rental or eviction process, and they do not say what happens next for the woman or for anyone else involved. They do not report whether she is challenging the eviction, whether she has found other housing or whether any agency is looking into the matter. The surrounding items on each site cover unrelated local news, such as weather, school funding and community events, and none of them adds to this story. The reports end with her account and give no follow-up.

stories.Headline: Fed official Goolsbee says AI investment drives up inflation now as firms report mixed productivity gains
stories.Summary:
Last week all the major stock indexes dropped by 8% or more, and tech firms led the way down, as investors dumped stocks while trying to predict how their big bets on artificial intelligence would pay off. The drop came even as Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, was raising a boatload of money by selling shares to the public for the first time. NPR's Scott Horsley reported the status of the economic effects of AI on Morning Edition on November 23, 2026, speaking with host Steve Inskeep. Horsley said futures markets suggested a rebound that morning, with investors possibly going bargain hunting after the steep drop in a shortened holiday week. He said the moment highlighted the real uncertainty investors feel about the huge sums being plowed into artificial intelligence when no one is really sure the big bet will pay off.

The National Association for Business Economics released a survey that morning asking firms about their experience with AI, Horsley reported. About 1 in 5 businesses said the technology is producing measurable, widespread productivity gains, and about half said they have seen some gains but not widespread ones. About 30% said either they are not using AI or it is too soon to tell what the results will be, so the economy is still in the early stages. Austan Goolsbee, who heads the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said the sheer size of the investment in AI is already having an impact on the broader economy whatever the payoff for businesses. Horsley said anything construction-related costs more because it competes with AI construction, and anything with electronic components, basically anything that uses computer chips, costs more too.

Goolsbee said it is fabulous that innovations are coming up that might raise productivity growth in the country and might make us rich, but with major trillion-plus-dollar IPOs you just have to be careful. He said the sizzling demand from the AI boom is adding to other price pressures, which is making inflation a little bit scarier. Horsley said boosters argue that over the longer term AI will help curb inflation by helping businesses crank out more stuff and more services at lower prices. Goolsbee said that will be great if it happens, but the Federal Reserve has to deal with inflation right now. He likened the AI build-out to a freeway expansion project in Chicago, where you can dream about how great it will be once the highway is widened, but in the here and now they have shrunk the number of lanes and the traffic is worse.

Goolsbee suggested the Fed may have to tamp down the resulting inflation by raising interest rates. He acknowledged that might not put the brakes on the AI boom but would instead hit other, more sensitive parts of the economy like housing and furniture and appliances. Horsley said overall spending has been very resilient, but shoppers have become more gun-shy and are spending less in some areas, for example in the grocery aisle. He said gasoline and airline tickets are both more expensive than they were a year ago, but that probably will not stop many people from driving or flying to see friends and family at Thanksgiving. Horsley delivered the report as NPR's chief economics correspondent, and Inskeep hosted the segment on Morning Edition.

Horsley said a chart of the stock markets last week looked like a ski slope, and he noted that artificial intelligence is shaping the economy in ways beyond the market drop. He described businesses as using AI a lot or at least experimenting with it, and he called the results a mixed bag. The survey by the National Association for Business Economics was the source for the figures on productivity gains, and Goolsbee's remarks came in the same interview. Horsley said the uncertainty surrounds the huge sums of money being plowed into artificial intelligence at a time when no one is really sure the big bet is going to pay off.

Horsley said futures markets suggested a rebound could come that morning, and he said investors might go bargain hunting after the steep drop. He said the Fed may have to raise interest rates to tamp down the inflation, though that would hit housing, furniture and appliances rather than the AI boom. He said boosters argue AI will curb inflation over the longer term by helping businesses produce more at lower prices, and Goolsbee said that would be great if it happens. The segment left open whether the rebound would materialize, whether the Fed would raise rates, and whether the longer-term gains boosters promise would arrive.

stories.Headline: Nvidia chief Huang returns as AI trade finds relief but faces open questions
stories.Summary:
The board of Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang after he had departed earlier in November 2026 following revelations of his extramarital affairs. This abrupt reversal occurred after the initial departure of the chief executive rattled investors and caused a slide in technology shares. The return of the leader brought a sigh of relief to investors in the battered artificial intelligence trade worth trillions of dollars. Some market participants viewed the move as a sign that the AI boom and Huang were simply too big to fail. The event halted a decline that had previously sent the benchmark S&P 500 index into a market correction.

The return of Huang caused Nvidia shares to soar more than 31 percent on Monday, adding over 950 billion US dollars in value. This single session cut the year to date losses of the company by two thirds and pushed the Nasdaq 100 up nearly 7 percent. In Taipei, production partners TSMC and Foxconn jumped by their daily limit of 10 percent on Tuesday following the news of the return. The company has previously bought shares in the South Korean provider Naver and the data centre operator known as CoreWeave Inc. Nvidia maintains its head office in California, where the company is based and where the attorney general's office is located.

President Donald Trump said he secured the deal to bring back Huang and told CNBC that the stock market reaction probably factored in. Trump stated that his view of the long term benefit of having Huang at the helm was the bigger weight in his decision. He also said the United States had no reason to believe that the return of the chief executive posed any security risk. King Lip of BakerAvenue Wealth Management said the return removes a significant piece of uncertainty that had created a crisis of confidence. Thomas Urano of Sage Advisory said the initial reaction was a big collective sigh of relief that puts confidence back.

Tom Plumb of the Plumb Balanced Fund said that nobody felt comfortable that anyone else could automatically fill the shoes of the visionary. Investors who were affected worried that the massive value of the company was tied up in the man who foresaw technology shifts. Shares of Naver and CoreWeave rose on the news, but they did not recover all losses logged since the resignation of Huang. Traders in Hong Kong noted that the Artificial Intelligence index remained flat due to risks of intensified scrutiny of exposure to China. James St Aubin of Ocean Park Asset Management said the return does not answer the big questions investors were grappling with.

The articles state that Nvidia has nurtured the AI ecosystem by acting as a lender and investor for its biggest customers. The company is credited with putting advanced chips at the heart of the AI boom, which drove the soaring profits of the firm. Before the leadership crisis, the market was dogged by questions about AI funding, profitability, regulation, and public resistance to data centre developments. The company is currently tied to an array of different firms involved in the sprawling buildout of artificial intelligence across the globe. The board had previously dismissed the idea of rehiring Huang before the abrupt reversal that took place earlier this month.

Huang will likely face questions from Congress next week regarding his relationship with a person who is an alleged spy for China. The California attorney general's office will continue a probe into what Nvidia told its investors about the company's ties to China. Yang Wang of Counterpoint Research said that while the CEO question is resolved, the governance and geopolitical questions have not been answered. Investors remain nervous about the outlook for the financing of customers and the broader trade as the relief rally runs its course. The articles leave open whether the board's independence is compromised and if regulatory issues will arise from the return of Huang.

stories.Headline: Fed chair Kevin Warsh presents three super intelligence scenarios for the economy
stories.Summary:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh discussed three economic scenarios regarding super intelligence at a recent conference. This event took place on November 16 at a meeting for the Productivity and Jobs Task Force. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco hosted the gathering where Warsh spoke. He explained that the Federal Reserve is currently modeling these three possible paths for the economy. These scenarios focus on how the economy might change as artificial intelligence continues to develop.

The first scenario involves rising productivity and growth that stays above the long run average. The second scenario requires super intelligence to work, but it could cause substantial labor market disruption. This second path might push the jobless rate above levels consistent with full employment in the United States. The third scenario is a letdown where super intelligence disappoints and returns on capital are lower than expected. This final path leads to a decline in valuations and a slowing economy before an eventual recovery.

Kevin Warsh is the chair of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors and manages these models. He stated that the three illustrative scenarios are not forecasts and he was not offering predictions. Warsh noted that many other outcomes could be drawn, including one that will prove most accurate. He has tried to avoid any kind of forward guidance since he became the chair. He stressed that these scenarios might not even happen as the Fed staff built them.

Some investors already share the concern that returns on capital for artificial intelligence could be lower than expected. Workers who are displaced by technology or forced into lower paying jobs are affected by these changes. These displaced workers are also consumers who power the economy through their regular household spending. The Federal Reserve is charged with managing concerns regarding growth, jobs, and inflation for the coming years. The stock market and the broader economy could face adverse implications from two of the scenarios.

President Donald Trump and his administration adopted the term super intelligence to describe artificial intelligence technology. This technology has become a driving force for both corporate spending and gains in the stock market. Business equipment spending jumped nearly 21 percent in the third quarter, which helped lift GDP growth to 3.4 percent. Consumer spending currently accounts for more than two thirds of the total economy in the United States. The Fed must figure out what is coming before it arrives to manage stable prices and employment.

The Federal Reserve will continue to monitor how super intelligence impacts the labor market and overall productivity. Investors are encouraged to consider these scenarios to ensure that their portfolios are prepared for different outcomes. The articles leave open which of the three scenarios, if any, will actually prove to be the most accurate. It remains unknown if the best case for technology is the best case for the American consumer. The articles do not state when the Fed will release new models or updated economic forecasts.

stories.Headline: Musk tells SpaceX staff the company cannot compete on AI and rents out its computing power
stories.Summary:
In August, Elon Musk changed the name of an engineers' group chat with hundreds of SpaceX employees to "Sell compute because we can't compete," according to a New York Times report published on Monday, November 23, 2026. In the same chat, the SpaceX CEO warned that anyone wasting GPUs on what he called bulls,  while the company was failing to compete would be asked to leave immediately, a step he described as a betrayal of the team. The report said Musk had privately expressed concerns that SpaceX was falling behind other artificial intelligence companies, even as the company leased valuable data centers to competitors such as Anthropic and Google. SpaceX had rapidly built data centers, including its Colossus facility in Memphis, Tennessee, to scale up its own AI business, but the company is now leasing compute to its rivals instead.

The report said SpaceX's AI unit now accounts for more than half of the rocket company's revenue through leasing agreements with other AI companies. Anthropic became SpaceX's biggest customer in October, surpassing the U.S. government, and is now paying an estimated $3.1 billion per month according to its prospectus, while Google is reportedly paying $800 million. The Times reported that xAI, which merged with SpaceX earlier this year, used less than half the capacity of its Colossus data center last year, citing internal documents. As income from leasing compute soared, SpaceX quietly shifted resources from several AI projects, including an AI companion feature, and laid off 60 employees working on Grok Imagine, an image and video generator, which The Information first reported the previous week.

The Times also reported that SpaceX shifted money away from the company's Digital Optimus project with Tesla, which was training AI models to do white collar work by first teaching them how to play video games. After Anthropic went public the previous week with a record-breaking initial public offering, both Musk and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made comments indicating their deal will likely continue in the near future. Asked on CNBC whether Anthropic planned to scale back its spending with Musk's company, Amodei said you can't be sure what you're going to do in the future, but that Anthropic was finding the compute to be high quality and enjoying working with SpaceX. Musk, speaking at the DealBook Summit the previous week, said he thought it was unlikely the company would stop leasing compute, and said Anthropic had told him its highest probability outcome was that it would like an incremental 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX, which he called a big number.

stories.Headline: Arizona teacher Kareem Neal uses AI to tailor lessons for special education students
stories.Summary:
Kareem Neal discussed the impact of artificial intelligence in schools during a recent appearance on NewsNation. Neal is Arizona's 2019 Teacher of the Year and a 2022 National Teachers Hall of Fame inductee. He explained how AI tools have been very helpful for both educators and students. The teacher uses these tools to help him plan lessons for his classes. He also uses AI to help his students better understand various pieces of information.

Neal teaches special education students in the ninth through twelfth grades. He uses AI to create content tailored to the specific learning levels of his students. He noted that many of his students read at prekindergarten or kindergarten levels. He can take an article written at a typical 10th or 11th grade level and rewrite it. This process makes the content accessible to students reading at a kindergarten or first grade level.

Kareem Neal stated that it can be difficult to find government articles that special education students understand. He believes that banning AI in schools would not prevent students from accessing it elsewhere. Neal acknowledged that the use of AI has made it easier for students to cheat. He emphasized that the tools are helpful for creating age appropriate and accessible content. These tools allow him to modify complex texts for his specific student needs.

New York City Mayor Eric Adams criticized a separate move by Google regarding AI in schools. Adams claimed that Google is using monopoly power to force AI into public schools. He stated that no corporation should dictate how children are taught in the public system. He argued that public schools exist to serve students rather than grow Big Tech profit margins. This conflict involves the integration of AI features into the Google search engine.

The articles state that AI is becoming increasingly integrated into classrooms across the United States. Google announced that students cannot use its search engine if schools block AI features in 2027. Chris Phillips is the vice president for education at Google. He told the New York Times that search and AI can no longer be separated. Access to these products will be off for K-12 accounts until administrators turn them on.

Google will turn off search for schools that do not use AI in 2027. The company provided this information in a recent update regarding K-12 student accounts. School administrators must explicitly turn on AI features to maintain access to the search engine. The articles do not state how many schools will block these features. They leave open how many districts will follow the lead of Mayor Eric Adams.

stories.Headline: DXC launches Frontier Code Assurance to find and fix software flaws using Claude Mythos
stories.Summary:
DXC Technology said on November 24, 2026 that it had launched DXC Frontier Code Assurance, a cybersecurity service that uses Anthropic's Claude Mythos AI model to help enterprises find, validate and help remediate vulnerabilities in mission-critical software, according to the company's press release. The release, issued from Ashburn, Virginia, described DXC as a leading enterprise technology and innovation partner and said the offering is available now, with an email address given for additional information and next steps. According to the release, the service can find flaws traditional scanners miss, with results validated by DXC cybersecurity specialists and ranked by business impact, and it delivers a prioritized remediation roadmap with auditable evidence at every step. The release said DXC then helps customers remediate and patch, and that organizations can start with a single application and expand over time or fold the service into ongoing security operations.

According to the release, Frontier Code Assurance builds on a multi-year global alliance between the two companies, announced in June 2026, to bring advanced AI capabilities into mission-critical enterprise environments, and DXC said it is a Global Premier partner in the Claude Partner Network. The release said the new offering is part of DXC's global Cybersecurity practice, which it said runs 12 Security Operations Centers across more than 40 countries with thousands of cybersecurity professionals. DXC said that as AI accelerates the discovery of vulnerabilities, the bottleneck has shifted from finding flaws to prioritizing and executing the remediation path, and that the service is built for that challenge. The release said Claude Mythos finds the potential vulnerabilities while DXC specialists decide what to do about them.

Raul Fernandez, CEO of DXC Technology, said in the release that through the Anthropic partnership DXC is able to combine its existing cyber incident detection, rapid response and recovery management with a new capability to run Claude Mythos for cyber vulnerability, discovery and detection. Fernandez said that with thousands of security professionals globally, DXC is very well positioned to assist its customers in what he called a rapidly emerging, critical capability. The release said the Frontier Code Assurance offering is available now and directed interested parties to email for additional information and next steps. The release described DXC Technology, listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker DXC, as delivering software, services and solutions to global enterprises and public sector organizations.

stories.Headline: Colorado hearing officer dismisses Kipp complaint over Independence Institute AI video
stories.Summary:
A hearing officer in the Colorado secretary of state's office dismissed a complaint last week regarding an AI-generated political video. State Senator Cathy Kipp filed the complaint, alleging that the video violated state laws against unlabeled deepfake political content. The hearing officer, Macon Cowles, issued his decision on November 19 to dismiss the case against the video. The video was produced by the right-leaning Independence Institute to criticize a specific ballot measure before the election. This legal dispute centered on whether the AI-generated content required a specific disclosure under current Colorado state law.

The 2024 law requires a disclosure when generative artificial intelligence depicts a political candidate close to an election date. The video criticized Proposition NN before the November 3 election, a measure sponsored by Kipp and referred by the Legislature. Proposition NN passed with over 57 percent of the vote to let the state retain more revenue for education. The AI-generated video showed Kipp as a grocery store cashier who refused to give a customer their change. While the video had a closing line stating it was AI-generated, it lacked the text required by law.

Hearing officer Macon Cowles stated that the law applies to content that falsely appears to be authentic and truthful. He determined the video was parody and satire, which he wrote are protected by the First Amendment of the Constitution. Cowles wrote that no reasonable viewer would believe Kipp agreed to play a cashier who keeps a customer's money. He noted that Kipp is a public figure and this AI criticism is akin to a political newspaper cartoon. The Independence Institute conceded the video was not true but asserted that no viewer would consider it true.

Independence Institute CEO Jon Caldara said they were grateful the officer saw the video as a joke with a point. Caldara stated that nobody believed Kipp moonlights at a checkout counter and that voters deserved to hear their argument. Senator Cathy Kipp expressed disappointment that the complaint was dismissed in a text message sent to the Colorado Newsline. Kipp stated it was important for the Legislature to find out how the law they passed would be interpreted. She argued that laws must keep up as AI-generated imagery and deepfakes become increasingly prevalent and harmful.

The law at the center of this case was passed by Colorado lawmakers in 2024 to regulate campaign materials. The Independence Institute used the video to illustrate what they believed Proposition NN would do with taxpayer money. The video portrayed Kipp stealing grocery change to give to children for their education, which the institute admitted was false. Critics had already raised free speech concerns about the disclosure requirements of the law after it took effect in 2024. The hearing officer concluded that reasonable viewers would not believe the events in the video actually happened.

The decision made by Macon Cowles is subject to review by the deputy secretary of state before it becomes final. The articles do not state when the deputy secretary of state will complete this review or what the result will be. There is no information regarding whether Senator Kipp intends to appeal the decision or take further legal action. The text does not mention if the Independence Institute plans to release similar AI-generated videos for future elections. It remains open whether the Legislature will amend the 2024 law based on this specific legal interpretation.

stories.Headline: DesignVerse finds AI coding tools without company context cost thousands of engineering hours
stories.Summary:
DesignVerse published its AI Coding Drift Report on 24 November 2026, examining 15 private enterprise codebases in sectors including aviation, banking and defense, each a complex legacy system between 15 and 20 years old containing more than one million lines of code. The research found that businesses using AI coding tools without knowledge of their existing systems and technical standards spend thousands of engineering hours correcting and rebuilding AI-written code. In one enterprise case, a year's work on a single product required an estimated 9,600 engineering hours without an enterprise context layer, a figure the report says fell to 4,000 hours, a 58% reduction, once such a layer was introduced. The 5,600 hours freed were valued at around $882,000, which the report describes as engineering capacity equivalent to about three engineers that could be redirected to other work rather than a direct reduction in staffing costs. The report also compared two unmanaged AI coding agents with DesignVerse's context-engineered system, which gives AI access to company knowledge, existing code, software architecture and technical requirements before it begins work.

The context-engineered system used the organization's own internal software components rather than inventing them or substituting public alternatives 92% of the time, compared with 55% to 59% for the unmanaged agents. The report introduces an Engineering AI Drift Index, which measures how much information an AI coding agent must read before producing code that can be accepted into existing systems, and across the examined codebases agents working without a dedicated context layer read a median of ten tokens for every token of accepted code, a ratio that reached 150 to one in a separate measurement on one client's legacy system. The report likens the problem to a skilled new hire with no handover, noting that an AI agent does the same on every task and forgets what it learned between sessions. Andrei Manolache, CEO and co-founder of DesignVerse, said businesses are investing heavily in AI coding tools because they expect to develop software faster and at lower cost, but there is a hidden bill many are not measuring in the time engineers spend checking, correcting and rebuilding code that does not fit their existing systems. He said companies paying for AI to write code only to pay engineers to fix it afterwards need to ask serious questions about the return on that investment, and that the next challenge for enterprise AI is not simply generating more code but generating code that fits the business.

He said an AI coding tool needs to understand the systems it works with, the company's architecture, its technical standards and the rules it must follow, and that without that context businesses risk creating more work for their engineers rather than less. The report sets out five recommendations, including building a persistent context layer of existing code, architecture, standards and project knowledge, giving AI tools access only to information relevant to each task, enforcing technical standards as code is generated, maintaining an audit trail of which company information and standards were used, and giving a named individual responsibility for keeping the context layer accurate and up to date. The full report, including its method, scoring rubric and limitations, is available online, and it sets out a two-week evaluation any engineering team can run on its own codebase. Businesses can also estimate the potential cost of engineering rework using DesignVerse's Cost of Drift Calculator.

This puts Musk in a position where he rents power to companies he is chasing. Anthropic is described as one of the biggest competitors and biggest customers for Elon Musk. The tension highlights a central conflict in the artificial intelligence push led by Elon Musk.

Musk started the company xAI one year after the 2022 release of the chatbot called ChatGPT. He has spent billions of dollars on data centers to catch up with his rivals. The New York Times viewed communications where Musk changed a group chat name in August. That specific name was Sell compute because we can't compete to reflect the current situation. These actions show the struggle to balance immediate revenue with long term product development goals.

SpaceX will continue to manage the use of its graphics processing units for training systems. The company must decide whether to prioritize internal AI development or external leasing for profit. stories.Headline: Brands use AI pricing tools to cut Black Friday discounts and protect margins
stories.Summary:
Consumer brands are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to help set prices, hoping to reduce discounts and protect profit margins, according to interviews with five firms that provide AI tools to brands and retailers. That could mean shallower bargains for inflation-weary US shoppers this holiday season, starting with Black Friday, an event synonymous with discounts. Brands from Gap to Under Armour are using AI tools to manage inventory levels, recommend retail prices and figure out when and how steeply to discount products. Often, the tools conclude that companies can reduce discounts without dampening demand, the AI pricing firms told Reuters. Software from retail decision-making company Impact Analytics, which counts Gap as a client, generally shows that brands need fewer promotions for less time on fewer products, chief executive officer Prashant Agrawal said.

Tools from AI pricing firm Kapnova advised a billion-dollar beauty brand to reduce its 2026 Black Friday discount on a skincare product to 30% from an initially planned 40%, CEO James Sun said, declining to name the client due to confidentiality. Tools from AI software company First Insight, whose customers include Under Armour and value chain Family Dollar, recently suggested that one brand scale back a buy-one-get-one promotion from 50% to 40% off, founder Greg Petro said, also declining to name the client. Holiday sales are set to rise 4.2% versus 2025 to just over US$1 trillion, National Retail Federation estimates show, though the bump would be largely attributable to an inflation rate currently at 3.7%. A Gap spokesperson said the brand uses Impact Analytics to make more informed markdown decisions based on demand and inventory signals, while Under Armour and Family Dollar use First Insight to decide what to charge for a product and to estimate how price changes will affect sales, the retail technology company said. Sun of Kapnova conceded that the practice is controversial, saying consumers want discounts but retailers are getting smarter and smarter with AI.

AI-driven planning platform Anaplan said LVMH-owned Tiffany, Dolce & Gabbana and Kering's Yves Saint Laurent use its software for pricing, and more than a dozen brands approached by Reuters, including those five, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The technology is not completely new, but it has become more sophisticated over the past two years at predicting demand for products at specific prices, and adoption is ramping up, experts and industry executives say. A 2025 survey by consultancy Simon-Kucher showed that a third of companies now use AI pricing for demand forecasting and 28% for real-time price optimisation, said Martin Crepy, the firm's global head of consumer. Predictive algorithms typically stop short of pricing items differently for individual customers, a controversial practice that retailers like Walmart and Target have said they do not engage in and that several states have taken steps to curb, but tools that allow retailers to quickly change prices, often called dynamic pricing, sit one layer removed from personalised pricing, according to former McKinsey consultant and e-commerce executive Sofia Serra, who said regulation is still evolving.

stories.Headline: Leibenluft and Sperling propose five policy planks to prepare US workers for AI job dislocation
stories.Summary:
Jacob Leibenluft and Gene Sperling wrote a report on November 23, 2026, regarding artificial intelligence. They proposed five policy planks to prepare the United States workforce for potential job dislocation. The authors argue that policymakers must begin these preparations now despite an uncertain outlook. These measures aim to support economic dignity for workers during a potential transition. The report suggests that the United States currently lacks the basic infrastructure to support these workers.

The plan requires universal job search assistance and universal income support for all displaced workers. It proposes expanded, progressive wage insurance and the use of automatic scaling-up strategies for labor challenges. The authors suggest supporting redeployment and shorter workweeks without pay reductions to discourage unnecessary layoffs. One proposal includes a universal worker adjustment assistance program providing up to 104 weeks of unemployment payments. These policies would be funded by better taxing corporate profits and capital.

Leibenluft and Sperling stated that the United States lags behind peer nations in providing transition infrastructure. They argued that policymakers should reject training nihilism and invest in successful workforce development strategies. The authors claimed that universal eligibility is the best roadmap forward for assisting displaced workers. They noted that any transition agenda is only one element of a broader policy response. They stated that no adjustment policies can succeed without a commitment to creating good jobs.

The authors noted that many workers already feel anxiety regarding the impact of artificial intelligence. They argued that the gains of productivity growth should be more equitably shared among workers. The report suggests that the lack of good jobs would limit the benefits of training. The authors believe that these policies would also help workers who lose jobs for other reasons. They claimed that previous economic disruptions would have been handled better with these robust measures.

The report notes that economists suggest scenarios ranging from minor transitions to the dislocation of tens of millions. It mentions that past trade assistance programs failed because they required complex adjudication processes for workers. The authors cite a period in the early 2000s when two million workers were dislocated by imports. They noted that Trade Adjustment Assistance then provided training to fewer than 50,000 workers per year. This background serves as a warning against targeting only those who prove AI caused loss.

The authors state that the federal and state governments should start this work immediately. They argue that the approach will require ongoing refinement and experimentation as AI impacts become clearer. The report leaves open the specific details of how to create new jobs if AI causes net losses. It does not specify the exact tax rates needed to fund these proposed worker supports. The authors acknowledge that full answers to the effects of AI on jobs remain unclear.

stories.Headline: US Energy Department leads project to test fuel cell power systems for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A three-year project led by the U.S. Department of Energy will examine how fuel cells, energy storage and power electronics can work together to meet the rapidly changing electricity demands of artificial intelligence data centers. The project, called StabilityMax, is led by the DOE's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory and FuelCell Energy. The effort will develop and validate testing and modeling frameworks to evaluate integrated power system architectures under operating conditions designed to reflect the fluctuating loads of modern data centers. As AI workloads expand, data centers are placing increasing demands on electricity infrastructure, and their power consumption can change rapidly as computing activity shifts, creating challenges for maintaining reliable power and managing impacts on the utility grid.

Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut that will serve as a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power systems. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will develop data center load profiles and simulation models to replicate the dynamic electricity requirements of AI computing infrastructure. Researchers will use the models and test facility to examine how fuel cells can operate alongside energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics to respond to changing loads. Argonne National Laboratory will contribute techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to evaluate potential deployment approaches.

The research will focus in part on the ability of fuel cell systems located alongside data centers to respond to power fluctuations while limiting impacts on the utility grid and other electricity customers. StabilityMax is part of the National Laboratory of the Rockies' broader work to develop modeling tools, planning platforms and testing environments for the growing energy requirements of AI-enabled digital infrastructure. The project also builds on FuelCell Energy's work with technology partners on integrated power architectures for data centers. Earlier this year, the company announced a collaboration with Siemens to advance a layered approach that combines multiple power technologies operating across different timescales.

stories.Headline: Appian report finds AI-written apps raise maintenance and security costs for UK enterprises
stories.Summary:
A report from Appian warns that enterprises rushing to use artificial intelligence for software coding face unexpected costs around maintenance and security for applications the company calls “aloneware.” Appian published the findings on November 24, 2026, and TechGig reported on the research the same day. The report says AI coding tools push time and costs further down the software lifecycle, which can make problems more difficult and expensive to resolve. Appian uses the term “aloneware” to describe apps developed using AI, noting their significant speed potential.

Two in three UK enterprise leaders, or 64 per cent, reported increasing time spent on testing, troubleshooting and deployment, even though actual software development with AI was faster. Four in five UK enterprise leaders, or 79 per cent, have already allocated at least 10 per cent of their technology innovation budgets to testing, deploying and maintaining non-commercially available software. Two in five, or 43 per cent, allocate at least 20 per cent of these budgets. The report highlights downsides such as generated code that is hard for developers to understand and maintain, limited documentation, complex integrations and awkward dependencies.

Three in five leaders reported unexpected post-launch costs associated with security or governance, and a further three in five struggle to access relevant technical support when apps do not come from enterprise-grade vendors. Appian CEO Matt Calkins said the most important applications in enterprises need support, and that if you vibe-code them there will be nobody to turn to when problems occur. Calkins added that using AI to build applications on a commercial platform combines the speed of AI with the reliability of supported technology. This suggests a middle ground for enterprises seeking both ownership and security benefits.

stories.Headline: Agoda reports 64 per cent faster code reviews with its modular monolith framework
stories.Summary:
Agoda introduced a modular monolith framework called Platform in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries between different parts of the system. The framework organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking and payments, and it avoids the need to rewrite the existing service from scratch. Agoda reported that the median code review time for changes backed by the framework was 64 per cent shorter than for legacy code. The company also said the time to initial substantive feedback fell by 34 per cent compared with legacy code.

The framework relies on several practices to keep the code organized, including the Data Mapper pattern, which separates repository-specific models from business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, and ArchUnit encodes architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration pipelines. Those tests fail builds when violations of the constraints occur, so the boundaries are enforced automatically rather than by manual review. Platform is now the default for new modules, and existing functionality is being migrated incrementally.

Agoda is the company responsible for the change, and it reported the 64 per cent and 34 per cent figures itself. The company said the approach shortened code review times without requiring a full service rewrite. The articles do not name any individual who spoke about the work or give any further statements beyond those figures and descriptions. The articles also do not say what happens next beyond the incremental migration of existing functionality to Platform.

stories.Headline: Google engineer says agents need scoped identities and sandboxes to limit insider risk
stories.Summary:
Amanda Walker, Google's senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security, spoke at QCon San Francisco about securing AI agents in production, framing them as an insider-risk problem that operates at machine speed. She said a rogue AI agent is like a rogue human insider but acts with superhuman speed and persistence, so controls must work at machine speed rather than relying on manual log reviews. She recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone. She cautioned that giving an agent raw human credentials is a fast path to production failure.

Scoped OAuth tokens can limit an agent's access in time and scope but are immutable once issued, while credential attenuation, where an orchestrator mints narrower tokens for its subagents, offers more flexibility, such as read-only access to logs. Eclipse Biscuit is a token format that lets holders append restrictions but not remove existing ones without invalidating the signature. For API keys, a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real key as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration. Walker noted that virtual machines protect the host but not the resources an agent can access, while container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies like Envoy offer finer control over file system and network access.

She said a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful without policies to constrain agent actions, and she highlighted risks from poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets. Snyk research found that over a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw. Agents can also cause harm unintentionally, such as one that invoked an emergency break-glass process after reading internal SRE documentation. Walker stated that tagging identities as agents provides auditability for risk decisions, supporting human-only rules like emergency access and agent-only rules like signed releases in regulated environments.
