stories.Headline: US military develops AI-enhanced simulation training for Pacific threat scenarios
stories.Summary:
The US military is developing training that can simulate real-world scenarios it may face in the Pacific, according to a Breaking Defense Game Changer published on November 24, 2026. The article says this kind of simulation will be critical to preparing for possible threats in the region. It explores tools and tactics that can be used to develop training and to quickly adjust it in response to future threat scenarios. The piece is described as a Game Changer, a Breaking Defense format, and it carries no further detail on dates, units or named officials.

The article frames the work as rehearsing the Indo-Pacific fight with AI-enhanced simulation, and it presents the effort as a way to keep training responsive as threat scenarios change. It gives no numbers, no contract values and no names of the people or organizations running the effort. The only date the article gives is its own publication date of November 24, 2026. It does not say what the simulation requires, what it changes or when it might be fielded.

stories.Headline: Pew Research Center rejects AI tools for coding religious restriction data after tests show inaccuracy
stories.Summary:
Pew Research Center tested two artificial intelligence tools to code data on religious restrictions. The center conducted these experiments between December 2024 and August 2025. Researchers wanted to see if AI could speed up the manual coding process. They compared AI results against data already hand-coded in prior studies. The center ultimately rejected adopting these tools into their current coding workflow.

The tests used Google's NotebookLM from December 2024 to February 2025 and Nexis+ AI from July to August 2025. NotebookLM reviewed 2021 sources for Germany, Iceland, Jamaica, Nigeria, Singapore, Canada, China, India, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, Indonesia, Serbia, and Syria. Nexis+ AI used 2020 and 2022 data for Canada, Egypt, Germany, Jamaica, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and South Korea. The process involves answering over 30 questions to produce the Government Restrictions Index and Social Hostilities Index. These indices cover 198 countries and territories with data dating back to 2007.

The researchers stated that the tools did not make things up but lacked completeness. They noted that AI missed many cases that human coders had previously found. For Nigeria in 2021, the tool listed four incidents while humans found 119 cases. The center said verifying AI citations took more time than the tools saved. They also observed that identical prompts produced different answers on different days.

The center noted that Nexis+ AI missed local reporting not translated into English. It failed to find a 2022 story about the detention of Jehovah's Witnesses in South Korea. The tool also cited Pew Research Center data back to the researchers through news stories. Human coders are affected because verifying AI results for Singapore took 10.5 hours instead of 4.5. The center said inconsistency would limit a dataset designed for comparisons over time.

The center manually codes data from national constitutions and publications from the United Nations and U.S. government. They also use sources from nongovernmental organizations like Human Rights Watch. A team of five trained coders typically spends four months combing through these documents. Two coders independently review each law, policy, or event to reconcile any disagreements. This demanding process ensures the integrity of the annual scores for each country.

The center may explore using AI to produce quick summaries to orient coders. They might test AI as a second coder to reconcile disagreements with humans. Future tests could involve updated tools to identify reliable sources for new research questions. The articles leave open whether newer versions of these AI tools will be more accurate. They do not state when further tests with updated tools will occur.

stories.Headline: Democrats seek stricter chip export controls and AI investigations after Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations into the Trump administration on Monday, November 23, 2026. This demand followed the decision by the board of Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer. President Donald Trump supported the move on Monday, stating that Huang did nothing wrong and had been communicating with the board. Nvidia claimed that input from senior United States government officials convinced the board that the return of Huang poses no national security risk.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., wants the 120th Congress to implement mandatory independent evaluations of artificial intelligence systems and update liability laws for internal development risks. He proposes a special joint committee on AI to study economic and workforce impacts, as well as greater transparency regarding industry debt and financing. Van Hollen also urges the Commerce Department to close loopholes that allow affiliates of banned companies or remote users to access advanced chips. Additionally, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.y., argues that the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation.

Senator Charles E. Schumer, D-N.y., stated that Democrats will use their power to investigate anyone who sells out national security for financial gain, including Huang and Trump administration officials. Jeffries echoed this call for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to prevent the Chinese Communist Party from exploiting AI technology. Senator Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued that the reckless decision to reinstate Huang increases the urgency for strict export controls. Meanwhile, Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said that Huang's testimony is critical for protecting the AI advantage of the United States.

Republican leaders have scheduled several oversight events, including a Senate Banking Committee hearing on December 3 featuring Huang as a witness. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., announced that Huang and general counsel Tim Teter will undergo transcribed interviews during the week of November 30. These interviews will be conducted by the House Intelligence Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. The committees have also requested the appearance of Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler.

stories.Headline: AMA adopts policy that AI can assist physicians but cannot be licensed to practice medicine
stories.Summary:
At its November interim meeting, the American Medical Association adopted a new policy stating that AI can assist with clinical tasks but cannot be granted physician licensure, professional titles or certification to practice medicine, Karen Blum reported for the Association of Health Care Journalists on November 23, 2026. The policy says AI-enabled technologies can be integrated into physician-led teams but must be used at the direction of the treating physician. It also calls for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability if they use AI products alongside their own clinical judgment and patient harm results, regardless of whether they follow the tools' recommendations. AI tools used for clinical functions like diagnosis or prescribing should have transparent, auditable evidence demonstrating their safety and efficacy, and be subject to appropriate regulation, documentation and liability requirements, according to an AMA news release. The policy also calls for legislation to prohibit misrepresenting nonhuman entities with titles reserved for physicians, according to an AMA news article that noted the Food and Drug Administration has authorized more than 1,450 AI-enabled medical devices as of December 2025.

AMA President Willie Underwood III said in a prepared statement that AI can help physicians analyze information, identify patterns and support clinical decision-making, but patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care. He said physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team. The AMA posits that when medical errors result from defective AI products, liability should rest with the vendors or manufacturers, or with hospitals or insurers that require the use of specific AI products. The Federation of State Medical Boards has enlisted regulators and industry associations to devise accountability guidelines, with recommendations expected next spring, AHCJ board member Randy Dotinga wrote for Medscape.

John D. Banja, professor emeritus at Emory University's Center for Ethics in Atlanta, told Medscape that until malpractice cases arise, it is unclear how liability scenarios will play out. Utah, which the article describes as the first state allowing residents to renew medications via AI without needing to speak to a doctor, has been expanding its testing of AI clinical programs. Last month, state regulators said they would allow an AI-powered service to assess patients for mild to moderate acne in part by analyzing photos of their skin, and determine whether to prescribe a low-risk drug, Mario Aguilar reported for STAT. In the early stages of this pilot, AI decisions will be reviewed by a licensed clinician to sign off on prescriptions, but the product may eventually be allowed to prescribe without this review, the article said.

This is part of a larger initiative allowing Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to waive regulations for companies looking to test their AI products under state supervision, Aguilar wrote. Additional agreements allow testing of a prescription renewal service focused on chronic disease treatment and the use of AI to evaluate patients for pelvic floor-strengthening physical therapy and guide treatment. These plans are continuing even though the state's Medical Licensing Board in the spring called for an immediate suspension of the first pilot allowing prescriptions, the article said. The Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy will now require third-party audits of participant claims and is introducing a network of authorized evaluators, according to the article.

In May, the state's Department of Commerce released the first five months of data from that program, showing that in 72% of cases, the AI tool recommended approving a medication renewal and routed it to a physician for approval, Forbes reported. Physicians agreed with that recommendation 91% of the time, requesting information such as updated labs in the remaining cases, and the department did not say how many total cases were reviewed. In about 28% of cases, the tool escalated the renewal request to a physician on its own, flagging complications or a need for new testing, and physicians agreed with the tool's recommendation 69% of the time. Zach Boyd, head of Utah's Department of Commerce, told Forbes that the tool has erred toward over-caution, routinely kicking uncontroversial decisions up to a physician.

stories.Headline: Nvidia adds AI motion generation and RTX updates for game developers
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA published its monthly game development update on 24 November 2026, describing new graphics, animation and local AI capabilities for game teams. Gaijin Entertainment integrated NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into the Dagor Engine for War Thunder, the article says. NVIDIA Kimodo became the first AI motion-generation model integrated into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's guided animation framework, according to the article. The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8, RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2, Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 also received updates. The article says the updates help teams balance image quality, performance and creative intent.

Gaijin adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map results back to linear HDR. Kimodo lets animators generate character motion inside Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's Sequencer using text prompts, spline paths and target poses at specific frames. In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 adds hardened RTX Spark platform support, updated llama.cpp and whisper.cpp backends, Parakeet automatic speech recognition through whisper.cpp, and Vulkan priority API integration. RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling, a fallback sample feature, enhanced reservoir visualization and RTX Spark support. RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds a nine-step introductory sample combining ReSTIR DI, SHaRC radiance caching and DLSS Ray Reconstruction, plus real-time subsampling and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation.

Gaijin said DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast the team had not been able to achieve before. The team said the result is a more natural, lifelike image with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism. Gaijin also said it tuned DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear and material properties. The team said it evaluated image quality and performance separately across air, ground and naval combat. The article says the interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with art direction.

The article says ON/OFF comparisons highlight rainy, overcast scenes in War Thunder. The article says Kimodo pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments. The article says the In-Game Inferencing SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics. The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues. The article says RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline.

The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries, displaying results in a separate window with its own camera. The article says developers can use the included sampler to attach the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process without changing a title's code. The article says the viewer offers visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state, plus per-pixel trace time heatmaps. The article says RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination and path tracing. The article says the RTX Path Tracing intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps.

The article directs developers to read the War Thunder DLSS 5 developer interview for practical lessons on balancing lighting enhancements with art direction. It directs developers to explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project to understand the guided animation framework. It directs developers to download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems to analyze DLSS Frame Generation workloads and use agentic AI tooling for graphics development. The article says Nsight Graphics 2026.4 and Nsight Systems 2026.6 introduce support for analyzing applications using DLSS Frame Generation, requiring Streamline SDK 2.12 or newer. The article says a new Nsight Graphics MCP server enables compatible AI agents to capture applications, inspect and debug captures, and analyze GPU traces.

stories.Headline: UC Irvine researchers combine physics and AI to reconstruct fluid flow from noisy sparse data
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Irvine developed a computational approach that combines fundamental physics with artificial intelligence to reconstruct fluid flow from limited and imperfect measurements. The work was published in the journal Physics of Fluids on November 23, 2026, in a paper titled "On physics-based reconstruction of incompressible flow fields from noisy and sparse data." Haithem Taha, professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering in UC Irvine's Samueli School of Engineering, and Arash Kheradvar, M.D., professor of radiological sciences in the School of Medicine and biomedical engineering in the Samueli School of Engineering, were leading collaborators. The research was led by first author Abdelrahman Elmaradny, who recently earned his Ph.D. at UC Irvine under Taha's supervision, with Kheradvar serving on his dissertation committee. The study also included Mohammad Saber Hashemi, a former postdoctoral researcher in Kheradvar's laboratory at UC Irvine.

The framework, called PMPG-based neural network, or PMPG-NN, combines neural networks with the principle of minimum pressure gradient, a principle of fluid mechanics advanced through earlier theoretical research by Taha and his collaborators. The method searches for a flow field consistent with both available observations and the physical principles governing fluid behavior, rather than relying exclusively on measured data. Unlike conventional physics-informed neural networks that frequently require explicit representation of fluid pressure, the new approach uses a physics-based minimization principle without needing direct pressure measurements. The researchers evaluated the framework using three fluid-mechanics problems: flow around a sphere, interacting vortices and time-dependent flow through a channel. They introduced measurement noise and limited the spatial or temporal availability of data to investigate how well the method could reconstruct the underlying flow.

Kheradvar said every medical imaging technique has inherent limitations in what it can measure, and that imaging blood flow with echocardiography or 4D Flow MRI obtains a representation of the actual flow field, not necessarily its complete physical description. He said the goal is to use the governing laws of fluid mechanics to reconstruct a more complete and accurate representation from the information the imaging system provides. Taha said the laws of physics offer insights into fluid motion beyond what experimental measurements alone can reveal, and that building these laws into the learning process allows reconstruction of a more complete flow field from a limited number of measurements. Kheradvar said the collaboration between engineering and medicine is particularly valuable because theoretical advances in fluid mechanics can provide a foundation for improving how medical imaging data is interpreted. Kheradvar said the exciting possibility is that more information may be obtained from the same imaging measurements, and that researchers can use fluid mechanics to estimate additional features of the underlying flow.

The results demonstrated substantial improvements in reconstructed flow accuracy, particularly when measurements were highly contaminated by noise, and the framework also performed well with spatially sparse observations and temporally limited measurements. The method improved the reconstruction of velocity gradients, which describe how fluid velocity changes across space and are essential for characterizing complex fluid motion. One potential application is echocardiographic particle image velocimetry, or Echo-PIV, a technique used to estimate blood-flow patterns within the heart from ultrasound imaging. Another is 4D Flow MRI, which can provide detailed measurements of cardiovascular blood-flow velocities in three dimensions over time but is constrained by the spatial and temporal resolution of the acquisition and the accuracy of velocity measurements. Elmaradny is now a scientist at Ford Motor Company, and Hashemi established his own research laboratory at Kansas State University last year.

The challenge extends beyond medicine, Kheradvar stressed, noting that whether scientists study blood moving through the heart, air flowing over an aircraft or fluids circulating through industrial systems, experimental measurements provide only a limited picture of the underlying flow. Measurements may contain noise, lack sufficient spatial resolution or capture fluid behavior at only selected locations and times, he said. Conventional computational approaches can smooth noisy measurements or interpolate between observed data points, but these procedures do not necessarily guarantee that the reconstructed flow obeys the laws of physics. Taha's research focuses on theoretical fluid mechanics, mathematical modeling and the physical principles that govern fluid motion, while Kheradvar's research focuses on cardiovascular mechanics, medical imaging to better characterize cardiovascular function and the development of medical device technologies. The study highlights how collaboration between UC Irvine's School of Medicine and Samueli School of Engineering can connect fundamental scientific discoveries to biomedical challenges.

The current study focuses on fundamental fluid-flow problems rather than clinical imaging, and its findings establish a foundation for future applications in cardiovascular research. The researchers emphasize that further validation using experimental and clinical imaging measurements will be necessary to establish the method's usefulness in these applications. Applying the framework to Echo-PIV or 4D Flow MRI could help researchers investigate whether physics-based reconstruction can improve the representation of complex blood-flow patterns, including vortices and other features that may not be fully resolved by existing imaging measurements. Beyond medicine, the framework may also offer opportunities in aerospace engineering and other areas of experimental fluid mechanics where measurement accuracy and resolution are limited. The articles do not state when or whether the method will be tested on clinical imaging data.

stories.Headline: Maryland comptroller Brooke Lierman releases AI tracker projecting 7 percent job losses
stories.Summary:
Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman released the Maryland AI Economic Impact Tracker earlier in November 2026, a public dashboard on how artificial intelligence could reshape the state’s economy. The tracker projects that Maryland could lose about 7 percent of its jobs to AI automation over the next two to five years. That is the third-highest rate in the nation, according to the dashboard. The tracker brings together data from government agencies, universities and private researchers on AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. Lierman’s office plans to update it regularly and to publish a series of research briefs next year.

The dashboard draws on the American AI Jobs Risk Index, a Tufts University project, which projects Maryland’s job losses from AI automation at 7.2 percent under a median adoption scenario. That rate is slightly behind Massachusetts and Virginia, which are both at 7.3 percent. The largest projected job losses in Maryland are in professional, scientific and technical services, the state’s third largest industry for employment, with 280,000 jobs in 2025. Based on the index, 44,000 Maryland jobs in this industry are at risk of displacement over the next 2-5 years, a loss of $5.3 billion in labor income. Educational services is projected to have the second most job losses at 24,000, and finance and insurance is projected to have the second largest labor income loss at $1.79 billion.

The Washington-Arlington-Alexandria metro area, which includes parts of Maryland, ranks as the second most vulnerable region in the country, with a projected 9 percent loss, behind only the San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara region of California at 10 percent. The comptroller’s office notes that Maryland has recorded 3,600 postings so far in 2026 requiring technical skills related to developing, running or maintaining AI systems. The data show Maryland trailing Virginia, the District of Columbia and Pennsylvania in AI-related job creation. In Maryland, AI job posting intensity is greatest in the Central Maryland counties, with Howard County highest at 3.1%, more than double the statewide rate of 1.5%. Prince George’s County has the second highest AI job intensity rate at 2.1%, and for some counties in Western Maryland and on the Eastern Shore there are very few or no AI job postings.

Lierman said in a statement launching the tracker that AI is reshaping the economy and that Maryland must meet this moment to support its workers and businesses. She said the dashboard consolidates the latest data on how AI could impact Maryland’s economy, giving state and local leaders information to make informed decisions and develop thoughtful policies. She said that by using these data to better understand the challenges and opportunities ahead, thoughtful safeguards can be developed while supporting innovation and economic growth. She said Maryland must be a leader in the national conversation on navigating the future of AI in the economy. The tracker also follows monthly counts of new AI jobs, based on postings compiled by researchers at the University of Maryland’s Robert H. Smith School of Business, who built an AI jobs mapping tool in partnership with LinkUp, a labor market data firm.

The comptroller’s dashboard incorporates information from the UMD-Link Up Maps Project, which captures job postings at the county level in Maryland. How many jobs have actually been lost to AI so far remains unclear, and the tracker notes that data on that is limited. One available gauge is the Challenger report of announced job cuts by U.S. employers: through September, AI was cited in 120,136 announced cuts in 2026, about 21 percent of all announcements nationally and the leading reason given. Other information in the tracker includes job automation risk by industry, with professional, scientific and technical services at the top spot, followed by educational services and then health care and social assistance. It also includes job automation risk by occupation, with software developers, customer service representatives and management analysts most at risk in Maryland, and how businesses in the state are adopting AI and its impacts on their staffing.

Maryland faces a gap of nearly $3 billion between expenses and revenues heading into the next fiscal year, and lawmakers will have to fill that hole to adopt the balanced budget required by law. Individual income taxes are the largest single source of general fund revenue, projected at about $15.8 billion in fiscal 2027, according to the state’s budget highlights. Fewer paychecks, or smaller ones, would ripple straight into state coffers. Lierman’s office plans to publish a series of research briefs next year on what AI adoption could mean for the state’s economy, revenues and budget. The articles do not say when the next update to the tracker will be published.

stories.Headline: OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger says AI can free staff for patient care if human dignity stays central
stories.Summary:
Michelle Conger, the chief executive officer of OSF HealthCare, spoke at the Peoria-based organization's OnCall Digital Health Symposium and said artificial intelligence can let providers and employees focus more on patient care if human interaction and dignity stay at the forefront. The all-day event was held at the Jump Trading Simulation and Education Center, and Conger described AI as a chance to free staff from administrative work at a time when healthcare organizations are coping with workforce shortages. She said the technology could free labor to do things far more rewarding than some of the work people do today. She also repeated the message of Pope Leo XIV's encyclical on artificial intelligence, calling on Catholic health organizations to put the personal aspect ahead of technological advancement.

Conger said human dignity must come before machines and that a person should always stay at the center of the care provided or the work done. She said technology and algorithms must serve people rather than reduce them. She said OSF's approach to AI adoption follows a governance process that weighs the potential impact on both patients and employees, and she described the challenge as balancing the potential of AI with the responsibility to keep technology a tool instead of a crutch. She said the governance process includes the human resources team, the mission people and the ethics people, who help the organization think through decisions and make sound ones.

Conger said she sees potential to apply AI toward making the healthcare system easier to navigate, since patients often struggle to determine where to access the services they need. She said she envisions establishing a digital safety net to help patients find the right entry point into the healthcare system. She also said the evolving technology could help OSF gain a better understanding of a person's situation and make it easier to direct that person to the appropriate care. The article does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Malmstrom engineer Rishub Goel beats a cybersecurity AI agent six times at DAFITC
stories.Summary:
Rishub Goel, a computer engineer with the 341st Communications Squadron at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, defeated an artificial intelligence agent in a cybersecurity challenge, according to a DVIDS story by Tech. Sgt. Aaron Thomasson posted on Nov. 23, 2026. The challenge took place at the Department of the Air Force Information Technology and Cyberpower Training and Education Event, known as DAFITC, held Aug. 24-26 in Montgomery, Alabama. Goel faced off against the AI six times over the conference and by the final day he had defeated it.

Among the thousands of attendees, he was one of only four people to beat the AI during the event. The contest was run by one of the companies exhibiting at DAFITC, and anyone at the conference could walk up and try to beat their specialized AI agent. The AI agent was specifically designed to be a superhuman expert in cybersecurity, and the company's aim, Goel said, was to show that AI could make cyber-defense calls more accurately and faster than people. Each scenario drew on MITRE ATT&CK, a free, public knowledge base of the tactics and techniques real attackers use. Players identified the evidence of an attack, then chose and ranked their defenses, such as adding a virtual private network or tightening security controls, by which would stop an attacker fastest.

Other prompts flipped the perspective and asked how to run the best offense, and answers were scored on accuracy and speed. In the scenarios, someone had been inside the network, files had changed without authorization, and an unfamiliar username had turned up where it didn't belong. Goel first attempted the challenge on the conference's opening day, and on a couple of attempts he topped the agent's score but not its time. He ended the first day sitting at fourth place on the leaderboard, behind the AI. Goel said the main thing that got him was not being able to beat the AI, especially if it was something he felt like he could do.

He described it as more of just the challenge, the thrill of asking whether he would beat it this time. Late in the conference, he moved into first place, then went back to the booth to make sure he stayed there, and he did. On the final day, Chief Master Sergeant Diane Schaefer, HAF/A6 Senior Enlisted Advisor for the Deputy Chief of Staff for Warfighter Comms & Cyber Systems, presented coins at the booth to Goel and the second-place finisher. Goel said he did not know they were going to get coined and that it was pretty cool. Lt.

Col. Danielle Shipman, 341st Communications Squadron commander, said Goel's performance reflects the squadron's technical readiness. Shipman said his impressive achievement reflects the technical skill and readiness expected from all of their cyber professionals, and that they are proud of his performance and the example he sets for the squadron. Goel said he does think AI is a very good resource, but sometimes it did better than other times, and that we still need humans to check it. Goel grew up in Orange County, California, where his father is an engineering executive in IT and his mother a chemist and educator.

Between watching his dad work in tech and his own interest in computers and video games, software was kind of the only thing he had in mind going into college, he said. Cybersecurity came later, partway through college at California State University, Fullerton, when he took a couple of cybersecurity electives and the subject came more easily to him than his other classes. Goel's work has seen him rotate through the squadron, from the client systems technician shop to infrastructure, where he learned the network, to his current job responsibilities, and because the squadron is small he said he has had a lot of opportunities. Back at Malmstrom, he works the defensive side of the same problem, spending most of his time on servers, applying patches and updates, managing the systems people across the base rely on, and keeping software infrastructure running. AI ran through much of DAFITC 2026, whose theme was "Accelerating the Digital Edge: From Enterprise to Orbit," reflecting the Department of the Air Force's shift toward an AI-augmented digital architecture, and Goel said attendees were excited about the technology.

As for AI, Goel expects it to play a bigger role in the work ahead, with people still involved in guiding and working alongside it. He said he thinks eventually we are gonna become pretty AI-oriented, but that he hopes it's not everything AI. The story lists the location as Great Falls, Montana, and gives a story ID of 580104. The story was posted on 11.23.2026 at 16:08 and had 40 web views at the time.

stories.Headline: AWS launches API Portal and WAF rule groups to discover and protect APIs and AI endpoints
stories.Summary:
On 23 November 2026 AWS announced new capabilities across AWS WAF, Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer and Amazon API Gateway to discover and protect the APIs and AI endpoints that services, apps and AI agents call. The launch covers API Portal, a new feature in Amazon API Gateway that discovers APIs and AI endpoints, and two new AWS WAF managed rule groups, API Security and AI Security. All three are generally available from that day, according to the AWS Security Blog post. The post says APIs have run digital businesses for more than a decade and that this changed in 2026, when AI endpoints joined them. It says teams now run large language model inference endpoints, Model Context Protocol servers and Agent2Agent servers beside their REST APIs on services such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service.

API Portal builds an inventory of APIs from their configuration and live traffic, identifies which are AI endpoints (LLM inference, MCP and A2A) and shows what to protect, analyzing configuration and traffic across CloudFront, Application Load Balancer and API Gateway. Discovery can be enabled for one account or for an organization in AWS Organizations, and resources can be excluded from the inventory. It reads the service logs and configuration records of API entry points, with nothing to attach, no logs to forward and no traffic to reroute, and lists endpoints by host, path and HTTP method. Every endpoint starts as a shadow API, becoming a managed API when promoted, and API Portal flags zombie APIs with no traffic and no configuration change for a set period and orphaned APIs whose owning account was closed or removed from the organization. API Security covers broken object level authorization, authentication attacks such as tampered tokens and credential stuffing, and reconnaissance such as probing for undocumented routes, using single-request rules and behavioral detections that learn traffic.

AI Security identifies AI traffic (LLM inference, MCP and A2A), validates MCP and A2A requests against their protocol and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for prompt attacks, harmful content and sensitive information. API Portal is in the Amazon API Gateway console and discovers APIs behind CloudFront, Application Load Balancer and API Gateway alike, while API Security and AI Security are in the AWS WAF console. The two rule groups protect the resources associated with a protection pack (web ACL), and they work together: API Portal shows which discovered endpoints AWS WAF protects, and security events AWS WAF detects appear on each managed API's detail page. The post says the single-request rules that identify token tampering and unsafe methods block, posture and schema discovery rules count, and behavioral detections block at high confidence and count at medium and low confidence. Every detection is a label under awswaf:managed:aws:api-security: that starts with a stage (attack, recon or warning) and names the finding, with behavioral detections also ending with a confidence (high, medium or low).

Mike Hasani, Senior Software Engineer at Principal Financial Group, said in the post that they can manage their API environment more effectively when they have a clear picture of what is running across AWS. He said API Portal gives them that visibility without requiring teams to change how they deploy APIs or route traffic, helping them create a more complete view across the enterprise. The post says APIs have always had two kinds of callers, other services and people who use an app, and now there is a third: AI agents that act on a person's behalf. It says a new MCP server or LLM endpoint takes minutes to stand up and can be placed behind a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution without passing through the API gateway, so it is missing from the API registry and the security review. It says an MCP client asks the server for its tools with tools/list and an A2A client reads the agent card the server publishes, and that the APIs behind web and mobile apps were built for one client, the app itself.

The post says the APIs are the same APIs they always were, and what changed is how they are exposed, who calls them and what threatens them. It says legitimate agents now call those same APIs directly, and so do attackers and fraudsters, none of whom have to follow the rules the app follows. It says the behavioral detections build a baseline from your own traffic and look for callers who do not fit it, with nothing to set up, no logging to turn on and no traffic to mirror. It says a nightly export job that reads thousands of records on a steady machine schedule looks like an attacker on volume and timing alone, so a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree and at least one is something your own traffic never does. It says high confidence also needs a caller AWS WAF can identify from a credential on the request such as a token, while a caller known only by IP address stays at medium confidence, and that the behavioral detections also flag credential stuffing and probing and take account of status codes such as a caller's rate of denied or failed requests.

The post says the rules that check the structure of a token in the Authorization header do not verify its signature, so the application still has to validate the token. It says API Security does not inspect the content of responses, and it points readers to the AWS WAF Developer Guide for the current list of supported resources, protocols and endpoint types and for the full list of rules and what each does by default. It says the behavioral detections cover more than object access, and that a caller stands out when, for example, its successful calls turn into a run of authorization failures. It says the APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows API Security detections over time, the detections that matched the most requests and how AWS WAF handled the labeled requests. The post gives no date for any further change and does not say what happens to endpoints already in a registry.

Articles.Title: Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection

stories.Headline: Corporate real estate leaders expect AI and economic pressure to reshape teams within three years
stories.Summary:
Corporate real estate leaders are expecting a shakeup to their teams over the next three years as AI, economic pressure and M&A activity force changes, CBRE said in a report released Nov. 17. Currently, 10% of corporate real estate departments are undergoing a major reorganization and 33% are exploring one, according to CBRE's 2026 corporate real estate organizational design study. Another 35% added roles in the past year to support what CBRE calls the industry's changing remit. The top five new or in-demand skills that teams are looking for are technology and AI, cited by 77% of respondents, and change management, cited by 52%, with reporting and analytics, financial acumen and CRM also named. As internal corporate real estate teams shift their focus to strategy and business enablement, named by over 90% of leaders as their department's top priority, organizations are shifting delivery to service providers, according to CBRE.

On average, 23% of staff are internal and 77% are Tier 1 service providers, with departments typically using one or two providers for each core function, like facilities, project and transaction management. One change already happening is an increase in outsourcing of real estate management services that were previously done by internal teams, according to CBRE. Real estate analytics software company Tango surveyed leaders at large enterprises, mostly in the C-suite or at the senior level in facilities, and all companies represented had over $500 million in revenue, with the majority in North America. The Tango survey found that the top challenges facing leaders are capital costs, volatile demand, lease inflexibility and limited high-quality space that meets their requirements. These issues are costing organizations, Tango says, with 53% reporting a shrinking set of acceptable compliant space and 43% having renewed or extended a lease on unfavorable terms due to a lack of time or decision support.

Just under 90% of respondents in Tango's survey said they have delayed at least one portfolio decision in the past year, and more than half said external factors were the most common reason a decision gets delayed. Leaders at CBRE, JLL and Cushman & Wakefield all said economic uncertainty did push at least some amount of deals to later in the year. CBRE CFO Emma Giamartino said on an earnings call that the volatility is what's driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027, and that the firm expects stability to come in the back half of next year, though results will differ if that doesn't come or things change. Still, the market has so far been surprisingly resilient, with 60% of U.S. markets showing positive net absorption over the past year, and Cushman & Wakefield CEO Michelle MacKay said during her firm's earnings call that companies are starting to make longer-term commitments.

Articles.Title: Corporate real estate leaders expect shakeup due to AI, economy: reports

stories.Headline: Arizona stop-motion artists teach claymation as Laika’s Travis Knight criticizes AI
stories.Summary:
Barrett Lanigan, who owns Barrett’s Studio in Scottsdale, teaches claymation and stop-motion to young artists ages 6 to 15 from her apartment four days a week, and she said the stop-motion course is her most popular offering. On Nov. 16, 2026, she helped a student photograph a handmade set inspired by the student’s real coffee cart business, The Daily Pedal, using a phone on a tripod. The same week, Cronkite News reported that Laika, the stop-motion studio based in Hillsboro, Oregon, had drawn critical acclaim for its film “Wildwood,” which premiered on Oct. 23. The film, directed by Laika President and CEO Travis Knight, is described as the longest stop-motion feature ever made, running 2 hours and 10 minutes.

“Wildwood” was created over a 16-year span, a timeline the article contrasts with artificial intelligence tools that can generate art in seconds, and most stop-motion films, including “Wildwood,” are shot at 24 frames per second. Knight has been an outspoken critic of AI, and the article describes that view as common among artists in the stop-motion world. Lanigan called claymation something beautiful because viewers can see a human made it, since it is imperfect. She asked how people could tell what is made by humans and what makes art valuable if AI can create work that looks human and imperfect, and she wondered what reason people would have to make art if it cannot turn a profit or match AI’s efficiency. She also said multiple parents of her students found her website through ChatGPT, which she said blew her mind.

Steven Hathaway, owner of Baby Cry Animation in Mesa, was filming a scene for a claymation music video in his studio on Nov. 17, 2026, featuring an air-conditioning unit falling from a building window. Lanigan was also putting together a course teaching students to create holiday-themed stop-motion films inspired by classics such as “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” and “Santa Claus Is Comin’ To Town.” The article lists other well-known stop-motion films, including Tim Burton’s “The Nightmare Before Christmas,” Wes Anderson’s “Fantastic Mr. Fox” and Laika’s “Coraline.” The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: AI can predict antidepressant response, but does not understand all patients equally
stories.Summary:
George Mason University researchers reported on November 23, 2026 that an AI antidepressant decision aid correctly identified medical information 82% of the time when patients used precise medical language. The team tested the aid across 500 simulated conversations using virtual patients built from National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program medical records. The work is part of an ongoing George Mason project led by Farrokh Alemi and Kevin Lybarger to develop conversational AI that helps clinicians pick antidepressants. The first study appeared in JMIR AI and the second in the Journal of Biomedical Informatics. The researchers introduced a patient simulator and an algorithm called Direct Effects Multiplicative Inference, or DEMI.

The aid matched patients' descriptions to medical terms 47.6% of the time for those with limited health literacy, 69.6% for functional health literacy and 81.9% for proficient health literacy. It identified 84% of medications mentioned compared with 94% of diagnoses. DEMI used 430 million relationships among medical concepts from the All of Us database. DEMI performed about as well as a conventional statistical model that relied on complete patient records. Both performed better for some medications than others.

Alemi, a professor in the Department of Health Administration, Policy, and Informatics, said the team wants the AI to help clinicians choose an antidepressant based on what patients are able to tell them. He said that by analyzing patterns in the medical histories of thousands of patients, the team hopes to predict which antidepressants have the best chance of working and reduce trial and error. He noted the system could recognize even misspelled medication names but struggled with vague descriptions. He said the team has not yet found a reliable solution to the health literacy gap. Lybarger, an assistant professor in the Department of Information Sciences and Technology in the College of Engineering and Computing, said mapping what clinicians write in their notes onto standard medical vocabularies is hard and mapping everyday patient speech is a much bigger leap.

Lybarger said people do not recite their whole chart, so the team is always working from a partial picture. The researchers said the stakes are particularly high in mental health care, where depression itself can interfere with communication. They said the new simulator gives researchers a way to pinpoint where the AI struggles and test whether changes actually help. The articles describe patients who might know a medication only as "the blue pills," lose track of questions or respond argumentatively. The articles state that the AI had to translate patients' words into standardized medical information before making treatment recommendations, and that errors in that translation could make recommendations less accurate.

The articles state that patients do not always describe their health in precise or accurate language. The researchers created virtual patients with different medical histories, health literacy levels and conversational styles. The second study introduced an algorithm that can predict antidepressant response without a patient's complete medical history. The method examines how diagnoses, past treatments and other medical details are connected rather than treating each as an independent factor. The articles state that the flexibility of DEMI makes it useful for conversational AI, which gathers patient information gradually.

The researchers are now exploring ways to help the AI make sense of imprecise medication descriptions, including using information from patients' medical histories. They also plan to give the system the ability to read prescription bottle labels. The articles state that the new patient simulator gives researchers a way to test potential improvements across different communication styles. The articles do not state when any of these next steps will be completed or tested. The articles do not state how the aid would perform in real clinical settings rather than simulated conversations.

Articles.Title: AI can predict antidepressant response, but does not understand all patients equally

stories.Headline: Trump reinstates Huang as Nvidia CEO and revives the AI trade
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump intervened to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, according to a StoneX market analysis dated Monday, 23 November 2026. The move followed weeks in which the AI trade had been getting pummeled, the article states. The return of Huang sparked more than just a rebound in AI stocks, it says. The article describes the AI trade as back following the intervention. It says Huang's return alleviates some near-term concerns surrounding the AI buildout.

The article says Nvidia plays a central role in the circular financing arrangements underpinning the AI buildout. It states that Huang's return does not put questions surrounding his conduct to bed. It says the return does not change the political landscape, with Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January. It says longer-term concerns remain about whether the sheer scale of investment in AI will deliver adequate returns. The article says a 25bp Fed hike in December is once again fully priced, with a small probability attached to a 50bp move.

The article attributes the intervention to Donald Trump, who acted to have Huang reinstated. It says Huang's return alleviates some near-term concerns surrounding the AI buildout. It says the return does not put questions surrounding his conduct to bed. It says the political landscape is unchanged, with Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January. It says longer-term concerns about AI investment returns also remain.

The article says the US economic exceptionalism narrative has roared back to life, sending the US dollar to fresh cycle highs. It says markets added to bets that additional monetary tightening will be required. It says the US Treasury curve bear flattened on Monday, with two-year yields climbing 5.9bp, five-year yields 3.8bp and 10-year yields 1bp, while 30-year yields fell 0.9bp. It says the financial conditions proxy registered its 17th largest daily easing since 2009, and the largest since Donald Trump announced his tariff pause in April last year. It says the DXY tagged 104.50 on Monday, closing in on 104.68, and that EUR/USD tagged 1.0900.

The article says the AI trade had been getting pummeled for weeks before the announcement. It says AI stocks had fallen violently heading into the announcement. It says the DXY had been attracting bids around 103.50, sitting just above 103.35, a level that acted as support and resistance on multiple occasions in late 2024 and again in 2025. It says EUR/USD fell to levels not seen since April 2025, briefly trading through a level it traded either side of in April 2025 around the Liberation Day episode. It says the price repeatedly ran into sellers at 1.1000 last week.

The article says a break above 104.68 would bring 105.44 into focus, a level that acted as support and resistance in late 2024. It says a sustained break beneath 103.35 would bring 102.95 into play, the high set on October 14. It says a sustained breach of 1.0900 leaves a vacuum of visible support until 1.0733, the swing low set in March 2025. It says 1.1000 is the first level of note overhead, followed by 1.1065, the former swing low set in May 2025. It says that barring another deterioration in sentiment towards the AI trade or a meaningful shift in the relative economic outlook for Europe and the US, EUR/USD remains a sell-on-rallies play.

stories.Headline: University of Wisconsin-Madison team pilots AI tool that transcribes student talk for teachers in Wisconsin classrooms
stories.Summary:
A team at the University of Wisconsin-Madison has built a tool called Content and Language with AI, which is going into pilot programs in urban, suburban and rural school districts across Wisconsin with a focus on fourth through eighth grade students, Wisconsin Public Radio reported on November 23, 2026. The tool records students while they discuss classwork in small-group projects and transcribes what they say in real time to a teacher's tablet, and the teacher can then filter through the conversations using keywords. It can translate and transcribe student answers when students speak a language other than English, and it can be used with English-speaking students as well. In the Arcadia school district in western Wisconsin, more than four in 10 students speak Spanish as a first language, and Carmen Lee, the district's director of curriculum, instruction and assessment, said many teachers there are not bilingual.

Earlier in November, the philanthropic initiative Multilingual by Design awarded $350,000 to the team to expand the project beyond Wisconsin science classrooms so it can be used in math classes. Shamya Karumbaiah, an assistant professor in the Department of Educational Psychology and director of The Responsible AI for Learning, or TRAIL, Lab at UW-Madison, is in charge of the pilot project, and she told WPR that she and her team are co-designing features for the tool using teacher feedback. She described one teacher who wanted a button to see whether everyone is participating equally and whether students' ideas are being taken up and built upon equally, and she said co-design means working with teachers to identify what is relevant and useful for their classroom. Karumbaiah said the project will use AI models running on local servers rather than proprietary models offered by OpenAI or Google to address security concerns, and she said the team is being transparent with its partners about where data is stored, how long it will be stored and what it would be used for.

Lee said a tool like this can be valuable for teachers who have limited capacity to closely follow the conversations among dozens of children in one classroom at the same time, and she said it allows a teacher to multiply themselves in some capacity and provide more directed feedback or recognize which groups they need to attend to next. Karumbaiah said the tool will be rolled out in six classrooms across Wisconsin next year to see if it can measurably change how teachers engage with students or if use of the tool increases how often students participate in classroom discussions. She said the decision to roll it out to other classrooms across the state will depend on how effective the tool is after it is used in more classrooms next year. She said the team hopes that in two to three years the tool could be available for teachers across Wisconsin, and that it would then begin thinking about how to make it accessible in terms of cost and maintenance.

Articles.Title: Pilot program uses AI to aid teachers, bridge language barriers for Wisconsin students

stories.Headline: Graduate instructor Travis Fraser builds Rubrica to grade exams using professor rubrics at UC Berkeley
stories.Summary:
Travis Fraser, a graduate-student instructor for a microeconomics course with 130 students in the spring, built an AI-powered grading tool called Rubrica, The Chronicle reported on November 23, 2026. Fraser was enrolled in his own MBA courses at the University of California at Berkeley’s Haas School of Business while responsible for assigning and grading coursework. It was not uncommon for Fraser to spend 30 hours grading a stack of exams, and he found most of the exam feedback he gave was identical. Fraser said he wondered whether he could apply the rubric process but have AI do it based on a professor’s rubric. Haas will pilot Rubrica in the spring with a group of 15 professors.

Fraser designed Rubrica to use only the rubric and the completed assignment to assign grades, so the tool will not work as intended if the rubric lacks specificity. The tool can also assign partial credit and is designed to flag any answers it is unsure about to the professor. Fraser emphasized that the tool is designed to have a human in the loop checking grades and making adjustments if necessary. Tom Tripp, executive director of Haas Digital, wrote that the team plans to start a second faculty test group in the fall of 2027 if the tool meets expectations on accuracy, time savings, increased face time with students, and improved feedback quality. During the pilot, the professors testing the tool will also be grading assignments regularly while Rubrica offers a set of its own grades to compare.

Fraser said that if colleges offload exams but do not replace that with hours spent with more students, the system can eat itself alive. He said that in a perfect world he sees every hour saved as reinvested, and that colleges implementing Rubrica must use the time saved for something productive. Sara L. Beckman, a mentor of Fraser’s and a professor at Haas who recently retired from teaching, said she has high hopes for Rubrica. Beckman said the tool could improve productivity and that there is a much deeper opportunity in what he has built that goes beyond grading. She said AI is better than human beings at spotting and analyzing patterns, and that for a subject like systems thinking a tool like Rubrica would have been useful in showing class-wide areas for improvement.

Jason Gulya, the AI-literacy coordinator at Berkeley College in New Jersey, said the issue is very nuanced because the reason we give feedback can be different depending on the assignment, the course, and the number of students. Gulya said he was impressed by how well some AI grading tools he has tested mimic his voice, though their percentages are sometimes off. He worried that colleges might say instructors will now teach 400 students instead of 100 because they have an AI grader. Hollis Robbins, a professor of English at the University of Utah who writes about AI in higher education, worried that tools like Rubrica could prevent students from coming up with innovative answers to exam questions. A study published in July found that an overwhelming majority of undergraduate students surveyed preferred instructor grading to AI grading, and about one-third found AI grading to be unfair.

Fraser and supporters of the tool hope the time saved will free up faculty members and their graduate assistants to focus on teaching and one-on-one time with students. Others worry that handing grading duties to AI could distance students from their teachers and remove administrators’ incentive to lighten the workload on teaching assistants and professors. Rubrica is just one pilot AI tool that Haas has embraced in recent years, and professors there are also testing out Rumi, a tool that allows students to show how they use generative AI in their research. Beckman said she thinks the tool could feasibly come to replace human graders who do not assume any teaching responsibility. Robbins said professors and administrators should be careful when deciding which types of coursework can use AI in content delivery or grading.

Fraser said student sentiment will be a consideration, and most respondents in the July study found AI feedback at least somewhat helpful for learning. Gulya said that if the goal is to evaluate baseline competency in a class of 200 students, it might make sense to bring in AI, but if the goal is to build an academic relationship with students, the technology might get in the way. The Chronicle reported that the plans for a pilot at UC-Berkeley are raising questions. The articles leave open whether Rubrica will meet the expectations set for the fall 2027 test group. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Should Professors Use AI To Grade?

stories.headline_source: Should Professors Use AI To Grade?

stories.Headline: Dr. Adetayo's AI User Safety Initiative names four pillars of its SAFE AI User Framework
stories.Summary:
KY3 published an episode of its All About AI series on November 23, 2026, in which the four pillars of the SAFE AI User Framework were discussed, and the segment was reported by Jazlyn Summers. The AI User Safety Initiative was founded by Dr. Gbemisola Adetayo, and the framework rests on four pillars, which are Structure, Accelerate, Filter and Empower. The episode set out to explain those four pillars to viewers, and the station directed people to a link for more information about the initiative. The article gave no further detail on what each pillar involves or on when the initiative was founded.

The framework belongs to the AI User Safety Initiative, which Dr. Adetayo founded, and the four pillars it names are Structure, Accelerate, Filter and Empower. The article does not say what any of the four pillars requires of users, developers or anyone else, and it does not describe a change in rules or law. It also gives no date for the founding of the initiative and no figure for how many people or organizations are involved. What the framework changes, beyond naming the four pillars, is not stated in the article.

Dr. Gbemisola Adetayo is named as the founder of the AI User Safety Initiative, and the four pillars of the SAFE AI User Framework are attributed to that initiative. The article does not quote Dr. Adetayo or anyone else, so it records no statement from her about the framework or its purpose. Responsibility for the framework rests with the initiative she founded, according to the article, and the episode presented the pillars as its subject. No other person or organization is named in connection with the framework.

The article comes from the All About AI series on KY3, and this episode was published on November 23, 2026, with an update posted about half an hour later. Beyond pointing readers to a link for more on the initiative, the article says nothing about what happens next, and it gives no schedule for further coverage. It closes with a note inviting readers to report corrections or typos by email. The article carries no other detail about the framework or the initiative.

stories.Headline: Nurse leader urges nurses to define clinical outcomes and govern AI across its lifecycle
stories.Summary:
Elizabeth Anderson, a registered nurse and director at Rauland, wrote the MedCity News piece published on November 23, 2026. She argued that AI is entering clinical workflows faster than many expected. She asked whether nurses are part of the decisions about how it gets used. She said AI may reduce administrative burden and help nurses find clinically relevant information faster. She said AI may support earlier recognition of patient needs and give nurses more time for professional judgment.

Anderson wrote that nursing leaders should ask what they are attempting to improve for patients and nurses. She said nurses should help identify the problems AI is meant to address and define desired clinical outcomes. She said nurses should take part in solution development and evaluate whether implementation produces meaningful improvement. She cited the American Nurses Association's position that nurses should have a leading voice in the design, implementation, evaluation, and governance of AI in nursing practice. She said nursing participation should extend across the AI lifecycle, from problem identification through testing, implementation, governance and outcomes evaluation.

Anderson said nursing leadership has an obligation to shape the direction of AI. She said nurse executives should set expectations for nursing participation in AI governance. She said they should create mechanisms for frontline nurses and nursing informatics experts to influence solution development. She said they should advocate for appropriate clinical validation and ensure implementation measures extend beyond efficiency. She said they should also take part in decisions about how capacity created through AI will be reinvested.

Anderson said AI may reduce one task while inadvertently creating another. She said AI may improve access to information while increasing notifications or adding steps to workflows. She said the National Academy of Medicine's Health Care Artificial Intelligence Code of Conduct emphasizes a human-centered approach. She said it identifies safety, effectiveness, equity, transparency, accountability and engagement as important principles. She said nurses must participate in determining whether an AI application produces the outcomes for which it was introduced.

Anderson said documentation, information retrieval, communication requirements and fragmented technology take time away from patient care. She said saving minutes on a task is an incomplete measure of success. She said organizations should define what they intend to accomplish with the capacity AI creates. She said that capacity could include time for assessment, patient and family education, mobility, symptom management, discharge preparation, care coordination and surveillance. She said time returned to nursing requires appropriate boundaries.

Anderson said efficiency gains could instead contribute to greater workload, expanded patient assignments or new responsibilities. She said organizations should examine whether AI lets nurses complete important interventions more consistently and coordinate care more effectively. She said success requires measures beyond productivity, including documentation burden, cognitive workload, missed nursing care, nurse satisfaction and patient experience. She said AI intended to affect nursing practice should be developed with an understanding of clinical context, workflow variability, patient safety and unintended consequences. She said the more important question is whether nursing will meaningfully influence AI.

Articles.Title: The Future of AI in Nursing Must Begin with the Outcomes We Intend to Achieve

stories.Headline: Researchers develop a statistical tool that tests whether synthetic data can stand in for patients in clinical trials
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Virginia Tech, the University of Maryland Baltimore County, Texas Tech University and Princeton University jointly developed a statistical tool that tests whether AI-generated synthetic data can accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials, and the model was published Nov. 23 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The work responds to a push by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to explore synthetic data alternatives that could compress trial timelines from years to a matter of months. Yulia R. Gel, a Virginia Tech professor of statistics, said the problem is that you have to verify the synthetic data is true to life, and that the goal is for trials using synthetic data to reach the same conclusions as trials with real people. The tool bridges computational topology and statistics to measure and compare complex image data, and the team tested it by comparing synthetic mammograms against real patient data while tracking how breast cancer responds to different radiation doses.

The proposed method let the researchers assess how faithfully the synthetic images could replace human data in trial evaluations, and the team is already in conversation with the FDA to customize the model for streamlined pre- and post-market evaluations. The researchers have also applied the model in materials science to verify synthetic representations of wood, fabric and metal. Jaidev Goel, a statistics graduate student and one of the leading authors on the paper, said AI is being used to generate new protein structures and new compounds in drug discovery, and that a materials scientist may want to make something with the properties of cotton, which the tool can check for density or texture. Down the road, the articles say, the model could verify synthetic data for power grids and 3D objects or help spot false assertions and restrict behavior in large language models.

Gel is quoted as saying the team wants clinical trials with synthetic data to reach the same conclusions they would get with real people, and Goel said we should not blindly buy into the hype of AI, adding that humans have always come up with ways to stress-test new tools and that statistics plays a crucial role in that history. The other researchers listed are Ansu Chatterjee of the University of Maryland Baltimore County, Asim Dey of Texas Tech University and Vincent Poor of Princeton University. The work was supported by the FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health, the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health through the NSF-NIH-FDA Foundations for Digital Twins as Catalyzers of Biomedical Technological Innovation program. The articles say the research will not stop with publication, given the ongoing talks with the FDA.

stories.Headline: Small and midsized businesses adopt edge AI to cut latency and bandwidth needs
stories.Summary:
Small and midsized businesses are exploring how to run artificial intelligence workloads at the edge, positioning data storage and computation closer to where it is needed, according to BizTech Magazine. Many of these businesses have relied on cloud platforms to access AI capabilities, while others have run AI workloads in on-premises data centers. Edge computing can reduce the need for bandwidth and lower latency in their workloads. The shift toward edge AI is happening rapidly at the enterprise level, and SMBs are looking to keep pace.

Cisco notes that by 2027, 75 percent of enterprise data will be created and processed at the edge due to evolving AI workloads. Edge AI processes data locally on devices such as smartphones and IoT sensors, at or near the point where it is created, rather than sending it to a service provider's servers. In a September 2025 white paper, IDC's Brandon Butler and Jennifer Cooke write that edge infrastructure minimizes latency, optimizes bandwidth utilization and enhances data privacy. Running workloads locally generally requires less power than cloud data centers, and sensitive data remains on local endpoints rather than traveling across a network. SMBs can scale by pairing cloud-based platforms with native edge capabilities on local devices.

Jeremy Foster, senior vice president and general manager for Cisco Compute, says AI is not waiting for the data center anymore and is happening right now in factories, at ports, in hospitals and in stores, where milliseconds matter. Butler and Cooke write that building an effective strategy for edge infrastructure begins with understanding the unique needs of highly distributed IT landscapes and industry-specific needs. They add that infrastructure and architecture choices need to consider the level of use case criticality and prioritize platforms that ensure data and physical security requirements. SMBs may face challenges, since existing edge infrastructure generally is not optimized for modern AI workloads and many sites have low power and limited footprints. Edge projects often take longer and cost more than planned as businesses deal with configuration drift and poorly managed large-scale updates.

Manufacturing and retail are two segments where edge AI may hold significant promise for SMBs, with edge devices monitoring machinery health, detecting defects and optimizing production, while retail uses it for personalized customer experiences, inventory management and loss prevention. A hybrid model may benefit retailers, with the cloud training large models and aggregating insights across locations while the edge handles real-time inference behind in-store intelligence. By rightsizing their computing infrastructure, SMBs can avoid overprovisioning while keeping performance and costs in check. For SMBs with lean IT teams, working with a trusted partner can make complexity manageable and speed up edge AI deployments.

Articles.Title: How AI at the Edge Can Help SMBs Improve Performance and Security

stories.Headline: Rob Baker argues AI literacy can help young Black men navigate banks and institutions
stories.Summary:
Dr. Rob "Biko" Baker wrote an op-ed published by civicmedia.us on Nov 23, 2026, at 10:00 AM CT, titled The New Gatekeepers: Black Men, Literacy, and the Age of AI. In it he describes a young Milwaukee entrepreneur who contacted him after his bank placed a hold on a check. For nearly three days the man had been getting the runaround, and eventually he asked Baker to get on the phone. Baker suggested asking for the branch manager, who was more polished but equally unhelpful and offered information that ultimately proved inaccurate.

The article cites the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress, under which only 8% of Black eighth graders in Milwaukee scored at or above the NAEP Proficient level in reading. Across all racial groups, just 11% of Milwaukee's eighth-grade boys reached that benchmark, figures the article says are not measures of basic literacy. According to Wisconsin's Department of Public Instruction, 62.7% of Black Milwaukee Public Schools students graduated within four years in 2024, compared with 79.2% of white students. The district's overall graduation rate improved to 72% for the class of 2025, though substantial disparities remain. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the national unemployment rate for Black men ages 20 to 24 was 9.1% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 6.8% for white men in the same age group.

Baker writes that he has spent much of his life as an advocate but is no expert at navigating bureaucracies, and still struggles with obstacles built into schools, healthcare systems, banks and government agencies. He says his fear of systems extended his time in grad school, with hours in the financial aid office trying to get a refund check processed. He says things were much easier at UWM, where he knew who to talk to solve his problems. He says he has learned which questions to ask, when to request a supervisor, and how to recognize when someone is giving him the runaround. He writes that many young Black men who seek his help lack the same experience or access to people who understand these systems.

Baker describes the young man as polite and professional throughout the encounter, wearing a Green Bay Packers hat and sweater with long braids, not yelling or behaving inappropriately. After leaving the bank, the man called Baker again, frustrated, and sitting in his car noticed what he believed were police officers moving through the parking lot. He wondered whether they had been called because of him, and Baker says he could not confirm his suspicions but understood why the possibility crossed his mind. Eventually they resolved the issue, and Baker talked with him about navigating such encounters, including that wearing more conventionally respectable clothing might influence how he is received when handling large financial transactions. Baker writes that he was uncomfortable giving that advice, because the man had done absolutely nothing wrong.

Baker writes that as artificial intelligence becomes integrated into banking, education, healthcare and employment, the ability to navigate institutions may depend even more on literacy, communication and understanding complicated systems. He asks what happens to young Black men already facing educational and employment barriers when artificial intelligence becomes another gatekeeper. He recalls loving books as a child, traveling the world through encyclopedias, novels, biographies and historical accounts, and calls the library his pathway to the middle class. He attended private Lutheran schools where he was challenged academically and developed reading, writing and critical-thinking skills that continue to serve him as an educator and advocate. He writes that reading taught him to ask questions, recognize patterns, understand unfamiliar language and challenge information that did not make sense.

Baker writes that schools must prioritize reading comprehension, writing, critical thinking and practical AI literacy, and that community organizations must teach young men how to navigate financial institutions, employment systems and public services. He writes that institutions adopting AI must remain accountable for the barriers their technology creates. He says artificial intelligence could democratize knowledge and help young Black men overcome obstacles that once required professional assistance, but that future isn't guaranteed. He writes that he does not want the next generation spending their lives looking for someone like him to get a banker, administrator or automated system to listen. He wants them to have the skills, knowledge and confidence to advocate for themselves.

Articles.Title: The New Gatekeepers: Black Men, Literacy, and the Age of AI
