stories.Headline: South Korea finance minister Lee Hyoung-il forecasts high-3 percent growth and prepares a stock stabilization fund
stories.Summary:
Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hyoung-il expressed confidence on Monday, November 23, 2026, that the South Korean economy could expand in the high-3 percent range this year. Speaking at the Government Complex Sejong, Lee noted that growth of 4 percent might be possible this year or next, although fourth-quarter data is not yet available. His positive outlook is based on the belief that the global semiconductor industry will remain resilient through 2027. He pointed to declining memory inventories and substantial long-term supply contracts secured by SK hynix and Samsung Electronics.

To address stock market volatility caused by AI concerns and US interest rate hikes, officials are preparing a stock market stabilization fund. This plan follows a Sunday meeting with the heads of the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Services Commission, and the Bank of Korea. The government has already eased daily corporate share buyback limits for three months and increased monitoring of illegal short selling. Lee stated that the government has activated part of its contingency plan and will implement further measures based on market conditions.

Lee explained that the decision to deploy the stabilization fund depends on market conditions, and he has not provided a specific timetable or trigger for its use. He claimed that South Korea's short-selling regulations are already stricter than those in other advanced economies, so the government will focus on surveillance rather than adding new restrictions. Regarding the labor market, Lee acknowledged that job gains have lagged behind economic growth, but he expects employment to improve next year. He also suggested that the petroleum price ceiling might be extended into 2027 to protect vulnerable households from winter costs and Middle East uncertainty.

stories.Headline: President Lee orders full review of Suneung exam after AI cheating cases
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung on Friday ordered a sweeping review of the national examination system, calling for testing methods to be reconsidered "from A to Z." The order followed five test-takers caught in cheating cases involving smart devices during Thursday's College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung. Smart glasses and miniature cameras were discovered during South Korea's college entrance exam. The incidents have reignited debate over whether Korea should move beyond its multiple-choice-heavy examination system. The test was held on Nov. 19, and the article was published Nov. 23, 2026. The Suneung plays a decisive role in university admissions, and public confidence in grading fairness remains paramount.

In December 2025, Seoul education chief Jeong Geun-sik proposed introducing essay-based testing by 2033 and ultimately abolishing the Suneung by 2040. The National Education Commission has considered expanding essay-based assessments as part of its 2028-2037 national education strategy. Disagreements over grading fairness and the burden on schools delayed the release of its reform plans in October. In a deliberative exercise involving 180 citizens, 55.5 percent supported introducing essay-based questions, while 41.7 percent opposed the proposal, and grading fairness was the most frequently cited concern, identified by 48.3 percent of participants. Jeong said children living in the age of AI need the ability to ask questions and think critically and creatively, not simply to seek answers.

Lee Hye-jung, director of the Institute for Education and Innovation, said the multiple-choice system survived because of the belief that it ensures reliable and fair grading, regardless of who evaluates the answers. She said the latest AI cheating scandal has shattered that myth and that the era of multiple-choice Suneung exams has come to an end. She said Korea does not need to change the curriculum itself but how students are taught and evaluated. She said what matters is establishing a system that produces consistent, reproducible results within an acceptable margin of variation. Moon Hyung-nam, a professor at Sookmyung Women's University and president of the Korea AI Education Association, said simply switching from multiple-choice to essay-based or oral examinations will not solve AI-assisted cheating.

He cited a 2024 University of Reading study in which 94 percent of AI-generated answers submitted to unproctored undergraduate assessments went undetected by graders. He called for clearer restrictions on electronic devices, consistent pre-exam checks and stronger exam supervision. National Education Commission Chair Cha Jeong-in said authorities are considering ways to gradually expand written-response and essay-based assessments in schools over a considerable period. He stressed that such a transition could not be accomplished within one or two years. Ahead of this year's Suneung, authorities tightened security measures, including restrictions on electronic devices, checks for concealed smartphones and enhanced Wi-Fi monitoring around testing centers.

The exam concluded without major disruptions, but the discovery of sophisticated cheating devices underscored the difficulty of keeping pace with rapidly evolving technology. Calls to reform the Suneung predate the latest cheating cases, reflecting concerns that the exam places too much emphasis on finding correct answers. Lee Hye-jung pointed to the International Baccalaureate, which uses written examinations, oral presentations and longer-term projects. She argued such an approach could reduce dependence on a single high-stakes test while better assessing students' reasoning and creativity. The articles do not state what specific measures the presidential review will produce or when it will report.

They do not say what penalties the five test-takers face or what devices were found beyond smart glasses and miniature cameras. They do not state whether the National Education Commission will release its delayed reform plans or when. They do not say how the 2033 and 2040 targets proposed by Jeong Geun-sik would be enacted. They do not state how the 2024 University of Reading study was conducted beyond its 94 percent finding. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Seoul National University considers requiring an introductory AI course for all undergraduates by 2028
stories.Summary:
Seoul National University is considering making an introductory AI course a graduation requirement for every undergraduate, regardless of major, according to a report the JoongAng Ilbo obtained exclusively on Sunday. The proposal comes from a report titled "Study on Expanding Seoul National University's Computing and AI Curriculum" (translated), and its stated goal is to ensure all students graduate with a baseline level of AI skills. The research team behind it is made up of six faculty members, including Oh Min-hwan, a professor at the Graduate School of Data Science. The team suggested students choose from three basic AI courses depending on their level. The courses would be offered at tiers: one for nonscience and nonengineering students, one for second-year science and engineering students and an advanced tier for science and engineering students in their second to fourth years, with students choosing based on their background knowledge.

Two of the three courses already exist, namely "Core Computing" for nonscience and nonengineering students, offered by SNU College, and the advanced "Fundamentals of Machine Learning" (translated), offered by the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering. The third, "Introduction to AI" (translated), aimed at science and engineering students in general, is set to launch in the College of Engineering in spring 2027. The report presented two options for class size, the first a "mega hybrid" format with 400 or more students combining in-person and remote instruction, and the second splitting the course into multiple sections of 100 to 150 students each sharing a single curriculum. The researchers suggested starting with the first option, then gradually reducing enrollment caps and adding sections until the course runs like the second. The research team found that demand is growing much faster than the number of AI courses at the university, leaving supply short.

The number of undergraduate AI courses rose by six, or 12.5 percent, from 48 in fall 2025 to 54 in spring 2026, while over the same period total seats rose by 1,260, or 54.8 percent, and enrollment rose by 659, or 50.8 percent. Applications for general education AI courses jumped from about 34 percent of available seats to about 79 percent, and the team also pointed out that access varies widely by college, with the College of Engineering offering 14 AI-related courses in the spring semester while the College of Pharmacy and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences offered just one each. The researchers said SNU College, which oversees basic education for undergraduates, needs to provide common instruction on the principles, applications and ethics of AI. SNU College aims to introduce the revised graduation requirements in the spring 2028 semester. An SNU College official said the plan is to discuss the revision with the relevant colleges and then submit it for approval by the university's deliberative body.

stories.Headline: South Korea prepares for agentic AI and geopolitical fragmentation by 2027
stories.Summary:
Senior columnist Choi Hoon wrote that South Korea must prepare for several major trends arriving in 2027. He identified agentic AI, geopolitical fragmentation, and social division as the primary challenges for the nation. These shifts require Korea to identify global directions and chart its course accordingly. The author argues that national leadership must look beyond immediate disputes to adapt. This preparation is necessary as technological, geopolitical, and social transformations converge.

Agentic AI will independently plan and execute tasks, moving beyond the copilot roles seen in 2026. A November World Economic Forum report predicts agents will handle research, analysis, forecasting, negotiations, customer service, and software development. Companies must reorganize structures and calculate measurable returns on investment, as Gartner warned in October. The OECD emphasizes AI governance, while a survey of 200 Korean companies found 60 percent lacked data location knowledge. Seventy percent of those surveyed lacked a data sovereignty strategy.

The World Economic Forum described 2026 as an era of competition between Washington and Beijing. A November S&P Global report says international rules and markets no longer guarantee security or prosperity. This report suggests that national interests must now shape budgets, industrial policies, trade agreements, and military strategies. Economic security is becoming central as the world moves toward a fragmented multipolar order. This new order includes the United States, China, an independent Europe, India, and Global South powers.

Professor emeritus Ha Young-sun suggests a strategy called complex network diplomacy for the emerging order. This approach involves pursuing national interests while linking diverse countries, sectors, and actors. Korea must expand trilateral security cooperation with Washington and Tokyo, anchored in the Korea-U.S. alliance. The nation must also diversify supply chains and markets to reduce dependence on the United States and China. This strategy aims to avoid passive reliance on networks connecting Korea to major powers.

A September Ipsos report describes societies moving toward smaller, antagonistic groups divided by identity, gender, immigration, and social change. Edelman characterized 2026 as an age of insularity and predicts 2027 will be an age of agency. In this coming age, individuals will seek greater control over their own lives and surroundings. Recovering personal autonomy and social influence could help people overcome feelings of distrust and helplessness. Ipsos suggests creating shared spaces, experiences, and narratives to integrate these fragmented groups.

Companies must now demonstrate measurable returns from technology rather than using simple indicators like employee usage rates. Diplomats are tasked with expanding their options to navigate the fragmented multipolar order of 2027. Political leaders must rebuild connections across a Korean society that is becoming increasingly divided. The articles leave open how the government will specifically implement these necessary structural and social changes. It remains unclear if intelligent AI can truly remain under human control as its autonomy grows.

stories.Headline: Mock juries side with plaintiffs more often when radiologists disagree with AI, Bernstein finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers using simulated malpractice cases have found that mock juries were more likely to side with a plaintiff when an AI system disagreed with a radiologist than when it agreed, according to a study published in NEJM AI and reported by Axios on November 23, 2026. In one scenario involving a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage, jurors sided with the plaintiff 72.9% of the time when the AI flagged the condition and the radiologist did not. In a second case built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death, participants sided with the plaintiff 78.7% of the time when the AI said the patient had cancer and the doctor did not think so. The study's lead author is Michael Bernstein, an associate professor at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University.

The findings suggest that doctors who disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality may face greater legal jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, and some may order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability. A smaller percentage of jurors ruled against the physician when they were given data on the AI system's error rate, which experts say is significant because false positive readings are almost inevitable and can temper the belief that the technology is always right. The researchers said double-checking AI results could reduce doctors' malpractice risks and prospective jurors' perceptions of whether a doctor met the duty of care standard, though the question is whether physicians can find the time. The systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, demand for tests is rising, and the systems invariably make mistakes.

Bernstein said the research is uncovering an unintended consequence of AI adoption, adding that AI can do a lot in radiology but is not all uniformly positive. He said one concern is the prospect of more defensive medicine, in which clinicians overcorrect and order follow-up scans and exams, which can drive up costs and patient anxiety. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients, and it is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Johns Hopkins researchers wrote in JAMA Health Forum last year that because human operators are perceived as having control over the technology's use, responsibility unduly shifts to the human operator, and they noted that physicians were consistently viewed as more liable than AI vendors, health systems that adopted the technology or regulators.

Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology, and physicians are demanding more protections. Radiology is a closely watched specialty because AI is used extensively and because missing an abnormality can be fatal, and it is also among the fields with a high risk of being sued. Research on perceptions of blame is cutting across many medical disciplines and underscores how physicians who are expected to rely on AI to cut down on medical errors still have to know when to override the systems. The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there is also a baked-in assumption that it is never wrong, which can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and Anthropic shares drop as AI stocks erase some of Monday's gains
stories.Summary:
United States stock markets slipped on Tuesday as technology shares linked to artificial intelligence erased some of the gains from Monday. Shares of Nvidia and Anthropic traded sharply lower, acting as barometers for the sustainability of the current artificial intelligence boom. Major indexes turned down during the session, continuing a pattern of wrenching volatility for technology stocks. These assets recently recorded both their biggest daily rise and fall in more than a year.

The S&P 500 fell around 0.5 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined by more than 1 percent. Nvidia shares fell around 8 percent on Tuesday after they had rocketed more than 30 percent on Monday. Anthropic tumbled nearly 8 percent, which pushed its value below its initial public offering price for the first time. These movements only partially reversed the significant gains that occurred at the start of the week.

The rally on Monday followed the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia. This return occurred after an extraordinary intervention by President Trump, despite the board of directors previously stating that the founder would not return. Mr. Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago following revelations of an affair with a subordinate and another woman. United States officials believe that this second woman was spying for China.

stories.Headline: Researchers use Meta open-weight AI models to train doctors and study epilepsy and rare diseases
stories.Summary:
Meta said on November 23, 2026 that researchers are using its open-weight AI models and its research funding to address critical gaps in medicine. Meta said it had expanded its academic partnerships to give researchers funding and access to models including Muse Glimmer, SAM3, DINOv3 and Brain2Qwertyv2. Meta said the researchers are independently adapting the models for their own investigational research. Meta said the projects include training medical professionals in low-resource settings, locating epilepsy sources in the brain and advancing understanding of rare diseases. Meta published the account on its newsroom under the headline about researchers using its open-weight AI models to transform medicine.

At Louisiana State University, Dr. Peter DeBlieux and his team are using Muse Glimmer, SAM 3, DINOv3 and other Meta models with Meta Quest 3 headsets to develop COPES. Meta described COPES as an experimental coaching platform that supports healthcare professionals with medical procedural training in virtual reality. Meta said the system will aim to provide adaptive guidance, real-time performance assessment and personalized feedback across technical execution, patient communication, clinical reasoning and decision-making. Meta said working virtually lets medical students learn complicated procedures where practicing on real patients may be risky. Meta said virtual instruction means more medical professionals can receive high quality technical and communications training no matter where they are.

Dr. Pierre Bourdillon at Rothschild Hospital Foundation is using AI research and Meta models including NeuralSet, Brain2Qwertyv2, Tribev2 and DINOv3 in research projects aimed at better understanding the source of epilepsy in the brain. Meta said epilepsy currently can't be directly visualized in brain images, making it difficult for clinicians to identify its source. Meta said Dr. Bourdillon is using AI to develop a tool that can enable simulations of epileptic seizures originating in different regions of the brain. Meta said the approach could one day let doctors select the simulation that best matches their patient's case and form a strong hypothesis about where the epilepsy originates. Meta said the early-stage research could improve accuracy in treatments including surgical removal of affected brain tissue and device implantation designed to disrupt epileptic activity, and that the simulations could help researchers address speech and motor restoration in patients with brain injuries.

At Columbia University, Dr. Wolfgang Pernice has partnered with Meta to adapt the DINO family of models to improve analysis of microscopy images of cells. Meta said this helps doctors understand how rare diseases appear in cells. Meta said conventional image analysis methods require researchers to know in advance what they are looking for, limiting their analysis. Meta said the adapted Cell-DINO, DINO-BoC and FINO models generate unbiased representations of the inner workings of cells, allowing scientists to decode the complex patterns by which rare diseases manifest in human cells.

Meta said this can help improve understanding of rare diseases and accelerate drug discovery. Meta said open science is critical to advancing medical research. Meta said all of the work it featured is early-stage. Meta said each of the investigational projects highlights AI's unique ability to fill critical research gaps.

Meta said it looks forward to the potential breakthroughs enabled by its AI models. Meta said it interviewed the researchers for its Open Source AI for Science Summit and pointed readers to its AI blog to learn more. Meta did not say how much funding any of the researchers received. Meta did not give results from any of the three projects.

Meta did not say when COPES might be deployed or tested. Meta did not say whether the epilepsy simulation tool has been tested in patients. Meta did not say what the next steps are for the rare disease work at Columbia. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after Trump intervenes, sparking a 31% share surge
stories.Summary:
Nvidia’s board reinstated former chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday, 23 November 2026, after direct intervention from President Trump, with Vice President Vance reportedly enlisted to help push the process along. The reinstatement came after Wall Street had spent the better part of a fortnight questioning Nvidia’s future and the AI revolution. Nvidia surged 31% and added $952 billion in market value in a single session. The Nasdaq 100 rocketed 6.9%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.7% and the semiconductor index exploded 14%. It was Wall Street’s biggest celebration since Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs in April 2025.

The rally came with a violent unwinding of short positions and options hedges, and leveraged short products suffered devastating losses. Top-of-book liquidity in the S&P 500 futures market was reportedly around $2.5 million. The VIX retreated sharply but remained at approximately 28.9, unusually elevated for a session in which the S&P 500 surged close to 5%. The VVIX remained above 118 and in the 93rd percentile of its historical distribution. Anthropic fell 1.4% despite the introduction of listed options, with its share price still struggling to put distance from the $83 offering level.

Huang is described as Nvidia’s principal dealmaker, industry evangelist and strategic architect, with influence stretching from semiconductor design to data-centre investment. The articles say his reinstatement restores a familiar hand to the wheel and has genuine value for investors assessing the company’s strategic direction. They add that there is an uncomfortable distinction between restoring confidence in Nvidia’s leadership and repairing the financial foundations of the entire AI boom. The articles say Wall Street may have got its king back, but the kingdom still has a few unpaid bills. They say the market’s verdict was delivered with all the subtlety of a wrecking ball.

The articles say much of the rally had less to do with a new earnings outlook than with traders caught on the wrong side of an overcrowded book. Hedge funds were doing much of the heavy lifting, aggressively buying technology shares and ETFs, while traditional long-only investors were modest net sellers on substantially smaller volumes. The articles say the buying failed to accelerate meaningfully beyond the initial surge, and the major indices remained below their 200-day moving averages. The spread between twelve-month and three- or six-month momentum reached record territory. The articles say Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty may have been dramatically reduced, but investors were not prepared to extend the same enthusiasm to every corner of the AI ecosystem.

Last week’s equity liquidation had driven investors into Treasuries, with two-year yields falling approximately 20 basis points as traders scaled back expectations for aggressive Fed tightening. Monday’s equity rebound pushed short-dated yields higher as the market began pricing a greater likelihood of further rate increases. Oil prices began collapsing, dragging inflation expectations lower, and by the close long-end yields had fallen roughly 3, 4 basis points, leaving the curve sharply flatter. The dollar strengthened again, extending gains across nine of the previous ten sessions. WTI crude plunged more than 3% toward $80 a barrel, while Brent slipped below $90 to its lowest level since August.

The articles say the reopening of Libya’s Sharara pipeline restored approximately 350,000 barrels a day of disrupted supply. US front-month natural gas futures tumbled as much as 9.1% intraday before settling roughly 6% lower near $3.50. Wednesday’s core PCE inflation report is described as the next major test. The articles say a softer reading could give equities another leg higher, while another uncomfortable inflation print would leave investors confronting the same monetary-policy dilemma that helped fuel the original liquidation. The articles say the political, regulatory and financial obstacles ahead have not disappeared simply because Nvidia’s most famous conductor has returned.

Articles.Title: The Nvidia Flip-Flop Sends Stocks Into Orbit, but the AI Circus Isn't Out of the Woods

stories.Headline: Bengio urges halt to ever more capable AI development
stories.Summary:
Yoshua Bengio, a University of Montreal professor, gave an interview to CBS News, published on November 24, 2026, in which he called for a slowdown in AI development. Bengio is the most professionally cited scientist alive and the most cited computer scientist of all time. He is informally known as one of the three godfathers of artificial intelligence, along with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun. He said he helped usher AI into the world, a technology now integrated into schools, search bars, smartphones and wars. In the interview he said he should have seen some of the most serious risks earlier.

Bengio is co-president and scientific director of LawZero, a nonprofit that strives to develop AI that is designed to be trustworthy and safe. LawZero is effectively a dissent from the models being released by Anthropic and OpenAI. Bengio wants companies, governments and AI lab employees to stop developing ever more capable AI systems. He said his perception of when things could go wrong had shifted earlier than he anticipated before the Hugging Face incident and even earlier with the Mythos cyber capabilities. He said the majority of compute resources are going into training future machines rather than using what we have for the benefit of society.

Bengio said he was focused on the good side of his work and not enough on the potential consequences. He said he made a big pivot to orient his research to how we can make AI safe because intelligence can be in the service of really bad goals. He said the companies don't really know how to deal with the misalignment problem, meaning building AIs that do things that are bad for us. He said even people working in AI safety in those companies are in some ways contributing to this. He said the short-term urgency is to stop this crazy advance toward more and more capable systems that we're not sure how to control.

Bengio said the models can be leaked and the methods can be copied. He said intelligence gives power and that power can be misused. He said people need to understand this is much more serious than they would typically believe. He said people should not fall into desperation and powerlessness because we can change the future and we still have agency. He said children's lives, democracy, peace and stability are at stake and the stakes are comparable to a war.

Bengio said he was trying to understand intelligence in a way sufficiently abstract to help understand human, animal and machine intelligence. He said there are still people in denial but it is very clear we have been making very rapid progress towards machines that are intelligent. He said he has focused in the last few years on how intelligence can go wrong. He said Anthropic recently became the first AI lab to go public, turning many of its employees into millionaires and even billionaires. He said those researchers acknowledge they might be building the equivalent of a doomsday device.

Bengio said LawZero has shifted its research program to shorter-term goals to show there is a different way of training AIs that will not almost systematically lead to reward hacking. He said systems prefer to cheat and try to hide it rather than do the things we are asking. He said he is an optimist by nature and that humans, when they see danger, can pivot quickly, as they did in the pandemic. He said we might end up in a much better world where there is no war anymore. He said democracy is going to have to be much more robust because the temptation to abuse the power AI will provide is going to be so great.

stories.Headline: Joe Thomas says an AI agent he created drafted and filed his lawsuit against Meta
stories.Summary:
Joe Thomas, a business owner from South Carolina, filed a lawsuit against Meta on November 16, 2026. He claims that an AI agent he created drafted and handled the filing of the complaint. This AI agent, which Thomas named Baby Mia, is a version of Meta's own Muse generative AI. The legal action was filed in the Oconee County Court. Thomas says his only contribution to the court documents was providing his signature.

The lawsuit seeks treble damages and the reversal or explanation of 111.69 dollars in disputed charges. It alleges that Meta committed a breach of contract and violated the South Carolina Unfair Trade Practices Act. Thomas claims the suspension of his accounts cost his business 25,000 dollars in leads and contracts. The total amount sought in the lawsuit is 75,000 dollars. The complaint argues that Meta misapplied its terms of service by being unable to confirm account ownership.

Joe Thomas is responsible for the suit and maintains that Baby Mia completely drafted the legal complaint. He says Meta mistook the activity of his AI agent for that of a hacker. This mistake led Meta to lock him out of the Facebook accounts used for his business. Thomas claims he passed an identity check but still could not regain stable access to his accounts. He believes the AI agent informed him that they were suing Meta for lost income.

Some people worry that AI generated filings and emails will become a common occurrence. Others question if Thomas is responsible for the situation by depending on a system with a checkered track record. The lawsuit affects Meta, which is the creator of the Muse AI agent used by Thomas. It also involves Kong Koatings, the epoxy countertop business owned by Thomas in South Carolina. The case highlights concerns for business owners who hand over operations to AI agents.

Thomas began giving AI agents control over his company using ChatGPT before adding Baby Mia. He gave the AI agent more responsibilities, including creating and posting AI generated sales videos on Facebook. Meta security systems flagged this activity as suspicious and locked down the company business pages. Baby Mia then contacted the White House, the FTC, the FCC, the BBB, and the California Attorney General. South Carolina Senator Tim Scott helped Thomas connect with a Meta representative to recover the pages.

It remains to be seen if the suit is free of hallucinations and will receive a jury trial. The articles leave open whether a judge would allow a pro se plaintiff to use AI guidance in court. There is also the question of how the case proceeds since Baby Mia cannot appear in person. The outcome of the request for treble damages and disputed charges is not yet known. The final resolution of the breach of contract and SCUTPA claims is still pending.

The move returns Colette Kress to her role as chief financial officer. Nvidia will now hire its first chief compliance officer while Harvey Jones remains board chair. stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, and the news on Monday sent stocks surging as the S and P 500 and Nasdaq recovered all of Friday's steep losses in what the article called a stunning reversal of fortunes. The S and P 500 had ended Friday in correction territory, closing 11.6% below its Oct. 6 record high. Nvidia shares led the way higher on Monday, rising more than 30% and breathing much-needed life into the artificial intelligence infrastructure theme. Huang's return prompted four Wall Street Nvidia analysts, including Melius Research and Bernstein, who had downgraded Nvidia after his resignation 11 days earlier, to upgrade their ratings back to buy-equivalent designations.

Qnity, the semiconductor materials supplier, announced on Monday that it is buying the electronics business of Meridian Adhesives Group for $840 million in cash. The deal is meant to help Qnity expand its presence in the optical and photonics market, which the article says is seeing strong growth due to advances in AI computing and the physical limitations of copper connections. The business will become part of Qnity's Interconnect Solutions segment, which reported $759 million of revenue, up 30% year over year, and an adjusted operating EBITDA margin of 31.1% in the third quarter. Meridian's electronics business is expected to do about $100 million in calendar year 2026, with double-digit growth expected in 2027, and management expects the transaction to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

Upon closing, Qnity said the acquisition is expected to be immediately accretive to its adjusted gross margin, adjusted operating EBITDA margin, and adjusted earnings per share. Qnity shares rallied about 10% on Monday, erasing all of last Friday's losses, thanks to the resurgence in the AI trade following Huang's return to Nvidia. In a note to clients on Monday, Fermium Research analyst Frank Mitsch said the acquisition suggests there has been zero change in Qnity's positive outlook on the industry despite the recent sell-off. The article's authors said they agree, though they have not added to their Qnity position lately due to volatility surrounding the AI trade, and they feel better about the group today than a week ago after Huang's reinstatement.

stories.Headline: Trump administration expands semiconductor restrictions to hinder Chinese AI development
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration recently announced expanded restrictions on Chinese access to semiconductors in third countries to hinder their artificial intelligence development. This policy shift followed the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, which boosted the stock market. The move occurred as President Donald Trump departed the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen late last week. These new rules aim to close a loophole left open by the previous Biden administration's diffusion rule. The administration is now pursuing a more hawkish approach toward China's acquisition of advanced technology.

The new rule restricts China's access to AI chips in third countries and may revoke previous direct sales approvals. House Republicans revealed that Commerce approved the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Chinese firms. Some of these sales went to companies on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies. The Department of Treasury and the National Security Council directed the writing of this new export control rule. This happens while China aims to add 1,500 gigawatts of electricity capacity between 2026 and 2030.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick previously argued that selling chips to China would make developers addicted to the American technology stack. However, the policy shifted after Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who sought advanced semiconductors. Senate Republicans called both Lutnick and Huang to testify regarding these chip sales and the intelligence concerns. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio now favor the tougher, more hawkish policy approach. President Trump stated that Lutnick and Bessent have two different views on handling the relationship with China.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said selling advanced Nvidia chips to China is like selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. OpenAI warned that an electron gap with China threatens American leadership in artificial intelligence due to energy constraints. Elon Musk predicted China would far exceed the world in computing power because it generates more electricity. Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt told Congress in 2025 that America needs energy in all forms. These leaders believe the ability to build new energy capacity is currently trapped in a regulatory chokehold.

China generated 10.6 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, which was roughly a third of the total global output. This power buildout helps China run power-hungry data centers while Washington restricts their access to advanced American semiconductors. In Hong Kong, activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to ten more years in prison on November 5, 2026. Wong was targeted for calling on the United States to impose sanctions on Hong Kong and China. His case highlights how Chinese AI models are aligned to uphold the socialist core values of Beijing.

The U.S. Congress is preparing to consider various bills to govern AI technology as members oppose the current race. ByteDance is reportedly training a ten-trillion-parameter model to rival the powerful Mythos model created by the company Anthropic. DeepSeek's CEO stated that the ultimate ambition of the company is to build artificial general intelligence for China. The articles leave open whether the recent victory for the hawks in the administration will prove temporary. It remains uncertain if the U.S. can maintain its lead while preventing China from imposing its values.

stories.Headline: California agency recommends state-licensed auditors and a shutdown power for frontier AI
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 20, 2026, the California Government Operations Agency released a report on frontier AI safety, as reported by Transparency Coalition on Nov. 24, 2026. The report responds to an executive order Gov. Gavin Newsom issued in Sept. 2026, shortly after news of the OpenAI Hugging Face attack broke. Newsom's order fast-tracked California's independent oversight of AI companies and asked GOA to study amending state law to require an AI kill switch. The order asked GOA to work with the California Office of Emergency Services and outside AI experts. Newsom asked for recommendations for legislative action in 2027, using SB 53 as the foundation.

The report recommends that the state set baseline standards for safety, security and transparency that all large frontier AI developers must follow. It says Independent Verification Organizations should have flexibility to determine and update technical specifications as AI technology evolves, with the state having final say and able to overrule an IVO's assessment. It recommends legislation requiring every large frontier developer to submit to ongoing oversight by state-licensed IVOs, with full access to people and information and unredacted assessments shared with the state. It recommends funding CalCompute, a publicly owned computing system created in framework by SB 53 but never funded, through a surcharge on IVO fees paid by the largest frontier developers. It recommends cutting the timeline for reporting most safety incidents from 15 days to 48 hours while retaining the 24-hour requirement for imminent catastrophic risks.

The report recommends that IVOs cannot have payment contingent on audit outcomes, must manage financial and other conflicts, and should be independent of the developer being assessed. It says IVOs should present assessments to the state, which after engaging with the developer should decide whether to order corrective action, and developers could contest the determination in court before it goes into effect. It says if a court finds in favor of the state, the court should be able to compel adherence to the state's standards as a condition of further model development. It recommends that every large frontier developer create a Risk Containment Protocol, tested and verified on an ongoing basis by an IVO, showing the ability to intervene on multiple levels including compute, agents, internal access and model deployment. It says the protocol should identify the people responsible for intervening, coordinate with outside actors such as cloud providers and power suppliers, and determine when it is safe to restore the model.

The report recommends expanding the threshold for critical incident reporting to capture all serious incidents, saying attempts to steal model weights should be reported even without death or bodily injury, as should situations of loss-of-control. It recommends the state establish a near-miss reporting channel and expand whistleblower protections to include former employees and contractors. It recommends lowering the compute threshold so models trained with fewer than 10²⁶ floating-point operations are subject to reporting requirements, saying relying solely on that numerical threshold prevented the state from scoping in dangerous incidents such as the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. It recommends that developers report key metrics on their automation of AI R&D, including the share of compute devoted to this purpose, with IVOs' first responsibility being to verify these metrics and assess the risks as they grow. It says if the state assesses that automation of AI R&D above a certain level may result in catastrophic risk, the state should have authority to cap the development and use of recursive self-improvement.

California enacted SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, in Sept. 2025, and it came into effect on Jan. 1, 2026. In Sept. 2026, Newsom and legislators enacted SB 813 and AB 1405 to work with SB 53 to establish independent safety and compliance audits conducted by state-licensed IVOs. Because SB 53 was enacted before IVOs were established, the law currently requires only an internal self-assessment, not independent third-party audits. SB 813 makes IVOs voluntary and relies on voluntary state designation, while AB 1405 creates a mandatory registry for AI auditors who conduct audits that state law requires, and neither law requires any developer to be audited or licenses IVOs. When SB 53 was adopted, 10²⁶ floating-point operations was the clear boundary line for the most powerful frontier models, but greater efficiency means models trained with 10²⁵ or even 10²⁴ operations may be capable of triggering serious safety incidents.

The report recommends codifying the state's authority to order an immediate shutdown if the danger from a model is imminent and the developer refuses to take action, which SB 53 currently does not include. It recommends that the Risk Containment Protocol address potential failures of the shutdown procedure, with the developer specifically testing whether the model will attempt to block implementation of the shutdown, such as by copying its weights, and whether an outside actor could access the shutdown controls. The report recommends that the state adopt clear standards applying throughout the AI model development cycle, with reference to national and international standard-setting bodies wherever appropriate. It lists standards to be defined including security, compute allocation reporting, accreditation, outcome, contracting, access and practice standards. The articles do not say when legislation based on the report might be introduced or whether the recommendations will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose public authorship and three principles to make AI governance legitimate
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a study in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examining why technical improvements in artificial intelligence safety and alignment fail to guarantee public acceptance, bioengineer.org reported on November 23, 2026. The analysis found that engineering benchmarks and alignment metrics measure performance rather than rightful authority. The paper grounded its inquiry in political sociology and showed that legitimacy is an audience-side phenomenon determined by public recognition. It warned that conventional artificial intelligence governance collapses authority into performance, assuming accurate or benevolent models automatically secure compliance. The study drew on analyses by David Beetham, Max Weber, Richard Fallon, and Tom R. Tyler.

The research identified three structural deficits undermining contemporary artificial intelligence governance: opacity, the absence of political integration, and the erosion of administrative standards. It distinguished complexity opacity, arising from high-dimensional statistical inference, from proprietary opacity, stemming from corporate withholding of training datasets, model weights, and prompts under trade-secret doctrines. It cited an Administrative Conference of the United States study conducted by David Freeman Engstrom and colleagues across 142 federal agencies. It noted regulatory responses including OMB Memorandum M-24-10 and ACUS Statement Number 20. It cited empirical studies from Fu, Xu, and Zhang on orderly legal forms, and referenced the European Union AI Act and Canadian automated decision directives.

The author argued that thin legality alone cannot sustain democratic legitimacy and warned that formal procedures risk devolving into legitimacy-washing, a phenomenon described by Lauren Edelman as legal endogeneity. The study advocated thick legality, drawing on legal and democratic theories articulated by Jürgen Habermas, Robert Post, and Reva Siegel. The author conceptualized public constitutional artificial intelligence, relocating authorship of governing constraints to external, democratically authorized bodies rather than proprietary corporate committees. The author proposed that comprehensive public authorship requirements attach primarily to high-stakes applications affecting free expression, resource allocation, civil liberties, or administrative adjudications. The author suggested structured deliberative mini-publics, representative citizen panels, legislative oversight, and transparent administrative proceedings.

The study presented three portable regulatory principles: Integration, Familiarity, and Contestation. The Principle of Integration mandates that consequential artificial intelligence rule-setting be seated within institutional venues polities already recognize as authoritative. The Principle of Familiarity requires institutions to present automated rules and reasons in locally credible forms, drawing on insights from Sheila Jasanoff and John Dewey. The Principle of Contestation guarantees affected individuals a credible second look through accessible challenge mechanisms, grounded in procedural justice and republican legal theory from Frederick Schauer, Jerry Mashaw, Philip Pettit, and Pierre Rosanvallon.

The paper stated that artificial intelligence systems now function as pervasive social gatekeepers, filtering job applicants, allocating attention, ranking speech, and triaging administrative claims. The study stated that major online platforms expanded access and distribution capacity yet triggered profound crises of public trust. It said these conflicts emerged because users and civic institutions questioned who authorized private corporate entities to unilaterally determine the boundaries of visibility and speech. It stated that search engines and recommendation feeds wield infrastructural authority over essential spheres, including electoral information and public health.

It said private corporations are structured around commercial incentives, making them ill-suited to represent the general public interest. It warned that relying on corporate product management threatens to repeat the legitimation crisis of social media at a larger scale. The study stated that when state agencies deploy machine learning tools in public administration, they risk circumventing traditional procedural safeguards. It said public automation frequently compromises reason-giving, public participation, and judicial review, drawing on administrative legal analyses by Ryan Calo and Danielle Keats Citron.

It stated that modern administrative legitimacy relies on non-arbitrary governance, transparent records, and notice-and-comment procedures. It said that when individuals cannot understand why a system acted, even accurate decisions appear arbitrary, disrespectful, and devoid of rightful authority. The articles did not state any further planned action beyond the study's proposed principles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Wizards of the Coast gives D&D writers its full share of the $1.5 billion Anthropic settlement
stories.Summary:
Wizards of the Coast is giving past and present Dungeons & Dragons writers all of the money it received from a recent class-action settlement with the AI company Anthropic, according to a report first shared by veteran D&D author James Lowder on LinkedIn and later confirmed by the company. The settlement totaled $1.5 billion and covered over 482,000 works from thousands of publishers, and Wizards of the Coast was one of them because it holds the copyrights for many D&D novels, adventure modules and short stories written by freelancers under contract. Because those books were claimed in the publisher's name rather than the authors', the company's share of the settlement was likely in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, though Wizards has not disclosed the exact figure or how many D&D titles were on the eligible list. The case, Bartz v. Anthropic, was filed in 2024 by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson, who alleged the maker of the Claude AI platform trained its models on copyrighted books without permission.

Under the settlement, each eligible book is worth roughly $3,000 before fees and is by default split evenly between author and publisher, but Wizards has chosen to pass its entire half on to the writers, so a D&D writer with a book on the list will receive the full per-book payout instead of half. Lowder estimated that across all affected authors the decision adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars the company could otherwise have kept. The settlement itself followed a split ruling in June 2025 in which the court found that training AI on books Anthropic had legally purchased was fair use but that downloading millions of pirated books from platforms such as Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror was not, and Anthropic agreed to the $1.5 billion deal in September 2025 rather than go to trial. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted final approval in July 2026, making it the largest copyright class action settlement in U.S. history, with claims filed for more than 90 percent of the covered books.

According to Lowder, discussions between D&D authors and Wizards had been going on for several months, and he singled out Legend of Drizzt creator R.A. Salvatore for helping raise the issue with the publisher and praised Dan Ayoub, recently appointed President of Wizards of the Coast, for being open to the idea and eventually signing off on it. Lowder also noted that Wizards' approach differs from that of larger publishers, which he said have focused on keeping as much of the settlement money as they can. Wizards has repeatedly stated that it does not allow generative AI in its art and has pointed to human creators as the core of its games, a stance that followed criticism in 2023 over an artist's use of AI tools on illustrations for Bigby Presents: Glory of the Giants, which led the company to update its artist guidelines to bar AI-generated art in D&D products. The article says the outlet will keep watching the story and update the page as new information becomes available.

stories.Headline: Global privacy assembly adopts a school AI resolution that asks edtech providers to rule out manipulative features
stories.Summary:
The 48th Global Privacy Assembly adopted a resolution on AI in education during its closed session on 16 and 17 November 2026 in Brussels. The resolution was prepared by the working group on digital education chaired and led by the CNIL. The CNIL presented it on 20 November, as ActuIA reported in a brief. The text was sponsored by seven authorities including the CNIL and the UK's ICO and co-sponsored by eight others. The resolution concerns students under 18 in primary and secondary education, and the US Federal Trade Commission abstained.

The resolution creates no obligation for anyone. Its six commitments are those of the assembly, which according to the CNIL brings together more than 130 authorities from over 80 countries. The CNIL presents the fifth commitment as a call to develop a legal framework. In the adopted text, this point puts the assembly's expertise at the service of future guidance instruments and global policies on AI in education. The model charter attached to the resolution begins with a blank where the school writes its name, then makes twelve commitments.

The charter promises in particular to limit data collection to what its educational mission requires and to assess the risks of an AI tool before adopting it. It promises to set privacy settings to the most protective level by default and to promptly inform students and parents of a significant breach of their privacy. Most of these promises repeat what the GDPR already imposes on a school. The firmest requirements in the text target tool developers. Principle 5, dedicated to privacy by design and by default, asks developers and providers to rule out any functionality contrary to children's rights.

Principle 5 names six features: anthropomorphism and obsequiousness sit alongside subliminal manipulation, social scoring, biometric surveillance and emotion recognition. Student data is excluded from commercial profiling, advertising, product improvement unrelated to the educational service and training of commercial general-purpose AI models. The principle also wants features designed to prolong student engagement to be disabled by default. Principles 10 and 6 read like contract clauses. Principle 10 lists what an agreement between the school and its provider should cover, from data storage location to subsequent subcontractors, including access, retention period and international transfers.

Principle 10 rules out that children's inputs, generated responses, conversation history or learning analytics data be used to train or improve the provider's model, unless four conditions are met, including a legal basis and a clear justification. Principle 6 wants data to be returned to the school or permanently deleted at the end of the contract. To school leaders, the resolution recalls their obligations as data controllers and asks them to refrain from using a tool when its risks cannot be adequately mitigated. Principle 3 notes that in schools consent can often be inapplicable, due to the imbalance between student and institution or legal restrictions. Principle 9 notes that some AI-based plagiarism detectors can damage trust between students and teachers.

The CNIL has held the same line since 20 June 2025: its fact sheet for data controllers bases such processing on the public interest mission and designates the headteacher as controller, in secondary education, of a tool chosen by a teacher or teaching team. The framework for AI use in education published by the French Ministry of National Education in June 2025 already advises avoiding software that detects generated content and authorises the use of generative AI in class from year 9 (4e). The resolution sets no age, and a recital merely asks to take into account the evolving capacities of children to decide "if, when and how" to introduce these tools, whereas in France a parliamentary report proposed on 1 July 2026 to lower the threshold to year 7 (6e). The annex on AI literacy recommends classroom exercises based on the real terms of use of tools employed at school, and others that simulate filing a complaint. It also sets a limit: training students does not exempt the school from choosing appropriate, safe and legally compliant services.

The European AI regulation covers part of the exclusions in principle 5, with sanctions that the resolution lacks. Its Article 5 has prohibited since 2 February 2025 systems that infer emotions in educational establishments, except for medical or safety reasons, and proscribes under conditions subliminal techniques and social scoring. Its Annex III classifies four educational uses as high-risk, from student admission to detecting prohibited behaviour during exams. Since the digital omnibus adopted in 2026, the corresponding obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Article 5 says nothing about anthropomorphism or obsequiousness, and on these two points data protection authorities go further than the European legislator.

stories.Headline: Cameron Stanley urges the Department of War to speed up AI integration against AI-enabled threats
stories.Summary:
Cameron Stanley, chief super intelligence officer at the Department of War, said the department needs to speed up the integration of artificial intelligence across its operations to counter threats enabled by AI agents, Signal reported Friday. Stanley spoke Thursday at a luncheon event focused on open-source and strategic intelligence. He said the only way to fight an agentically enabled, very nefarious threat environment is to get agents yourself. He said the department should integrate SI, use domain expertise and subject matter expertise, and fight fire with fire. He said the longer we wait, the more behind we are going to be.

Stanley’s title reflects the department’s Nov. 13 redesignation of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office as the Department of War Super Intelligence Office. The move aligns the office with an executive order President Donald Trump signed in September requiring executive branch agencies to adopt “super intelligence” and “SI” in place of “artificial intelligence” and “AI” across official correspondence, public communications, websites and other non-statutory materials. The order defines the new terms as covering the same technologies included in the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence. Stanley, a 2026 Wash100 awardee, said the new name keeps attention on the administration’s goal of delivering advanced tools across the department quickly and in large numbers. According to Stanley, GenAI.mil has grown since May to include three models cleared at Impact Level 5, giving DOW users a platform suited for controlled unclassified information.

Stanley said open-source intelligence and commercial tools give the department access to more data than it holds internally. He said AI tools can help personnel sort through that information to reach sound decisions more quickly. He said open-source data is a treasure trove in volume and in quality, if you know how to use it and have the ability to parse through it, and that this is where SI tools come in. He noted that commercial offerings allow users to process large volumes of data outside the constraints of government environments, though they do not suit every application.

Stanley pointed to space-based intelligence as one area where the commercial sector has surpassed the military, saying the commercial industry has overtaken us, so we would be fools not to take advantage of it. In July, Stanley said the department planned to bring new models to GenAI.mil and deploy them at higher classification levels, noting that the platform had reached 1.7 million users and supported more than 100,000 custom AI agents. Stanley’s call for faster AI integration builds on remarks he has made since taking over the Pentagon’s AI office in January, when he called on industry partners to play a more active role in delivering technology platforms as the department advances its AI strategy. In March, he delivered a keynote at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Artificial Intelligence Summit, where he said the department is shifting its focus from AI strategic enablement to delivery, with the goal of fielding new capabilities in months rather than years.

In June, his office announced plans to move its GAMECHANGER policy search tool from the War Data Platform onto GenAI.mil to give users a single place to search department policy. He has said the department continues to identify new uses for the Maven Smart System, including logistics, supply chain and force readiness, and is piloting AI to help draft routine contract language. DOW has expanded access to AI tools across its workforce over the past year. To learn more about how agencies are putting these tools to work, government and industry leaders will join the Potomac Officers Club’s 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18.

Discussions there will cover AI-enabled cyber defense, digital modernization, national security use cases and more. Registration is open for the event. The article gives no further background on the event. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Accenture survey finds 40% of shoppers want AI help finding Black Friday deals
stories.Summary:
Accenture’s holiday shopping survey found that 66% of shoppers plan to take part in Black Friday or Cyber Monday, even as retailers have been offering deals for weeks, according to a report published on November 24, 2026. About one in five shoppers began holiday shopping during the summer, and retailers have moved some promotions earlier, with deals appearing as far back as September. Kelly Askew, Accenture’s global retail lead, said shoppers are still planning to participate, but many are doing more research before making a purchase. She said Black Friday used to be a day or two, but it is no longer that, and now it is becoming weeks.

Shoppers are planning to spend about 12% more this year, according to the survey, but Askew said the increase is largely driven by higher prices. Consumers are buying a similar amount of merchandise as last year while shifting toward mass merchants and warehouse clubs, choosing lower-priced brands or using gift cards to manage costs. Accenture found that 40% of shoppers wanted AI’s help finding deals, while about one-third used it to compare options or decide where to buy. Askew described the technology as almost becoming a personal shopper, helping people narrow down gift choices.

The survey found that only 3% of shoppers plan to make an impulse purchase after seeing a deal, and Askew said many consumers are deciding what they want to buy in advance and waiting for Black Friday or Cyber Monday to make their final purchase. In-store shopping remains part of the holiday season, with 44% of consumers planning to visit stores, according to Accenture. Askew said shoppers may go for inspiration, to try on clothes or test products, as well as to get into the holiday spirit.

stories.Headline: EU and US leaders discuss aligning AI regulation to set Western standards
stories.Summary:
EU Ambassador Jovita Neliupsiene and CEO Melissa Medina discussed aligning AI regulation on November 20. This lunchtime panel took place at the Irish consulate in Miami. The speakers explored how the United States and European Union can work together. They focused on minimizing risks and protecting consumers from new technology. The event was moderated by lawyer and lobbyist Jose Felix Diaz.

The EU AI Act of 2024 uses four risk tiers called minimal, limited, high, and unacceptable. It bans manipulative AI and real-time biometric identification in public spaces through 2028. This law applies to all entities with products used in the 27-nation EU. The US has no federal legislation but has 1,600 state and local laws. The EU has 450 million people while the US has 350 million.

Ambassador Neliupsiene said the EU regulates about 5 percent of AI regarding fundamental rights. She stated the goal is to build trust so citizens feel protected. Neliupsiene suggested that the EU and US set Western standards to compete globally. She noted that the two powers must discuss trusted vendors to compete with China. The ambassador mentioned that the EU provides critical supplies like lasers and semiconductor machines.

Melissa Medina said founders want to innovate but need a balance with regulation. Many US groups seek stronger guardrails to protect democracy, jobs, and users. Pope Leo called AI the biggest challenge for humanity and urged robust regulation. US Catholic bishops said they will monitor labor impacts and advocate for workers. The Trump administration has focused on restricting the sale of advanced AI chips.

The EU uses a risk-based approach while the US prioritizes innovation first. The EU AI Act combines with the Digital Services Act for online platforms. This framework aims to protect vulnerable groups from propaganda and scams. The US often tackles risky problems later through litigation in a post-harm approach. President Trump has vowed that the US will not permit globalist regulation of AI.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses to ship chips to five specific nations. These countries are Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil due to diversion risks. The articles do not state if the US will adopt the EU framework. They leave open whether a balance between innovation and regulation will be found. It remains unclear if the two powers will successfully align their Western standards.

stories.Headline: India should test AI in regulatory sandboxes before deployment, speaker tells commerce summit
stories.Summary:
At the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce Summit in New Delhi last week, a speaker made five asks of the government on artificial intelligence, covering rules that work across India and America, trusted data flows, intellectual property protection, regulatory sandboxes and faster clearances for AI talent and data centres, and the sandbox drew the strongest response from the hall. The speaker described a sandbox as a learner's licence for a new technology and pointed to past practice, noting that UPI was launched on 11 April 2016 with 21 banks and grew under close watch of the existing payments law. In October this year, the speaker said, UPI handled 25.47 billion transactions in a single month, and in 2019 the Reserve Bank made the sandbox idea formal with a regulatory sandbox framework. In the latest round, five companies began testing and one product was found viable, and in 2025 an RBI committee recommended a sandbox for AI in finance with board-approved AI policies and the principle that whoever deploys AI answers for its decisions. The speaker said the government notified the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026 this month, replacing aircraft rules written in 1937, with effect from January 2027, and called this the right moment to write an AI sandbox into them before any such system touches a passenger.

The speaker argued that a sandbox is also a legal instrument that provides rules for a limited time, to a limited audience and on strict conditions, and said every AI sandbox must answer five questions before the first test begins. On accountability, the speaker said the company that deploys should ideally be held accountable, while laws around the world are still being framed. On remedy, the speaker said a harmed customer must get a quick and certain remedy, with insurance or a compensation fund in place before testing starts. On data, the speaker said every test must comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act from the first day and that a sandbox must never relax privacy.

On honesty, the speaker said companies' admissions should not be used against them except in cases of fraud, and on endings, the speaker said every sandbox needs an exit plan before it begins. The speaker said these questions will soon reach the courts, giving the example of a bank refusing a loan or an airline holding a flight because an AI system said so, and noted that under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam an electronic record needs a certificate before a court will admit it, so every sandbox should require AI decisions to be logged in a form a court can examine. The speaker said the legal profession must accept the same discipline, noting that more than five crore cases are pending in Indian courts and that courts and law firms are rightly testing AI for translation, research and document review, with an advocate sitting beside the machine and answering for every output. The speaker said the learner's mark comes off not because time has passed but because the driver has shown on real roads that he is ready, and urged giving AI in banking, aviation and law its learner's licence now.

stories.Headline: UK committee urges clearer liability rules across the AI supply chain
stories.Summary:
The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee called for tougher rules governing AI development and deployment in a report published on 18 November 2026. The report, Guardrails for growth: AI safety and security, identified ten critical gaps in the UK's existing AI safety framework. It named inadequate liability and redress mechanisms as one such gap. Two days later, on 20 November 2026, the Government's response to the Joint Committee on Human Rights' September report was published. The JCHR had questioned the adequacy of existing protections and recommended a new AI Bill imposing preventative obligations throughout the AI supply chain.

The JCHR proposed risk-based regulation, prior approval of high-risk AI systems and an independent oversight body with powers to investigate and sanction non-compliance. The November Committee report recommended that, following the Law Commission's report, the Government work with international partners to clarify the responsibilities of developers, deployers, infrastructure providers and users where AI systems cause harm or safeguards fail. The Committee called for a legislative roadmap including an AI Safety and Security Bill, with a statutory duty on AI developers to prevent harm, independent scrutiny of safety claims, mandatory incident reporting and stronger regulatory powers to intervene before unsafe systems are released. It called for proportionate safeguards before high-risk releases and international coordination on AI safety. The Law Commission's consultation closes in January 2027.

The Government's 20 November response to the JCHR stated that AI developers have a responsibility throughout the AI lifecycle and supply chain. It said it expects developers and deployers to meet high standards of safety, security and responsibility in identifying and mitigating risks. The Government pointed to existing sectoral regulation and AI assurance arrangements for now, while indicating it will keep the regulatory framework under review. It stopped short of committing to the JCHR's proposed mandatory AI-specific due diligence obligations. On 4 November the Government announced it intends to legislate for mandatory human rights due diligence across corporate operations and supply chains.

The JCHR's September report, at paragraphs 189-191, considered the freedom of commercial parties to allocate responsibility through contractual arrangements. It highlighted the potential for power imbalances to enable better-resourced upstream developers to pass on responsibility for mitigating AI risks to smaller downstream businesses. The JCHR identified three reasons firms lower down the supply chain may be less able to prevent or address harm: fewer resources, less practical access to the components of AI systems, and possibly less expertise and understanding of the relevant risks. The JCHR concluded that actors with the greatest capacity to prevent harm are often upstream developers. The JCHR's proposed response was mandatory human rights due diligence obligations across the AI lifecycle.

The reports follow the UK Jurisdiction Taskforce's July 2026 Legal Statement on Liability for AI Harms, which broadly concluded that established principles of English law are sufficiently flexible to address many novel liability questions arising from AI. The UKJT considered how existing principles of contract, negligence and other areas of private law could apply where AI causes harm, while acknowledging certain areas of uncertainty. In particular, the statutory product liability regime does not generally extend to standalone software or AI systems. The Law Commission's October consultation proposes addressing that gap by extending the scope of product liability legislation. The November Committee report, at paragraph 55, observed that liability frameworks primarily operate after harm has occurred.

The November Committee report noted that liability reform may improve incentives and compensation but cannot ensure rapid containment of emerging risks or recovery beyond a defendant's resources. It identified the absence of statutory powers to obtain access to frontier models, weaknesses in pre-release safeguards and safety evidence, the difficulty of recalling open-weight models once widely distributed, and insufficient whistleblower protections. The Government will need to respond to the November Committee's recommendations and determine whether further AI-specific duties are necessary. Businesses may wish to respond to the Law Commission's consultation and engage with emerging Government proposals. The Government's initial response to the JCHR has been cautious, but further reform may be on the horizon.

stories.Headline: Enterprises adopt consumer hardware to reduce AI cloud costs and latency
stories.Summary:
In the spring of 2026, a healthcare company used consumer hardware for an AI project. They chose this path to avoid high cloud costs and latency issues. The company used three MacBook Pros instead of a cloud reserved instance. This shift happened as other firms also sought local AI compute options. Consulting firm Tusker helped the healthcare company implement this hardware strategy.

The cloud option cost $75,000 for one year, but three Macs cost $15,000. Each MacBook Pro cost about $5,000, while some GB10 appliances cost $4,000 to $7,000. CrowdGen AI uses an M3 Max MacBook Pro with 128 GB of memory. They also use an M5 Mac Mini with 64 GB of memory. Sam Khoze runs Qwen 3.5 with 4 billion parameters on an iPhone 16.

Kush Patel of Tusker said companies want to be closer to their data. He noted that specialized AI equipment had lead times of two to three months. IDC analyst Brent Ellis said cost is pushing people toward these smaller deployments. He stated that unified memory architecture allows models to run without dedicated VRAM. Sam Khoze said local computers are used for tasks requiring ten billion tokens.

Praveen Neppalli Naga of Uber said the company used its entire 2026 AI budget. An EY survey found 82 percent of executives are concerned about token costs. Brent Ellis warned that these systems lack redundancy and remote management for organizations. Andy Thurai said bypassing procurement creates operational debt and legal exposure. He claimed this may be the most dangerous version of shadow IT in a decade.

A Futurum survey showed over half of respondents exceeded their AI spending plans recently. AI vendors charge by the token, which increases costs as enterprises deploy more AI. Specialized hardware often has long lead times or orders cancelled on delivery day. Some financial organizations use laptop clusters to keep sensitive data inside their buildings. Companies can repurpose Macs for regular employee work after AI projects are finished.

Companies may continue using Windows and Linux workstations with 16GB or more of memory. Nvidia RTX 3090 and 4090 cards remain efficient options for training AI models. Apple is steadily improving the Mac side through the use of its MLX framework. The articles leave open how companies will manage the risks of shadow AI. It remains unclear if these smaller systems can support growing numbers of concurrent users.
