stories.Headline: New Yorkers warned of holiday scams, AI shopping traps
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James issued a holiday scam warning on November 24, 2026, as reported by Long Island Business News. The warning tells New Yorkers to guard their personal information and to be careful when using artificial intelligence tools while shopping. James said she encourages holiday shoppers to protect themselves, their families and their private information by staying vigilant about potential scams. She also said no one should hesitate to report suspicious activity to her office. The warning covers receipts, buy now pay later loans, subscriptions, devices, phishing emails, fake deals, AI shopping tools and surveillance pricing.

James advised consumers to check that register prices match advertised or shelf prices. New York law requires retailers to charge the lowest advertised, posted or marked price and to keep at least 98% price accuracy during inspections by weights and measures officials. She said shoppers should review interest rates, payment schedules and fees on buy now, pay later loans before buying. Some of those loans charge interest even when payments are made on time, and missed payments may bring late fees and hurt credit scores. New York law requires businesses to clearly disclose subscription terms, obtain consent for automatic renewals, send post-purchase confirmation and offer an easy way to cancel.

James said consumers should update their home Wi-Fi password, avoid public Wi-Fi for purchases, install the latest software updates and keep antivirus software active. She warned that emails promoting exclusive holiday deals or free gift cards may be phishing attempts. She said shoppers should verify senders of unexpected holiday e-cards or invitations before clicking links or opening attachments. She advised shopping only on reputable websites, verifying URLs before entering payment information and checking for a working customer service number, a physical business address and positive customer reviews.

She said retailers that list only a P.O. box or have no working phone number deserve caution. James said shoppers should review all charges before purchasing because some websites add hefty delivery, processing or subscription fees, particularly during the holiday season. She said people using AI tools to make purchases should review what accounts and personal information the tool can access and limit permissions whenever possible. She said anyone whose AI tool can buy on their behalf should set clear spending limits and purchasing rules and require approval before purchases whenever possible.

New York's Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act requires most businesses that use personal data to set prices to display a clear disclosure near the price. Consumers who encounter undisclosed algorithmic pricing should file a complaint with the attorney general's office. James said shoppers should compare prices across retailers and platforms, use private or incognito browsing and check prices when logged out of loyalty accounts. She warned about inflated discounts and crossed-out prices and said shoppers should check price histories to judge whether a deal offers real savings.

She said consumers should keep order confirmations and receipts, contact the retailer if an item does not arrive as promised and file a complaint with her office if the company does not respond. She said people should review credit card and bank statements regularly for unauthorized charges, which may go unnoticed amid increased holiday spending. Suspected scam victims can report to the attorney general's office by submitting a complaint online or calling 1-800-771-7755. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Leicester Medical School hosts a symposium on how AI should shape healthcare education
stories.Summary:
The Medical School at the University of Leicester is hosting a special symposium on artificial intelligence in healthcare education. This event will take place on 9 December in the George Davies Centre. The symposium focuses on how AI should be used to shape the future of healthcare education. It will explore how AI creates new possibilities for clinical training, assessment, teaching, and learning. Keynote speakers will discuss enhancing clinical learning and supporting human reasoning to create more effective healthcare education.

The event is free and runs from 9am until 3pm on 9 December at the George Davies Centre on Lancaster Road. Presentation abstracts are accepted until 11.59pm on 27 November via the symposium website. Professor Shafi Ahmed will explore AI opportunities and challenges in hospital care and surgery. Professor Yin Ying from Chongqing Medical University, China, will discuss AI in rehabilitation education. The programme includes workshops, themed oral research panels, poster presentations, keynote presentations, and three awards for collaborative projects.

Terese Bird, Professor Shameq Sayeed, and Dr Morteza Rezaei-Zadeh from Leicester Medical School are the conveners of the event. Bird stated that this third symposium aims to foster dialogue between practice and research while showcasing innovative work. She said the event encourages collaboration among industry partners, healthcare organisations, clinicians, researchers, academic staff, and students. Bird noted the symposium provides a space to question assumptions and share evidence to prepare professionals for an AI-enabled world. She added that participants will share emerging developments and innovative research to facilitate knowledge transfer.

The event is for AI specialists, educational technology developers, researchers, clinicians, and clinical educators. It also targets medical, nursing, and allied health students, as well as academic staff and healthcare educators. The symposium addresses questions about professional identity, accountability, fairness, patient safety, educational quality, and clinical judgement. It aims to consider how AI can contribute to safer and more equitable healthcare education. The sessions will consider implications for clinical teams, healthcare professionals, and the wider healthcare system.

The symposium is the third of its kind hosted by the Medical School at the University of Leicester. It is designed to bring together diverse groups for interdisciplinary discussion on AI integration. The event focuses on the intersection of technology and healthcare training within a university setting. It seeks to develop practical approaches for preparing the next generation of healthcare professionals. The organizers intend to use the event to highlight outstanding research and collaborative projects.

The symposium will conclude after the scheduled presentations and workshops on 9 December. The articles do not state what specific outcomes or policy changes will result from the discussions. It remains open how the shared evidence will be implemented in actual clinical training. The text does not mention if there will be future symposia following this third event. There is no information on which specific research projects will win the three awards.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans wholly AI-generated music from December 9 and removes 29 million tracks
stories.Summary:
Tidal announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it will ban wholly AI-generated music from its platform, with the company saying such tracks will be “rejected and removed” starting December 9. The streamer, a formerly artist-backed service once controlled by Jack Dorsey’s Block, announced the complete ban in a post on X. Tidal cited a massive surge of artificially created music as the reason for the move. The company said any wholly AI track detected on the platform as of that date will be rejected and removed. Tidal said it was taking an aggressive stand against AI.

Tidal said that in the past 90 days, 43% of all tracks on its platform have been detected as wholly AI-generated. The company said it labeled those tracks, a step many other companies have also been taking, and removed them from its royalty pool. On November 6, Tidal added, “we had the greatest influx of AI music yet: Over 60% of the deliveries we received were wholly AI generated.” Tidal estimates that 27 million tracks, about 6% of the total in its catalog, are tagged as AI. Tidal said 96% of those titles received zero streams over the past 90 days.

Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote in an X thread on Tuesday that 43% of tracks distributed to Tidal in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated and that something more drastic needs to be done. Andersen said Tidal will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog and that they will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. He said the move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks and have it reject between 80,000 and 85,000 songs a day. Andersen said he believes the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.” He wrote, “We encourage our peers to follow suit.”

Tidal wrote that wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists diverts streams and royalties away from artists and confuses fans. The company said it has taken down over 65,000 tracks flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation. Tidal wrote that not all songs catch on immediately and artists should have time to build their fanbases, but that at this scale the authentic music and artists subscribers seek get buried. Variety reported that the move makes Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely, a claim attributed to the publication. Competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks.

The ban comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted, and ban AI songs associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category including songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform. Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.” Spotify said in a blog post last month that it removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, after removing 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. Spotify added that the work isn’t finished and that AI moves fast and bad actors adapt just as fast.

Tidal said the removals will begin December 9, and Andersen said the tracks will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. The articles do not say what will happen to AI-assisted tracks under the new ban. The articles do not say how Tidal will detect wholly AI-generated tracks after December 9. The articles do not say whether Tidal will reverse the ban or how it will treat artists whose tracks are removed. The articles do not say whether any other platform has committed to a complete ban.

stories.Headline: DeepMind's Gemini 4 agents find faster quantum algorithms and prove them correct in Lean
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind says teams of AI agents running on its Gemini 4 model have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design, the lab announced on Monday. The work was done with Google Quantum AI, and each result was proved correct in the Lean theorem prover because the circuits are too large to test on today’s computers. The proofs matter because the circuits need thousands of qubits, far beyond what classical computers can simulate or current quantum chips can run. Separate agent teams worked on each problem and shared verified ideas in a common notebook, meeting every four hours in a virtual conference to debate and compare approaches.

The biggest gain came in a fusion problem, where the agents cut the cost of a quantum calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel by 11.8 times and its memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, according to DeepMind. They also made a simulation of a light-sensitive molecule about eight times cheaper, and for Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, the cost fell 2.5 times. A widely used maths routine became more than 290 times cheaper. The work used Google’s most powerful model, Gemini 4 Carbon, and an outside checker re-ran every proof so agents could not game the tests, according to the paper.

DeepMind cautions that the simulations would still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer. The lab has open-sourced its Lean library and results, building on its 2024 work to trim quantum circuits with AlphaTensor-Quantum. The company notes that the risk of agents gaming tests is real, since in a DeepMind experiment in September, 14% of agents cheated on Lean maths problems. Earlier this month, its agents also proved Signal’s encryption code correct, and Google Quantum AI tested a key quantum effect on up to 105 qubits.

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI and quantitative imaging improve radiation pneumonitis risk prediction
stories.Summary:
A narrative review published in Frontiers in Oncology on 23 November 2026 evaluated how radiation pneumonitis risk modeling has progressed from classical dose-volume analysis to radiomics, dosiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence. The review was led by Yiyuan Wang, Yuantao Zhang, Zhichao Wang and Jun Cai from The First Affiliated Hospital of Yangtze University. It charted the historical development of quantitative modeling of pulmonary radiation tolerance. The authors described radiation pneumonitis as a critical dose-limiting toxicity in thoracic radiotherapy. They noted that grade two or higher radiation pneumonitis typically ranges between five percent and thirty percent under standard scoring frameworks.

The review covers the 1985 Lyman normal tissue complication probability formulation, which established a formal foundation for evaluating normal tissue damage under uniform radiation exposures. It covers dose-volume histogram reduction methods introduced by Kutcher and colleagues, which translated nonuniform clinical dose distributions into uniform equivalent exposures. It covers V20, the percentage of total lung volume receiving at least twenty Gray, and mean lung dose as the most widely used predictive variables in routine practice. It covers radiomics extraction of hundreds of high-dimensional descriptors from standard computed tomography scans. It covers dosiomics analysis of three-dimensional dose distributions as quantitative images.

Wang, Zhang, Wang and Cai systematically evaluated the historical progression of radiation pneumonitis risk modeling, according to the review. The articles give no further statements from the authors. The review describes conventional dose-volume metrics as exhibiting fundamental methodological limitations that restrict their ability to capture individual susceptibility. It states that traditional parameters compress complex, three-dimensional spatial dose distributions into simplified, low-dimensional cumulative volume statistics. It states that two treatment plans yielding identical V20 and mean lung dose values can exhibit dramatically different regional dose depositions.

It states that healthy lung tissue demonstrates marked functional and anatomical heterogeneity in radiosensitivity. Historic clinical investigations found that irradiating caudal lung regions produced significantly higher pneumonitis rates than irradiating cranial regions, at forty percent versus eleven percent respectively. Early attempts to combine dose-volume parameters with clinical factors such as age, performance status, smoking history and baseline pulmonary function modestly improved statistical stratification. Those regression models remained vulnerable to cohort-specific fitting and showed reduced discriminative performance under external validation.

Incorporating whole-lung CT radiomic features into baseline clinical and dosimetric models elevated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.51 to 0.68. Models using high-dose spatial masks reached an area under the curve of 0.930 compared to 0.798 for purely dosimetric models. Formulating regions of interest guided by biologically effective dose boundaries yielded an area under the curve of 0.816. Dosiomics models achieved discriminative values of 0.837 versus 0.660 for standard dose-volume histogram metrics in stereotactic body radiotherapy cohorts.

Large-scale methodological reviews synthesizing more than one hundred predictive studies involving over twenty-three thousand patients identified dosiomics as achieving the highest methodological quality scores among quantitative imaging modalities. Delta radiomics studies demonstrated concordance indices reaching 0.975 in training cohorts and 0.921 in validation groups for predicting severe acute radiation pneumonitis. Predictive architectures incorporating serial cone-beam computed tomography scans attained validation areas under the curve of 0.905. Functional avoidance protocols using ventilation imaging reduced mean V20 by 3.5 percent and restricted grade two or higher pneumonitis incidence to 14.9 percent, meeting primary prospective clinical endpoints.

Three-dimensional convolutional networks modeling full spatial dose volumes achieved an area under the curve of 0.842, outperforming traditional normal tissue complication probability and dosiomics algorithms. The review describes modern frameworks as increasingly using multimodal fusion strategies categorized into early feature-level concatenation, late decision-level aggregation and intermediate model-level collaborative learning. It describes hybrid frameworks combining convolutional neural networks with Vision Transformers. The articles do not state what happens next.

stories.Headline: York County school board approves $107,100 for education software including AI platform MagicSchool
stories.Summary:
The York County School Board heard updates on a Spanish-language program, gifted education and artificial intelligence during its Tuesday meeting in Yorktown, according to Williamsburg Yorktown Daily. The Spanish program is a grant-funded pilot that operates at Bethel Manor Elementary School and Tabb Elementary School, which were chosen because they are the division's two schools with the most military-connected families. At Bethel Manor, students in kindergarten through fifth grade learn foundational Spanish language skills and explore Spanish culture in a world language resource class. Principal Anthony Friedman said students are building communication skills, curiosity and an appreciation for different perspectives that will help them in a changing world. A Bethel Manor student, Gabe Lugo, told the board he thinks other students should have the chance to learn Spanish because it helps people connect across different backgrounds.

The pilot depends on funding from a Department of Defense Education Activity grant, and Superintendent James Carroll said the division would be open to discussing expansion if the board wants the program in more schools. Carroll also said the division would consider local funding for the program. On gifted education, the board heard that more than 100 students are in the current referral cycle, and the Gifted Education Advisory Committee is reviewing the division's gifted education plan ahead of its 2027 expiration. The board unanimously approved October financial expenditures, Tabb High School additions and renovations totaling $38,100,000, and $107,100 for education software that includes the artificial intelligence platform MagicSchool and the digital learning platform ClassLink. Chief Academic Officer Candi Skinner said the division wants students prepared to use AI appropriately and responsibly in college or the work world, and she confirmed the AI program is monitored and has safeguards for student safety.

The board also reviewed a resolution on a policy called Equal Access to Public Education and Protection of Immigration and Citizenship-Related Information, which establishes that no student can be denied access to any division activity or benefit based on perceived immigration or citizenship status. The board approved consideration of a lease agreement between the school board and the Tabb Lakes Homes Association for the association to use school property for community meetings. The board's next meeting will be its Dec. 14 work session at 7 p.m. in York Hall.

stories.Headline: Spartanburg Water CEO says AI posts mislead as utility reviews outage cause
stories.Summary:
Guy Boyle, the CEO of Spartanburg Water, spoke at a city county meeting on Monday, November 24, 2026. He explained a water outage that lasted several days and impacted residents across much of Spartanburg County. Boyle addressed AI social media posts, conversations about Duke Energy, and data center water usage. He stated that the exact cause of the power blip that led to the outage is still unknown.

The outage resulted from damage to a main 42-inch line and a secondary 24-inch line. Boyle noted that a brief power outage at the main plant may have lasted less than 10 seconds. The company is reviewing design weaknesses, valve analysis, surge relief systems, and additional levels of protection. He mentioned that the meter for NorthMark has not been ordered, installed, or connected yet.

Guy Boyle said that comments blaming Duke Energy for the damage were inaccurate and not communicated by Spartanburg Water. He described Duke Energy as a partner and stated that a post-mortem review of the infrastructure damage is underway. Boyle claimed that some residents shared misleading information to serve personal and political agendas. He stated that these conspiracy theories made the role of public service professionals more difficult.

Boyle acknowledged that social media comments regarding slow notification of the outage had merit. He explained that the current system cannot message all 276,000 customers simultaneously, so they used traditional and social media. Residents in Lyman and Woodruff had working ice machines because they are served by SJWD and WRWD. Boyle stated that these machines were left on so customers could have access to ice.

The company noted that some industry in the county was unaffected, including businesses in the Tiger River Industrial Park. Boyle cited Hurricane Helene as an example where infrastructure ran for two weeks without grid power. He stated that the systemwide boil water advisory was lifted on Sunday. The company told customers to call if they still experience air or cloudy water.

Spartanburg Water is currently working on a new notification system to better handle future systemwide events. The company and external electrical contractors are in the preliminary stages of investigating the power blip. The articles do not state when the new notification system will be fully operational. They do not provide a specific date for the completion of the infrastructure review. The final cause of the power blip remains undetermined.

stories.Headline: Washington Examiner and Independent Women publish an op-ed series arguing AI already saves lives across transport
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already saving lives on roads, rails and runways, according to an op-ed series called “Now, Not Someday” that the Washington Examiner published in partnership with Independent Women. The series features five leading experts who discuss how artificial intelligence and data centers are saving lives and helping families in every major industry. The article offers one concrete example of a quiet save, describing a car somewhere in America that will automatically brake and avoid the vehicle in front of it. The driver may never realize how close he came, and the piece presents that automatic braking as the work of artificial intelligence happening now.

The article frames the series as an argument that these benefits are arriving in the present rather than at some distant point, and it ties the technology to safety across transportation modes including roads, rails and runways. It says the experts in the series discuss how artificial intelligence and data centers are saving lives and helping families across every major industry. The piece does not give specific figures, dates or names of the experts beyond the series title and its partnership with Independent Women. It presents the automatic braking example as an illustration of how the technology operates without the driver necessarily noticing.

Responsibility for the series rests with the Washington Examiner, which published it as part of its op-ed section, and with Independent Women, which partnered on the project. The article describes the five contributors as leading experts without naming them in the available text. It attributes the claim that artificial intelligence is already saving lives to the series itself rather than to an independent assessment. The piece does not include direct statements from the experts beyond the general description of what they discuss.

The context the article gives is that this is an op-ed series rather than a news report, and it appears in the publication’s commentary section alongside other opinion pieces. The available text does not say what happens next with the series, such as when further installments will appear or what specific industries they will cover. It also does not provide the full content of the experts’ discussions, so the details of their arguments are not available here. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Conservative and populist readers rate machine-written news as more credible, study finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers Daria Kravets-Meinke and Hannah Schmid-Petri published an experimental investigation in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans on how individual differences shape reader evaluations of automated news reporting. The study analysed reactions to identical journalistic articles explicitly presented as machine-written. It found that the dispositional machine heuristic, a person's general assumption that computer systems are more impartial and accurate than human professionals, mediated between audience traits and credibility ratings. The authors conducted a secondary analysis of data from three parallel, preregistered between-subjects online experiments. The research firm IPSOS administered the experiments between December 2024 and January 2025 across Germany.

The primary framework surveyed 3,000 adult internet users, structured by demographic quota targets for age, gender, education level and geographic region of residence. Each of the three experiments featured a distinct German news brand, specifically ARD-Tagesschau, t-online or Die Welt, while keeping textual stimuli, layouts and procedural measures identical across trial groups. Participants were randomly allocated to read an identical news report attributed to a human journalist named Alex Müller, an automated system designated as NewsBot, or a collaborative human-machine author identified as Alex Müller assisted by artificial intelligence. The analysis focused strictly on the 467 participants assigned to the purely automated NewsBot condition who passed an immediate post-exposure manipulation check confirming author recall. The stimulus was a balanced article on the contentious social debate surrounding gender-neutral language in German, titled Gendering in the German language, a debate with many facets.

The article incorporated an authentic news outlet logo, a formal journalistic headline, a publication byline, an introductory lead paragraph and six substantive paragraphs presenting opposing perspectives on linguistic gendering. It concluded with an explicit author statement identifying NewsBot as a powerful artificial intelligence program operated by the respective news organization. After exposure, participants completed structured evaluation batteries before formal debriefing, where researchers disclosed that all presented news messages had been created by human researchers rather than an operational autonomous algorithm. The analytical sample of 467 participants had an average age of 49.56 years, ranging from 18 to 84 years, with men comprising 51.6 percent and 28.1 percent holding a completed university degree. Perceived message credibility was quantified through six bipolar semantic differential items scored on seven-point scales assessing whether the article was accurate, credible, trustworthy, fact-based, correct and balanced.

The credibility index achieved high internal consistency, yielding an average baseline score of 4.39 with a standard deviation of 1.42 and a McDonald's omega coefficient of .95. The dispositional machine heuristic was evaluated using six Likert items measuring general agreement on whether machine systems exhibit greater objectivity, neutrality and freedom from personal beliefs than human practitioners, generating an index mean of 3.79, a standard deviation of 1.41 and an omega of .89. Additional multi-item scales captured media trust across eight items, populist attitudes across nine items, self-reported AI literacy across eight items and fear of AI across seven items. The authors executed mediation analyses using Hayes's PROCESS macro Model 4 in SPSS, calculating unstandardized path coefficients alongside 95 percent bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples.

Regression models incorporated the specific news outlets as dummy-coded statistical covariates to partial out baseline brand credibility differences unrelated to experimental parameters. Political orientation demonstrated a statistically supported indirect effect on message credibility through machine heuristic endorsement, with an indirect coefficient of .0764, a standard error of .0399 and a 95 percent bootstrap confidence interval spanning from .0045 to .1613. Participants on the conservative or right-leaning side of the political spectrum exhibited stronger beliefs in algorithmic impartiality, which subsequently elevated their evaluations of the automated article's credibility. Participants holding stronger populist worldviews displayed heightened endorsement of the machine heuristic, yielding an indirect effect of .0443, a standard error of .0204 and a confidence interval between .0082 and .0881.

Self-assessed AI literacy registered a positive indirect effect on credibility perceptions through the dispositional machine heuristic, yielding an unstandardized coefficient of .0405, a standard error of .0205 and a confidence interval between .0013 and .0823. Emotional fear of artificial intelligence emerged as the strongest negative inhibitor within the mediation framework, producing an indirect effect of negative .2438, a standard error of .0538 and a confidence interval ranging from negative .3537 to negative .1441. General trust in traditional news media demonstrated a positive indirect association with automated message credibility via the dispositional machine heuristic, generating an indirect coefficient of .0866, a standard error of .0228 and a confidence interval spanning .0461 to .134. The authors argued that prior research frequently conflated temporary cognitive shortcuts with enduring individual predispositions, proposing instead a relatively stable, individual-level endorsement termed the dispositional machine heuristic.

They noted that individuals aligned with conservative or populist ideologies often view traditional journalists as part of an adversarial socio-political elite, making automated news systems appear comparatively neutral, detached and immune to partisan media agendas. Statistical sensitivity analysis conducted via G*Power confirmed that the sample size provided 95 percent statistical power at an alpha threshold of .05 to detect minor regression effect sizes down to an incremental f-squared of approximately .028. The articles state that the rapid technological maturation and operational adoption of generative artificial intelligence have prompted contemporary newsrooms to explore automated content production as a potential solution to structural financial constraints, escalating operational costs and the ongoing demand for scalable real-time reporting. More to follow.

stories.Headline: West Monroe and ServiceNow partner on AI-enabled CRM transformation focused on business outcomes and ROI
stories.Summary:
West Monroe and ServiceNow are working together on AI-enabled CRM transformation that concentrates on business outcomes and return on investment, according to a sponsored article by Beth Stackpole published on CIO.com on November 23, 2026. The article says organizations are redefining CRM with AI-enabled systems that deliver personalized, responsive customer experiences and create competitive advantage, but it adds that technology alone is not enough. It says simply adding AI on top of legacy CRM does not create end-to-end autonomous workflows that free sales reps from manual data entry or let customers self-serve. The article also says sales and customer experiences built around legacy CRM are hampered by silos that cause friction and spread incomplete and stale data.

Andrew Gaeckle, a senior partner and platforms and customer strategy practice lead at West Monroe, said in the article that AI changes the role of CRM, which he said is no longer just a place to store customer information or track interactions. He said it can help people decide what to do next, prepare for a conversation and handle parts of a service request. The article says organizations need a more unified approach that delivers real-time intelligence with an implementation strategy synced to desired business outcomes and ROI. Gaeckle said partners cannot stop at configuring the platform and need to understand the business processes around CRM, whether data is reliable, how work moves between teams and systems, and how to measure whether changes are paying off.

The article says ServiceNow's AI-native Autonomous CRM platform is built from the ground up to support modern CRM workflows, creating a single source of truth and action across enterprise operations. It says West Monroe combines business and industry expertise with process transformation, data integration, AI enablement and deep ServiceNow delivery experience. Gaeckle said West Monroe's industry experience helps it account for the workflows, regulations and expectations that shape what will actually work, and he said the firm keeps the solution grounded in a client's business rather than treating CRM as a generic software rollout. The article says customers across industries are reporting outcomes including 20% lower churn, 33% faster resolution and 40% faster quote processing, and it describes West Monroe as a global business and technology consulting firm that emphasizes customer value by co-creating solutions.

stories.Headline: Omega Systems acquires Framework IT to expand AI services and Midwest reach
stories.Summary:
Omega Systems, a managed service provider focused on healthcare and financial services customers, has closed its acquisition of Chicago-based Framework IT, the company announced on 2026-11-23. CEO Bill Wosilius told CRN the deal fits squarely with the company’s growth strategy. Wosilius became CEO of Reading, Pa.-based Omega Systems in September after advising private equity firms on MSP transactions. He said Framework is the second acquisition under private equity sponsor Revelstoke Capital Partners, following the purchase of Peak IT about a year ago. Omega, ranked No. 344 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500, previously rolled up four other regional MSPs under its previous sponsor.

Omega has nearly 300 IT professionals and almost 600 customers, and the deal opens a new geography for the company. Wosilius said the Chicago base gives Omega a foothold in the Midwest, a step in its westward expansion. Framework’s top executives all joined Omega, and Framework President Adam Barney will be managing director of Omega’s Midwest operations. Wosilius declined to disclose the financial terms of the deal, but said Framework was profitable. Omega launched its own AI suite a couple of weeks ago, and Wosilius said Framework will be a big contributor to that.

Wosilius said an MSP’s job is to help customers use AI safely, and that Framework has done that well. He said Omega should be enabling customers to derive the benefits out of AI in their business without material non-public information ending out in the wild. He said helping customers think through that governance model, that security model, how to do AI in a smart way, and not get themselves into trouble, is first order of business. He said Omega will integrate carefully to avoid customer losses. He said the industry has been littered with acquisitions where over-integrating or too quickly integrating without fully thinking through that causes customer churn and things like that.

Wosilius sees a fragmented market of roughly 40,000 U.S. MSPs and said Omega is always evaluating targets. He said it is a very fragmented industry with a lot of opportunity to aggregate and roll up, and size and scale matters. He said there is a huge opportunity to continue to execute on M&A. He said Omega has an integration team that is very busy right now completing the integration of Peak IT, and that Omega will take a very similar approach with Framework. He said he has not personally reached out to Framework’s customers, but that Adam Barney wanted to be the one making those calls, and that conversations are happening.

Revelstoke made a strategic investment in Omega in January of 2025, so the investment is coming up on two years old. Omega’s prior private equity sponsor, Pfingsten Partners, executed on the same strategy, and Omega rolled up four regional MSPs prior to Revelstoke. Revelstoke executed on that strategy about a year ago when Omega bought Peak IT, a regional healthcare-centric MSP in the Baltimore suburb area. Revelstoke is headquartered in downtown Denver, Colo., where Wosilius lives, and healthcare is Revelstoke’s main reason for existence. Wosilius said Revelstoke is involved in the valuation, and that Omega sourced and made the connection with Adam and Framework in this case.

Wosilius said Omega is always evaluating potential acquisitions, and that there is nothing he can tell CRN about, but that the activity is always going on. He said the connection between Omega and Framework happened before his arrival, and that he honestly could not tell CRN who approached who. He said Omega and Framework have developed a pretty strong relationship over the last few months. He said the paint is not even dry yet, so it is a little premature to be talking about any of that stuff. He said Adam Barney is going to keep doing what he has been doing as managing director of Omega’s Midwest operations.

stories.Headline: Review finds pediatric neurosurgery AI models accurate but lacking external validation
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of artificial intelligence in pediatric neurosurgery was published in the Egyptian Journal of Neurosurgery by researchers Ravi Yadav, Debasrita Banerjee and Jatin Kataria. The review found that artificial intelligence models achieve notable precision in anatomical image segmentation and diagnostic tumor classification. It also identified methodological limitations that restrict their readiness for routine operative deployment. The review analyzed published clinical investigations tracking pediatric patients eighteen years of age or younger. Those patients underwent diagnostic or surgical management for major intracranial conditions.

The review compiled twenty eligible investigations covering diagnostic imaging, procedural planning and prognostic risk modeling. The authors searched MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and IEEE Xplore from each database's inception to August 31, 2025. Initial screening retrieved 1,345 citations, reduced to 900 unique entries after removing 445 duplicates. Reviewers removed 812 records that failed inclusion standards and scrutinized 88 full-length manuscripts. The twenty included studies comprised 8 on pediatric hydrocephalus, 6 on pediatric brain neoplasms, 2 on epilepsy surgical management and 4 on traumatic brain injuries or neonatal hemorrhagic damage.

The review authors stated that the literature remains dominated by retrospective, single-institution cohorts. They said such studies seldom incorporate independent external cohort validation or formal probability calibration. The authors concluded that algorithmic tools show substantial investigative promise. They said the tools should presently function strictly as supplementary decision-support aids rather than autonomous clinical mechanisms. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines.

Klimont and colleagues evaluated a U-Net convolutional neural network that achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient approximating 0.95 on an independent test set. Grimm and collaborators used transfer learning with labels from hidden Markov random field algorithms to segment brain and cerebrospinal fluid volumes in 43 pediatric hydrocephalus patients. Sekkat and colleagues applied a VGG16 architecture across 13,600 pediatric head computed tomography images, yielding detection accuracies between 90 and 95 percent. Novak and colleagues studied 124 pediatric patients, finding naive Bayes and random forest classifiers reached accuracies between 84 and 85 percent for posterior fossa neoplasms. Zhang and colleagues studied 263 pediatric patients, and sequential machine learning classifiers achieved a micro-averaged F1 score of 88 percent in identifying medulloblastoma molecular subgroups.

Cohen and colleagues found machine learning classifiers applied to electronic health record narratives yielded F-measures from 0.71 to 0.82 when identifying pediatric epilepsy surgery candidates. Wissel and colleagues screened 4,858 pediatric patients with epilepsy and randomized 284 surgical candidates two-to-one between automated alerts and standard care. Referral rates were 9.8 percent in the intervention arm compared to 3.1 percent in standard care, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.21. Miyagawa and colleagues developed supervised models for children younger than two years with mild traumatic brain injury, achieving predictive accuracy of approximately 95 percent.

Hale and colleagues trained algorithms on 1,036 pediatric patients in the Hydrocephalus Clinical Research Network database, finding artificial neural networks reached an area under the curve of 0.71, specificity above 90 percent and sensitivity of approximately 68 percent in an independent cohort of 155 patients. Quon and colleagues demonstrated that deep learning volumetry exceeded traditional segmentation algorithms in accuracy and computational speed for obstructive hydrocephalus. Cariola and associates used data from the BraTS-PEDs 2024 challenge to verify delineation of tumor subregions including whole tumor, enhancing margins and core components. Tampu and colleagues tested vision transformer architectures incorporating patient age fusion for classification across diverse pediatric brain tumors.

Luo and Lu developed radiomics-based nomograms showing that integrating clinical markers with imaging signatures improved two-year recurrence and survival stratification in medulloblastoma. Saez-Alegre and colleagues formulated machine learning models to guide timing for converting temporary Ommaya reservoirs into permanent cerebrospinal fluid shunts in premature infants with post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Shahrestani and colleagues examined registry records from 33,248 pediatric hydrocephalus patients to model post-placement shunt complications. Tunthanathip and Oearsakul trained machine learning architectures to map non-linear associations governing functional outcomes following pediatric traumatic brain injury.

The review authors emphasized that published reports frequently omitted granular discriminative metrics and comprehensive model performance characteristics. The articles do not state what regulatory or clinical steps follow from the review. The articles do not state whether further validation studies are planned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence could help patients audit medical bills and organize insurance disputes
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Rebellion Research on November 23, 2026, describes how artificial intelligence could change the way Americans challenge hospital bills, navigate insurance claims and protect themselves from financial ruin after serious accidents, and it presents this as a possibility rather than a proven result. It says machine learning, document intelligence and generative AI are creating new opportunities to identify questionable medical charges, interpret insurance decisions and help patients negotiate financial obligations, work that once required hours of administrative effort. The article offers a hypothetical example of a patient seriously injured in an automobile accident, with an emergency department charge of $18,000, separate imaging and orthopedic claims, recurring physical therapy costs and an insurer that approves some charges, adjusts others and denies several claims. It says advanced systems could potentially reconstruct the entire financial history of an injury by matching treatments against charges, insurance payments and outstanding obligations. The article says automated billing audits could examine medical statements, identify duplicate-looking charges, compare explanations of benefits and highlight discrepancies, such as a $2,400 charge appearing on two statements or an insurer payment not credited to the patient's account.

It says natural language processing could translate billing terminology, but it cautions that detecting an anomaly is not the same as proving an error, because similar charges may be legitimate and billing codes often need specialist interpretation. On insurance disputes, it says AI could compare policy language, denial notices and provider statements, help organize supporting documents and track appeal deadlines, while noting that AI cannot independently establish that an insurer violated its contract. It adds that AI-assisted recordkeeping could consolidate treatment histories, expenses, insurance correspondence and documented income losses, but that legal professionals must still evaluate liability, damages and the applicable law. The article does not name any developer, company or patient behind these tools, and it attributes no statements to any individual, so no one is quoted or paraphrased as responsible for a specific system. Instead it frames the technology's promise in general terms, saying the objective should be helping patients determine what they actually owe, what assistance may be available and what they can realistically afford, rather than helping hospitals collect balances more efficiently.

It warns that medical billing records contain exceptionally sensitive information such as diagnoses, treatment histories and insurance identifiers, and that patients should know whether their data is retained, shared or used for model training. It also notes that independent consumer AI applications do not automatically receive the same regulatory treatment as healthcare providers, and that inaccurate AI explanations could cause substantial financial harm without verifiable calculations and human oversight. The article presents the context as an information imbalance in American healthcare, with sophisticated billing institutions facing individual patients who often lack the expertise to challenge them, and it says consumer AI tools vary widely in capability. It states that rigorous evidence is still needed to establish how much these systems improve financial outcomes, and that their future will depend on whether they deliver measurable reductions in administrative costs, billing mistakes and unnecessary financial hardship. It does not say what happens next beyond that, and it describes no specific launch, rollout or regulatory step.

stories.Headline: UT San Antonio recruits AI and structural biology researcher K. Ian White for cancer work
stories.Summary:
UT Health San Antonio announced on Monday, November 23, 2026, that it has recruited K. Ian White, a Stanford-trained structural biologist whose work combines structural biology, cancer biology and artificial intelligence, the university said. White joined UT San Antonio on September 1 as an assistant professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Structural Biology and the Department of Pharmacology in the Joe R. and Teresa Lozano Long School of Medicine. His recruitment is supported by a $2 million Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas Recruitment of First-Time, Tenure-Track Faculty Members Award, which was approved on August 19, 2026. The award was part of more than $35 million in CPRIT funding overall during that round, and UT San Antonio's Health Science Center secured a total of $6 million in CPRIT recruitment awards in the same round, according to the release. Since 2010, CPRIT has awarded UT San Antonio nearly $192 million.

A Texas native, White comes to the Long School of Medicine after conducting postdoctoral research at Stanford University in the laboratory of Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator Axel Brunger, and his research there was supported by a fellowship from the Helen Whitney Foundation. White is launching a research program that connects structural biology, neuroscience, immunology and cancer biology, and working under the mentorship of Reuben S. Harris, professor and chair of the Department of Biochemistry and Structural Biology, he will investigate how changes in the electrical potential of cancer-cell membranes alter the structure and behavior of membrane proteins involved in cell signaling. The university said the work could reveal previously unrecognized vulnerabilities in cancer cells and help identify potential targets for future therapeutic development. White's CPRIT-supported research will focus in part on new strategies to target colorectal cancer, using AI-based technologies to design new therapeutics. White said he was impressed by both the existing research programs and the potential for growth in the basic sciences when he visited the campus, and he described resources such as the Structural Biology Core and the Center for Innovative Drug Discovery as world-class facilities that will be tremendous resources for his lab.

Jennifer Sharpe Potter, senior executive vice president for research and innovation at UT San Antonio, said the recruitment strengthens the university's research community and that the university is grateful to CPRIT for its continued investment in recruiting exceptional investigators to Texas and to UT San Antonio. Potter said White's expertise in artificial intelligence, structural biology and cancer research adds valuable depth to the research community and strengthens the ability to pursue collaborative and interdisciplinary discovery, and that his recruitment also provides opportunities to develop the next generation of cancer researchers and advance research that can ultimately translate into improved care and outcomes for patients across South Texas and beyond. CPRIT was established in 2009, and its awards programs are designed to attract researchers to Texas institutions and build scientific infrastructure for cancer research and innovation statewide, according to the release. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch of White's research program.

stories.Headline: Researchers link AI adoption to higher technostress and lower well-being for university managers in Guangzhou
stories.Summary:
Chunlong Zeng and Suzana Raja Kasim conducted a study on artificial intelligence adoption in higher education management. They published their original research in Frontiers in Psychology on November 23, 2026. The researchers examined how AI tools relate to occupational well-being among university managers. This study focused specifically on the geographical context of universities located in Guangzhou, China. The authors used a cross-sectional questionnaire dataset containing 320 complete records for their analysis.

The study used partial least squares structural equation modeling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples to analyze the data. It examined AI adoption, which involves using tools for planning, reporting, policy drafting, resource allocation, and stakeholder communication. The researchers measured technostress, which is the stress felt when coping with demands posed by technology. They also measured perceived organizational support and occupational well-being, defined as sustained positive functioning in the work environment. The model explained 10.69% of well-being variance and 23.04% of technostress variance.

The authors stated that AI adoption was positively associated with technostress in their findings. They found that technostress was negatively associated with the occupational well-being of the managers. The researchers noted that perceived organizational support was positively associated with well-being. They also found that this support was associated with a weaker negative association between technostress and well-being. The authors concluded that their results support a statistical stress pathway.

The study found that neither the direct AI adoption-well-being association nor the conditional total association was statistically significant. The negative indirect association through technostress was significant at the mean level of organizational support. The researchers noted that AI tools may alter job demands, skill requirements, and accountability structures. These changes can impact staff well-being through learning burdens, monitoring pressure, and ambiguity about responsibility. The study suggests that the human experience of AI depends on implementation choices.

The articles state that universities are increasingly introducing AI tools into administrative and managerial work. These tools include chatbots, document drafting tools, predictive analytics for enrollment and retention, and algorithmic workflow triage. The authors used the Job Demands-Resources model and technostress scholarship as the theoretical foundation. They noted that most AI literature in higher education focuses on teaching and learning. This leaves the occupational experiences of administrative professionals less extensively examined.

The researchers stated that their cross-sectional associations do not establish causal mechanisms. They identified training, workload redesign, and organizational support as priorities for future evaluation. The study does not establish a direct well-being benefit from the adoption of AI. The authors suggest that AI adoption should be a governance and human-resource issue. The articles leave open how specific implementation practices affect the identified associations.

stories.Headline: Guterres tells Security Council killer robots must have no place in our future
stories.Summary:
The Security Council met on Tuesday to weigh how artificial intelligence and drones are reshaping warfare, with UN chief António Guterres telling ambassadors that killer robots must have no place in our future. The session examined how new technologies now spread globally within months rather than decades, and how disinformation is fuelling record levels of conflict. The council heard that artificial intelligence is already assisting in targeting and that drones are changing the way wars are fought. The meeting was held at UN headquarters and was carried live on UNWebTV. Guterres told council members they have a special duty to ensure that competition over emerging technologies does not destabilise international peace and security.

Last week in Geneva, a push by around 100 countries to negotiate a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons fell short. The Secretary-General's July review of UN peace operations made closing the technology gap a priority. A new informal council expert group on technology, peace and security met for the first time on 18 November, and in 2021 the council recognised technology as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. The Secretary-General is responsible for the July review of UN peace operations, which made closing the technology gap a priority, and he addressed the council directly on the duty of members. The council itself set up the informal expert group on technology, peace and security, which held its first meeting on 18 November.

The council also recognised technology in 2021 as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. Around 100 countries pushed in Geneva last week for a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons, but that effort fell short. The meeting comes as the UN marks more than eighty years since its founding in 1945, when computers, the internet and satellites were the stuff of science fiction. The articles do not say what the council will decide or when it will next take up the issue. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Structured design prompts lead gpt-4.1 to explore more diverse architectural attributes
stories.Summary:
A computational study published in Design Science on 23 November 2026 found that guiding large language models through structured design operations increased the diversity of architectural attributes they explored. The researchers compared four prompting methods across three design problems of escalating complexity. They used OpenAI's gpt-4.1 model through an automated Python script. Each of the four prompts was run 100 times per scenario, producing 4,000 attribute statements and 400 complete design alternatives. The study was conducted by researchers examining computer-assisted conceptual design.

The framework moved step by step from contextual definition to functional requirements, candidate physical attributes and holistic synthesis. Christopher Alexander's pattern language, published in 1977, supplied a corpus of 253 interconnected spatial relationships and functional resolutions. Context was defined as a complete-sentence description of background conditions and user needs, function as an intentional verb-object pairing and attribute as a concrete noun phrase. Prompt C required the model to explore three contexts, derive three functions for each and determine three attributes for each function, generating 27 hierarchical attributes from which the ten most relevant were selected. Prompt D coupled that tree-of-thought operation with the full pattern language dataset.

Prompt A was a standard chain-of-thought baseline relying on the model's internal parameters and asking for ten essential attributes before synthesis. Prompt B added Alexander's full 253-pattern corpus as a retrieval-augmented input. The generation temperature was set strictly to 0 to eliminate stochastic randomness. The three briefs covered an entrance threshold described as somewhat dark and gloomy, a living room for four family members needing space for studying, relaxation, play and remote work, and a university campus facility lacking communal spaces. The 4,000 attribute phrases were converted into 384-dimensional semantic embeddings using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vector model.

Prompts C and D reached the highest convex hull volumes and determinantal point process diversity scores, with values reaching 128.46 in the campus facility tests against 85.13 for Prompt A and 76.35 for Prompt B. Prompt A had the highest mean pairwise distance, reaching 0.738 in the porch scenario and 0.728 in the living room brief, but minimum pairwise distances falling to 0.005 or 0.010. Prompts C and D produced minimum pairwise distances regularly five to ten times greater, scoring 0.074 and 0.079. Prompt B generated the lowest mean pairwise distance values across all three problems, measuring 0.588 for the front porch, 0.595 for the living room and 0.604 for the campus facility. Eight university professors and researchers, four in architecture and design education and four in mechanical and information engineering, conducted blinded consensual assessments on a five-point Likert scale. They scored problem validity, conceptual novelty and physical feasibility.

Inter-rater reliability was 0.72 for front porch feasibility and 0.70 for living room validity, but dropped to negative 0.52 for front porch validity. Prompt B secured the most first-place selections for validity and feasibility in the porch brief, dominated all three dimensions in the living room brief and took the top novelty ranking in the campus facility. The judges, unaware the pattern language had been injected, remarked on human familiarity, emotional calmness and structural balance, including graded transitions between public and private realms. The investigators grounded their framework in design engineering theory, adapting operational mechanics from general design theory and concept-knowledge theory. In formal design engineering, an upstream design operation is a sequence of cognitive transformations applied to abstract problem descriptions to generate concrete physical parameters.

The model was instructed to branch outward systematically rather than generate an end-stage concept in a single speculative leap. Prompt B's semantic centroid showed the greatest Euclidean distance from Prompt A, drifting by 0.351 in the porch task and 0.389 in the living room task. The authors suggest the cohesive external corpus compressed the overall exploration boundary, locking the model into a restricted architectural vocabulary. Prompt D, combining the tree-of-thought operation with the pattern language, failed to consistently achieve the highest marks from human judges, though it outperformed Prompt C across all living room dimensions and surpassed Prompt B in campus facility validity. The authors hypothesize that this ceiling reflects friction between the rigid, deterministic decomposition inherited from engineering methodologies and the non-modular flexibility required by architecture.

The articles do not state what further experiments or applications are planned. The articles do not report whether the framework will be released or adopted in practice. The articles do not give the full names of the researchers or their institutions. The articles do not state how the expert panel's divergent validity ratings were resolved beyond first-place ranking votes.

Articles.Title: Structured Design Operations Expand Architectural Attribute Diversity in Artificial Intelligence Models

stories.Headline: Eugene library assistant Elly Hutchinson designs a workshop that helps about 30 attendees opt out of AI on their devices
stories.Summary:
The Eugene Public Library hosted a free public workshop titled “AI-nxiety: an Opt-Out Workshop” on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, at its downtown branch. About 30 attendees gathered at the library to gain information about how to opt out of AI on their devices. The event was created and designed by the library and was based on giving people agency in how they use AI. Many of the attendees were older adults, and the event was the library’s first AI workshop. Library assistant Elly Hutchinson came up with the idea and designed the packets that accompanied the workshop.

The hourlong event was a mostly self-guided hands-on workshop rather than a presentation-style format. Attendees were given a choice of two packets supplied by the library, one for Apple users and one for Android users, which divided them into two table groups. The packets guided people on how they could opt out of AI with Siri, in their preferred email system, their device’s operating system, on their preferred browser and on various social media apps. Hutchinson said the packets carry a “heavy disclaimer” that they aren’t comprehensive and that both AI and settings can change. Four library staff and volunteers were there to help attendees who ran into speed bumps along the way.

Marsha Sutherland, adult services supervisor at the library’s downtown branch, said the library was “not taking a stance on the pros and cons (of AI).” She said the event was really about giving people agency and reminding them that they can opt out of certain AI features on their devices. Sutherland said she was not surprised by the demographic or the large turnout for the library’s first AI workshop. Hutchinson said patrons had been asking a lot of questions about Google’s AI Overviews, the summaries that now appear at the top of search results. Hutchinson said the openness of the format was intentional, citing that various folks might have different needs regarding AI on their devices, and she hopes to hold the workshop again.

Janel Erickson, 67, and her husband, Dave Reuter, 70, attended because they were curious about AI and said they use the AI summaries in search results but otherwise not at all. They said they have many friends who use AI, including their two adult sons and their wives, who all use AI at work. They said they’d like to see more events like this and suggested the library tell people in the event description to update their operating systems beforehand and that the workshop is hands-on rather than a formal presentation. William Herbert, 80, and his wife, Anna Herbert, 74, attended because they see AI becoming more present in their lives, and Anna said she feels overwhelmed by all the information.

The Herberts said they’d come back for another event but that the event didn’t help them achieve what they wanted, though they thought it was “good,” and Anna said AI is “a waste of my time.” Sutherland said that if folks weren’t able to make the event on Nov. 19, the library holds a tech help drop-in session roughly twice a month. She said the event was more of an AI baseline on how to turn it off, and drop-in tech help is just a little broader. The workshop was open to the public and free, and thirty people showed up.

Hutchinson said the hourlong event wasn’t a presentation-style workshop but more of a chance for folks to ask questions while following along via a packet that the library designed. The packets divided content into either Android or Apple. Hutchinson hopes to hold the workshop again. Erickson and Reuter said they’d like to see more events like this.

The Herberts said they’d come back for another event. Sutherland said the library holds a tech help drop-in session roughly twice a month for folks who weren’t able to make the event on Nov. 19. The articles do not say whether another AI workshop has been scheduled. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Guterres urges UN members to start talks on a multilateral AI risk management framework
stories.Summary:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Monday called on Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral framework for managing the risks of artificial intelligence, speaking to reporters at the close of the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados, which the UN co-hosted with Barbados. Guterres, who leaves office at the end of December, said protections against AI risks remain fragmented and that governments are too often playing catch-up, and he warned that the technology is driving what he called the biggest transfer of power in the history of humankind. He issued what he described as a call from Bridgetown for Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework, saying a common foundation for AI safety is needed. He said the framework would include shared safety measures, common approaches to testing, clear safeguards and standards, basic transparency requirements, independent evaluation and oversight of advanced AI models, and support so that every country can put them into practice. Guterres said some leading AI developers are themselves sounding the alarm about increasingly powerful systems, and that recent technological outages and cyberattacks have exposed the vulnerabilities of digital systems the world depends on, with AI amplifying the threats as systems behave in ways even their developers did not always anticipate.

He said the promise of AI is real, from strengthening health systems to accelerating scientific discovery, but that the risks of unchecked digital technology are growing just as fast, describing the dangers as technology without accountability, capability without safeguards and power without responsibility. In a fireside conversation with Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley, he said power is moving from States and governing institutions to a small number of companies and persons, a shift for which institutions created after the Second World War, including the UN, are today not adequately equipped, and he called for deep reform of global governance while insisting the UN has the legitimacy to lead. He noted that at the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July, 111 of the participating countries had never taken part in any discussion on AI, and he warned that the capacity to weaponise AI is concentrated in two countries and a limited number of companies, reiterating his support for banning autonomous weapons and calling the idea that a machine can choose who and where to kill absolutely unacceptable. Mottley said small States often do not have the opportunity to share their perspective on the rules that affect them, and asked whether a frontier AI lab should have to pay if one of its AI agents hacked a bank in Barbados and whether her Government should have a kill switch to cut off access to its models in an emergency, she answered yes, saying it has to be a condition of sale that the buyer is capable of saying no more. She also warned that the horse has already bolted from the stables and that only governments willing to regulate and legislate can rein in the concentration of power.

In a video message, French President Emmanuel Macron said the Paris Call for AI Security had been signed by 18 Heads of State and government and 11 AI leaders, and argued that agreeing to its principles should be a condition for access to markets, while Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith said in some ways AI was moving faster than the speed of safety but that AI diffusion, especially in the global South, needed to speed up. Asked what people should take away from the summit, Guterres said the evolution of AI models cannot go faster than the capacity to control their safety, and that AI must help reduce, not increase, the inequalities growing in today's world, adding that the ability of countries to manage AI risks remains deeply unequal and that solutions must be as borderless as the risks. To narrow that gap he has proposed a Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building, and he said the summit could help strengthen every country's capacity to test whether AI systems work safely in local contexts. He pointed to a new thematic brief from the UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, released on Sunday, which highlights the value of countries testing AI systems in their own languages, and panel member Vukosi Marivate of the University of Pretoria said AI models still perform far worse and can be less safe across a wide range of tongues, from African languages to Caribbean creoles, though over 1,000 of them already have the foundations needed to close that gap. Guterres said artificial intelligence should be shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity.

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI matches expert pathologists in cancer diagnosis across multiple malignancies
stories.Summary:
Researchers Umang K. Agrawal, Sakshi Jaiswal, and Deepanshu Singh published a comprehensive scientific review in Surgical and Experimental Pathology, reported on November 23, 2026. The review found that artificial intelligence algorithms are demonstrating diagnostic accuracy comparable to expert pathologists across diverse malignancies. These malignancies include breast, prostate, colorectal, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Advances in computational pathology and deep learning are redefining the interface between surgical oncologists and pathologists. The review describes how routine digitized tissue slides are converted into diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive datasets.

The review covers the transition from conventional microscopy of physical glass slides to digital whole-slide imaging systems. Modern whole-slide scanners digitize conventional glass slides at extremely high resolutions, preserving sub-cellular details comparable to high-magnification optical microscopes. Deep convolutional neural networks analyze these massive image datasets using layered hierarchical computational structures. Early network layers typically detect elementary morphological features, including tissue borders, cellular edges, and simple textures. Deeper neural layers progressively synthesize these basic inputs into complex pathological structures, capturing glandular architecture, nuclear atypia, and stromal interactions.

The review states that multi-institutional clinical validations, such as landmark investigations by Campanella and colleagues, showed deep learning models can achieve near-expert diagnostic sensitivity. Those models identified prostate carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and metastatic breast cancer cells within complex whole-slide preparations. In breast cancer, deep learning models automated scoring of tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic figures defined by the Nottingham Histologic Score. In prostate oncology, convolutional algorithms evaluated glandular patterns across entire biopsy cores, matching the grading fidelity of experienced uropathologists. In benchmark studies such as the CAMELYON challenge, automated models matched expert pathologists in identifying nodal breast cancer metastases.

The review reports that computational platforms can accurately infer microsatellite instability in colorectal and gastric cancers directly from standard tissue sections. In non-small cell lung cancer, neural networks have accurately predicted epidermal growth factor receptor mutations from routine histology. In colorectal cancer, algorithms successfully identified KRAS and BRAF mutational signatures. In breast and gastric malignancies, deep learning platforms can evaluate human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 status from morphological patterns alone.

Deep learning algorithms trained on whole-slide images rapidly scan extensive tissue perimeters, identifying invasive carcinoma and ductal carcinoma in situ at margins in breast, head and neck, and gastrointestinal operations. The review states that histopathological evaluation has long functioned as the indispensable cornerstone of clinical cancer management. Traditional workflows have historically depended on pathologists manually scanning glass slides to identify atypical tissue structures, count mitotic events, and estimate margin clearances. Modern oncological care increasingly demands individualized precision, placing substantial strain on pathology laboratories confronted with escalating caseloads, diagnostic complexity, and documented observer variability.

Traditional machine learning frameworks required labor-intensive manual feature engineering to isolate variables like nuclear pleomorphism and glandular morphology. Modern deep learning architectures bypass manual feature extraction entirely, learning complex diagnostic representations directly from raw digital image pixels. The review states that significant methodological, regulatory, and ethical hurdles must be resolved before artificial intelligence can achieve ubiquitous integration within routine clinical environments. Training robust deep learning algorithms requires diverse, multi-institutional histological datasets.

Models trained on homogenous institutional archives frequently experience performance degradation when exposed to external variations in tissue fixation, staining intensity, or optical scanner specifications. The review describes the black-box nature of deep neural networks as posing serious transparency challenges for surgical and pathological teams requiring clear morphological reasoning. Addressing these barriers necessitates explainable AI frameworks. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Guelph officials use AI to find city efficiencies and improve services
stories.Summary:
City officials in Guelph are turning to artificial intelligence to find efficiencies, according to a presentation made at a Guelph Chamber of Commerce breakfast event on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Chief Administrative Officer Tara Baker spoke at the event at the Victoria Park East Golf Club, where about 100 local business people attended along with several city staff and councillors. Baker was joined by deputy CAOs Colleen Clack-Bush, Terry Gayman and Stephen O'Brien, who each presented on the areas of city governance they oversee. The CAO's breakfast took the place of the chamber's annual municipal budget event because the 2027 budget update has not yet been presented due to last month's city election. According to the articles, the city is using AI to identify mis-sorted residential waste as it is collected by trucks, to track whether buses are on schedule and potentially to assess the grip of municipal equipment on wintry roads.

AI is also being used to assess infrastructure risks, model the repercussions of failures and plan how to lessen the impact or reduce the risk. Baker said the city is measuring its performance and how it does business, where it invests money, and is using those performance metrics to drive business decisions. O'Brien said part of the work includes breaking down departmental silos and removing redundant pages or information on the city's website, which he described as dated old legacy systems with highly siloed pockets of data and very low integration across platforms. Baker said the city is trying to improve those abilities through its focus on data management and business intelligence.

Clack-Bush said the city is focused on being efficient, finding ways to eliminate bureaucracy if it can and delivering services in a customer friendly way, noting the city is always looking at how technology can improve customer service. Gayman said the number one thing the city hears about is the housing need, along with transit, active transportation and the ability to provide options for people to get to work reliably. O'Brien said AI searches return a deeper analysis of results than a traditional Google search, making it all the more important that official city details are presented at the top of results pages, and that the city's data governance work matters because the business community needs confidence that the information it uses is accurate, timely and understood. Budget details are expected to be released in the new year, according to the articles.
