stories.Headline: Teradyne grows robotics revenue 28% as AI automation demand rises
stories.Summary:
Teradyne is benefiting from growing adoption of artificial intelligence-powered robotics, expanding automation demand and increasing investments in AI data center infrastructure, according to an article published by Zacks Investment Research and carried by Yahoo Finance on November 23, 2026. The article was written by Nilanshi Mukherjee and appeared at 10:04 AM CST. Teradyne's expanding robotics portfolio strengthens its competitive position against KLA and Cohu in the AI space, the article states. Growing investments in physical AI and robot-assisted assembly and testing are creating significant opportunities for the company's Robotics business, according to the article. The article asks whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu.

In the third quarter of 2026, Teradyne's Robotics revenues increased 28% year over year to $96 million, marking its highest third-quarter revenues on record, the article states. The segment also turned a profit during the quarter, reflecting improving demand and operational performance. Electronics and semiconductor manufacturing has emerged as Robotics' largest vertical, supported by growing automation needs in complex server and rack assembly processes. Teradyne's Universal Robots Gen 7 collaborative robot platform and PolyScope X software are strengthening its competitive position, and these solutions are designed to support physical AI applications and improve automation flexibility across electronics assembly operations. The company is expanding its physical AI ecosystem through partnerships with NVIDIA, Analog Devices, Scale AI, Generalist, Bright Machines and Sereact, collaborations expected to accelerate adoption of intelligent robotics solutions across industrial applications.

Teradyne expects continued Robotics revenue growth in the fourth quarter of 2026, according to the article. Broader automation deployments by a major customer are expected to support growth in 2027, while emerging physical AI applications could create additional opportunities in 2028 and beyond. The article states that Teradyne's expanding AI-powered robotics portfolio, strategic partnerships and growing automation demand strengthen its long-term growth prospects, positioning it favorably against competitors like KLA and Cohu. Teradyne currently carries a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), the article states. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2026 earnings is pegged at $9.41 per share, which has increased 3.29% over the past 30 days and suggests 137.63% year-over-year growth.

KLA is benefiting from growing demand for AI through its leadership in process control and ability to address growth markets in wafer fab equipment, including high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging, the article states. Cohu's exposure to AI infrastructure is expanding through adoption of its Eclipse handler and active thermal-control technology for high-power processors, according to the article. Cohu's management raised the estimated annual high-performance computing opportunity pipeline by 18% sequentially to approximately $1 billion in the third quarter of 2026, including about $230 million in qualified opportunities, $440 million in qualification and $330 million in engagement. Cohu also raised its fiscal 2026 high-performance computing revenue outlook to approximately $120 million from $100-$110 million, the article states. Eclipse supports multiple processor generations, helping customers manage capital investment and accelerate production ramps.

Teradyne shares have gained 5.8% year to date, outperforming the Zacks Computer & Technology sector's 6% decline and the Zacks Electronics - Miscellaneous Products decrease of 5.7%, according to the article. Teradyne stock is trading at a premium with a forward 12-month Price/Sales of 5.06X compared with the Computer & Technology sector's 4.27X, and Teradyne has a Value Score of D. The article states that Teradyne is facing stiff competition from KLA and Cohu, and that both companies are expanding their footprint in the AI space. The article originally published on Zacks Investment Research. The article carries a trading disclosure linking to Coinbase and states that Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser.

The article leaves open whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu in AI, posing the question in its headline without answering it. It gives no date for when Teradyne might outpace its competitors or what measure would settle the comparison. It does not state the size of KLA's or Cohu's AI-related revenues for comparison with Teradyne's $96 million in third-quarter Robotics revenues. It gives no figures for Teradyne's total company results, only the Robotics segment. It does not say what the major customer's broader automation deployments in 2027 involve or name that customer.

stories.Headline: Organized crime groups steal high value AI hardware during transport to data centers
stories.Summary:
Transnational organized criminal gangs have stolen high value AI hardware during transport to data centers. These thefts have occurred in recent weeks and throughout the past year. The criminals include cartels that operate with their own finance and human resources departments. They target shipments moving across the country on roads leading to data center facilities. Some of these thefts have reached values in the tens of millions of dollars.

The thefts involve Blackwell chips on pallets worth between 15 and 20 million dollars. Some truckloads moving across the country now carry a total value of 100 million dollars. Stolen items also include generators, transformers, bus bars, and both high and low voltage switchgear. Criminals use signal jammers, fake paperwork, and resprayed trucks with changed license plates and DOT numbers. Some gangs buy legitimate trucking companies to gain traction on load boards before stealing cargo.

David Warrick is the executive vice president of enterprise at the risk detection company Overhaul. He stated that the economics of these thefts have become crazy from a criminal perspective. Warrick said that chips are easier to move than narcotics because they are legal goods. He noted that some large thefts remain private because there is a level of embarrassment. He advised shippers to treat their high value inventory as if it were cash.

Hyperscalers and neo cloud providers are affected because stolen components are often part of just-in-time builds. These victims face direct monetary impacts because there is no automatic way to replace scarce components. The thieves may ship the stolen hardware to destinations such as Russia, Iran, and China. Some shippers now use smaller transit vans or box trucks to avoid building huge truckloads. This change in behavior allows thieves to steal 15 million dollar pallets in Sprinter vans.

The AI infrastructure boom has created a level of spending that exceeds previous freight security experiences. Global spending on this infrastructure now runs at about double the cost of the U.S. interstate highway system. A secondary market for components has emerged due to scarcity during the current year. The vulnerability exists on the roads leading to data centers rather than the facilities themselves. Overhaul tracks cargo using a data set that adds 200 million data points every month.

Overhaul continues to work with local law enforcement agencies around the world to recover stolen loads. Warrick expects the trend of theft to continue as more money flows into the build-out. He believes more work is needed regarding legislation to create punishments that stick for offenders. The articles do not state if any specific criminal gangs have been identified or arrested. They leave open whether new legislation will be passed to deter these organized crime groups.

Paul Vacquier, CEO of the plumbing company Beagle Services, which recently added the L7 to its product offering, said in a statement that the move helps shift the focus from responding to water damage after a loss occurs to identifying issues earlier and potentially reducing the impact. The article does not say what the device requires of a household beyond learning its water-use patterns. The article does not say what happens next for the L7 beyond the company's announcement, and it gives no timeline for pricing or availability. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mercedes-Benz deploys Arena Physica AI agents to speed electrical repairs at its Alabama plant
stories.Summary:
Mercedes-Benz and Arena Physica announced on Nov. 23, 2026, a global agreement to deploy Arena's Atlas platform, which applies AI agents that reason about complex hardware to speed up electrical and electronic repair on the production line, according to the press release issued by Arena Physica. The release said deployment starts at the Tuscaloosa plant in Alabama for the new GLE and GLS, with pilot deployment planned at additional Mercedes-Benz plants. According to the release, Atlas is integrated as an add-on into Mercedes-Benz's existing electrical and electronic rework assistance system and runs a closed-loop optimization that aims to direct technicians to the most likely root cause, refine the repair plan as new measurements come in, and capture causes and repair outcomes. The release said that in the initial testing phase Atlas enabled technicians to diagnose and repair 20 to 30 percent faster, across both new and experienced skill levels.

The release said the expected results are higher first-time-fix rates, reduced rework and disassembly costs, faster onboarding of new technicians, and improved production quality through quicker root cause detection and prevention of repeat electrical and electronic issues. According to the release, Atlas learns to understand hardware the way an experienced engineer does by combining deterministic and probabilistic reasoning, and it is underpinned by the Metagraph, a digital representation of pins, connectors and wires in the vehicle and the mapping of their functional importance and physical location. The release described the Metagraph as a flexible foundation that grows richer as new data comes in and extends to new systems and applications over time. The release said Mercedes-Benz plans to bring Atlas's diagnostic intelligence directly onto global production lines, complementing its existing engineering and quality systems.

Jason Hoff, CEO of Mercedes-Benz North America, said in the release that as the company's vehicles grow more sophisticated, so does the expertise required from technicians on its lines, and that Atlas puts additional diagnostic intelligence into the hands of its teams so they can repair complex electrical systems with greater speed and precision. He said this aligns with the company's global AI strategy of using AI wherever it empowers team members and benefits customers, according to the release. Pratap Ranade, Co-Founder and CEO of Arena Physica, said in the release that one challenge in advanced manufacturing is encoding decades of engineering expertise and scaling it across an organization to support all team members, and that Atlas helps capture deep diagnostic knowledge that takes engineers years to build and makes it available to every technician on the line. He said working with Mercedes-Benz, which he described as a company that has defined the industry standard for automotive quality, shows what is possible when AI is deployed to help skilled people be even better at what they do, according to the release.

The release said the partnership follows a human-centered approach to AI in production at Mercedes-Benz, in which AI provides additional support to experts performing diagnostic tasks as electrical complexity in modern vehicles increases. According to the release, Arena Physica, which calls itself the electromagnetic superintelligence company, was founded in 2019 and is based in New York City, and its Atlas platform is described as the agentic harness for hardware engineering that applies physics-informed AI to verify, debug and optimize complex hardware across its lifecycle. The release said the company works with hardware companies including AMD, Anduril, Bausch + Lomb and Mercedes-Benz. The release did not say when the pilot deployment at additional plants would begin or which plants would be involved.

stories.Headline: Arrive AI sells $100,000 of stock to strategic investor at 50% premium
stories.Summary:
Arrive AI Inc., a company listed on Nasdaq under the ticker ARAI, announced on November 23, 2026, that a strategic investor had completed an initial purchase of $100,000 of its common stock at a 50% premium to the stock's closing price on November 20, 2026. The investor also received one-to-one warrant coverage, exercisable for cash at a 75% premium to that same November 20 closing price. The investor has the ability to purchase up to $400,000 in additional common stock, which could raise its aggregate direct equity investment to $500,000. Any future stock purchases would be priced at a 50% premium to the market price at the time of the applicable transaction.

The arrangement contemplates one-to-one cash warrant coverage for any investor share purchase, and the investor holds an initial tranche of warrants that have not yet been exercised. If all contemplated additional share purchases and cash warrant exercises occur, Arrive AI could receive greater than $1 million in aggregate gross proceeds, though future purchases, warrant issuances and exercises are not assured. The new investment follows Arrive AI's recent exchange of debt into preferred equity, which the company said eliminated its debt and strengthened its balance sheet as it pursues additional growth capital. Additional details of the transaction are set out in the company's Current Report on Form 8-K, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission concurrently with the announcement.

Piyush Phadke, Chief Financial Officer of Arrive AI, said completing the initial investment at a 50% premium brings fresh capital into the company on terms reflecting its disciplined approach to issuing shares. He said the company continues to believe there is substantial value to unlock at Arrive AI and that the investment reflects confidence in that opportunity. He also said the premium pricing reinforces the company's commitment to securing capital on terms that support its shareholders as it executes its growth strategy. The release describes Arrive AI as a physical AI and autonomous logistics infrastructure company building a network of intelligent delivery endpoints.

The release states that the forward-looking statements in it, including those about potential additional equity investments, future transaction pricing, future warrant tranches, cash warrant exercises and potential aggregate proceeds of up to $1 million, are contingent on future transactions or the exercise of warrants for cash, none of which is guaranteed. It says these statements reflect management's current expectations and assumptions as of the release date and that risks and uncertainties may cause actual results to differ materially. Readers are directed to review the risk factors in Arrive AI's registration statement and other filings at www.sec.gov and to avoid undue reliance on these statements. The company says it has no obligation to update the statements after the release date except as required by law.

stories.Headline: Du launches National HyperAI sovereign AI platform for UAE government and enterprises
stories.Summary:
UAE telecoms provider du launched a sovereign AI platform called National HyperAI on November 23, 2026, according to a report by Georgia Butler for datacenterdynamics.com. The platform is built on du Tech's National Hypercloud, which the article describes as a sovereign cloud platform, and it offers AI inference, GPU as a Service, Model as a Service and autonomous agent workflows. National HyperAI is designed to serve government entities as well as enterprises of all sizes across the United Arab Emirates. The platform is already available to organizations, and its hardware is housed in du's five data centers across the region. Because the platform is sovereign in nature, it will ensure that data remains within the UAE, the article says.

According to du's website, the company's data centers are located in Dubai and Abu Dhabi and include third-party locations such as the IMPZ Equinix data center. The article states that in November 2025 du deployed a cluster of Nvidia B300 GPUs at its DSO data center in Dubai for NextGenAI, with an IT capacity of 13MW. It also notes that in April 2025 the company signed a $544.54 million deal with Microsoft to develop a new hyperscale data center in the UAE, with Microsoft set to be the facility's main tenant. Jasim Al Awadi, chief ICT officer of du, said the UAE's leadership has set a clear vision to lead the global shift toward an agentic, AI-driven economy. He said organizations in the public and private sectors have proven what AI can do in isolated pilots, but scaling into production requires sovereign assurance, predictable economics and unified accountability.

Al Awadi said du brings together something no other provider in the nation can offer, namely complete ownership of the data centers, national connectivity, sovereign inference compute and an end-to-end delivery journey under one roof. He said du is proud to stand as a trusted partner supporting the UAE's AI ambitions by enabling government entities and enterprises to turn AI opportunities into practical and measurable outcomes. The article places the launch in the context of du's earlier infrastructure work in the UAE, including the Nvidia GPU cluster and the Microsoft data center deal. It gives no further details about what happens next with National HyperAI beyond the statement that the platform is already available to organizations. The report does not say how many customers have signed up or what the platform costs.

stories.Headline: AFL whitepaper urges unified fiber planning across edge, regional and core AI tiers
stories.Summary:
A whitepaper published on November 23, 2026 by AFL examines how fiber infrastructure should be planned across edge, regional and core tiers as AI workloads spread out, and it asks when a brownfield retrofit stops making sense compared with a greenfield build. The paper describes AI infrastructure as a distributed system, with training in hyperscale campuses, inference in metro facilities and small models at the edge. It says every tier depends on fiber, which raises the retrofit question for existing sites. The whitepaper was announced by datacenterdynamics.com on the same date.

The paper asks operators to plan edge, regional and core fiber infrastructure as one connected strategy rather than as separate projects. It sets out the capacity, density, resilience and connectivity that each tier of AI infrastructure demands, so planners can compare requirements across the whole system. It also asks operators to assess existing pathways, installed fiber and route diversity before choosing between a retrofit and a new build. On design, it recommends separating long-life and short-life elements so that future speed upgrades can add capacity without pulling new cable.

AFL is responsible for the whitepaper, which appears in the DCD whitepapers and reports section under the compute, storage and networking channel. The articles do not quote any named person, so no individual is credited with specific remarks. The paper frames the retrofit or greenfield decision as a practical question that existing sites must answer before committing. It presents the connected planning approach as guidance for operators weighing that choice.

The articles give no figures, dates or named sites beyond the November 23, 2026 publication date, and they do not say what any operator has decided to do. They also do not describe next steps beyond the planning and assessment the whitepaper recommends. The paper is tagged under AI, AI infrastructure, architecture, brownfield, DCI, distributed infrastructure, fiber, greenfield and retrofit. No outcome or follow-up announcement is reported.

stories.Headline: Can AI help with manage your money? What to know before you ask - WKMG
stories.Summary:
More consumers are turning to artificial intelligence for help with their finances, and one of them is Toni Moore, who is blind and said she began asking AI about her money after using it to answer other questions. The conversations led her to budgets and spreadsheets and helped her review recurring charges, and she said the tool helped her organize subscriptions and cut costs by dropping ones she did not need. Moore said text-based AI tools make financial information easier for her to access because the format is already accessible to her. She said AI helped her learn how to talk with creditors, negotiate and keep a budget, skills she had to teach herself. Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency, reported that the number of clients who found it through organic generative AI searches, primarily ChatGPT, rose 48.8% year over year through September 2026.

That increase came as more people sought help with debt, and MMI said its counseling volume was up 9.5% year over year through September. Its clients carried an average of $40,200 in unsecured debt year-to-date, up 4.8% from $38,300 during the same period in 2025. Ted Rossman, MMI's principal consumer finance analyst, said in the release that the story behind the numbers is about the rising cost of living and that on average the price of everything we buy has risen 30% since the pandemic. He said credit card debt often stems from medical bills, car and home repairs, and everyday expenses such as gas and groceries. The article says AI can help users organize expenses, build a basic budget, understand common debt-payoff approaches, or prepare questions to ask a creditor.

The article warns that AI-generated answers can be inaccurate or incomplete and says they should be treated as a starting point, not a substitute for advice from a qualified financial professional or a nonprofit credit counselor. It advises checking important information against trusted sources before making a financial decision, especially when it involves debt, taxes, investments or legal rights. It also says to protect personal information by not entering a Social Security number, date of birth, account numbers, passwords or other details that could identify you or give someone access to your accounts, and it suggests asking general questions with rounded or hypothetical figures instead of sharing exact identifying details. For Moore, the article says, AI is not making her financial decisions but is helping her make more informed ones. The article's tips include starting with a general task, verifying the answer with a bank, creditor, government agency or qualified counselor, keeping control of decisions, and considering nonprofit counseling for anyone struggling with debt.

stories.Headline: South Korea builds a national research base to develop AI scientists for the K-Moonshot project
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT held a meeting with experts from industry, academia, and research on November 23. This gathering took place at the National AI Science Research Center to discuss linking national science AI resources. The participants focused on advancing the AI scientist mission under the K-Moonshot project. They aimed to move beyond using AI as a support tool to using it for setting hypotheses and designing experiments.

The government is building a national science AI research base by combining computing resources, training data, AI models, agents, and skilled personnel. This initiative requires the National AI Science Research Center, established this year, to work with government-funded institutes in fields like nuclear power, nuclear fusion, and biotech. The plan includes running a pilot integrated science AI platform service before the end of this year. Experts also discussed securing dedicated computing resources, such as supercomputer No. 6, and establishing a standard system for training data.

Yong-kyun Yoo, the head of the National AI Science Research Center, presented missions to consolidate resources, operate the integrated platform, and foster an ecosystem. Seong-bin Lim, a PD, presented the specific roadmap for the K-Moonshot AI scientist mission. Deputy Prime Minister and Science and ICT Minister Gyeong-hun Bae stated that an era is coming where AI scientists verify hypotheses alongside human scientists. He promised full government support to ensure the research center becomes a hub and the K-Moonshot project delivers results.

stories.Headline: AMD and US Energy Department unveil Lux supercomputer at Oak Ridge to advance AI-driven science
stories.Summary:
AMD, working with the U.S. Department of Energy and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, unveiled the Lux supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, according to a Small Business Trends report published on November 23, 2026. The system is designed to support advanced artificial intelligence and scientific research, and it is ranked 14th on the TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers. Lux is now accessible to scientific users working on the Genesis Mission, a Department of Energy initiative aimed at advancing AI-driven science. The machine combines AMD EPYC processors, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software, all built by HPE. The Genesis Mission projects include AI-assisted design of fusion power plants, development of materials for advanced manufacturing, and predictions of earth systems to assess water availability and forecasts in regions such as the Tennessee Valley Authority area.

Small businesses in tech-driven fields like manufacturing, energy or environmental consulting could use Lux to run simulations, refine AI models and analyze large datasets that typical in-house computing resources may not handle. Accessing the system requires navigating the application processes set forth by Oak Ridge's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, and the report notes that the supercomputer is primarily aimed at researchers and may cater more to academic and governmental initiatives. Small business leaders should also weigh whether their projects align with the goals of the Genesis Mission, since work in fusion technology or environmental prediction may fit Lux particularly well. Thomas Zacharia, AMD's Senior Vice President, said the partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that can benefit researchers across the country. Georgia Tourassi, Associate Laboratory Director for Computing and Computational Sciences at ORNL, said that by expanding the computational resources available to the scientific community, Lux will help accelerate the integration of simulation, modeling and experimental data to advance discovery.

Trish Damkroger, Senior Vice President and General Manager at HPE, said the company, together with Oak Ridge and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation to advance the nation's scientific computing resources. The report frames access to high-performance computing as a possible advantage for smaller companies seeking to stay competitive in an increasingly tech-centric landscape, while cautioning that the barriers to entry must be weighed against the potential for breakthroughs. Businesses interested in using Lux can visit the ORNL Lux resource page, and the report suggests speaking with the OLCF team to streamline the process and clarify essential considerations. Engaging with advanced computing resources can also foster connections within the scientific community and open the way to partnerships that enhance business operations, according to the report.

stories.Headline: National Governors Association proposes splitting federal and state AI oversight
stories.Summary:
On November 22, 2026, the National Governors Association published bipartisan principles for artificial intelligence governance. These principles split regulatory authority between the federal government and the individual states. The federal government would oversee frontier models, cybersecurity, and international AI. States would maintain authority over workers, children, privacy, and daily AI deployment. This coordinated signal came just before a new session of Congress.

The plan requires a risk-based framework for frontier models, which are the most advanced general-purpose systems. It calls for independent audits of these models and reporting of safety incidents to federal and state authorities. Washington would set national standards for threats to financial systems and chemical, biological, or nuclear security. Maryland Governor Wes Moore and Indiana Governor Mike Braun lead the Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance. North Carolina Governor Josh Stein and Utah Governor Spencer Cox serve as co-chairs.

Governor Moore stated that humans must stay in control while protecting kids, consumers, and workers. Governor Braun linked the technology to efficient government services, jobs, and wages. Governor Cox argued that states already run thoughtful policies that protect consumers and foster adoption. Governor Stein urged federal action that preserves state authority as states retool service delivery. CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal policy works without input from the governors.

The plan affects AI builders who must now navigate both federal audits and state disclosure rules. It specifically impacts developers of frontier models who face new reporting and evaluation obligations. Workers are affected by state-led efforts to address job disruption and fund transition infrastructure. Small entrants are protected by rules that prevent large incumbents from using compliance as a moat. Consumer protection agencies in states like New York may continue their own testing programs.

The association previously established a cybersecurity advisors institute and a working group on AI and work. They also created a one million dollar RAISE US partnership regarding the future of work. These existing resources provide the infrastructure for implementing the new governance principles. The framework responds to a fragmented legal landscape where states already regulate hiring and health. It also overlaps with the safety frameworks suggested in the SAFE AI Act outline.

Congress will return in January to develop a federal framework consistent with these federalism principles. Developers are advised to tag features by regulator type and draft unified incident templates. The articles leave open whether Congress will adopt these specific separation-of-powers recommendations. It remains uncertain if federal preemption will override state child-safety and privacy statutes. The document is a coordinated signal rather than a statute or law.

stories.Headline: Irish startups need clearance or a licence to train AI on copyrighted works in 2026, guide says
stories.Summary:
The article is a guide published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, about training AI on copyrighted content in Ireland. It was written for founders, CTOs, heads of machine learning, product managers and in-house counsel at Irish startups building, fine-tuning or deploying AI models. The guide was last updated in September 2026 and lists Dean Cunningham of Cunningham Solicitors in Ireland as its featured expert on the matter. It sets out the legal framework, the situations in which training on protected content is lawful, how to license data properly, a risk matrix, sample contract wording and a 30/60/90 day action plan. The guide states that in 2026 training a model on copyrighted works in Ireland will in many cases need clearance or a licence.

The guide says the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, as amended, is the foundational statute and gives rights holders exclusive rights including reproduction. It states that copying a protected work, even temporarily and even into a training pipeline, needs authorisation unless a statutory exception applies. It names the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which applies across member states on a phased timeline with different obligations starting at different dates. It says the Act requires certain general-purpose and generative models to have a policy to respect EU copyright law and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content. It adds that the GDPR applies where training data holds personal data, supervised in Ireland by the Data Protection Commission.

The guide states that Ireland has transposed the EU Digital Single Market Directive, which introduced text and data mining exceptions. It says one exception covers scientific research by research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, and a broader one covers other mining subject to rights holders reserving their rights in machine-readable form for online content. It says Ireland follows a fair dealing model rather than the open-ended fair use doctrine familiar from the United States, and that fair dealing applies only to listed purposes. It advises startups to follow legislation and statutory instruments through the Oireachtas for final text, the designation of competent authorities and enforcement mechanisms. It warns readers not to assume a particular bill title, section number or penalty figure.

The guide says the cleanest basis for training is an express licence from the rights holder that specifically allows the work to be used to train an AI model. It states that content being publicly accessible does not make it free to copy, that publication is not a waiver of copyright, and that most website terms of service prohibit automated collection and reuse. It says commercially licensed datasets are the lowest-risk source provided the licence expressly permits AI training, and that many older data licences predate generative AI and say nothing about model training or weights. It says open licences often impose attribution, share-alike or non-commercial conditions, and that a non-commercial restriction is incompatible with a revenue-generating model. It says scraping carries the highest content risk and can trigger copyright infringement and breach of contract.

The guide says copyright applies automatically under the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, and that most text, images, code and audio scraped or ingested is protected. It says databases have their own protection, including the sui generis database right, which is directly relevant when scraping structured content. It says authors keep moral rights, including attribution and the right to object to derogatory treatment, which survive a sale or licence and must be dealt with expressly in contracts. It says an output that reproduces a substantial part of a protected input can itself infringe, so risk attaches to what a model produces and not only to what it ingests. It says Ireland is building its national governance and enforcement structure for AI, largely to give effect to the EU AI Act.

The guide recommends that startups build dataset manifests and provenance metadata now, and keep one compliance record covering copyright, AI transparency and data protection. It sets out a decision path asking whether an express licence covers AI training, and if not, whether a specific exception clearly covers both the copying and the intended commercial use. It says that if neither is satisfied, a team should not ingest the data but should seek a licence, find a compliant substitute or leave it out. It advises deciding how to respond to a demand letter before one arrives. It states that because the detail of national governance is still developing, readers should check the current position whenever they start a project.

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on AI chatbot toys over child safety risks
stories.Summary:
New York has enacted a five-year pause on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of artificial intelligence chatbot toys, and Gov. Kathy Hochul cited concerns about potential risks to children. Hochul signed the legislation on Tuesday in Harlem, and it targets stuffed dolls and animals that have internet access and integrated AI capabilities. The governor said these toys can let children of any age hold conversations with software that runs with minimal safety controls. She spoke at Grandma's Place, a Harlem toy store owned by retired schoolteacher Dawn Harris-Martine, who is known to customers as Grandma Dawne.

Under the law, toy manufacturers that do not comply could face penalties of up to $15,000 per day, according to Hochul. The governor said technology is evolving rapidly and that laws must adapt to keep pace with it. Supporters of the measure say AI-powered toys have raised concerns about child safety. Muna Heaven, a Harlem mother and member of Mothers Against Media Addiction, said the group has identified examples ranging from inappropriate or sexual conversations to dangerous advice, including instructions on how to find knives, tied to AI chatbot toys.

Hochul said parents buying gifts for the holiday season should hear a warning that some toys out there could be harmful to their children. Harris-Martine said a good toy for a child is one that stretches their imagination, and she encouraged parents to be actively involved in their children's play. She said parents should not put an iPad in a child's hands and let them sit and play with it alone, and she urged them to be present and get off their phones. Harris-Martine, who opened the store in the late 1990s, said she plans to keep offering what she described as an AI-free environment for children and families. She said it is really necessary when a three-year-old can sit and listen to a teddy bear telling them to do strange things, which she called not a good thing.

Articles.Title: New York pauses AI chatbot toy sales, citing child safety concerns - ABC7 New York

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes law to give all citizens a cash bonus from AI industry tax revenues
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed the Special Act on Sharing Economic Gains with All and Stabilizing Livelihoods on November 20. This legislation, which is also called the AI Bonus Act, aims to return tax revenues from the artificial intelligence industry boom to the public. The bill was passed with a narrow margin of fifty votes in favor and forty six against. It was pushed forward under the leadership of the main opposition Kuomintang party.

The act requires a payment of NT$20,000, which is about 810,000 won, to every resident of the country. This bonus is intended for all citizens regardless of their income levels or any other exclusion criteria. However, the ruling Democratic Progressive Party had proposed a smaller payment of NT$10,000, or about 400,000 won, in its 2027 budget. Several further steps must be completed before these payments can actually be distributed to the people.

The Kuomintang party appealed for public support by stating that local election results will determine if the bonus is paid. The Democratic Progressive Party opposed the higher amount, arguing that fiscal conditions make it difficult to increase the payment. Because the two political parties continue to disagree, it will likely take time to finalize the payment amount. An online poll by China Times News Network showed that 92 percent of over 8,000 participants strongly support the cash payments.

Taiwan has a history of distributing cash and consumer vouchers to stimulate the economy and boost consumption. The government issued vouchers of NT$3,600 in the late 2000s and NT$3,000 and NT$5,000 during the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021. In 2023, the state paid NT$6,000 in cash per person to help the national economy. Last year, the government distributed NT$10,000 per person to counter the economic impact of reciprocal tariffs from the United States.

stories.Headline: A study finds AI systems displace legal certainty, accountability and enforceability
stories.Summary:
A conceptual legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examines how artificial intelligence systems displace the core structural foundations that historically uphold legal legitimacy. The study conceptualizes these foundational conditions as the Tripod of Legal Legitimacy, consisting of legal certainty, accountability, and enforceability. Across public and private domains, the normative authority of law is increasingly challenged by opaque, adaptive, and privately administered algorithmic infrastructures. Rather than merely assisting human decision-makers, artificial intelligence technologies embed regulatory functions such as adjudication, classification, and enforcement directly into their computational architecture. These systems frequently operate outside the scope of democratic authorization, legislative scrutiny, or judicial review, raising fundamental questions about the capacity of legal orders to maintain normative authority.

The study defines normative legitimacy as the capacity of legal systems to justify authority through principled reasoning, procedural fairness, and democratic accountability. Legal institutions comprise public authorities such as legislatures, regulatory agencies, and courts charged with creating, interpreting, and enforcing rules. Legal certainty requires laws to be clear, general, prospective, and intelligible so that individuals and institutions can understand rules to comply or seek contestation. Accountability provides vertical oversight through public and electoral scrutiny, alongside horizontal checks via judicial review and inter-agency evaluation, ensuring decisions remain contestable and subject to justification or reversal. Enforceability ensures legal norms produce concrete behavioral effects through compliance mechanisms, coercion, or institutional alignment, preventing rules from decaying into symbolic declarations.

The author diagnoses how specific characteristics of artificial intelligence destabilize this legal tripod through institutional erosion, technical substitution, and infrastructural control. Modern machine learning models rely on statistical inference, automated optimization, and probabilistic classifications rather than human deliberation or causal deduction, creating an inherent black-box problem. The study distinguishes between two distinct layers of opacity: the internal architecture of deep neural networks that impedes legal explainability, and the institutional opacity of corporate structures that shields proprietary code and training data behind trade secrecy and platform terms of service. Accountability diffuses across fragmented supply chains of developers, deployers, and institutional adopters, producing a responsibility vacuum where fault-based liability falters. Enforceability erodes as transnationally deployed cloud platforms operate beyond the reach of domestic regulators, leaving state authorities with fragmented oversight.

In the Netherlands, the predictive algorithmic profiling system SyRI, deployed to detect social security fraud, operated with minimal transparency until the Hague District Court invalidated it for violating fair trial guarantees and European human rights transparency standards. European Union border operations examined by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency demonstrated that automated border management tools significantly constrain individuals' access to legal redress. Italian data protection authorities issued a moratorium on real-time facial recognition in public spaces, Spanish regulators suspended artificial intelligence systems in public schools over biometric profiling concerns, and Canadian provinces paused predictive policing programs due to discrimination risks and absent procedural safeguards. In the United States, police departments widely adopted facial recognition technologies within regulatory vacuums, demonstrating how technical systems hollow out legal protections in practice without explicitly repealing statutes. The study introduces a comparative process-based model that contrasts the recursive feedback cycles of traditional public law against artificial-intelligence-induced governance cycles.

Under the traditional legal-governance framework, legitimacy is maintained through four interlinked stages: norm formulation through deliberative processes such as legislative drafting and public hearings; institutional implementation by public bodies; behavioral adjustment alongside procedural contestation in administrative or judicial venues; and normative recalibration, wherein legal disputes and observed failures feed back into statutory reform. The European Union's Digital Services Act incorporated over 3,000 public submissions during drafting and established Digital Services Coordinators to oversee algorithmic risk management, while the AI Act mandates supervisory reviews and five-year revision cycles under Article 84. The artificial-intelligence-induced governance displacement framework traces how private infrastructures substitute code-based mechanisms for public law across five distinct stages. The cycle begins with design-based norm encoding, where private actors embed governance choices directly into technical system parameters, as seen in Meta's Community Standards or OpenAI's behavioral guidelines and prompt engineering. The second stage, infrastructural adoption, occurs when public institutions, educational bodies, and individual users integrate these unregulated models into everyday practice in the absence of statutory review.

Third, functional displacement emerges as platform-based systems simulate legal functions, such as adjudication and content moderation, exemplified by Meta's Oversight Board issuing non-binding rulings or OpenAI defining internal safety rules without judicial oversight. The fourth stage, epistemic dependency, manifests as public regulators face substantial technical knowledge gaps and increasingly rely on private developers for expertise, auditability, and regulatory guidance. During 2023 United States Senate hearings, lawmakers invited OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman alongside academic and civil society witnesses to suggest regulatory approaches, highlighting how technical elites increasingly influence public agenda-setting. Finally, legitimacy closure occurs when platform operators deploy internal ethics boards, transparency portals, system cards, and corporate audit reports to signal normative compliance. In July 2025, major artificial intelligence developers including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral signed the European Union's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI, pledging adherence to transparency, copyright, and traceability provisions, while Meta rejected the voluntary Code, publicly citing overregulation.

The author notes that no major United States court, including the Supreme Court, has yet adjudicated cases regarding artificial-intelligence-generated pornography. The author outlines six structural policy priorities necessary to reconstruct legal authority rather than merely extending existing compliance checklists. First, legal frameworks must establish enforceable traceability through statutory algorithmic registries, mandatory version-update documentation, and publicly accessible audit trails to ensure administrative legibility. Second, statutes must clarify liability across the entire artificial intelligence supply chain, establishing tiered liability models that apportion responsibility among system developers, practical deployers, and institutional adopters. Third, enforceability must be re-anchored in binding statutory entitlements, guaranteeing enforceable rights to explanation, mandatory justification protocols, and independent third-party appeals. Fourth, democratic jurisdictions must advance transnational coordination through interoperable regulatory standards and mutual recognition to prevent private jurisdictional arbitrage.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Los Angeles schools disable Google AI summaries for students
stories.Summary:
Officials from the Los Angeles Unified School District disabled automatic artificial intelligence summaries on Google searches for students in November 2026. This action removes the AI Overviews that previously appeared above standard search results and links for learners. The district had already blocked students from using Gemini in search via school accounts in September of this year. These combined efforts aim to curb the use of generative AI tools across all grade levels.

The current restrictions require that students no longer see automatic summaries while keeping general search tools open under review. This follows a districtwide generative AI moratorium established in September and the disabling of conversational AI mode earlier in the term. Google announced on November 3, 2026, that accounts for students from pre-K through 12 will need administrator approval to access Search and Gemini. A community survey was distributed on November 16, 2026, to gather input from families, students, and staff.

District leaders are responsible for these changes and expressed concerns that AI tools might encourage shortcuts for students. They believe these tools could reduce original research and produce inaccurate output across various classroom search queries. Officials stated that they are evaluating how digital tools support learning without banning the Google Search platform entirely. They intend to provide age appropriate experiences for learners while a board committee prepares recommendations for a potential vote.

The district continues to use Google products while reviewing how these digital tools can best support the educational process. Google noted that schools rejecting AI outright may lose search access on those accounts, though the district has not explained how it will resolve that specific gap. Latino families are encouraged to check with their schools because rules may vary depending on the specific account or device. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Perth and Kinross Council officials say AI-generated requests overwhelm staff and raise costs
stories.Summary:
Leaders at Perth and Kinross Council in Scotland said artificial intelligence is fuelling an “incredible” rise in the volume and complexity of correspondence from the public. Officers dealing with complaints, data compliance and freedom of information requests must wade through thousands of pages of AI-generated “gibberish” to work out which communications are genuine. Lisa Simpson, head of legal and governance at Perth and Kinross, told the council’s scrutiny and performance committee on 18 November that AI lets people produce 10, 11 or 12-page requests at the flick of a button. She said 80% of this material is “nonsensical”, so “an awful lot of time and resources” is taken up processing it. Jillian Walker, the council’s data protection officer, told councillors at the meeting that subject access requests had risen by 100% in the last two years, partly due to AI.

Subject access requests let people obtain the data an organisation holds on them by law. According to Scottish newspaper The Courier, Walker said compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025 despite the pressures. A report presented to councillors showed the 1,849 freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 was the highest number in figures going back seven years, and 21% more than in 2024-25. Walker said much of the increase in communications is also related to Scotland’s Redress Scheme, which provides survivors of historical child abuse in care homes with redress payments, emotional support and official apologies. She said staff dealing with these requests must process “thousands of pages of highly distressing records” and reply to those seeking redress in a compassionate, trauma-informed and sensitive way.

Walker praised her “highly conscientious” small team but said there is “just no way we can sustain the compliance rate we have achieved previously”. Asked whether the council could use its own AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, she said that though it is “very low-tech”, staff had found the best way to decipher AI-generated text and requests was to print them off and go through them with highlighter pens. Simpson acknowledged that AI could be valuable but said there was a “time and a place” for its use. She said that in some cases the tools and technology are not being used responsibly and their purpose is to tie the council up in knots and almost grind things to a halt. She said this does not help when the council is trying to help people with genuine requests, genuine issues and genuine complaints.

According to the BBC, officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level. In a paper published in September, researchers from the UK-based Centre for the Governance of AI and from the Hertie School in Berlin identified 84 cases across 11 countries. In those cases public bodies or “credible observers” attributed surges in requests to public use of AI, including freedom of information requests, planning consultation responses and civil court claims. The report, “Characterizing agentic flooding of government services”, defines “agentic flooding” as a surge in the volume or complexity of requests to a service caused by AI use that substantially strains the body’s capacity. The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity.

The report presented to councillors covered freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 and compared them with figures going back seven years. Walker linked part of the rise in communications to Scotland’s Redress Scheme for survivors of historical child abuse in care homes. Simpson and Walker both addressed the scrutiny and performance committee meeting on 18 November. The Courier reported Walker’s statement that compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025. The BBC reported that officials said the council is working with other local authorities on whether the problem could be addressed at a national level. The September paper by the Centre for the Governance of AI and the Hertie School set out the 84 cases and the definition of agentic flooding.

Officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level. The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity. The articles do not say what the council’s own next steps will be, or what the other local authorities have found. The articles do not say whether the council will adopt any new AI tools to handle the correspondence. The articles do not say what response, if any, the Scottish or UK government has given to the council’s concerns.

stories.Headline: Trump threatens penalties for US companies building data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Trump threatened to impose penalties on American companies that build data centers in other countries. He made these remarks to reporters at the White House on November 20, 2026. The president specifically mentioned Finland as a place where American computing capacity was escaping. He claimed that China would take all the facilities if this trend continued. He promised that the government would not allow these overseas projects to happen.

The president promised tremendous penalties but named no specific rate, tax base, or start date. He did not specify a legal authority for these penalties or a timeline for implementation. He admitted that he had not yet discussed the plan with his own staff. No implementing document or formal policy had appeared as of November 23, 2026. A new federal tax would require authorization from Congress to become law.

President Trump stated that the United States would not allow its companies to build data centers abroad. He warned that such actions were necessary to prevent China from taking over the industry. The White House summary of the briefing repeated these remarks without setting out a policy. The president also advised local communities to make the data center companies pay them. He framed the issue as a matter of keeping computing capacity within the country.

The threat affects American companies that seek to invest in AI infrastructure outside the United States. Some companies have already faced delays in Finland due to incomplete environmental impact assessments. Police in Oulu opened an investigation into suspected environmental damage at a Muhos worksite. Google's subsidiary Tuike Finland suspended preparatory work at sites in Muhos and Kajaani in October. These companies must now navigate both presidential threats and local regulatory hurdles.

The administration has already implemented other controls through the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. An interim final rule on remote access to advanced semiconductors took effect on November 19, 2026. This rule requires licenses for exports to overseas data centers serving companies in countries of concern. It also adds license requirements for advanced chips sent to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These regulators focus on who uses the computing power rather than where the building stands.

The White House has not yet provided a formal policy or a legal basis for the penalties. It remains unclear how the administration will enforce these threats without congressional authorization for taxes. The government has not specified which companies will be targeted or when penalties will start. Future developments depend on whether the administration creates a statutory basis for these penalties. The articles leave the specific nature of the promised tremendous penalties open.

stories.Headline: Sompo's Jon Monks warns AI must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers
stories.Summary:
Jon Monks, executive vice president and head of distribution, business development and client engagement for Sompo North America, warned in an interview published by Insurance Business on November 23, 2026, that artificial intelligence must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers. He said the industry will obviously all use AI to create efficiencies, but he cautioned that if technology takes over the work of digging into policies and coverage structures, the industry risks losing what he called the core building blocks of building specialty expertise. Monks said the industry needs to make sure it continues to teach the next generation those skills, so that it develops critical thinkers and not just order takers. He joined Sompo in 2018 after more than two decades at Marsh and AIG. Monks said the role of the wholesale broker is changing, and that the next generation will be valued for specialty expertise rather than simply for placing business.

In his view, a broker should be seen as a technician and a specialist rather than just a placement. He said wholesalers have done a good job of hiring college graduates and putting them through training programs, and he credited the Wholesale & Specialty Insurance Association's internships and networking events with enriching that pipeline. The harder step, he said, is that a broker with one to five years of experience really needs to propel into the expertise of a broker with eight to twelve years, to the point of taking a deal from cradle to grave by understanding the risk, building a solution, taking it to market and defending it at renewal. Monks is not arguing against AI, and he said Sompo, like every carrier, expects to use it to make processes more efficient across the business.

His concern is which work gets handed to machines first, since the traditional way of bringing on talent has been to have people dig into policies, understand coverage and learn how programs are structured. He said that pushing all of that onto technology could cause the industry to miss out on developing opportunities to create critical thinkers, which he said it will need going forward. He is not alone in raising the issue, and Jimcor's Kristen Skender has described how automation is reshaping entry-level underwriting roles at MGAs, the jobs where many new entrants have traditionally learned the business. In Monks's view the graduates are arriving and the early training is working, and what will decide the next generation's quality is whether the industry keeps giving young brokers the kind of work that turns them into specialists, even when a machine could do it faster.

stories.Headline: Julia Louis-Dreyfus files trademarks to protect her voice and image from AI
stories.Summary:
Julia Louis-Dreyfus filed four trademark applications on November 20, 2026, seeking protection for her voice and her image as part of an effort to guard against artificial intelligence recreating them without permission, according to Gerben IP. The filings cover the Soup Nazi scene from Seinfeld, the glass door scene from Veep, her voice saying a sentence introducing her podcast Wiser Than Me, and her image. The article describes the filings as unusual because she is seeking protection for recognizable moments from her acting career rather than a traditional logo, slogan or brand name. Taylor Swift and Jimmy Kimmel are among the high-profile figures who have pursued similar trademark filings involving their recognizable voices and images.

The article says whether trademark law can provide the broad protection these celebrities seek remains an open legal question, and that courts have not answered whether a registration covering one recorded sentence would reach AI-generated imitations of her voice saying different words. It notes that sounds and motion marks can function as trademarks, citing the Netflix sound and the MGM lion, but that protecting an individual scene from a television show is very different. The article says it is likely the United States Patent and Trademark Office will refuse both motion mark applications, because recognition alone does not make a scene a brand identifier in the marketplace. It adds that even a pending application might be used under AI platforms' intellectual property policies to restrict use of a voice or image.

The article is by Josh Gerben, a trademark attorney and founder of Gerben IP, who writes that the legal strategy makes sense even if some applications are ultimately refused, because celebrities are looking for additional legal tools in a world where AI can reproduce voices and likenesses with remarkable accuracy. He says trademark law offers an established intellectual property framework that technology companies already recognize, and that many AI platforms have policies addressing trademark infringement. He states that it will ultimately be up to the courts to determine how far trademark law can be used to restrict what AI generates. He also notes that such filings rely on the premise that we still have control over AI itself.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams in Paris to assess AI risks in public services
stories.Summary:
The first HUDERIA academy on responsible AI governance at local level took place in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026, organised by the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the event, which was the first of its kind. The participants were 18 municipalities and two counties from 18 European countries, ranging from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies. It was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit, and served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe.

The academy provided the teams with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over the three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion in Greece, Bălți in the Republic of Moldova, Bergen in Norway, Bitola and Resen in North Macedonia, the City of Arezzo in Italy, the City of Vigo in Spain, Diyarbakır in Türkiye, Fingal County in Ireland, Harghita County in Romania, Kutaisi in Georgia, the London Borough of Camden in the United Kingdom, Lviv and Rivne in Ukraine, Nõo in Estonia, Shkodër in Albania, Szentendre in Hungary, Turnišče in Slovenia, Valongo in Portugal, and the Ventspils Education Board in Latvia.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla of Estonia, Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens, and for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles describe her remarks as a call to automate tasks rather than democratic responsibility, and they present the academy as putting into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

The articles say that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls, with local and regional authorities on the frontline of this AI revolution. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in the efficiency gains promised by AI, but they also face hard questions, such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say authorities lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities, and the academy sought to rectify that problem. The articles do not say what follow-up the academy will have beyond its place in the Road to Geneva programme and the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

stories.Headline: Italy decree presumes causation and creates a criminal offence for high-risk AI oversight failures
stories.Summary:
Italy’s Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapts Italian law to the EU AI Act on civil and criminal liability, according to Global Advisory Experts. The decree was published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale on 15 September and entered into force on 30 September 2026. It applies alongside Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 on artificial intelligence and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act. The measures concern businesses that build, deploy or insure high-risk artificial intelligence in Italy. Global Advisory Experts published its guide to the rules on 23 November 2026.

The decree presumes causation where damage follows a breach of an AI Act obligation, unless the defendant disproves it. It creates an offence of failing to adopt security or human oversight measures on high-risk AI systems where this endangers life or safety. It adds that offence to the Decree 231/2001 catalogue of predicate offences. It gives claimants a court-ordered route to evidence about how an AI system worked. It lets claimants sue the defendant’s liability insurer directly.

Under Decree 231/2001, entities can be held administratively liable for certain crimes committed in their interest or to their advantage. A company can avoid sanctions by showing it adopted and effectively implemented an adequate organisational and management model and appointed a supervisory body. Sanctions work through quotas, with the court fixing the number of quotas and the money value of each according to the entity’s economic condition. The regime also allows interdictory or disqualification measures, including limits on carrying on the activity, suspension of authorisations and bans on contracting with the public administration. Global Advisory Experts said boards should treat any significant development in AI criminal law as a reason to review the whole 231 model.

Global Advisory Experts said compliance with the AI Act’s harmonised requirements is useful evidence for a defendant but does not of itself necessarily exclude civil liability. It said a system can be compliant on paper and still fail in operation, be used outside its intended purpose, or cause harm through weak oversight in the field. Providers carry the heaviest design-stage duties on risk management, security measures and human oversight, while deployers must run systems within their intended purpose and keep up oversight in real use. Injured parties rarely understand how a system reached the decision or output that caused their loss. Courts can order redaction, confidentiality arrangements and protective orders for trade secrets and confidential information.

The AI Act applies directly in Italy and defines provider, deployer and high-risk AI system, with provisions applying on a staggered timetable running through 2025 to 2027. The AI Act identifies high-risk categories through its annexes, capturing uses such as certain law-enforcement tools, critical-infrastructure management and safety components of products such as medical devices. Italy’s national AI law sets national principles and sector rules and changes criminal provisions on the misuse of AI systems. Prosecutors in Italy have traditionally had to fit AI-related harm into existing offences, such as negligence, endangerment, or offences on workplace and product safety. The revised Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853) must be transposed by member states and expressly brings software and AI systems within product liability.

Global Advisory Experts said AI legislation is moving quickly at EU and national level and that the exact text and commencement dates of any measure should be checked against official sources before acting. It said the Italian transposition of the revised Product Liability Directive and its commencement should be confirmed against official sources. It said exposure crosses borders, so a provider established elsewhere in the EU that places a high-risk system on the Italian market, or whose system causes damage in Italy, may face Italian civil claims. It said the first task for any Italian business is to establish whether anything it builds or deploys falls into a high-risk category and which obligations follow. It said existing 231 programmes need reviewing for AI, with risk assessments covering high-risk AI and evidence that the model genuinely operates rather than sitting on paper.

Articles.Title: Italy AI Liability: Criminal, Civil and Insurance Risk - Global Advisory Experts

stories.Headline: OpenAI reports GPT-6 models design protein shapes and sequences using reasoning and code alone
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 24, 2026 that its GPT-6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. OpenAI published the claim in a preprint titled “GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models.” An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks, OpenAI said. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT-6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets, and redesigned antibodies also retained binding.

Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing, OpenAI said. OpenAI tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab, and 35 of them, or 10.9%, tested positive for binding to their intended target. OpenAI found 5 hits for PD-L1, 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. For three targets, OpenAI saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). Of 107 proteins made from GPT-6.2’s new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes, 14 (13.1%) showed binding, and of 182 designs for six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind IL-4Rα, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding.

OpenAI said the models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. When designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, OpenAI said, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction. OpenAI said an internal model followed an instruction on how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. OpenAI said the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give strong evidence that GPT-6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. OpenAI said the results also suggest it could use GPT-6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

OpenAI said it compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT-6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while its latest internal models scored higher. OpenAI said the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. OpenAI said predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness. OpenAI said it used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design, and other specialized protein models helped select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. OpenAI said it tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab, and of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

OpenAI said proteins do much of the work in living cells, driving the chemical reactions that sustain life, carrying oxygen through the blood, and defending the body against infection. OpenAI said incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. OpenAI said proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids, and the order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. OpenAI said scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do, and the challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. OpenAI said using and coordinating specialized biology models requires substantial expertise, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training.

OpenAI said it asked GPT-6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein, and when it already knew which two atoms formed a bond, it could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. OpenAI said it could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. OpenAI said it also asked its models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where it wanted a minibinder to attach, and the model then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders without using specialized protein AI models. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones.

Articles.Title: OpenAI says GPT-6 models can design new protein shapes and sequences using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate them (OpenAI)
