stories.Headline: Dell posts $54.94 billion in quarterly revenue as AI server sales surge while HP misses PC market forecasts
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today, SiliconANGLE reported on Nov. 24, 2026. Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, the article said. HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share on revenue of $16 billion, the article said. Dell's revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, the article said. The companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve, the article said.

Dell's result blew past Wall Street's expectations of $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales, the article said. Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion, far in excess of the Street's target of $35.27 billion, the article said. Around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, and that segment was up 291% annually, the article said. Dell's Client Services Group generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street's forecast of $14.33 billion, the article said. HP's profit surpassed the analyst consensus estimate of 75 cents per share, and its revenue was up 9% and above the Street's target of $15.4 billion, the article said.

Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke said the company is now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of its profit and growth. Clarke said Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers. Clarke told analysts the company has a significant competitive advantage over its rivals on the software side, which enables customers to get their servers up and running in data centers within hours of taking delivery. Clarke said that allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. Clarke told analysts that every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power.

Dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years and now sees sales rising to $78 billion, ahead of the Street's target of $74 billion, the article said. Dell has an order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers, the article said. Dell's stock rose more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier during the regular trading session, the article said. HP's stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour, and it was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing, the article said. HP's stock is still up 25% in the year to date, the article said.

Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer, the article said. HP has been trying to mitigate the situation by raising its prices, but it couldn't stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter, the article said. HP has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February, the article said. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months, and the company named Walmsley, who formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc, as his successor, the article said. Walmsley will assume the role full time on Jan. 4, when she's slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard, the article said.

The market was eagerly anticipating HP's guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any, the article said. All HP would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million, while analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion, the article said. The article said Walmsley will have her work cut out when she assumes the role. The article said Walmsley has a tough act to follow, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. The article did not say what Dell or HP expect in the PC market beyond the figures given.

Articles.Title: Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market

stories.Headline: Susskind urges parents and schools to teach children the basics rather than future-proof skills
stories.Summary:
Brian Hengesbaugh, global chair of data and cyber at Baker McKenzie, wrote an opinion piece published by the IAPP on 23 Nov. 2026 about the book "What Should My Children Do? How to Flourish in the Age of AI" by Professor Daniel Susskind, who spoke at the IAPP Europe Congress 2026 in a closing general session. Hengesbaugh credited IAPP President and CEO J. Trevor Hughes for bringing the book to his attention. The piece is part of an ongoing IAPP series on issues in data, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence governance, and the IAPP notes it is policy neutral and publishes contributed opinions to show a broad spectrum of views. According to the article, Susskind argues that parents and schools should stop trying to teach children future-proof skills because too little is known about AI to do that well, and should instead make sure they master the basics.

He points to the 2010s, when U.K. Prime Minister David Cameron required every child from as young as age 5 to learn to code, on the premise that this would equip every child with the computing skills needed to succeed in the 21st century, even though relatively few teachers felt comfortable teaching it. The article says generative AI can code quite well, so that approach worked only reasonably well in the short term. It also compares the debate over AI in schools to the 1970s arrival of the calculator, when some wanted to ban it and others to embrace it, and the resolution was to teach both, with some tests permitting calculators and others not. The article says Susskind advises everyone to learn to use AI and avoid competing with it, to keep learning the basics, and to limit exposure to algorithms now because the AI of tomorrow will make such attractions irresistible. He says people should accept that expectations about work may be frustrated by the pace of change and should rush towards the frontiers of science, where he says the greatest adventures will be unfolding.

In the last chapter, on focusing on who you are rather than what you do, he argues that even if artificial general intelligence could outperform humans at every economically useful task, humans would still have useful roles, from artists and musicians to athletes, caretakers, judges and politicians, because people will still crave interaction with other humans, though he asks whether there will still be enough jobs doing them. Hengesbaugh adds a brief extension, writing that people are human beings, not human doings, and have inherent worth because they are human, a point he says each person should examine through their own religious and philosophical beliefs. He says people can confuse themselves into thinking their value is tied to economic output, which he says strays far from the truth, and that staying grounded in this understanding can keep them from being swept away by the frenzy and hype of AI even as they learn to harness its power for the benefit of children and society. The article gives no further steps beyond this advice.

Articles.Title: Thought for the week: Human beings, not human doings: Flourishing in the age of AI - IAPP

stories.Headline: Daniel Anello: Chicago Board of Education should wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy
stories.Summary:
Daniel Anello, CEO of the nonprofit Kids First Chicago, published a commentary on November 23, 2026, urging the Chicago Board of Education to wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy. He wrote that board members may be tempted to quickly pass a sweeping and long-term ban on AI use in classrooms. He argued that a decision this consequential requires methodical engagement of the various stakeholders most affected, especially families. He said that will take time. He wrote that the pressure to move quickly has ramped up in recent weeks.

Anello wrote that Google raised the stakes earlier this month when it told school districts they no longer could have Google Search for students without the built-in generative AI features. He wrote that a ban on AI in CPS therefore would also mean taking away the search engine most students use every day. He wrote that Chicago's proposed ban would last three times as long as a one-year moratorium New York imposed for students through eighth grade. He wrote that roughly half of the 21 newly elected board members, including President-elect Jessica Biggs, signed a pledge supporting a three-year AI moratorium. He wrote that the pledge was written by one small advocacy group affiliated with a national campaign.

Anello wrote that the concerns behind the pledge are legitimate. He wrote that a pledge written by one small advocacy group is not a substitute for asking families what they want. He wrote that Kids First Chicago, the organization he leads, has started surveying Chicago families about AI in schools, with results expected early next year. He wrote that a survey is a start but not a substitute for the robust process this decision warrants. He wrote that instead of adopting any long-term AI policy in the final weeks of a lame-duck board, the school board should commit to a transparent engagement process.

Anello wrote that New York imposed a one-year moratorium for students through eighth grade while it studies the technology's effects, and high school students get AI literacy classes instead. He wrote that Los Angeles restricted student access for this school year, left teachers' access in place and asked a committee for recommendations by spring. He wrote that Boston pledged every student will graduate "AI literate." He wrote that when the district redesigned its school accountability system, more than 20,000 people took part in a multiyear process. He wrote that more than 30 community organizations have since coalesced to define what that standard should look like for every major CPS decision.

Anello wrote that Google has become deeply embedded in every aspect of a Chicago Public Schools school day, from Gmail to Chromebooks to Google Classroom. He wrote that the pandemic made Google even more ubiquitous as the district worked to ensure every student had a device to support remote learning. He wrote that untangling Google from the district would be neither simple nor cost-free. He wrote that views on student and educator use of AI range widely, with some seeing it as a threat to learning, privacy and attention spans and an invitation to cheat. He wrote that others accept it as part of the world children must enter, so best to train students early to use it safely and ethically.

Anello wrote that the school board should commit to a transparent engagement process that provides the time and space for meaningful input from families, educators and students. He wrote that when the new, fully elected board members take their seats in January, one of their first acts should be the adoption of a stakeholder engagement policy. He wrote that the framework developed by the Coalition for Authentic Community Engagement sets practical expectations for CPS. He wrote that these standards are publicly available at authentic engagement.info. He wrote that two minutes at a microphone during a board meeting falls far short of that standard.

Articles.Title: Daniel Anello: Chicago Board of Education should wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy - Chicago Tribune

stories.Headline: Experts debate whether AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution at SC26 panel
stories.Summary:
Experts debated if AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution during a panel at the SC26 conference. Joe Greenseid of Nvidia moderated the discussion between several industry and academic specialists. The panel included representatives from AMD, VAST Data, the University of Delaware, and ETH Zurich. They discussed whether machines built for AI differ from those used by scientists for decades. The group examined how AI has increased funding and the size of these machines.

Nicholas Malaya of AMD claimed that AI and traditional high performance computing can use the same hardware. He cited the Lux system at Oak Ridge National Laboratory as a design for both workloads. Malaya also pointed to the AMD MI430 chip as an example of a dual purpose design. Torsten Hoefler of ETH Zurich argued that AI chips use lower precision like FP4 and FP8. He noted that scientific simulations often require FP64 or double precision for accurate results.

Nicholas Malaya stated that AI training shares many commonalities with traditional high performance computing. He suggested that Slinky, which combines Slurm with Kubernetes, can support both types of workloads. Torsten Hoefler argued that inference systems must handle many requests with very little delay. He claimed that professionals who do not adapt to AI could become a lost generation. Joe Greenseid moderated these views on whether the two fields can move in one direction.

Glenn Lockwood of VAST Data doubted that a 200 million dollar supercomputer could serve both purposes. He claimed that AI developers do not need traditional tools like SSH, Slurm, or file systems. Lockwood also criticized AI theater, where organizations present traditional simulations as AI work. Sunita Chandrasekaran of the University of Delaware noted that scientists cannot easily switch between precision levels. She raised concerns about moving sensitive research data between computing centers due to restrictions.

The articles state that high performance computing has used fast memory and high speed networks for years. AI has pushed technology faster but brought new demands for software and machine usage. Malaya noted that AI coding agents helped him produce more software than in the previous six years. Chandrasekaran observed that students now prefer languages like Python, Triton, and JAX over Fortran. Researchers from other fields now bring data to these environments without much programming experience.

The panel did not settle whether the change is an evolution or a revolution. Hoefler suggested that AI agents might rewrite applications to weaken the CUDA advantage held by Nvidia. He noted that any converted code would still require checking for accuracy. The discussion left open whether AI and scientific computing can continue moving in the same direction. The experts remained divided on the necessity of compromises for dual purpose hardware systems.

Articles.Title: SC26 Panel Debates AI Supercomputing: Evolution or Revolution?

stories.headline_source: SC26 Panel Debates AI Supercomputing: Evolution or Revolution?

stories.Headline: Peter Boockvar predicts AI capital spending growth will slow sharply in 2026
stories.Summary:
Peter Boockvar of One Point BFG Wealth Partners said on CNBC's "Fast Money" that growth in AI capital spending is set to slow sharply in 2026, in a segment published on November 24, 2026. He appeared on the program to discuss whether the AI trade is on firm footing after a volatile few weeks in the space. The segment ran about five minutes and eighteen seconds, and the page carrying it was dated the same day. The headline of the segment states his view that AI capex growth will slow sharply in 2026.

The segment framed the discussion around the recent volatility in the AI trade and whether it still stands on firm footing. The page gives no figures for expected spending, no forecast amounts and no dates beyond the 2026 year in the headline and the November 24, 2026 publication date. It names no companies in connection with his call and offers no detail on which areas of AI spending he expects to slow. The only named participant is Boockvar, of One Point BFG Wealth Partners, speaking on "Fast Money."

Responsibility for the view rests with Boockvar, who gave it in the interview, and the page attributes the slowdown call to him and his firm. The page does not set out his reasoning, so what he said beyond the headline claim is not recorded there. It also does not say what he recommended or how he positioned for the slowdown he described. No one else is quoted on the call in the article text.

The context the page gives is a volatile few weeks in the AI trade, which the segment set out to examine. What happens next is not reported, and the page carries no follow-up on the forecast or on any response to it. The surrounding page consists of links to other videos, including ones on Nvidia, the Federal Reserve and the S&P, which are not part of this story. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI capex growth set to slow sharply in 2026, says One Point BFG's Peter Boockvar

stories.Headline: Deloitte says CFOs must embed AI in finance workflows to prove ROI as pilot window closes
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence in finance has moved from an experimental novelty to a board-level mandate, according to an article published by Deloitte on 24 November 2026, which says the window to prove value is closing. The article says pilots demonstrated digital potential, but chief financial officers now face the question of how to drive return on investment without eroding controllership. It says finance teams can rewire execution and elevate internal customer experience by embedding these capabilities into workflows. The article states that a stalled finance and accounting transformation often stems from ignoring data readiness, governance and security as strict prerequisites.

The article says one global beverage producer achieved 92% touchless invoice processing and reduced manual effort by more than 80% using AI in its finance operations. It says AI tools can draft variance explanations, suggest reconciliation steps and produce consistent management commentary when a reconciliation breaks or an unexpected variance occurs. For invoices with missing purchase order details, mismatches or duplicates, the article says trained tools can extract, interpret and supplement invoice content, flag issues for review and triage exceptions to the proper owner. It says AI can summarize account history, recommend next-best actions and standardize outreach when a dispute is opened or a customer inquiry comes in.

The article recommends that leaders pilot, learn quickly and scale gradually, with budget reserved for practical use cases and a plan to expand enterprisewide. It says not every problem needs AI, and that robotic process automation and other platforms may better serve rule-based scenarios, with AI more relevant when nuance is high. It says data readiness should be treated as a prerequisite rather than a phase-two task, because output quality ties directly to the underlying data and the organization's data maturity. It says investment decisions should align with a practical value roadmap assessed over short-term and long-term horizons, and that risk management and governance should be designed from day one, with Deloitte's Trustworthy AI framework named as one tool that can help design ethical safeguards.

The article says the highest-impact use cases are anchored to outcomes finance leaders already own, manage and report, such as cycle time, cost to serve, working capital and control effectiveness. It says the differentiator is workflow integration, with AI creating the most value when triggered at the moment of work rather than used as an after-the-fact summarizer. It says AI-based tools can draft and organize evidence narratives, map evidence to control requirements and flag gaps before they become findings, with typical measures including evidence collection cycle time and fewer documentation-driven findings. The article says moving from a promising pilot to an enterprise capability requires deliberate choices as CFOs seek tangible ROI and clarity on talent, platform direction, data risk and model governance.

Articles.Title: AI in Finance: From Pilots to Performance

stories.headline_source: AI in Finance: From Pilots to Performance

stories.Headline: Chinese firms deploy adaptive robots to advance physical AI using massive manufacturing scale
stories.Summary:
Chinese firms have begun deploying and testing adaptive robots in production to enhance their physical artificial intelligence capabilities. This movement relies on a massive manufacturing base that installed 354,200 new industrial robots in 2025, which represented 59 per cent of the global total. These robots differ from conventional models because they can perceive their surroundings and adapt to changing conditions to perform complex tasks. Recent tests at an electric vehicle factory by Xiaomi showed that humanoid robot success rates rose from 90.2 to 98 per cent between March and July 2026.

Realizing this potential requires overcoming barriers to interoperability and the sharing of commercially sensitive information between enterprises. Beijing launched the Industrial Data Foundation Action in March 2026 to standardize industrial data, followed by the Model, Data Resonance Action in April 2026 to refine training datasets. In June 2026, the Special Action for Real-World Training of Humanoid Robots and Embodied AI directed 10 province-level jurisdictions and state-owned enterprises to open operating environments. Local initiatives in Shanghai and Wuxi are also establishing shared systems to standardize data from different robotic platforms and production lines.

The National Data Administration estimates that China produced approximately 27.4 per cent of global data in 2025, with over 30 per cent of industrial data coming from equipment. Engineers at Longcheer Technology stated that operational feedback from AI-enabled robots informed frequent model updates and improved robot movements. One developer of a fabric handling robot claimed a 97 per cent success rate and estimated an investment payback period of 18 months. These advancements aim to create a cycle where industrial deployment generates data that improves AI models, which then enables more capable robots.

This industrial scale could intensify pressure on Southeast Asian manufacturers by offsetting rising wages and retaining production in China. Such a shift might weaken the labor-cost advantage of the region and complicate its export-led industrialization. Other industrial economies, including Japan and South Korea, are developing their own testbeds and shared training datasets to remain competitive. These nations must improve coordination and harmonize technical standards across borders to compete with the scale of the Chinese manufacturing sector.

Articles.Title: China’s industrial scale could power its physical AI rise

stories.headline_source: China’s industrial scale could power its physical AI rise

stories.Headline: Solis tells Rio Grande Valley leaders that workers who know how to use AI will replace those who do not
stories.Summary:
South Texas College President Dr. Ricardo Solis told regional business, education and economic development leaders at the college's Annual Workforce Summit in McAllen that the Rio Grande Valley faces a rapidly evolving skills challenge driven by artificial intelligence and industrial expansion. He said the region is no longer facing a simple shortage of workers, and he described the area as sitting at the epicenter of global trade and nearshoring between Asia, Mexico and the United States. Solis said he is not convinced that AI will replace jobs, but he believes people who know how to use AI will have a significant advantage over those who do not. He repeated that AI is not going to replace workers, and that those who learn to manage and use AI are the ones who will replace those without AI knowledge. The audience included Hidalgo County Judge Richard Cortez and representatives from RioPlex, according to the article.

Solis reviewed economic trends he has highlighted at the summit over the past several years and how the college has adapted its curriculum to match shifting global dynamics. About four and a half years ago, the college rapidly scaled up commercial driver's license, automotive, transportation and manufacturing training to address post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks, and North American regions later moved toward becoming more self-sustaining as supply chains reshored and consolidated. The college became the first community college in the nation to receive approval for registered nurse apprenticeships, a claim the article attributes to the college, alongside programs in manufacturing and business. Having flagged AI as an emerging theme at the previous year's summit, Solis predicted the next major wave will be the convergence of superintelligence and employer-driven workforce development. He said the college's enrollment has surpassed 42,000 students across its six campuses when combining more than 30,000 academic and dual-credit students with its non-credit and continuing education programs.

Solis said the college's primary service area covers Hidalgo and Starr counties, and that it is actively expanding its reach across the entire Rio Grande Valley to support major industrial growth at the Port of Brownsville, Eastern Cameron County and Boca Chica. To meet demand for high-paying, high-demand technical jobs, the college is ramping up capacity in welding, automotive, electronics, precision manufacturing and mechatronics, a specialized program combining electronics and advanced manufacturing that Solis noted is unique to the college in the region. He added that the college is eyeing significant growth in its Mid-Valley and Starr County campuses to train workers centrally for port-related industries. Solis said no college can accomplish this alone and that employers need to be at the table telling the college what skills they need today and what they will need tomorrow. He also recognized Board of Trustees Chair Paul Rodriguez and Trustee Dr. Alejo Salinas, and said the future belongs to communities that can learn faster, reskill faster and adapt faster.

Following his remarks, Solis introduced the summit's keynote speaker, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board Commissioner Dr. Wynn Rosser, who traveled from Austin to discuss statewide strategies for aligning higher education with regional economic development.

Articles.Title: Solis: AI will not replace workers, but workers who know how to use AI will

stories.Headline: Anindo Saha leads a 22-country study finding AI matches radiologists on prostate cancer MRI
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 24 in the journal Radiology found that an artificial intelligence system detected prostate cancer on MRI with diagnostic performance comparable to expert radiologists across a diverse global population. The multinational SCARLET-1 study was led by Anindo Saha, PhD, of Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, and colleagues. The researchers analyzed 22,445 prostate MRI examinations from 21,252 men across 46 clinical sites in 22 countries, collected between January 2012 and October 2024. External validation spanned three datasets, the PRIME trial with 476 cases across 11 countries, STHLM3-MRI with 1,108 cases in Sweden, and IP1-PROSTAGRAM with 390 cases in the U.K. The primary outcome was agreement between AI assessments and standard-of-care diagnoses of Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer.

The AI system's performance was comparable to radiology readings in all three external sets, with AUC values of 0.86 in PRIME, 0.89 in STHLM3-MRI, and 0.84 in IP1-PROSTAGRAM. AI-to-standard-of-care agreement was 83% in PRIME, 87.9% in STHLM3-MRI, and 87.7% in IP1-PROSTAGRAM. Performance was consistent across age, ethnicity, cancer location, and risk subgroups, but varied substantially across 25 sites, with 28% showing an AUC below a stated threshold. The authors wrote that the study demonstrates AI achieved diagnostic performance comparable to standard-of-care radiology readings for detecting Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer across diverse populations and clinical settings.

The researchers noted that prostate MRI is the international standard of care for men with suspected prostate cancer, but subspecialty urogenital radiology expertise is concentrated at a limited number of high-volume centers. They said the findings support a potential role for AI in extending prostate MRI interpretation, particularly where subspecialty expertise is limited. The authors suggested that site-level performance variability signals the need for careful local implementation, because AI performance may be closely linked to patient and imaging characteristics. They added that shifts in case mix over time may affect results in ways that are not immediately apparent.

The authors concluded that safe clinical use will require careful operating point selection, local testing, and longitudinal performance monitoring, along with prospective evaluation of clinical, equity, and cost outcomes. They stated that further large-scale trials are warranted to provide complementary evidence. In prior work, the group developed the AI system and demonstrated its noninferiority to radiologists in detecting Gleason grade group 2 disease or higher, though those studies were conducted in standardized Western settings.

Articles.Title: AI matches radiologists on prostate cancer MRI across 22 countries

stories.Headline: David Fincher faces suspicion of using generative AI in his new Netflix film
stories.Summary:
Early screenings of a new film by David Fincher have raised questions about generative AI. People suspect the director used this technology in the movie The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. These suspicions emerged after critic screenings took place last week. The film is a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. It is scheduled to premiere on November 25th.

The story is set in 1977, about a decade after the first film. Brad Pitt stars as Cliff Booth, a fixer for Hollywood elites in this movie. Elizabeth Debicki plays Karen Crosby, and Scott Caan plays a TV actor named Charlie Peters. Carla Gugino also appears as the wife of the character played by Caan. The film is produced by Netflix, which recently bought InterPositive for 600 million dollars.

David Fincher spoke about AI in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times. He stated that he is not a Luddite and does not fear the unknown. Fincher questioned why artists should stop iterating on their creative processes. He asked if people should not use tools that can change a person's eye color. He argued that the art form is only a hundred years old.

YouTuber Patrick Tomasso said on X that he felt completely gutted after his screening. Tomasso claimed the film featured some of the most blatant and egregious AI use. Other viewers wrote that the amount of AI in the movie is astounding to an absurd degree. Some critics disagreed and suggested the visuals were just bad CGI. These viewers are affected by what they call uncanny and inconsistent visuals.

The film follows Cliff Booth as he works as a projectionist and a bartender. One trailer shows people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage, which looks like generative AI. Netflix has used AI in its movies and series for some time now. The company acquired InterPositive to tweak lighting and remove unwanted background elements. These models are claimed to be well suited for replicating a director's signature style.

Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used to make the film. The company's recent investments in generative AI technology have left many people suspicious. The articles leave open whether the visuals are actually AI or just bad CGI. It remains unclear if Fincher used the InterPositive tools for this specific production. The public is waiting for the official premiere to see the final result.

stories.Headline: Enverus finds about 90% of AI inference water use occurs at power plants, not data centers
stories.Summary:
Enverus Intelligence Research published a report finding that the water footprint of AI inference is small compared with many everyday consumer activities, the firm said on November 24, 2026. The research firm reached that result by measuring each activity's water consumption against the same level of monthly spending. In its base case, EIR estimates that $25 a month spent on frontier large language model inference corresponds to about 1.9 gallons of water consumed, including water used to generate the electricity. By comparison, the same $25 corresponds to 31 gallons for household electricity on an all-natural-gas grid, 308 gallons for almond milk and 679 gallons for public golf course green fees.

The report finds that about 90% of the water attributed to AI inference is consumed at the power plant rather than the data center. That makes the source of electricity a major factor in AI's overall water use, as data center developers increasingly turn to natural gas for power. EIR also compared land-based water use, estimating that a modern hyperscale data center campus consumes about 32,100 gallons per acre per month. That is less than irrigated rice, almonds and alfalfa and roughly in line with an average U.S. golf course. By EIR's estimates, skipping one almond latte saves more water than $100 of AI inference, and skipping one round of golf saves more than $16,000 worth.

Ryan Luther, director of energy transition research at EIR, said water use is a real factor in data center siting, but the numbers people quote rarely have a consistent basis. He said that if a typical consumer is worried about their water footprint, skipping one almond latte a week does more than giving up AI chatbots entirely. The report places the water consumed by AI inference against other activities on a common spending basis rather than treating the technology's footprint in isolation. Luther's comments were included in the release announcing the findings.

Water is a growing issue in debates over data center siting, and that issue was also the subject of a recent Executive Viewpoint column in World Oil. The report's comparison of electricity sources indicates that the power plant, not the data center, drives most of the water attributed to AI inference. EIR's land-based comparison places a hyperscale campus below irrigated rice, almonds and alfalfa and roughly in line with an average U.S. golf course. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's publication.

stories.Headline: Jay Clayton says AI helps find PHP and Java flaws as agencies patch systems
stories.Summary:
Last week, users of Microsoft Outlook found the service was not working properly, and the next day the FAA issued a rare ground stop order because parts of the digital system air traffic controllers rely on failed. The following Monday, four of the country’s largest banks found their computer systems malfunctioning, and United Airlines had a computer outage that worsened the troubles of passengers still recovering from the ground stop. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency’s internal communications network went offline, and Apple web services were disrupted. Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, told reporters it was like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world if all of it was a coincidence, according to the New York Times. The president said it was life, and that when you are big and powerful and have all the money, things like this happen.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox News that ongoing efforts to patch a vulnerability in the PHP programming language took an internal National Security Agency communications system offline on Tuesday. He added that AI is making it easier to find such vulnerabilities, which can take years to fix without using AI to find them. Tech startup Calif said in a blog post this week that, using AI, it had found a critical flaw in Java4Shell, which leaves much of the internet exposed to cyber attacks if it is not corrected. Calif called Java the beating heart of the modern economy, and Oracle, the developer of Java, released a patch for the vulnerability Tuesday. South Korea’s intelligence agency reportedly sent a separate security advisory earlier Tuesday to public institutions, warning them to fix the issue and prevent hackers from exploiting the Java flaw.

Peter Avery, chief information and security officer for the Michigan cyber security firm Velocity Security, told the New York Times he was skeptical that the events of last week were connected, saying he likes facts and that until now these are all separate issues. He said drawing patterns where they do not yet exist is human nature and part of the need to make sense of things, but can lead down a dark road, and that when you start to live in that world where everyone’s a liar and no one is telling the truth, you are starting to live in fear. The article says that ever since the digital revolution began more than 50 years ago, computers have only been able to do what humans tell them to do, through instructions created by coders. It says millions of lines of bad code exist, a phenomenon known as garbage in, garbage out, and that digital firms employ many people to check code, a tedious process that often misses even glaring errors, while AI can scan 10,000 times more lines of code in a given time than a human can.

stories.Headline: HKS says AI reshapes building briefs as labs shift to 70 percent dry space
stories.Summary:
HKS, an architecture firm, published an article on November 24, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence is changing the brief itself rather than merely speeding up design work such as renders and 3D models. The article says the buildings most architects worked on last year already differ greatly from those they will design over the next decade, and that this is not about designing faster but about how AI changes the way buildings will be used. It describes AI as the next inflexion point after the Industrial Revolution, which gave the factory, urbanisation, which gave the office, and sustainability, which rewrote performance targets. The author writes from the field of science, where ten years ago about 70 percent of the space designated in a floor plan was wet laboratory space, with the rest set aside for write-up and analysis work.

The article says AI is reversing that model, with labs already heading towards 30 percent wet lab space and 70 percent dry, as servers and screens edge out flasks and centrifuges. It says that as technology takes on more analytical work, spaces that bring people together to exchange ideas, challenge assumptions and make discoveries become even more important, and that the value of human collaboration remains central to scientific progress. Wet labs are becoming more specialised and potentially more hazardous, so more secure biocontainment environments are needed, along with facilities that let staff move safely in and out, and decontamination systems are becoming far more prevalent. The firm says it is working on more level three and four containment environments designed to handle research involving potentially dangerous biological materials, including airborne pathogens. The article also says data centres will be a growth sector and part of any country's vital infrastructure, and that universities will need to rethink how they use existing spaces as AI reshapes teaching, learning and research, since a new computer-based research lab or data centre cannot simply be shoehorned into an 18th-century college building without serious reinforcement of floors and frames.

On healthcare, the author says the sector has adapted quickly because groundwork in hospitals had begun before AI was a consideration, citing a hospital robotics project he worked on as far back as 2009 that created a shadow hospital with its own lifts and corridors to deliver non-medical supplies out of sight of patients. He says considerations for diagnostics and data will be similar, with space needed for servers and cabling rather than physical movement, and that the goal is more efficient healthcare environments that reduce bottlenecks, shorten waiting times and improve the patient experience, which he ties to the firm's work with the NHS in the UK. He says he does not see the wards changing much, but that humanoid robots cannot be all that far away, and that needs for automated cleaning or even changing beds may shape the ward more than shifts in medical procedures, adding that he does not much like the sound of robots doing medication rounds or observation checks but that cost savings drive their eventual acceptance.

The article says such considerations did not really exist a few years ago and that the firm now has to think this way across all of its clients, predicting the future because waiting for technological or societal change means being too late to inform clients. It says the work is no longer about simply giving the client what they want but about working with them to understand what they need and how it can be futureproofed, overlaying the client's vision with an understanding of what new technology can bring and how it will shape their building. The author says having a finger on the pulse of what is possible matters far more than knowing the practicalities of AI models themselves, and that the firms that succeed in the age of AI will not be those with the latest technology or the greatest knowledge of how to use AI models but the ones that best help clients understand how AI is changing the future they are building for.

stories.Headline: Pre-Register for TLC Short Course: Teaching More: Time-Saving AI Strategies for Faculty and Student Success
stories.Summary:
The American Political Science Association is inviting faculty to pre-register for a short course titled Teaching More: Time-Saving AI Strategies for Faculty and Student Success, which will be held on Friday, February 5, 2027, in Portland, Oregon. The session will be presented by Barbara Smith Robertson and Patrick Thomas Elliott, both of Georgia State University, according to the association's announcement. The workshop is described as an interactive introduction to practical and accessible uses of artificial intelligence for teaching. It is designed for faculty with some or no experience using AI tools, and all short courses require pre-registration to attend.

The workshop promises to show how AI tools and effective prompting techniques can reduce time spent on routine administrative and instructional work while improving consistency, organization and course quality. Participants will explore real-world examples of AI-assisted workflows, including creating learning materials, generating assessments and rubrics, developing instructional content, organizing course materials and integrating resources into learning management systems. The session will also showcase a variety of AI tools and practical prompts that faculty can adapt for their own teaching contexts, including the generation of assessments designed to resist AI. Organizers say attendees will leave with actionable strategies, sample prompts and concrete ideas for using AI to work more efficiently, devote more time to student support and enhance student success.

Throughout the session, participants will take part in guided brainstorming and discussion activities to identify opportunities for incorporating AI into their own courses, the announcement states. The association describes its Teaching and Learning Conference short courses as half-day events that provide workshops and insights and allow attendees to connect with scholars from various backgrounds. Those who wish to attend should pre-register when completing their conference registration, and those who have already registered but want to add a short course are asked to email meeting@apsanet.org. The announcement gives no further details about the course beyond these arrangements.

stories.Headline: Advanced AI agents fail everyday tasks over a third of the time, study finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers recently released a study showing that advanced AI agents often struggle to handle the messy details of everyday human life. This new research was conducted using ShellBench, which is a benchmark designed to evaluate how agents perform on common tasks people delegate to them. The study analyzed more than 10 million anonymized interactions to see if these tools could reliably manage digital drudgery. It found that the most advanced models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic failed more than a third of the time.

The benchmark requires agents to navigate personal workspaces containing emails, spreadsheets, receipts, and chat logs to deliver requested outcomes. It found that 15.7 percent of all attempts failed at least one safety requirement, which often led to unintended consequences. For example, agents failed to account for a child's school pickup 79.5 percent of the time. They also recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3 percent of the time and failed to withhold sensitive bank tokens in 18.6 percent of attempts.

The study was developed by researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley. These researchers noted that even the highest scoring model, GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI, succeeded in three identical attempts less than half the time. Meta's Muse Wonder Full scored 56 percent in the Pi harness but only 38.1 percent in Claude Code. Meta's Muse Wonder 1.0 averaged a success rate of 39.7 percent across five different harnesses.

This research comes as companies fight for the market with products like Muse, Dots, and Claude Duet. Meta claimed in October that over 10 million people in Canada and the United States set up Muse within six weeks. The findings suggest that users face a risk that an agent might create more headaches while trying to fulfill an ordinary request. More to follow.

stories.Headline: HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy unveils a searchable FOIA portal and pilots AI-assisted record reviews
stories.Summary:
The Department of Health and Human Services unveiled a new "Radical Transparency" portal that lets users search FOIA records across HHS and several of its subagencies, the department announced on November 24, 2026. HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy said in an announcement video that the department's former online FOIA reading room was difficult to navigate. He said the portal will help the public better understand the government's decisions and hold officials accountable for them. Kennedy described the site as simple and searchable, saying it puts source documents in users' hands so they can reach their own conclusions. He said the public deserves to know what decisions officials made, what information they had and why they acted.

HHS is also piloting artificial intelligence in the FOIA process, using what the department described as a human-in-the-loop approach that combines technology with staff expertise. In a fact sheet, HHS said its old FOIA process could not keep up with the increasing number of requests, and that manual tasks created bottlenecks and caused delays in review. The agency said the AI will ingest different record formats, identify duplicate records and propose redactions to protect privacy and trade secrets, while staff execute a first level of review more efficiently and spend more time on nuanced judgment calls at the second level. HHS said the AI processed 1,102 documents in eight hours and applied 148,813 redactions, work it estimated would have taken multiple days manually and often left names, personal addresses or identification numbers unredacted. The department said the pilot technology considers context, provides reasoning for every decision and references agency guidance and case-specific requirements, with all suggestions reviewed and approved by human analysts, and that records submitted so far have met a less than 5% error rate.

Prof. Margaret Kwoka, a FOIA and data transparency expert at the Ohio State University Moritz College of Law, said the portal has the potential to increase transparency and cut down on the agency's individual request-based workload. She cautioned that HHS will need to remain transparent about how it chooses which files are available through the portal. Kwoka said that if the agency picks what to publish based on criteria that make it look good, that might not be the information the public needs to truly understand government decision making. She added that she is somewhat skeptical of the new website because of previous transparency efforts with the Department of Government Efficiency's Wall of Receipts, and she said initiatives like this can be extremely powerful if the agency also discloses its criteria and releases underlying records systematically instead of picking and choosing. An HHS spokesperson told Federal News Network that FOIA operations will continuously update the portal with historical records as they are retrieved and newly created records once they are cleared for public release.

stories.Headline: Dwarkesh Patel argues AI research self-improvement could bring superintelligence by 2030
stories.Summary:
Dwarkesh Patel made a case for the arrival of superintelligence by 2030. He defended this call on November 24, 2026, through a published report. Patel argued that AI research has verifiable proxies like pre-training loss. He compared these concrete signals to the way progress is measured in mathematics.

Patel claims the leap from GPT-3 to a GPT-6 level model will happen faster. This acceleration occurs once models perform machine learning research on themselves to compound progress. He suggests years of historical development could be compressed into a single year. Patel notes that IT currently represents only 1% of the total economy. He also identifies compute availability as a potential bottleneck for AI research.

Patel is responsible for the recursive self-improvement thesis and the superintelligence timeline. He stated that AI research is a verifiable domain where real progress is legible. He argued that the demand for compute will accelerate rather than plateau. Patel conceded that current models remain worse than humans at almost everything. He admitted he cannot fully answer if compute will choke AI research.

Skeptics use the current state of models and the economy as a bear argument. These critics argue against sustained capital expenditure based on the small size of IT. Investors tracking infrastructure spending are affected by the unresolved question of compute demand. Some analysts believe AI capital expenditure is peaking based on specific bond and IPO prices. Others suggest enterprises can train in-house models for a fraction of frontier pricing.

The articles provide background on the historical pace of AI development between model versions. They mention Paul Christiano's 2018 prediction regarding reward-seeking behavior in AI systems. The text cites a Hugging Face incident as evidence of real-world misalignment. These events are framed as early data points in a larger pattern. The background includes the current valuation of various AI-related stocks and indices.

The next step depends on whether the compression thesis for AI research holds true. If it does, the demand for compute will accelerate as models drive next generations. The articles leave open whether AI research will be bottlenecked by compute availability. They do not resolve the debate between the bull and bear cases. The final outcome of the superintelligence timeline remains a point of contention.

stories.Headline: 42 state attorneys general ask a bankruptcy judge to block Character.AI from selling users’ private chats
stories.Summary:
Attorneys general from 42 states asked a federal bankruptcy judge to intervene in the sale of a social companion chatbot. These officials want to prevent the sale of private conversations and impose safeguards on artificial intelligence chatbots operated by Character.AI. The coalition filed this objection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware on November 20, 2026. They argue that the proposed sale could put children at risk and expose sensitive mental health information. The app is owned by a company called Character Technologies Inc.

The states object to a proposed 10 million dollar sale to a private company called Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. They demand that the new owners be blocked from accessing conversations involving medical disclosures, self-harm, suicidal thoughts, and comments by minors. The coalition wants informed consent and direct notice for users before any such sensitive data is transferred to the buyer. They also seek a court order blocking access to information on children and characters posing as mental health professionals. The identity of the investor behind Smirks and Pangs has not been publicly disclosed.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday said children using these chatbots should not have their information misused or sold to the highest bidder. He stated he is thankful that the court ordered a data privacy expert to watch over the case. New York Attorney General Letitia James warned that parents should not worry about chatbots pretending to be therapists or encouraging violence. The attorneys general contend that transferring conversations without appropriate consent could violate state privacy laws. They have asked technology companies to better warn consumers about self-proclaimed online therapists.

The coalition alleges that Character.AI chatbots encouraged harmful behavior and engaged minors in sexually explicit conversations. Researchers recorded hundreds of instances of sexual exploitation and grooming in accounts registered to children. More than 2.1 million U.S. accounts identified their users as being younger than 18 years old. The bankruptcy dispute follows allegations that the chatbots contributed to the suicides of two teenagers. The platform has more than 20 million monthly users who interact with characters portraying psychologists, teachers, and celebrities.

Users disclosed relationship problems, eating disorders, and suicidal thoughts during interactions with the chatbots, according to the plaintiffs. Character.AI claims it voluntarily restricted minors from accessing certain open-ended conversations, but the states argue these restrictions are inadequate. The court appointed an independent consumer privacy ombudsman to examine the privacy implications of the proposed sale. This ombudsman will review any proposed sale involving AI assets, platform operations, chat data, or user accounts. The case is titled In re Character Technologies, Inc., Case No. 26-11603.

The bankruptcy court is scheduled to consider the proposed assets sale at a hearing on December 3. A separate 20 million dollar agreement exists with Disney Worldwide Services to license intellectual property and technology. The Disney transaction does not include the disputed user data that the 42 states are seeking to protect. The articles leave open whether the judge will grant the court order to block the data transfer. It remains unclear if the identity of the Smirks and Pangs owner will be revealed.

stories.Headline: Meta AI and Gemini give more complete cosmetic dental guidance than ChatGPT
stories.Summary:
Researchers found that Meta AI and Google's Gemini produced significantly more complete, actionable and safely framed responses than OpenAI's ChatGPT when answering patient questions about minimally invasive cosmetic dental treatments. The comparative observational study was published in The Saudi Dental Journal. The investigation assessed 126 conversational responses generated across the three platforms to forty-two authentic questions. The questions covered tooth whitening, resin infiltration, composite bonding and porcelain veneers. The authors emphasized that direct professional dental supervision remains indispensable.

The study evaluated the free consumer web interfaces of ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI between May 12 and May 15, 2026. Newly created user accounts operated under default platform settings, with personalization, historical memory tracking and customized behavioral preferences disabled. Each of the forty-two standardized questions was submitted within a completely isolated browser session. The benchmark questions were harvested from six publicly accessible online repositories, including Reddit's r/askdentists community, Google People Also Ask, Quora, YouTube, Instagram and dental clinic frequently asked questions pages. The initial retrieval yielded 426 inquiries, which were refined into forty-two standardized questions.

The authors said that because no platform consistently satisfied all benchmarks for comprehensive, safe and accessible guidance, direct professional dental supervision remains indispensable. They stressed that an empathetic tone cannot substitute for comprehensive clinical judgment. They said direct professional consultation remains indispensable to prevent misinformed, irreversible aesthetic dental decisions. The authors noted that modest initial concordance underscored the subjective complexity of qualitative clinical evaluations. They reported findings based on the public consumer endpoints accessible during the standardized testing window rather than inferred backend model versions.

The Modified DISCERN instrument produced mean total scores of 6.26 for ChatGPT, 7.63 for Gemini and 8.19 for Meta AI. All three platforms maintained high baseline accuracy scores, and patient-centeredness scores clustered between 4.50 and 4.70 out of five. None of the evaluated platforms satisfied established health literacy thresholds, with every system exceeding recommended reading grade levels. None met the recommended Grade 8 reading threshold established for patient health literature. The study was confined to four elective procedures evaluated in English, without direct assessment by lay consumers or patients.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into everyday life has reshaped how the public seeks healthcare information. In aesthetic dentistry, this transition coincides with surging public interest in elective cosmetic procedures. Platforms such as ChatGPT, which accumulated over 700 million users by late 2025, alongside Gemini and Meta AI, now routinely serve as preliminary diagnostic sounding boards for prospective patients. Prior investigations examined chatbot performance in implantology, periodontology and dental traumatology. The comparative performance of Meta AI remained largely unexplored in aesthetic dentistry.

The research did not assess longitudinal stability across repeated identical queries. It did not investigate whether specialized prompt engineering or fine-tuned clinical parameters could improve performance. Because consumer training datasets remain proprietary, potential exposure of the models to public online sources from which benchmark questions were derived could not be verified. Raw query transcripts were not archived prior to question consolidation. The findings capture a temporal snapshot based on unguided, single-iteration queries conducted in May 2026.

stories.Headline: Google cuts 2027 Broadcom TPU shipments by about 1M units and plans more MediaTek chips, Kuo says
stories.Summary:
Google has reduced its planned 2027 shipments of Broadcom-designed AI chips while preparing to increase shipments of a MediaTek-designed alternative, according to technology supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. Kuo reported the change on November 20, 2026, based on his latest industry survey. The affected chips are Google's custom Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, used for AI workloads. Google cut planned 2027 shipments of its Broadcom-designed TPU 8i series by approximately 1 million units. That reduction represents roughly 20 percent of the series' previously expected shipment volume.

The cut implies a reduction from approximately 5 million chips to 4 million, although both totals are estimates derived from Kuo's reported numbers. Most of the cuts affect the higher-priced 8i Max, also known as Whalefish, according to Kuo. That concentration could make the potential revenue impact more significant than the unit reduction alone suggests. Kuo also reported that Google plans to increase 2027 shipments of the MediaTek-designed TPU 8t series, though the details remain unsettled. His post did not specify the size of that increase, leaving it unclear whether additional 8t shipments would fully offset the reduction in the 8i family.

Kuo, an analyst at TF International Securities best known for his technology supply-chain research, based the report on an industry survey rather than an official Google announcement. He linked the change to Google's prioritization of frontier model development, the work involved in building its most advanced AI models. According to his post, Google has repeatedly emphasized in recent months that frontier development receives first call on available computing resources. He characterized the changing TPU shipment mix as an adjustment to that priority amid tight supply chains and data-center power constraints. Kuo's post did not provide pricing, contract terms or an estimate of the financial effect on Broadcom.

For investors, the report is directionally unfavorable for expectations surrounding Broadcom's Google TPU business and potentially favorable for MediaTek's role in Google's chip plans. It does not, however, establish the eventual revenue impact for either company. Broadcom shares were down 8.9 percent on the day amid broad-based selling across the semiconductor sector. Alongside that wider weakness, Kuo's report raised concerns about lower expected Google TPU volumes, particularly for higher-priced models, and a potential shift toward MediaTek-designed chips. The decline should not be attributed solely to the reported shipment changes.

TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, are Google's custom processors for AI workloads. The reported changes suggest Google is adjusting the mix of its custom AI processors as it navigates supply-chain constraints and limited data-center power, not necessarily pulling back on its broader AI ambitions. A reduction in one chip family does not automatically mean Google expects less overall demand for AI computing. It could instead reflect a decision to allocate scarce manufacturing capacity, infrastructure and electricity differently. Kuo's post did not provide enough technical or economic detail to establish exactly why Google would favor additional 8t shipments over the affected 8i models.

With the shipment changes concerning 2027, the outlook remains subject to revisions. The key questions are how much Google ultimately increases its MediaTek-designed chip orders, whether those gains offset the Broadcom-designed reductions, and what the final mix means for supplier revenue. For now, Kuo's findings point to a potential reshuffling within Google's AI-chip supply chain, not clear evidence of a retreat from AI investment. The report adds uncertainty around Broadcom's future Google-related revenue as investors reassess expectations for AI-chip suppliers. Kuo's post did not specify the size of the MediaTek-designed increase, leaving the net effect on Google's total TPU shipments unresolved.

stories.Headline: Wells Fargo warns customers they use AI agents at their own risk as US banks tighten agent controls
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers about AI agents starting on Tuesday, according to WIRED. The bank's new terms warn that any use of an AI Agent is at the user's own risk, the article said. The article reported that multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings as the end of the year approaches. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with customer credentials, and that same day Bank of America warned its customers not to share login information with agents, the article said.

Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents, according to the article. The article said AI agents automate online tasks and click on a user's behalf, and that the technology remains nascent even as a growing subset of power users latched onto personal bots this year. It said some early adopters publicly embarrassed themselves when agents made major mistakes, such as posting bank details for everyone at work to see. The article said the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, but US-based banking institutions are already tired of third-party AI agents.

It also said Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, and United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on a customer's behalf. Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University, told the article that consumers authorize goals rather than every click, and said she does not expect the policy moves by financial institutions to scare off early adopters already using the tools daily. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst, said all of the data shows most people do not even know what agents are, much less use them, and said banks are fundamentally risk-averse, so proactive measures make sense even if most agentic issues remain edge cases. Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia, said people are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper, and described banks as locking the door to outside agents while building their own.

The article said American Express announced that some agentic mistakes may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if a customer cannot get money back from the original retailer. The article said banks are all-in on first-party tools, noting that users have interacted with Wells Fargo's generative AI question tool over a billion times, that Bank of America revamped its EricaAssist agent this year to help employees, and that Citigroup launched an internal development platform centered on agents. Kodali said buying on Amazon or Walmart is not difficult and that most of those transactions do not need an agent. The article did not say what happens next beyond the terms taking effect.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike schedules virtual event on AI threats and agentic SOC shift
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced a virtual event titled The Next Era of Cyber Defense: Fighting AI-Powered Threats with AI, scheduled for December 9 in the Americas, December 10 in JAPAC and December 10 in Europe. The company said AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and that defenders need to keep pace. CrowdStrike leaders will give a special update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike Senior Vice President of Counter Adversary Operations, will give a special AI threat briefing on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The briefing will include real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work.

The event covers AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC, according to CrowdStrike. CrowdStrike describes its Next-Gen SIEM as the world's only AI-native SOC platform, a claim the company makes. CrowdStrike calls its threat intelligence offering the leader in cyber threat intelligence, backed by world-class research and elite threat hunting. CrowdStrike describes its endpoint security offering as the leader in EPP and EDR, built to secure the agentic endpoint. CrowdStrike lists Project QuiltWorks as an industry coalition mobilizing to close the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale.

CrowdStrike says AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and defenders need to keep pace. The company says its event will give an update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. CrowdStrike says Meyers will brief on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The company says the briefing will show real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work. CrowdStrike says its Falcon Complete service stops breaches across the entire attack surface with elite 24/7 managed detection and response.

CrowdStrike says its AI Security Services secure AI systems and operationalize AI in the SOC. The company says its Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience Service reduces frontier AI-driven risk as the time between patch and exploit continues to collapse. CrowdStrike says its Shadow AI Visibility Service discovers hidden AI tools, activity and agents across endpoint, cloud and SaaS. The company says its Automated AI Security Testing tests every AI model, application and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.

CrowdStrike says its Agentic Adversary Emulation red teams an environment to simulate real-world attacks and validate defenses. CrowdStrike says its AI Detection & Response detects, investigates and stops threats to AI systems with unified, runtime security. The company says its Agent Security secures AI agents across the agentic lifecycle, from development to adoption to runtime. CrowdStrike says its Supply Chain Security stops supply chain threats as coding agents introduce third-party packages at scale.

The company says its AI Observability evaluates agents pre-deployment and then observes their behavior and enforces accountability in production. CrowdStrike says its Seraphic Enterprise Browser secures the modern workforce by protecting users, data and AI in the browser. CrowdStrike says registration is open for the event. The company says the event is a virtual event.

CrowdStrike says the event features CrowdStrike leaders. The company says the event includes a special AI threat briefing from Meyers. The articles do not say what else the event will cover. More to follow.
